In the third part (which is placed as it were for a close in the last position in the disputation, whose beginning is: Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth ) he calls to mind the vanity 122Aof mortality, so that the human soul may as it were hear at the end that which it is the more needful to perceive with intent consideration, and to recall to memory the more often. These things we have prepared, according to the grasp of our understanding, for the opening of Ecclesiastes, which is the second of Solomon's books, for those entering upon the reading of it. But we confess that to explain worthily its whole breadth is above our powers: in matters of this kind, covered over with deep profundity, seeking rather to hear a teacher than to snatch a teacher's place. For it is better, as Plato says, modestly to learn what is another's than shamelessly to thrust forward one's own. But if we have been able to say anything fitting upon this, let it be beyond hope and expectation. If anything usefully, not beyond our intention. First, as it were 122Ba certain proem, he sets before his book: in which he distinguishes that threefold matter of the following work which we have called to mind, concerning which he afterwards enters more amply into disputation. The proem therefore is: Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, as far as: The sun riseth, and goeth down. From there the first part of the book is begun, and the rest as we have said. Now let us consider the very words of the letter, whether we may be able to grasp in them anything of the things which have been said above.

Vanity of vanities (said Ecclesiastes), vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. With weight is that to be pronounced which he speaks of himself as though of another: said Ecclesiastes. For because for authority's sake he set down his own person, he fittingly spoke of himself not as of himself, but as of another, so that, since he had to speak of himself as some great one, as the matter 122Cdemanded, he might more becomingly and more maturely say this of himself in another than in himself. So Balaam, speaking of himself, says: He hath said, the hearer of the words of God, who hath beheld the visions of the Almighty, who falleth and hath his eyes opened (Num. XXIV). And John in his Gospel. He speaks of himself as though of another, saying: This is that disciple whom Jesus loved, who giveth testimony of these things, and we know that his testimony is true (Joan. XXI). And Paul speaks of himself as though of another to the Corinthians, saying: I know a man in Christ, whether in the body, or out of the body, I know not, God knoweth, such a one caught up even to the third heaven, and such a one caught up into paradise, and that he heard secret words, which it is not granted to man to utter (II Cor. XII). But this kind 122Dof speech, as often as it is taken up in Scripture, is done either for the sake of humility, or of admiration — namely, that when we would say great things, we should rather ascribe them as it were to others, lest it seem either proud or excessive, if we should attribute them to ourselves. For we ought both to remove great things from ourselves for humility's sake, and to show wondrous things as it were from afar, for admiration's sake. For those things are less wondrous which come nearer to knowledge. Therefore, that the minds of all may be raised up to the utterance that is to come, and may awake as at some miracle of newness, it is rightly said: Said Ecclesiastes. As if it were said: What so great and such a one has said could not be vain, even though he said it concerning vanity. The common teacher and the instructor of all, Ecclesiastes himself, has said it. What did he say? Hear what he said, and attend. For they are no small things 123Athat are said: Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. If all is vanity, then he also is vanity who said this. And how will it stand firm that what vanity said concerning vanity is not vain? But if it is true that what he said is vain, it is not to be heard, but spat out. What then shall we say? Either not all is vanity, as he said, and he said what is false; or all is vanity, as he said, and he himself is vanity, and said a vain thing. But assuredly, as he himself said: All is vanity, and he himself, who said it, is vanity; and not only vanity, but even universal vanity: and yet what he said is not vanity, but truth; because in that which he said he himself was not vanity, since he said against vanity what he said concerning vanity; and it is agreed that he could not be contrary to vanity in that in which he was vanity 123B. Something therefore was in him which was not vanity, and that could speak not vainly against vanity. But what was this, or where was it? Assuredly, if we shall say that this body was it, or something in the body, which spoke without vanity concerning vanity: then could the body, which is corrupted, subject to vanity and born for vanity, at some time be without vanity — a body which wholly lives in vanity? We remember the saying of the Psalmist: Universal vanity, every man living (Psal. XXXVIII). For that which dies is the very thing which lives: which is born that it may live, and lives that it may die. But what is it that dies, save that which is deprived of life? That therefore dies in man which is extinguished from life. And what is this, save the body and the bodily sense? For it is not itself after the living creature, 123Cfrom which it is a living creature, and when it ceases to be capable of sensation, the sense ceases to be. Therefore that which dies in man is the very thing which lives in man; which is for that reason subject to vanity, because it is liable to mortality. Therefore the bodily sense could not reprove vanity, in which nothing can be found free and pure from vanity. What then must be said this was? Was it perhaps the soul? Have we not shown above that it too is subject to vanity? For in it we placed the vanity of iniquity: which stands forth so much the more deformed than all other things, in that from it alone the others have either that they are harmful, or that they are at all. For without this vanity, neither would there be the vanity of mortality, nor would the vanity of mutability be harmful 123D. How then can the soul, which is subject to so great a vanity, truly reprove vanity? Or is something surviving found in it free from vanity, and was it said without cause: Universal vanity, every man living? For man is universal vanity, because in body and in mind he is subject to vanity. What man? Every man living. Not every man life, but every man living. For man is both life and man is living. Where the life, and where the living. Life in that which quickens; living in that which is quickened. And the flesh lives from the soul, and the soul from the flesh: and both live, but the flesh has wholly from the soul that it lives? the soul has not wholly in the flesh that it lives. For it lives also in God, and would that it did live? What lives in the flesh is vain. What lives in God 124Ais not vain, but is true, because it is from truth. In that part therefore in which it lives from truth, it truly reproves vanity, and it is found how vanity reproves vanity, not through vanity but through truth. Rightly therefore Ecclesiastes, who in mind was lifted above all vanity and had come through to truth itself, saw sublimely in that same truth what he truly said concerning the reproving of vanity: Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. The driving home of the words with the affection of the speaker signifies both the greatness of the matter and the newness of the wonder. And it is a sentiment uttered with heightening. For there are certain degrees, and as it were certain progressions, for one going both to the better and to the worse. For thus is it said the Song of songs, and the age of ages 124B, just as here it is now said: Vanity of vanities — so that by a certain like distance and a similar difference the Song of songs may be understood to excel above the song only so far as a song excels a word, and next a word silence. And an age of ages to excel an age only so far as an age alone excels a moment, or again a moment nothing. And with a like progression made here by the contrary: that vanity of vanities is worse than simple vanity by so much as simple vanity is worse than a solid and abiding essence. Thus by driving home the sentiment may be read: Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity — so that in all things vanity of every kind may be expressed, and out of all things a certain sum may be understood to be made up, which contains every vanity, so that as it were each single 124Cthing is by itself vanity, and the universe gathered out of them all is vanity of vanities. So in the creation of things, when God was completing his works, each single work is by itself called good (Gen. I), and last of all, all things being perfected, the universe is named very good. For if that which in part is good is found better in the whole, that also which in part is evil must needs be worse in the whole. Therefore vanity is of vanities, and the vanity of all vanities is universal vanity, and the universality of vanity is all vanity. Or else that vanity of human minds is here reproved by comparison with the other vanities: which, as risen out of the other vanities, and having surpassed all vanities by comparison of vanity, is deservedly called vanity 124Dof vanities. It can also not incongruously be that this threefold repetition of vanity is referred to the three kinds of vanities recalled above, so that as it were one of the vanities is the work of man, another mortal nature, the third this whole world with its universe of mutable things. For this man considered the works of mortals, and saw of each single one that with labor and grief they come to their effect. When made they subsist for a brief time; but passing away they leave no fruit behind them. He saw with how great affliction and misery human life is worn down daily without ceasing, even in those things which it works for its own consolation, and how it almost always suffers more loss in seeking a remedy than it receives of consolation in obtaining a solace. And in all these things, at how vainly every man living is troubled, wondering and amazed 125Ahe says: Vanity of vanities. Then, attending to the very condition of mortals, and finding in it a greater and more miserable vanity, he saw that if it is reckoned a great vanity when that which man makes passes away, then that vanity is altogether to be grieved over and pitied when that which man is cannot stand. Upon this therefore, redoubling again, he cried out and said: Vanity of vanities. Last of all, beholding the inconstantinam and the fluctuation of all mutable things hastening to their setting, concluding as it were in a sum he added and said: All is vanity.

What hath a man more of all his labour that he laboureth under the sun? What hath he more — it is understood — than that which has been said of all things: Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity? As 125Bif he were saying: If all things are subject to vanity, how can the works of men be alien from vanity? If according to something that is vain which God created, how is that not much more vain which man makes? If that is temporal which the Eternal made, what is that which the temporal makes? Therefore what hath a man more of all his labour that he laboureth under the sun? He laboureth under the sun, namely either as acting or as suffering. Distinguish these two: he who acts and he who suffers labors under the sun; each labors, both he who acts labors, and he who suffers labors. But this is the difference, that the one labors as though unwilling, the other willingly. For he who acts labors, and himself makes that from which he labors. But he who suffers labors, and does not himself make, but sustains, that from which he labors. These two kinds of men live in this world, namely those who labor 125Cand act, and those who labor and suffer. Who are they that labor and act? Hear the Psalmist: Nevertheless universal vanity, every man living. Nevertheless man passeth as an image; yea and he is disquieted in vain. He storeth up, and knoweth not for whom he shall gather these things (Psal. XXXVIII). Who are they that labor and suffer? Hear Paul the apostle: The creature, he says, was made subject to vanity, not willingly; but by reason of him that made it subject, in hope (Rom. VIII). Therefore both labor: both those, namely, to whom this life is sweet, and those to whom this life is bitter. Those labor to enjoy its delights; these labor to be freed from its misery. Those labor in fear lest they go hence quickly; these labor in dread lest they remain here long. The labor of the former is reproved for vain solicitude. The labor 125Dof the latter is crowned for patience. To the former it is said: Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof (Matth. VI). And that: Be not solicitous, saying: What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or wherewith shall we be clothed? (Ibid.) To the latter it is said: Be you also patient, strengthen your hearts (Jac. V). And that: If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him. If we die with him, we believe that we shall live also together with him (II Tim. II). To the former it is said: Ye sons of men, how long will ye be dull of heart, why do ye love vanity, and seek after lying? (Psal. IV.) To the latter it is said: Blessed are all they that fear the Lord, that walk in his ways. For thou shalt eat the labours of thy hands, blessed art thou, and it shall be well with thee (Psal. CXXVII). Therefore the labor of the former has a penalty in the work, and a penalty in the recompense. 126ABut the labor of the latter has indeed a penalty in the work, but a reward in the recompense. In the labor of the former there is true misery. In the fruit of their labor, a false and vain consolation. In the labor of the latter, a temporal and transitory affliction. In the fruit of their labor, eternal blessedness. Therefore the labor of the former is empty in its fruit, true in its misery. The labor of the latter is transitory in its penalty, eternal in its fruit. But there, for the evil man, what of good seems to be present is vain; the evil of these men which appears is as it were vain, because it is transitory; but the good which does not appear is perpetual. Let it not therefore seem wondrous that we call the evil in this life laboring and acting, but the good only laboring and suffering, since if we look more closely upon the truth, we shall find the evil always laboring by acting, and the good always by suffering. 126BFor as incontinence harasses the evil even then when they seem to be at rest, so patience keeps the good tranquil even when they are set in labors. Wherefore in a certain wondrous manner all the good and the just, when for God's sake they waste themselves with voluntary affliction, then also labor by suffering; because, setting themselves against themselves, what outwardly they inflict by raging in strictness, inwardly, remaining quiet and without disturbance, they bear in patience. But all the perverse and lovers of the carnal life, even then when they sustain evils brought upon them from without by another's violence, because inwardly they disturb themselves with the goads of fury and of impatience, they rather themselves make that from which they labor. Therefore the good labor in this life, but the evil labor even for the sake of this life; because the temporal labors to which all the depraved 126Cand perverse subject themselves for the obtaining of temporal sweetness, the good bear patiently for the sake of eternal consolation. But because this mortal life, in which and for which men labor, tends daily through the spaces of living to the end of life, rightly is all the labor of man reckoned in the number of the vanities, when it is said: What hath a man more of all his labour that he laboureth under the sun? It is understood: apart from vanity.

It is to be noted, however, that he does not say: What more is the labor of man? But: What hath a man more, he says, of all his labour that he laboureth under the sun? Whence it stands firm that here the matter treated is not so much the labor of man as the fruit and profit of human labor; 126Dbecause it is not asked what or of what sort the labor of man is, but what fruit man obtains of all his labor by which he labors under the sun. And all this fruit is declared to be nothing other than vanity, when it is said: What hath he more? As if it were said: Man hath nothing more than vanity of his labor. Therefore vanity is the whole fruit of man's labor, and every man labors in vain, being about to receive nothing but vanity of all his labor. Was the labor then of the saints also vain, who faithfully served God, and for love of him suffered so many torments and kinds of tortures? Who would presume to say this? For how was the labor of those men vain who, vexed indeed for a little while, came through transitory griefs to abiding joys, and through a temporal death obtained everlasting life? 127AOr is that labor to be called vain for this reason, because what they suffered has passed away: and yet according to something not vain, because what they received abides? For that even the labor of the just is vain — so far, that is, as regards the transitory penalty and this as it were imaginary appearance of misery — the Psalmist seems to hint, when he says: Thou who framest labour in commandment (Psal. XCIII). For God as it were frames labor for his elect, when outwardly, as though angry, he inflicts upon them by judgment a temporal penalty, for whom inwardly, by the providence of his mercy, he keeps the rewards of eternal blessedness. Since therefore the Psalmist names the labor of the just, and this imaginary grief, because it has the appearance of misery but does not have true misery, a framed thing, he assuredly shows 127Bthat this same labor can also, according to something, be not unfittingly called vain. Behold therefore the labor of the work passes away. What was vain passes away; what was transitory has passed away: the labor has passed away, the grief has passed away. Has the fruit of the work passed away, or the wage of the labor? Therefore it is permitted: behold, according to a certain manner of speaking, the labor itself and the temporal grief is not unfittingly called vain. Yet will the wage of that same labor ever rightly be called vanity? God forbid! How then shall that stand which was said: What hath a man more of all his labour? For it was said of the reward of labor and not of the labor itself, of the profit, not of the work: What hath a man more of all his labour? Behold, man hath more, and much more hath he, 127Cand thou sayest: What more hath he? Therefore he added and said: That he laboureth under the sun. Behold, we have the difficulty of this question resolved. For here he openly shows what labors he reproves of vanity. Those which are done, he says, under the sun. What is it, to be done under the sun? Perhaps what he says, under the sun, is to be taken simply; because men, dwelling in this lower part of the world, receive from above the light of the sun, and are lighted so that they may see for the doing of the works necessary to human uses. For on this account the times of human life have been so distributed by divine providence in alternating turns, that the very vicissitude of the alternating times might repair sick bodies wearied by too great a stretching out of their actions. Therefore night and day unceasingly succeed one another 127Dwith mutual evenness, so that by day the sun, passing over from its rising to its setting in its course above, may pour out its light on every side upon the things beneath it, and, illuminating human eyes by its presence, may rouse both those eyes and those of the other living things of the earth to the exercise of acting, and at the same time afford the means of working. But by night, withdrawing itself from human sight, and, as with certain swaddling-bands of infancy, spreading over them the veil of darkness and covering the eyes of mortals, it may foster their weary limbs to rest and slumber, that it may restore them again, repaired and more eager, to labor and to the day's exercise. This wondrous order of the divine dispensation the Psalmist beheld, when, commending God's works, he calls this to mind among the rest as something excellent and worthy of no small praise, saying: He hath made 128Athe moon for seasons; the sun knoweth his going down. Thou hast appointed darkness, and it is night: in it shall all the beasts of the woods go about. The young lions roaring after their prey, and seeking their meat from God. The sun ariseth, and they are gathered together, and they shall lie down in their dens. Man shall go forth to od his work, and to his labour until the evening (Psal. CIII). Hence also is that which God promises to Noah as he goes out of the ark after the flood, as for some great sign of his loving-kindness and gift of his bounty, saying: All the days of seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day shall not cease (Gen. VIII). Beautifully therefore he said that men, distended down below in this ark of the world through the various runnings-about of the occupations of mortal life, labor under the sun, so that this too belongs to the vanity 128Bof human work: that a light passing over from above, and to be ended in darkness, gives light to man for his working. For he considered how abject and wretched is the condition of mortals, who upon the surface of the earth, like certain worms creeping in vain curiosity, are roused by a light suddenly poured in from above, as though to be mocked, to snatch at what they vainly desire, and, the same being withdrawn after a little, are wrapped about again in a sudden blindness, and can in no wise go forward further into effect. Therefore the very light by which they are lighted is shown to them from afar and at a distance from above, and unapproachable to man, so that it may be proved to stand in no way in man's power; so far that man receives from it only so much as the graces of God, who bestows and orders all things, shall have permitted, not so much as 128Cman's perverse will, serving cupidity, desires. A great vanity therefore it is to labor under the sun, and small confidence to labor under the sun: whose light, however pleasant to look upon and delightful to the sight it be, yet cannot always be present to human eyes nor profit them. But if it please us to push our consideration yet higher and to look into the matter more subtly, we can take time to be signified by the name of the sun, so that what he said, under the sun, may be the same as if he had said, under time. For because chiefly by the sun both the course of the times is distinguished and the nature of temporal things is varied, time itself is fittingly expressed by the sun, when it is said under the sun it is the same as if he had said, under time. But has he perhaps in this too willed to intimate in nuere something to us, in that he did not say in time or with time, 128Dbut under time: and must a discernment be had by us, that we may understand that some things are those which were as it were made with time; but others those which were either made in time, or are done under time? Let us discern therefore, if we can, whether perchance we may be able to find the reason why he said rather that the works of men are vain as made under time than either with time or in time. All things which were made were either made with time, or in time. For those things were made with time whose rising time did not precede: such as the angelic nature, and that formless matter of visible things, which in the beginning God created. Those things were made in time whose rising time preceded, such as those works of the six days in which God perfected and completed 129Athe fabric of this sensible world; but those things also which afterwards were made formally, or essentially, were all made in time. Again, of those things which are done in time, some are done in time and under time, others are done in time only, not under time. Those are done in time and not under time which indeed begin in time, but are not ended in time. Those are done in time and under time which both begin in time and are ended in time. Likewise, of those things which are done under time, some are done for the sake of time, others are done for the sake of eternity. Those therefore which are done for the sake of time are vain both in act and in fruit. But those which are done for the sake of eternity are indeed vain in act; but in fruit they are not vain, because, even if they pass away in the work, yet they abide in the recompense. For a good work 129Bis not this alone which appears outwardly transitory; because it consists both of a visible action and of an invisible devotion. For, as man consists of a living thing and of life, and the living thing indeed dies, but the life does not die; so without doubt the good has both a visible action in itself, and an invisible devotion. The visible action is as it were the body; the inward devotion is as it were the spirit. The action lives through devotion, as the body through the soul. But devotion quickens the action, as the soul the body. For every action which is without devotion is dead. Therefore the visible action itself as it were lives, and the invisible devotion itself is life. But that which lives, this dies; but that which is life, this does not die. Because a transitory action, just as it has its beginning from time, so indeed it is ended in time. That therefore which dies, 129Cwhich is ended, which passes away, which is given over to mutability, is itself liable to vanity. But that which is life, which abides, which does not admit of an end or of corruption, does not itself admit vanity. Let it be said therefore: What hath a man more of all his labour that he laboureth under the sun? it is understood: apart from vanity. Nothing more, because all things which are done under the sun are vain. And what would he have of vain things but vanity? What then? Will good works which are done under the sun be able to confer nothing more upon those who work them than vanity? And how did we say above that this question was resolved by that which he says, under the sun? Behold, the same question rises up for us again, no less difficult than the one above, because we cannot deny that good works too are done under the sun, that is, under time, according to what 129Dhas been expounded above; and yet we do not dare to say that nothing but vanity follows from them. And behold, the book plainly says: What hath a man more of all his labour that he laboureth under the sun? But if we are willing to consider the very words more diligently, it is plainly shown what those works are which are reproved as vain. For he did not say: What hath a man more of all his labour which is done, or which was done, under the sun? But rather he says, which man himself laboureth under the sun. He does not therefore reprove the labor so much as the laborer as being under the sun. So that because man himself, set under the sun, labors, therefore what he labors at is vain. But who is he who labors under the sun? He who, pressed down by love of temporal and transitory 130Athings, labors for the obtaining of the same, if he does not have them, or for the keeping of them, if he has them. This man, set under the sun, labors, and this man labors in vain. But he who exercises good works for the hope and desire of eternal things, this man does not labor under the sun, even though the labor in which he labors is under the sun; because, although the work which he carries through is temporal, yet he himself transcends all temporal and falling things in mind and in devotion. This man therefore does not labor in vain, even though that in which he labors is vain; because that for which he labors is not vain. And when that which is vain, in which he labors, has passed away, he has ready that which is not vanity, for which he labors. Such a man therefore does not belong to that sentiment in which it was said: What hath a man more of all his labour that he laboureth under the sun? Because he does not 130Blabor under the sun, but above the sun, who does not set the wage of his labor in things rolling and passing away with time.

One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh. Behold vanity. One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh. This human nature conceived, corrupted in the first root of its stock, and, sown together with this same corruption, it sprouted out into the whole offspring of posterity. For the first parent of the human race, as soon as he heard: Earth thou art and unto earth thou shalt go, from that time made mortal, because he fell from the state of incorruption, began as it were to pass over from life to death through mortality. This way therefore all men after him pass through, who descend from him by the birth of the flesh. This is that vanity of which the Psalmist spoke, saying: Nevertheless 130Cuniversal vanity, every man living. Nevertheless man passeth as an image (Psal. XXXVIII). This vanity therefore, as greater than the rest and more horrible to human minds because of the dread necessity of death, he added in the last place, so that man might hear this at the end, in which he may more evidently recognize the misery of his own condition. For the first vanity is not even in the name; nor is it referred to man. The second vanity is indeed not in man; but yet it is referred to man. The third vanity both is in man, and is referred to man. Accordingly, as though advancing by certain steps always to higher things, he set first that vanity which is neither the penalty of man nor his fault. Then he added that vanity which is not the penalty of man, but the fault. Last of all, that which is not the fault, but the penalty: 130Dalthough yet neither can such a fault ever be without penalty, nor is such a penalty — at least in those to whom the sacrament of salvation does not come to aid — altogether free from fault. But I have called that the fault of man, not the penalty, and this the penalty, not the fault; because in the one man's desert is discerned, and in the other judgment is found. This penalty therefore, as heavier and more monstrous than the rest, he set last: which, though it be not more wicked than the fault, is yet more grievous to the flesh, and more effectual for the rousing of carnal minds. Let him say therefore: One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh. As if he were saying: If you think it is to be neglected that everything you do is vain, is even this to be neglected, that you yourselves are vanity? One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh. If the dying 131Adepart and those who are to die follow after, what joy is there? The grief of the living seems indeed to receive consolation in those who are born; but from that whence it is thought to be ended so that it should not be, from thence it receives that it should always be. For that the dying depart is grief. What consolation follows in that those who are to die come on? A consolation which is bounded by mourning. And what can be vainer in either? One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh. If some lamentable chance were to involve only a few, or at least not all, it would seem tolerable; but as it is, a savage plague drags all with it to destruction. One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh. If it passeth away, whither does it go? If it cometh, whence does it come? Alas, dread lot! How canst thou be secure, O man, wrapped in such great darkness? Behold, thou knowest that by living thou tendest to death. But canst thou know 131Bof what sort, or where, thou art to be after death? Consider therefore in how great a vanity thou livest, thou who daily seest that which thou art pass away; nor yet canst thou by any reasoning know of what sort is that which thou art to be. One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh.

But the earth standeth for ever. Hearken, O man, and blush. The earth standeth for ever. Why does the earth stand, and thou canst not stand, for whose sake the earth was made? Perhaps thou wilt say, because it stands for thy consolation. It stands that it may send forth those who come, bear those who pass over, and receive those who depart. For those who are born come from the earth by the origin of the flesh, and the living pass over upon the earth by the mutability of the flesh, and the dying return into the earth by the corruption of the flesh. Therefore it stands for thy consolation; nay rather it stands for thy confusion 131C. How? See of what sort it stands, of what sort it bears, and whom it bears, and out of what sort it bears. Of what sort therefore does it bear? Hear of what sort: Cursed is the earth in thy work; thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to thee (Gen. III). And whom does it bear? Hear again: Cursed art thou upon the earth (Gen. IV). And out of what sort does it bear: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat thy bread; and thou shalt eat the herbs of the earth? (Gen. III.) Therefore the cursed bears the cursed. And yet it bears them. But from that whence it bears, it has something for thy consolation and something for thy penalty. What is for thy consolation is with thy labor; what is for thy penalty is through thy labor. It has bread, and it has thorns also. Bread with thy labor, for thy consolation; thorns through thy labor, for thy penalty. In the sweat of thy face 131Dshalt thou eat thy bread: this is for thy consolation, with thy labor. When thou hast worked, the earth will not give thee its fruit, but thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to thee. This is for thy penalty, through thy labor. Therefore it stands not only for thy consolation, but much more it stands for thy confusion. It stands not only for the easing of thy misery, but it stands for the testimony and the penalty of thy fault. The earth standeth, and thou standest upon the earth. Stable is she who bears, and thou fallest in ruin who art borne. Why is this? Art thou too not earth? What then was said to thee: Earth thou art, and unto earth thou shalt go? Therefore thou art earth, and thou art upon the earth, and thou art of earth. Why then dost thou not stand for ever? Hast thou been made weaker than that earth from which thou wast taken? What then did the hand of the craftsman work, if it did not advance 132Aits work to something better? Was there then no knowledge with him, or was he found weak, so that in his hands that good matter should be made worse? God forbid! Nay rather, he made thee much better than that had been out of which he made thee; because he had made the earth stable, but thee he made out of earth immortal. Therefore he made thee better than that had been out of which he made thee. Not therefore from the craftsman did thy corruption proceed, who made thee with so great power and with such goodness that nothing could be less than perfect, nothing would he have worse than the best. And so the best craftsman made a good thing formed, whose eternal incorruption and immortal goodness neither begets a fault nor receives a fault.

But perhaps the matter is to be blamed, which was such that nothing else could be made of it. For the matter was earth, and there came forth an earthen vessel. What? This is a wonder. 132BThou therefore, in saying this, oughtest to have looked to this: that, if thou art an earthen vessel, then thou wast hardened out of soft mud into a potsherd, and thy clod, if it had not the nature of firmness, yet had the nature of confirmation. If it had not that this should be by nature, yet it had by nature that this could be by grace. Therefore thy matter did thee no harm, which both keeps whole what nature conferred, and does not itself diminish what grace gave. For the earth standeth for ever. What is standeth? It perseveres in that which it was made; it keeps its own nature; it does not desert its own condition; what it received, this it retains uncorrupted. Earth it was made, and earth it remains; never is it other than what it is. And when it is other, it is other not by the failing of corruption, but by the advance of exaltation. Just as in thee 132Cit has been made other, and is to be other, than it was born; but by exaltation, not by corruption. And when in certain earthly things it seems to carry itself over from one thing into another, yet it is never other than it is; because it is earth, and always it is earth, and that which passes over is earth and that into which it passes over is earth; and when this passes over into that, or into that other, yet that which is earth does not pass over, which in this and in that is the same. Therefore the earth has to be moved within the bosom of its own nature, and has to work out of that which it is, that which it is: it has not to pass over beyond the bounds of its own nature out of that which it is into that which it is not: and for that reason, the earth standeth for ever in that which it is not. Why therefore hast not thou too stood in that in which thou wast made upon the earth, just as 132Dthe earth stands in that in which it was made? Why hast thou degenerated, so as not even to imitate thy matter, which so far keeps what it is, that even when thou hast been made together with the earth, thou canst not be other than the earth is? As far as that thou flowest away by thy own fault; beyond it thou art not permitted to go forward by its nature. Behold how much it guards what it is, so that even when it has received thee, flowing and unstable, it does not suffer thee to pass over further into another thing which itself is not. Whence then is it for thee to flow away? Search diligently, and think. Neither thy craftsman nor thy matter did this for thee; because she, both by standing for ever, keeps in thee also what she herself is, and he, by making thee for eternity, gave also more than she is. Whence therefore is this for thee, save from thy own fault, out of which it is now a penalty for thee that thou returnest into her, to whom this had been given of grace, that thou shouldest stand always 133Aabove her? Therefore thou passest away, and the earth standeth in testimony against thee, so that, reproving thee as mortal and receiving thee as dying, it may convict thee before it punishes thee. Therefore the earth standeth for ever. One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh; but the earth standeth for ever.

These things we have said, according to the littleness or the scantiness of our understanding, upon the opening of the book of Solomon which is called Ecclesiastes, in no way presuming that we have said what most of all had to be said, since it is so great a thing for us only not to have said what had not to be said. But for the rest it must be known that this book requires a certain new kind of exposition; because, since it wholly aims at moving the affections of the human heart, one must more often form one's discourse in it as though by conversing than by expounding. Whence 133Bit is needful in these matters sometimes even to dwell longer upon words in those things which seem plain and open, so that the very driving home of the utterance may touch more strongly and penetrate more effectually the heart of the hearer. He who shall wish to handle this Scripture otherwise, even if he serves conveniently the understanding of his hearers, yet, not retaining its force and property, profits perhaps less unto edification.

HOMILIA II. De probatione vanitatis omnium sub coelo: per elementorum corruptionem, per rerum generationem, successionem, et eorum, quae fuerunt oblivionem.

Verba Ecclesiastes, quae cuncta sub sole vana esse testantur, nescio quo pacto, modo cum legerentur dulcia facta sunt in auribus nostris. Et ecce coepimus libenter audire mala nostra, et quae non diligimus 133Ctamen audire diligimus. Mala enim nostra non diligimus, et mala nostra audire diligimus; quia audiendo mala quae non diligimus, bonorum recordamur quae diligimus. Et ipsa haec bonorum recordatio (etiam inter mala) dulcis animo est, et tanto utique dulcior quanto amariora sunt ipsa mala, quae vel audiendo, vel sentiendo agnoscimus longe esse ab iis bonis ad quae, vel saltem per recordationem suspiramus. Hoc totum erat, quod in hac relatione nobis modo tantum sapuisse miramur, in qua exsilii nostri nobis aerumna describitur, et nostra miseria atque calamitas qualis ac quanta sit declaratur. Mens enim nostra in auditu malorum suorum quasi de quodam somno pristini temporis evigilans subito 133Dagnovit ubi esset, stupensque et mirans tantum ruinae barathrum, simul etiam considerare coepit de quanta sublimitate in hoc ipsum miseriae profundum cecidisset, et ad illam quia necdum effectu potuit miro quodam ardoris intimi desiderio suspiravit. Hoc ergo erat quod in illis verbis, quae nostram recitabant miseriam, nostrum traxit affectum. Hoc fecit ut mala nostra sic nobis semper audire libeat, nec possit amarum esse quidquid illud est, quod cum eo percipitur quod tam dulce est. Hoc quotidie miseris lamenta ipsa dulcia facit, et inter suspiria ac gemitus lacrymis delectabiliter pascit afflictos; quia eorum quae diliguntur inter adversa recordatio suavior est, et ipse animus desiderio absentium amplius inardescit, praeteritorum memoria dulcius tangitur, 134Adilatione futurorum validius inflammatur. Hoc noster Ecclesiastes optime noverat, qui in omni narratione sua tam diligenter exsequitur vanitatem rerum transeuntium, ut ex ejus consideratione cor humanum admoneat coelestia meditari et evigilare in desiderio aeternorum. Scivit enim quod quanto evidentius eorum, quae temporaliter praetereunt vanitas agnoscitur, tanto sublimius intus mentis oculus ad statum aeternitatis aperitur. Incipiens ergo, in hac prima parte operis sui, ostendit omnia vana esse, quae sub sole sunt, id est, quaecunque visibilia sunt corruptioni subjecta esse, vel obnoxia mutabilitati. Ostendit enim neque in coelo, neque sub coelo, neque super terram, neque in terra aliquid esse perpetuum, quod vicissitudinem non patiatur nec 134Btranseat in alterationem. Ideoque nihil vere esse ex omnibus iis, quae semper sine cessatione in id trahuntur quod non sunt, et quod sunt, stabile vel incorruptum servare non possunt.

Oritur sol, et occidit, et ad locum suum revertitur: ibique renascens gyrat per meridiem, et flectitur ad aquilonem. Hoc per se distinguendum est. Deinde sequitur:

Lustrans universa in circuitu pergit spiritus, et in circulos suos revertitur. Et hoc per se ponendum est. Postea sequitur:

Omnia flumina intrant in mare, et mare non redundat: ad locum unde exeunt flumina revertuntur, ut iterum fluant. Et hoc simul conjungendum est.

Tria ergo quaedam proponere videtur in argumentum 134Cmutabilitatis omnium, solem, spiritum, flumina, id est ignem, aerem, humorem, ut per solem quidem ignem, per spiritum aerem, per flumina humorem, velut a parte totum significatum intelligatur. Superius namque terram quasi fundamentum immobile medio loco constituit. Nunc caetera tria elementa, id est ignem, aerem, aquam circa ipsam motu instabili fluctuantia disponit, ut in procreandis mutabilibus, his tribus elementis motum agendi, et quodammodo vicem artificis attributam ostendat. Terram vero quasi materiam quamdam procreandorum omnium immobilem subjacere; impotentem quidem agendi, sed aptam tantummodo, ut ex ea caeteris operantibus formentur, quae creanda 134Dsunt. Per haec igitur tria elementa in illo quarto vim suam natura exercet, quae circa illud, et in illo discurrentia lege mirabili, et se invicem contemperantia, tam innumerabiles formas et species rerum ex ea producunt, quot annuis menstruis, diurnis temporum vicissitudinibus in eorum accessu et recessu jugiter sine cessatione alternantibus demonstrantur. Quia igitur cuncta nascentia quae de terra oriuntur et ex terra substantiam nutrimentumque accipiunt, ab his tribus elementis vitalis motus naturam sortiuntur, recte in eis, et mutabilitatis originem posuit, et mutabilium omnium naturam proprietatemque expressit, ut in his pariter videamus et unde sit quod stare non potest, quidquid sub tempore oritur, et qua via adesse prodeat quod non est, vel quod 135Aest, ad non esse revertatur. Oritur sol, et occidit, et ad locum suum revertitur, ibique renascens gyrat per meridiem, et flectitur ad aquilonem. Paucis verbis rem magnam comprehendit: de quibus aliqua nos pro tempore dicere oportet, non tamen animum auditoris diutius in ejusmodi detinere, ne videamur contra propositum nostrum sacram expositionem relinquentes, ad describendos siderum cursus devolvi. Omnia quidem haec ob id solummodo dicta sunt, ut humanus animus earum rerum quas novit relatione, commodius excitetur, et ut per haec ad cogitanda ea, quae non novit, evigilet: et idcirco non nobis pigrum esse debet, aut indignum videri, ad ea diligenter intendere, quae nobis divinus sermo studuit diligenter enarrare. Demonstrat ergo quali via 135Bluminare hoc magnum, quod sua praesentia universa illustrat, incessabili agitatione in hoc mundi sensilis globo circumferatur, suoque accessu et recessu varias rerum mutationes efficiat. Oritur sol, et occidit, et ad locum suum revertitur. Primum ostendit eum circularem habere motum, et ad id semper unde progreditur reverti, ut, quia in circulo finis non potest inveniri, cursus ejus perpetuus demonstretur. Oritur sol, et occidit, et ad locum suum revertitur. Deinde anfractus progressionis ejus describit, dicens: Gyrat per meridiem, et flectitur ad aquilonem, ut idipsum ad magnam rerum mutationem pertineat, quod non semper eodem modo neque in directum cursum suum dirigit incedens. Oritur sol, et occidit. Oritur quotidie, quando emergens 135Chumanis praesentatur aspectibus. Occidit, quando descendens ad inferiores partes secundum convexitatem circum actionis suae oculis nostris se abducit. Revertitur ad locum suum; quia impellente volubilitate subtus rursum ad ortum revocatur. Post ortum vero ad occasum tendens, primum flectitur ad meridiem, quia obliquo ductu praecipue cum in aestivalibus commoratur signis, ab ortu ad lineam meridianam conscendit. Deinde autem ad occasum descendens, rursum obliqua progressione ad aquilonem inclinatur. Potest alia adhuc in his verbis expositio satis conveniens adhiberi, scilicet ut haec omnia non de diuturno, sed de annuo cursu solis dicta accipiamus. Oritur quippe nobis sol, quando 135Dper vernale aequinoctium ingrediens ad nostrum polum consurgit. Occidit autem, quando per autumnale aequinoctium exiens ad inferiora descendit. Gyrat per meridiem, quando in hiemalibus signis commoratur. Flectitur ad aquilonem, quando in aestivis signis, quae polo boreali viciniora sunt, circumfertur. Oritur ergo sol, et ipso oriente omnia pariter, oriuntur, quae ex ejus calore reviviscunt. Occidit, et statim igne vitali subducto universa occumbunt, quae ex ejus praesentia viguerunt. Gyrat per meridiem, ut aestiva incendia algor temperet hiemalis. Flectitur ad aquilonem, ut quae brumae gelu, et torpor glacialis astrinxerat, aestivis ardoribus rursum calefacta animentur. Vides igitur unum corpus quantas secum trahat rerum mutationes.

136ALustrans universa in circuitu pergit spiritus, et in circulos suos revertitur. Si per spiritum, aerem accepimus, congruo ordine, postquam instabilitatem coelestis elementi descripserat, eamdem quoque inferiora legem pati demonstrat, dicens: Lustrans universa in circuitu pergit spiritus. Ac si diceret: Si ea quae in coelo sunt vis naturae stare non patitur, necesse est ut ea quoque quae sub coelo sunt eadem conditio mutabilitatis moderetur. Sane quemadmodum soli? ita quoque aeri orbicularem tribuit motum, ut ejus agitatio perpetua esse demonstretur. Quod autem pluraliter subjungit: In circulos suos revertitur: hoc significare potest quod motus aeris non semper ubique idem est, sed cum alibi vehementius, alibi moderatius agitetur, ipsa ejus fluctuatio 136Bversa vice in semetipsam refusa dissimiliter moveatur; et non uniformiter conquiescat, ut non cogamur motum semel coeptum usque ad extrema extendere, ut singulae motiones impulsionesque quasi in se factae; et paulatim spatio motu languente quiescant. Sed, et illud quod ait: Lustrans, apte huic elemento tribuitur, quod sordes universas sua mobilitate ubicunque aspersas sive collectas purget ac dissipet. Sive quod sua subtilitate cuncta penetrans ubique se diffundat. Vel ad superiorem hoc verbum sententiam copulatur sic: Oritur sol, et occidit, et ad locum suum revertitur; ibique renascens gyrat per meridiem, et flectitur ad aquilonem, lustrans universa in circuitu. Et hic distinctione facta, deinde sequens sententia subinfertur ita: Pergit 136Cspiritus, etc. Sol enim cursu suo universa in circuitu lustrat; quia omnes partes mundi per diversa signa oriens, vel occidens attingit. In cancro enim oriens, et occidens, aquilonem tangit. In capricorno, meridiem. In libra, et ariete, per orientem, et occidentem medium pertransit. Sequitur: Pergit spiritus, et in circulos suos revertitur. Secundum praecedentem expositionem, spiritum nunc non incovenienter accipere possumus igneam vim quae ab ipso sole procedens, per cuncta se diffundit, et universa invisibiliter penetrans vegetat et movet. Unde et veteres naturam esse dixerunt. Ignem artificem procedentem in res sensibiles procreandas. Vitalis enim motus, et vegetationis sensibilis in cunctis nascentibus 136Dignea vis origo est: quae rebus omnibus incrementum subjicit, et invisibili eas nutrimento alens ac fovens, ad invisibilem tandem producit substantiam. Hanc autem occultam naturae vim cuncta moventem, et alentem poeta quoque spiritum nominavit: et nota sunt ejus verba: Principio coelum ac terras, camposque liquentes, Lucentemque globum lunae, titaniaque astra, Spiritus intus alit: totamque infusa per artus, Mens agitat molem, et magno se corpore miscet. (Aeneid. VI, 688.) Quamvis in his verbis illum potius errorem probare videatur, qui mundum hunc sensilem quasi anima constans ex anima et corpore, ipsamque ejus animam spiritum esse cuncta moventem asseveret. Sed 137Aquomodolibet opinio errantium exponatur, nos sano intellectu spiritum pergentem in omnia, et in circulos suos revertentem occultam naturae vim accipere possumus, quae universa invisibiliter nutrit et vegetat, et unumquodque ad certum finem legitimumque terminum perducit. Hic ergo spiritus, id est, occulta naturae vis omnia lustrat; quia per omnes rerum partes invisibiliter se diffundens, unicuique secundum suae naturae capacitatem, propriam qualitatem distribuit. Pergit, et revertitur quia universa, qui oriuntur in tempore prius per incrementum provehit, ac deinde senescentia ad originem suam reducit. Pergit enim quia in nascentibus egreditur, in crescentibus usque ad certam mensuram procedit. Revertitur, quia in senescentibus, et per defectum 137Bnaturae suae retro labentibus, usque ad originis suae principium revocatur. Sic igitur singularum rerum cursus et progressiones, quasi circulos quosdam et orbes in semetipsos recurrentes recte accipimus; quia omnia temporaliter orta illuc tandem per occasum redeunt, unde per nativitatis principium exiverunt. Et unumquodque quidem secundum propriam mensuram, et tempus quo subsistit, differentem ab alio, id est, majorem minoremve excursum habere probatur. Omnia autem sicut originem unam, sic et finem unum habere noscuntur; quia omnia per occasum ad terram redeunt, quae in ortus sui principio de terra exiverunt. Sicut ergo sol oritur et occidit, et ad locum suum revertitur, sic spiritus pergit, et in circulos suos revertitur. Quia 137Csicut in corpore solis localiter ignis progrediens, ad ortus sui principium reducitur, sic etiam naturaliter in cunctis nascentibus, motum quem per incrementum rerum erexit, per defectum et occasum earumdem ad originem suam reducit.

Sequitur tertia clausula in qua tractatur de elemento aquae, quod in ordine rerum, tertium post ignem ponitur in procreatione secundum sociatur. Quantum enim attinet ad dispositionem et ordinem rerum, primum et supremum locum ignis possidet; aer secundum igni proximum. Postea aqua tertium vendicat locum; novissimo et imo loco terra residet. In his quatuor ignis et aqua, natura quidem maxime repugnantia confoederatione 137Dtamen aequabili amica, omnium nascentium origo sunt. Et ideo si locum vel naturam attendimus, a se invicem duo haec disparata cernimus. Si efficientiam respicimus, proxima sibi utraque et amica invenimus. Igitur de elemento aquae, quod alterum cum igne fomentum vitale praebet nascentibus, quasi post ignem, et aerem tertio, vel cum igne secundo inter rerum mutabilium naturas tacendum non fuit. Et idcirco hujus quoque circuitum, et excursum in res sensibiles procreandas describit, dicens: Omnia flumina intrant in mare, et mare non redundat. Et causam statim adjungit, quare non redundet mare omnibus in se fluminibus receptis: Quia scilicet rursum ad locum unde exeunt flumina revertuntur, ut iterum fluant. Ductus enim aquarum per omne 138Acorpus terrae intrinsecus, et deforis in modum venarum humorem trahunt, ut aequabiliter irrigatio in omnem partem diffundatur. Haec autem infusio ut jugis et perpetua esse possit, idcirco aquarum cursus in orbem dispositus est, et in illa perenni circuitione, ut nunquam deficiat quod desuper infunditur; quantum in parte altera deorsum fluit, tantum in altera parte per occultos meatus ad ortum revocatur. Sic et cibus corporis quodam circuitu fertur, et primum a palato in alvum descendens, ac deinde in secessum pertransiens, et in ipso ejus transitu, quasi quadam instillatione naturae, deficienti nutrimentum subjicitur, quo evaporato et exinanito, necesse est rursum ut membris fatiscentibus reparandis edendi subsidio concurratur. Quasi ergo circulus 138Brenascentis semper indigentiae in suam originem recurrens ducitur; quia dum sine cessatione quod sumptum est praeterit, semper iterato sumi necesse est, quod supplendo defectui substantiam ministrare possit. Quale ergo nutrimentum substantia cibi assidua iteratione alendo corpori subjicit: tale omnino elementorum refluxio nutrimentum in terrae corpore procreandis fetibus seminibusque vivificandis infundit. Hoc ignis, hoc aqua, hoc aer perpeti accessu et recessu sine intermissione agere non cessant, ut semper accidentia repleant et recedentia evacuent ut quia subsistere non potest vigor infusionis praeteritae ex necessitate denuo iteretur irrigatio plenitudinis reparandae. Quam ergo rerum alimenta fiduciam perpetis subsistentiae praestare poterunt, 138Ccum in rebus omnibus sic semper sine cessatione, et reparantia transeant, et deficiant reparata? Licet enim huic defectui qualemcunque consolationem praestare videatur repetita infusio; magna tamen est miseria semper ad indigentiam accipere, et nunquam indigentia accipiendi posse carere. Unde manifestum est quod omnia transitoria, et caduca vana sunt, quae a sui status soliditate jugiter, vel transitu vel defectu inanescunt. Magnum ergo hic spectaculum sanctis mentibus praeparatum est, quae norunt ex visibilibus trahere invisibilium cognitionem. Quae norunt dicere Creatori suo: Omnia in sapientia fecisti, Domine (Psal. CIII). Delectasti me, Domine, in factura tua, et in operibus manuum tuarum 138Dexsultabo. Quam magnificata sunt opera tua, Domine, nimis profundae factae sunt cogitationes tuae (Psal. XCI).

Ecce enim quomodo in circuitu feruntur omnia transitoria et vanitati subjecta. Et scimus quia circulus finem non habet. Quae ergo in circuitu currunt, currunt quidem, sed ad finem nunquam perveniunt. Quae ergo requies sperari potest, ubi status nullus esse potest? Ubi enim perpetuus cursus est, status nullus est. Ubi autem circuitus via est, ubi cursus certe finem habere possit, non est. Quae ergo in circuitu currunt, semper currunt et nunquam ad statum perveniunt. Semper transeunt, et nunquam subsistunt. Semper finiuntur, et finem invenire non possunt. Cum praeterierint, futura sunt; cum supervenerint, 139Anon subsistunt. Haec est via omnium mutabilium, et via omnium mutabilia amantium, et mutabilia sequentium. Nam et de impiis dictum est: In circuitu impii ambulant (Psal. XI). Et iterum: Caput circuitus eorum (Psal. CXXXIX), et pone illos ut rotam, Domine (Psal. LXXXII). Caput quoque impiorum omnium de se testatur, dicens: Circuivi terram, et perambulavi eam (Job I). Et de ipso apostolus ait: Circuit tanquam leo rugiens quaerens quem devoret (I Petr. V). Vides ergo quemadmodum perversi semper circuitum diligunt, et a circuitu non recedunt. Idcirco quae a perversis perverse amantur, etiam ipsa in circuitu omnia currunt in testimonium illis, quod circuitum sequuntur, et ipsi. Econtrario amator aeternorum dicit: Pes meus stetit in directo 139B(Psal. XXVII). Et iterum: Dirige me in semitam mandatorum tuorum, quia ipsam volui (Psal. CXVIII). Et iterum: Rectus est callis justi (Isai. XXVI). Et alibi rursum: Ibunt, inquit, directe emissiones; et ad certum locum deducet eos Dominus Deus noster (Sap. V). O via recta, o circuitus, quo ducis tu. Et tu quo ducis? Tu ducis, et perducis. Tu vero ducis, et seducis; quia quos ducis, perdis, non perducis. O circuitus, quomodo involvis, quomodo complecteris sequaces tuos? Tu currentibus per te, neque exitum tribuis a te, nec in te perventionem. Ergo omnia transitoria et caduca per circuitus volvuntur dum transeunt, ut in eis bonum aeternitatis non quaeramus, quae cernimus semper, et sic advenire ut transeant, et sic transire ut non subsistant. Videamus 139Cergo adhuc circuitus istos vanitatis. Dei enim sapientia, ut jam dictum est, hoc mirabiliter providit, ut rerum omnium motus in orbem ageretur, quatenus corporea natura, quae effluendo aliquando defectum sentire potuisset, semper in suam recurrendo originem dum sine intermissione recipit quod effudit, sine defectu effundat quod recipit, et sit defectus sine defectu; nec unquam desit quod possit deficere, ut semper deficiat. Unde in una eademque re, et miserum est, quod est; et mirabile quod factum est, quia in eodem opere et fragilis invenitur materia, et ratio artificis admiranda. Et contemptum quidem mundi suadet natura corruptibilis, sed succumbit mens admiratione in contemplatione rationis. 139DAd hanc ergo rationem intuendam post explicitum cursum rerum mutabilium noster Ecclesiastes se convertit, ut in ea mentis aciem per contemplationem exerceat; quia eam scientia sufficienter non valet comprehendere, digna studet venerari admiratione. Nam, quia mutabilitatem omnium, in tribus rerum generibus igne, aere et aqua, secundum motum moventem explicuit quam inexplicabilis eadem sit secundum motum qui movetur per singula quaeque orientia et occidentia in universitate subsequenter ostendit.

Cunctae res difficiles non valet eas homo explicare sermone: non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris impletur auditu. Cum res quaelibet in superficie sua cernitur, nondum adhuc vel causa ejus occulta, vel 140Anatura penetratur. Videtur namque quod est, sed quale sit illud quod videtur, vel quam in occulto (quo sensus corporeus accedere non potest) retineat qualitatem: cur etiam sic sit ut videtur, vel unde sic sit, vel ad quid sit, quis hominum (non dicam in rebus omnibus, sed nec in una qualibet re) ad plenum comprehendere valet? Quantis ergo tenebris homo involvitur; quanta ignorantiae caecitate coarctatur, cujus sensus vix etiam superficie tenus pauca rerum potest attingere? Qui etsi cuncta, quae sunt secundum speciem exteriorem, cerneret, nondum tamen vim latentem rerum, invisibilemque naturam penetraret. Ergo universitas rerum utroque modo homini incomprehensibilis est; videlicet et secundum exteriorem speciem, et secundum interiorem 140Bqualitatem. Singulae autem rerum, aliae quidem ex parte foras specie ad sensum veniunt, aliae prorsus absconduntur, vel quia localiter remotae sunt, vel quia etiam loco praesentes, subtilitate sui tarditatem sensus humani excedunt. Vix ergo aliqua sensus humanus in rebus attingere sufficit; nihil autem universorum, perfecte ut est, comprehendit. Ergo cunctae res difficiles sunt: et secundum universitatem videlicet, ut nec valeant attingi, et secundum singula quaeque difficiles, quia nullo sensu possunt vel intellectu plene comprehendi. Quae si ratione perfecte investigari non possunt, multo minus sermone possunt explicari. Nam hoc ipsum in rebus magis omnibus ineffabile est, quod in tanta mutabilitatis confusione nusquam bene consideranti 140Cratio evidens et manifesta deest: quod tam bene disponitur id etiam quod in rebus bonum non est, ut quodammodo singulorum corruptio, universorum sit pulchritudo. Propterea sensus humanus in consideratione horum succumbens suaviter ex defectu suo reficitur; quia in eo quod secundum corruptionem displicet, in ordinatissima pulchritudine universitatis, etiam ipsa corruptio pulchra est et placet. Sic miro et ineffabili modo, Conditor in creatura sua simul et per corruptionem rerum punit malitiam, et per pulchritudinem delectat naturam, ut agnoscat homo in poena sua quid per culpam meruit, et in delectatione quid amisit. Quantam enim in Creatore rerum dulcedinis affluentiam esse credimus, si 140Dtam miram in creaturarum pulchritudine suavitatem invenimus? Propterea cum dixisset in tam multiplici et perplexa variaque rerum profunditate defectum humanae intelligentiae, subdit statim in pulchritudine earumdem jucunditatem naturae.

Non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris impletur auditu. Cum omnes sensus corporei in rebus conditis oblectamenta sua, et quasi proprias quasdam delicias singuli praeparatas inveniant, utpote visus speciem, auditus melodiae dulcedinem, olfactus odorem, saporem gustus et tactus lenitatem. Caeteri quidem omnes corporeae necessitati, vel etiam voluptati serviunt. Hi vero duo sensus, id est visus et auditus alimenta sua magis ad spiritalem jucunditatem trahunt. Unde et illorum refectio defaecationem 141Anon habet, quia cum perceptione dulcedinis nullam trahunt massam corruptionis. Propter quod illorum refectio ad dulcedinis satietatem non pervenit; quia a percipienda dulcedine appetitum illorum nec percurrens difficultas tardat, neque succedens molestia ulla restringit. Purum ergo atque sincerum hoc alimentum sine omni mole corporea totum in refectionem animae transit; quia licet a specie corporali emanet et per corporis sensum transeat, non potest tamen retineri a corpore, quia corporeum nihil habet, nec ingerit corpulentum. Idcirco ergo visus et auditus quasi excellentiores caeteris et nihil ponderis deprimentis habentes, sublimiorem in corpore sedem sortiti sunt, ut libere et sine obstaculo ad suas delectationes effluant, vel 141Binfluentes, in se sine difficultate admittant. Sane duo sunt, quae ex rerum specie per visum intrant ad animum. Et duo item, quae ex vocum perceptione ingrediuntur per auditum. Per visum namque ad animi cognitionem ex rebus pervenit substantia et forma. Ex vocibus per auditum, significatio et melodia. Et idem operatur in animo per visum substantia ex rebus, quod per auditum significatio ex vocibus. Itemque idem facit per visum in animo forma ex rebus, quod per auditum melodia ex vocibus. Duo quippe sunt, quibus animae rationalis natura tota disponitur, videlicet cognitio et affectus, id est sapientia et amor. Quae duo si anima perfecte obtineat et legitime disponat, beata est. Si vero vel in his quantum natura expetit obtinendis 141Cdeficiat, vel obtenta, contra naturam pervertat, in ea procul dubio parte qua vel defectum vel confusionem horum patitur, misera, necesse est, efficiatur. Tota ergo animae rationalis substantia his duobus regitur, id est cognitione et affectu, ut per sapientiam quidem veritatem inveniat, per amorem autem amplectatur virtutem. Ut igitur ob beatitudinem rationali animae etiam exteriora servirent, posita sunt in corpore humano haec duo instrumenta sensuum, ut per ea ad animam notiones visibilium ingrederentur atque in ipsa sapientiam sive virtutem, vel si omnino non esset, efficerent, vel si minus esset augerent. Ergo essentia rerum per visum ad animam ingrediens, et vocum significatio per auditum scientiam pariunt. Forma vero rerum per visum 141Dintrans, et melodia vocum per auditum ad jucunditatem animum accendunt. Quoties enim foris sive rerum specie visus afficitur, sive auditus vocum dulcedine demulcetur, evigilat animus intus miris affectibus, illi quo exterius tactum se sentit, respondens. Et fit nonnunquam, ut per eam quam sensu corporeo trahit dulcedinem, redeat ad invisibilium bonorum recordationem et quodammodo ex similitudine, admonitus inenarrabili desiderio illud incipiat concupiscere: cujus quasi umbram et imaginem in affectu corporali se sentit percepisse.

Dicat ergo Ecclesiastes: Non saturatur oculus visu nec auris impletur auditu. Quia per hos sensus, visibilium pulchritudo, dum animum jucunditate in 142Asui contemplatione afficit, inenarrabilem in eo concupiscentiam invisibilium bonorum accendit. Quae videlicet concupiscentia ineffabilem dulcedinem sitiens, visu vel auditu corporeo quo excitatur quantamcunque jucunditatem afferant, irritari potest potius quam expleri, et sermone humano quantumlibet profusus fuerit vel disertus, etsi tenuiter vix dicitur, nunquam perfecte explicatur. A specie enim visibilium rerum, quasi quaedam tantummodo rationalis animus semina concipit gaudiorum; sed excrescente mox in immensum desiderio parturit ipse et non se capit in tanta jucunditate. Nemo ergo visibilium rerum aspectum castis mentibus noxium putet; quia, si videre opera Dei omnino noxium foret, nequaquam ab ipso videndi usus 142Bcreatus fuisset. Opus enim Dei quasi verbum illius est, per quod nobis loquitur, et ipsi oculi quasi instrumenta sunt quibus per contemplationem verba Dei percipiuntur. Sicut ergo auris instrumentum est ad percipiendum verbum hominis, sic oculus instrumentum est ad percipiendum verbum hominis, sic oculus instrumentum est ad percipiendum verbum Creatoris. Propterea congrue in humano corpore, et oculi coram positi sunt, et aures a latere constitutae, quasi per hoc nobis significetur quod nostra intentio secundario dirigi debeat ad proximum, principaliter ad Deum. Recte ergo ut ostenderetur qualiter ex consideratione rerum visibilium, nascitur in animo desiderium aeternorum, soli oculi et aures commemorantur. Quia his solis fere sapientiae 142Cet virtuti via patet ad animum, quia, dum visibilium pulchritudinem prae caeteris sensibus meram percipiunt, soli interius amorem invisibilium bonorum sincerius accendunt. Cunctae res difficiles non valet eas homo explicare sermone.

Non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris impletur auditu. Mirum est. Cor humanum toti mundo non sufficit, et totus mundus cordi humano non sufficit. Quare cor humanum toti mundo non sufficit? Quia cunctae res difficiles nec valet eas homo explicare sermone. Quare cordi humano totus mundus non sufficit? Quia non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris impletur auditu. Ergo scientia succumbit, affectus transcendit. Tendit se scientia quantum potest, et totum capere non potest; amor vero totum haurit, 142Det adhuc satiari non potest. Quare hoc? Quia scientiae charitas supereminet, nec dicit: Sufficit cor humanum, donec ad illum pervenerit, et illum invenerit a quo factum est ut esset, et ad quem factum est ut in illo beatum esset. Omnis jucunditas, omnis suavitas, omnis pulchritudo rerum conditarum afficere cor humanum potest; satiare non potest, nisi sola illa dulcedo ad quam factum est. Nam species rerum visibilium quasi venae tantummodo quaedam sunt, per quas invisibilis pulchritudo se manifestans ad nos usque emanat. Et ideo, cum ista sensum nostrum atque affectum in se naturaliter provocant, non quidem desiderium replent, sed ad inquirendam Conditoris speciem et ejus pulchritudinem 143Aconcupiscendam irritant. Ergo ista omnia quae foris videntur ad provocandum affectum humanum, non ad satiandum facta sunt, ut ab eis excitatus surgat et ea auctus transcendat. Quapropter non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris impletur auditu. Quia delectat quidem quod pulchrum factum cernimus, sed non sufficit, nisi illum qui fecit, inveniamus.

Vel sic intelligi potest quod dicit: Non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris impletur auditu. Quia enim praemiserat cunctas res esse difficiles, nec posse hominem eas explicare sermone. Ne forte putaretur vel scientia eas comprehendere posse, adjunxit: Non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris impletur auditu. Ac si diceret: Non est mirum si homo rerum difficultatem 143Bcultatem sermone explicare non potest: qui nec sensu earum profunditatem capere vel pervestigare potest. Sive enim persemetipsum invenienda quaerat, sive ab alio jam inventa audiat, infra plenitudinis satietatem est omne quod capere potest. Nam, si per semetipsum contemplari incipiat, non saturatur oculus visu. Si erudiri quaerat ab altero, non impletur auris auditu. Angustiae enim corporalium instrumentorum, si se foras effundant, profunditati rerum sive immensitati explicandae non sufficiunt. Si autem se infundant, capacitatem cordis humani implere non possunt. Quia enim cor hominis peccati tenebris caecatum intus oculum non habet, quo lumen veritatis plene videat, nec aurem qua Dei verbum intrinsecus sonans percipiat, ad ariditatem 143Cignorantiae suae rigandam corporeos oculos et aures aperire cogitur, ut foris aliquam saltem in rerum specie veritatis stillam hauriat, qua sitis ejus licet non valeat omnino exstingui, vel ad modicum valeat temperari. Hoc est enim quod Dominus per prophetam populo suo improperat, dicens: Duo peccata fecit populus meus. Me dereliquerunt fontem aquae vivae, et foderunt sibi cisternas dissipatas, et non valentes aquas continere (Jer. II). Scimus namque quia cisterna idcirco foditur, ut aqua extrinsecus collecta in eam defluat, et ex ea rursum in usus hominum transitura hauriatur. Sed haec quia venam vivam non habet, quantumlibet magna et aquarum collectione redundans videatur, aliquando exhauriri potest 143Det exsiccari; quia, cum sublatum fuerit, et consumptum quod aliunde infunditur, nihil ei de suo superest unde reparetur. Sed fons qui vivam habet venam etiamsi modicus est, deficere tamen omnino non potest, neque effusionis suae defectum aliquando sentit, cui sine defectu semper de proprio incrementum accedit. Corporales igitur oculi et aures, licet praecipua sint instrumenta, quibus via disciplinis aperitur ad animum, quia tamen intus a fonte veritatis non veniunt notiones rerum visibilium, ad cor hominis per angustos suae capacitatis ductus et quasi aquas sparsim collectas in cisternam deducunt. Et quia in eisdem rebus quas percipiunt, neque universitatem comprehendere, neque intima penetrare valent, recte nunc dicitur: Non satiatur oculus 144Avisu, nec auris impletur auditu. Quia humanus animus vel vivendo vel audiendo, etiamsi aliquid quantulumcunque de veritate percipit: longe tamen ab ejus plenitudine, suae eum conditio infirmitatis repellit. Non ergo mirum est si humani sermonis ariditas ad explicandam rerum difficultatem non sufficit; quia sensus etiam humanus in ejus consideratione succumbit. Ideoque cunctae res difficiles, nec valet eas homo explicare sermone: non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris impletur auditu.

Quid est quod fuit? Ipsum quod futurum est. Quid est quod factum est? Ipsum quod faciendum est. Nihil sub sole novum; nec valet quisquam dicere: Ecce hoc recens est. Jam enim praecessit in saeculis, quae fuerunt ante nos. Existimet fortassis aliquis errorem 144Bhic illum confirmari, quo philosophi gentilium de saeculorum revolutione, et rerum omnium recursu in idipsum, mira dementia temporum aeternitatem astruere conati sunt. Dixerunt quippe rerum mutabilium seriem ab aeterno eodem ordine quo nunc cernitur cucurrisse, et sine fine, lege eadem, mundo in sua universitate nec principium nec finem habente, per saecula quaedam sibi succedentia cursuram. Saeculum magnum autem in quindecim millibus annorum constare (quem annum appellant) quo expleto, omnibus sideribus ad locum suum unde singula quaeque ab initio saeculi progressa fuerant revocatis, rursusque in exordium alterius saeculi simili ratione ac modo motum inchoantibus, subjectamque naturam simili itidem ratione moventibus: rursus eadem 144Cprorsus omnia, quem in saeculis praecedentibus ordine praecessissent, eodem nihilominus ordine, eadem essentia, eadem forma, eisdem omnino et locis et temporibus, iterato consurgere, cursumque suum ac fatum simile priori atque idem peragere: eamdem quoque legem pati, fortunamque subire; ita ut eosdem homines nasci, itidem eosdem filios gignere, eadem fortuna vivere, eadem sorte mori contingat: eumdem rerum eventum, eamdem prorsus qualitatem, eumdemque statum et procursum omnium, quae praeterita prioris saeculi tempora tenuissent. Talem autem rerum omnium revolutionem atque iterationem, in idipsum semper fuisse semperque futuram esse sine fine, ut quemadmodum 144Drecursu unius sideris per singulos annos, ad pristinum ista tum renovantur omnia; ita recursu omnium siderum totiusque naturae ad ortum per singula saecula et magnos annos ad primam conditionem reparentur universa. Hic vero error quantus sit, facile arguet ratio manifesta. Nam tempora aeterna esse non posse in hoc evidentissime comprobatur: quod omne tempus initium habuit; et sine contradictione constat quod omne quod initium habuit, aliquando non fuit. Amplius omne tempus praeteritum, aliquando praesens fuit. Omne autem tempus quod aliquando praesens fuit, antequam praesens esset, nondum fuit. Alioquin si semper praesens fuit, non jam tempus fuit, sed aeternitas. Si ergo omne tempus praeteritum aliquando non 145Afuit, fuit quando nullum tempus fuit. Itaque, tempora aeterna esse non potuerunt; sed erat ante tempora aeternitas sine tempore, quam tempora quidem nec auxerunt cum inciperent, nec cum finientur, consument. Liquet ergo falsam esse assertionem eorum qui saeculorum aeternitatem praedicaverunt, et mutabilitatis principium sine principio fuisse testati sunt. Sed, ne forte in hoc loco error hujusmodi confirmari videatur, cum dicitur: Nihil novum sub sole; neque valet quisquam dicere: Ecce hoc recens est. Jam enim praecessit in saeculis, quae fuerunt ante nos. Quo intellectu id accipiendum sit: statim subsequentibus verbis ostendit, dicens:

Non est priorum memoria; sed nec eorum quidem, qui postea futuri sunt, erit recordatio apud eos, qui 145Bfuturi sunt in novissimo. Nam, si priora et novissima cum praesentibus prorsus eadem essent; nequaquam praesentes homines a prioribus, et a futuris in novissimo alios diceret; nec diceret, apud eos qui post nos futuri sunt in novissimo, sed diceret, apud nos qui futuri sumus in novissimo. Nisi forte primos et novissimos ad principium et finem ejusdem saeculi referendum quis dicat, alioquin nec primos esse nec novissimos qui sine principio fuerunt, et sine fine futuri sunt. Sed primos et novissimos ad principium et finem ejusdem saeculi referre prohibet, quod ait: Jam praecessit in saeculis, quae fuerunt ante nos. Quia, dum alia saecula praecedentium, atque alia subsequentium dicit nequaquam se primos et novissimos ejusdem saeculi significasse ostendit. 145CErgo, quia non solum a catholica veritate, sed a ratione quoque sententia abhorret, nos dictum hoc referamus ad rerum similitudinem, quae in suis generibus sic a principio institutae sunt, ut unumquodque secundum similitudinem et formam primam originis suae propaginem extendat et nihil sit quod terminum primae dispositionis in suo genere excedat. Sic in ipsis elementis mundi, sic in iis, quae ex ipsis procreata sunt vel procreantur, omnibus natura primam dispositionem custodit, ut nihil a primo alterum, id est diversum, aut dissimile inveniri possit sub sole. Ut verbi gratia, ab initio coelum sursum, et terra deorsum. Ab initio luminaria in coelo, sol, luna et stellae, aves in aere, pisces in aqua, bestiae in terra. Ab initio volatus avibus, natatus 145Dpiscibus, gressus hominibus, et bestiis quibusdam reptatus, et tractus serpentibus. Et haec omnia sicut fuerunt, sic sunt, sic permanent. Et si quando forte miraculo aliquo praeter usitatum naturae cursum accidente, aliud fiunt quam semper sunt; non tamen in toto fiunt, nec semper fiunt, ut prima illa institutio etsi aliquando intermitti videatur, nunquam tamen videatur dissolvi. Ergo et hanc confusionem regit sapientia Dei. Et quod nobis confusum est, ipsi non est. Et ideo sub sole nihil novum est; quia ab illo qui est supra solem quod temporaliter transit, ab aeterno ordinatum est. Atque ideo singula quaeque, quia in semetipsis per immutabilitatem stare non possunt, in suo tamen genere 146Aper similitudinem statum custodiunt, ut licet quod sunt, semper esse non possint singula; nunquam tamen inveniuntur aliud esse universa, quam singula. Ergo nihil novum sub sole. Quanto magis supra solem? Nam et ideo nihil novum sub sole; quia aeternum est supra solem. Sub sole et luna novum non est; nec est tamen aeternum. Aeternum enim non est sub sole aliquid, quia omne quod sub sole est, in semetipso praeterit; tamen novum non est, quia in similitudinem sui generis subsistit. Ergo sub sole nihil novum est, et nihil aeternum. Quia enim praecessit in saeculis quae fuerunt ante nos, ideo novum non est: et quia non est praeteritorum memoria, ideo aeternum non est. Ideoque quia omne quod venit, praeterit et non subsistit, aut permanet 146Bquidquam sub sole; non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris impletur auditu; quia, dum intrat elabitur, et fugit, omne dum teneri putatur; et completur sententia: Vanitas vanitatum, et omnia vanitas. Quid ergo quia sub sole non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris impletur auditu? Supra solem eat ubi non solum novum non est aliquid, sed nec transitorium; ubi et priorum memoria et praesentia futurorum, imo omnia praeterita et futura praesentia sunt; quia nec praeteritum nec futurum aliquid ibi est, ubi praesens est omne quod est, et omne quod est ibi est. Ibi ergo et oculus visu satiari et auris auditu impleri potest: ubi consummata et plena perfectio percipitur, et percepta plenitudine aeternitas non evacuatur. Sic ergo tota haec sententia, qua sub sole nec novum 146Caliquid nec aeternum esse dicitur, ad hoc spectare videtur, ut agnoscat homo quid vel fugere debeat vel sequi. In eo enim quod sub sole nihil novum est aeterna dispositio ostenditur. In eo autem quod nihil sub sole permanens esse potest, in iis quae sub sole sunt aeternitatem quidem significari, non tamen esse demonstratur. In ipsis ergo quae sub sole sunt, simul agnoscimus, et in eo quod nihil aeternum est, fugiendum esse quod sunt. In eo autem quod nihil novum, sequendum esse quod non sunt. Quapropter recurrat ad summam sententiam, ut quia in iis quae sub sole sunt oculi satiari, et aures impleri nec scientia possunt, quia non comprehendunt totum quod est; nec desiderio possunt; quia, etsi comprehendant, non sufficit totum quod est, 146Dnec quantum possunt permanet quod praesens est. Sciunt vanitatem esse omne quod sub sole est, et quod nihil de universo labore suo, quo laborat sub sole, homo amplius habere potest.

Dicat ergo: Cunctae res difficiles, ut comprehendantur ab humano sensu, quae nec numerari possunt multitudine, nec comprehendi quantitate, nec profunditate pervestigari. Et ideo non mirum est si sermo deficit, ubi intelligentia succumbit; et ob hoc non valet eas homo explicare sermone, ut rationem reddat de singulis quia omnia non novit: Non enim saturatur oculus visu cum per se considerat; nec auris impletur auditu, cum eruditur ab altero, ut vel intentio exiens ad inquisitionem rerum quantum extra 147Aest, totum comprehendat, vel cognitio ingrediens quantum intus est, totum repleat.
