Ergo oculus et auris nec toti mundo sufficiunt, ut totum capiant; nec toti animo, ut totum impleant. Et tamen per ea quae foris sunt, admonentur ut pergant illuc ubi vita est, ubi totum inveniant, et totum capiant, quia omnia in ipso vita erant, et vita erat lux hominum (Joan. I). Illuc ergo pergant ubi simul totum inveniant, et totum capiant totumque possideant ubi in aeterna dispositione jam facta sunt, quae sunt futura in tempore. Nam quid est quod fuit? Ipsum enim idem, et non aliud futurum est in tempore quam quod fuit ante tempora, in aeterna Dei dispositione. Nec aliud subsequens in rerum ordine explicatur mutabile, quam quod fixum et permanens 147Bsemper fuit in illa rata et invariabili divina dispositione. Et ut manifeste patescat quod subsequens rerum effectus cum providentia concordat, ideo etiam in ipsa rerum serie, futurum a praeterito non discordat. Quid est enim quod factum est? ipsum quod faciendum est. Ergo quod fuit in providentia semper, aliquando futurum est in re; et quod factum est jam in re, per similitudinem adhuc est faciendum. Sed non praetereundum mihi videtur quod non ait. Quid est quod futurum est, ut deinde subjungeret. Ipsum quod fuit, cum praeterita magis certa sint futuris, et quia etsi non sunt, fuerunt tamen aliquando et visa sunt. Futura autem nunquam fuerunt.

Et ideo magis in quaestione ponendum videretur 147Cquod minus certum est. In responsione autem, quod magis notum esse constat. Sed notandum quod effectus rerum secundum causam, providentia posterior est; in nostra cognitione, prior. Quia donec in actu suo rem cernimus, quid de ipsa in aeterna providentia dispositum sit prorsus ignoramus. Atque ideo recte cum quaereret, dicens: Quid est quod fuit? (quia ipsa per se providentia occulta est) statim ad intelligendam eam auditores ad actum rerum mittit, dicens: Ipsum quod futurum est; quia scire non possumus quid in praescientia praecedat, donec viderimus quid in effectu rerum subsequatur. Sed et in rebus ipsis, praeteritorum qualitatem quae non vidimus, ex futurorum comparatione 147Dcum supervenerint colligemus. Dicat ergo: Quid est quod fuit? Ipsum quod futurum est. Quia sicut dictum quod praecedit in providentia: hoc idem et non aliud in effectu rerum subsequitur. Et deinceps: Quid est quod factum est? ipsum quod faciendum est. Quia eadem rerum natura in singulis generibus eamdem similitudinem actu exhibuit in praeteritis, quam producet supervenerint in futuris. Et ideo nihil novum est in rerum generibus sub sole, cujus similitudo non praecessit. Nec valet quisquam dicere: Hoc recens est, quantum ad similitudinem generis sui. Jam enim praecessit in saeculis quae fuerunt ante nos in genere suo, cujus ipsum est. Et tamen fluunt omnia, nec permanet quidquam sub sole. Et quae in dispositione ordinantis fixa 148Asunt a nostra praesentia simul et a memoria in semetipsis transeuntia recedunt. Nam prius a praesentia nostra subtrahuntur, ut non subsistant per speciem; deinde etiam a memoria oblivione delentur, ut nec subsistant saltem per recordationem. Et ne forte dura corda hominum transitus praeteritorum ad contemptum rerum visibilium trahere non sufficeret, si illis sublatis ii qui praesentes sunt de statu suo fiduciam habere potuissent. Ideo postquam illorum transitum commemorando ait: Non est priorum memoria, statim istorum etiam interitum demonstrat, dicens: Sed nec eorum qui post nos futuri sunt. Nam si post nos futuri sunt, alii profecto constat quod nos qui modo subsistimus, cum venerint qui post nos futuri sunt, et nos quoque eadem 148Bforte sublati, etiam in recordationem viventium tunc nequaquam veniemus. Quid ergo nobis prodest, quod illis qui per mortem sublati sunt, in hanc vitam successimus; quia et nos quoque cum tempus nostrum advenerit descendentes, alios successores relinquemus. Si ergo scire volumus quales erimus apud eos qui post nos futuri sunt, consideremus quales modo apud nos sint qui nos ab hac vita jam olim sublati praecesserunt. Et ut omnis improbis mentibus spes praesentium tollatur, ii quoque qui post nos futuri sunt non permansuri dicuntur; nec in recordationem apud suos posteros venturi, ne vel hoc in consolationem pravis mentibus veniat, si is qui in semetipso stare non potest, saltem in suo haerede aut successore subsistat. Propterea, 148Cpraeteritorum, praesentium ac futurorum omnium unum ostendit interitum. Non est priorum memoria; sed nec eorum qui post nos futuri sunt erit recordatio, apud eos qui futuri sunt in novissimo, ut omnia vanitati subjiciat, et humanum animum ab amore eorum, quae sub sole videntur, ad desiderium aeternorum convertat.

Si quis autem simplici expositione contentus esse non velit, habet aliud quod in his verbis, quae supra exposita sunt, convenienter satis et forte manifestius intelligere possit. Quia enim dixerat nec oculum visu satiari, nec aurem impleri auditu, confestim causam adjungit, quare nec oculum visus, nec aurem possit implere auditus; quia videlicet 148Drerum transitoriarum species per sensum quidem advenientes, concupiscentiam excitant, sed cito fugientes transitu desiderium fraudant. De hoc enim transitu sententiam subjungit, dicens: Quid est quod fuit? Jam non est: praeteriit enim, et jam non est. Ipsum idem tale erit et id quod futurum est: nam et ipsum cum venerit pertransibit, et cum pertransierit amplius non erit. Quid est quod factum est? Etiam ipsum jam pertransiit, et non est ipsum. Ergo idem tale erit et illud quod faciendum est; quia et ipsum cum factum fuerit, pertransibit, et amplius non erit. Sed quaeri potest quare praeterita solum et futura commemoravit, cum praesentium rerum potius contemptum persuadere intendat? Sed hoc ipsum ad magnum contemptum pertinet eorum quae 149Avidentur, quod ea solum in numero eorum commemorare voluit, quae sola sensus carnis praesentia comprehendit, quasi illa solum non esse videat, quae sola esse videntur, ut ne dicere quidem possit, quod est. Quod est, dum est, pene nihil est: nam praesentium momenta ita cursu festino et veloci elapsu fugiunt, ut etiam de se loquentium sermones exspectare non possint. Nam etsi aliquando ab interrogante secundum quid recte dici possit, est, a respondente tamen semper verius dicitur, fuit, et non est. Sic ipsa interrogatio responsionem quidem quaerit, quae nondum est. Sed responsio veniens interrogationem non invenit, quae jam non est. In vera igitur consideratione hoc solum quasi non esse vidit, quod solum esse videtur. Quia dum simul et 149Besse incipit ex eo quod nondum est, et esse desinit in id quod jam non est; pene nihil est, quod est. Et idcirco nequaquam interroga, quid sit quod est? quia et ipsum interrogantis est respondenti quantumvis proximo, fuit jam, et non est. Recte ergo dicitur: Quid est quod fuit? Ipsum quod futurum est. Quid est quod factum est? Ipsum quod faciendum est. Ac si diceret: Ex praeteritorum consideratione perpendite, quid debeatis de supervenientibus exspectare, idem enim est utrumque. Et quod fuit, et quod futurum est. Quod factum est, et quod faciendum est. Idem est, non per essentiam, sed per consimilem naturam. Quod enim fuit (quantum ad res), et quod factum est (quantum ad actiones) utrumque pertransiit. Et non est jam vel quod factum 149Cest. Similiter quod futurum est in rebus, et quod faciendum est in actionibus, totum pertransibit, et non erit aliquid sub sole perpetuum. Unde hoc? Quia eadem est conditio praeteritorum, et eorum quae futura sunt, et natura consimilis. Nihil enim novum est sub sole, nec valet quisquam dicere: Ecce hoc recens est. Jam enim praecessit in saeculis quae fuerunt ante nos. Et quia similis conditio est; ergo sicut praeterita, sic et futura. Et qualia sunt putas ipsa praeterita? Audi qualia: Non est, inquit, priorum memoria. Ergo non solum praesentia eorum interitu sublata est, sed memoria quoque oblivione deleta est. Magna ruina. Talia sunt et ipsa, quae futura sunt. Nam et eorum qui post nos futuri 149Dsunt, non erit recordatio apud eos qui futuri sunt in novissimo. Veraque sententia est: Vanitas vanitatum, vanitas vanitatum, et omnia vanitas.

HOMILY II. On the proof of the vanity of all things under heaven: through the corruption of the elements, through the generation of things, the succession, and the forgetting of those things which have been.

The words of Ecclesiastes, which testify that all things under the sun are vain, have — I know not by what compact — just now, when they were read, been made sweet in our ears. And behold, we have begun willingly to hear our own evils, and what we do not love 133Cwe nevertheless love to hear. For we do not love our own evils, and we love to hear our own evils; because by hearing the evils which we do not love, we remember the goods which we do love. And this very remembrance of goods (even amid evils) is sweet to the soul, and assuredly so much the sweeter the more bitter are those evils themselves, which, whether by hearing or by feeling, we recognize to be far from those goods for which, at least by remembrance, we sigh. This was the whole reason why we wonder that this recital alone has just now been savory to us, in which the hardship of our exile is described to us, and it is declared of what sort and how great our misery and calamity is. For our mind, in the hearing of its own evils, as though awaking out of a certain sleep of former time, suddenly 133Drecognized where it was, and, amazed and wondering at so great an abyss of ruin, began at the same time also to consider from how great a height it had fallen into this very depth of misery, and, because it could not yet do so in effect, it sighed after that height with a certain wondrous desire of inward ardor. This therefore was what in those words which recited our misery drew our affection. This made it that it should ever be pleasing to us thus to hear our own evils, and that whatever that be which is perceived along with that which is so sweet cannot be bitter. This daily makes their very laments sweet to the wretched, and amid sighs and groans feeds the afflicted delightfully with tears; because the remembrance of the things that are loved is sweeter amid adversities, and the soul itself burns the more with desire of things absent, is touched the more sweetly by the memory of things past, 134Ais the more strongly inflamed by the deferring of things to come. This our Ecclesiastes knew excellently well, who in his whole narrative so diligently pursues the vanity of passing things, that out of the consideration of it he may admonish the human heart to meditate upon heavenly things and to awake in desire of things eternal. For he knew that the more evidently the vanity of those things which pass away in time is recognized, the more sublimely within is the eye of the mind opened to the state of eternity. Beginning therefore, in this first part of his work, he shows that all things are vain which are under the sun, that is, that whatsoever things are visible are subject to corruption, or liable to mutability. For he shows that neither in heaven, nor under heaven, nor upon the earth, nor in the earth is there anything perpetual which does not suffer vicissitude nor 134Bpass over into alteration. And therefore that nothing truly is out of all those things which are always without ceasing drawn into that which they are not, and cannot keep stable or uncorrupted what they are.

The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place: and there rising again, he goeth about by the south, and turneth again to the north. This is to be distinguished by itself. Then follows:

Surveying all things round about, the spirit goeth forward, and returneth in his circuits. And this is to be set down by itself. Afterwards follows:

All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea doth not overflow: unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return, to flow again. And this is to be joined together.

Three things therefore he seems to set forth as an argument 134Cfor the mutability of all things: the sun, the spirit, the rivers, that is, fire, air, moisture — so that by the sun fire, by the spirit air, by the rivers moisture may be understood to be signified, as the whole from a part. For above he set the earth as it were an immovable foundation in the middle place. Now he disposes the other three elements, that is, fire, air, water, fluctuating about it with unstable motion, so that in the procreating of mutable things he may show that to these three elements the motion of acting and, in a certain manner, the office of the craftsman has been assigned. But that the earth lies subject, immovable, as a certain matter of all things to be procreated; powerless indeed to act, but only fit that out of it, while the rest work, there may be formed those things which are to be created 134D. Through these three elements therefore nature exercises its power in that fourth, which elements, running about that fourth and in it by a wondrous law, and tempering one another, bring forth out of it so many innumerable forms and species of things as are shown by the yearly, the monthly, the daily vicissitudes of the seasons, alternating continually without ceasing in their approach and their withdrawal. Since therefore all things being born which rise out of the earth and receive from the earth their substance and nourishment obtain the nature of vital motion from these three elements, rightly did he place in them both the origin of mutability, and did he express the nature and property of all mutable things, so that in these we may equally see both whence it is that whatever rises under time cannot stand, and by what way that which is not comes forth to be present, or that which 135Ais returns to not being. The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place, and there rising again he goeth about by the south, and turneth again to the north. In few words he has embraced a great matter: concerning which we must say some things according to the time, yet not detain the hearer's mind longer upon such matters, lest we seem, against our own purpose, to be rolled away from the sacred exposition into describing the courses of the stars. All these things indeed have been said for this alone, that the human mind may be the more conveniently roused by the recital of those things which it knows, and that through these it may awake to think upon those things which it does not know: and therefore it ought not to be a weariness to us, nor seem unworthy, to attend diligently to those things which the divine discourse has taken care to recount diligently to us. He shows therefore by what way 135Bthis great luminary, which illuminates all things by its presence, is carried round in this globe of the sensible world with unceasing agitation, and by its approach and withdrawal works the various changes of things. The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place. First he shows that it has a circular motion, and always returns to that from which it goes forward, so that, because in a circle no end can be found, its course may be shown to be perpetual. The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place. Then he describes the windings of its progression, saying: He goeth about by the south, and turneth again to the north — so that this very thing may belong to the great changing of things, that it does not always in the same manner nor in a straight line direct its course as it goes. The sun riseth, and goeth down. It riseth daily, when emerging 135Cit is presented to human sight. It goeth down, when descending to the lower parts according to the convexity of its circum actionis it withdraws itself from our eyes. It returneth to his place; because, its rolling driving it on, it is called back beneath again to its rising. But after its rising, tending to its setting, it is first turned toward the south, because by an oblique course, especially when it tarries in the summer signs, it climbs from the rising to the meridian line. But then, descending to the setting, it is bent again by an oblique progression toward the north. Still another exposition, fitting enough, can be applied to these words: namely, that we take all these things to be said not of the long-continued but of the yearly course of the sun. For the sun riseth to us when, 135Dentering through the vernal equinox, it rises toward our pole. But it goeth down, when going out through the autumnal equinox it descends to the lower parts. It goeth about by the south, when it tarries in the winter signs. It turneth again to the north, when it is carried round in the summer signs, which are nearer to the northern pole. The sun riseth therefore, and at its rising all things equally rise which revive from its heat. It goeth down, and at once, the vital fire being withdrawn, all things fall which flourished from its presence. It goeth about by the south, that the winter's cold may temper the summer's burnings. It turneth again to the north, that those things which the winter's frost and icy torpor had bound fast may, warmed again by the summer's heats, be quickened. Thou seest therefore how great changes of things one body draws along with it.

136ASurveying all things round about, the spirit goeth forward, and returneth in his circuits. If by the spirit we have taken the air, then in fitting order, after he had described the instability of the heavenly element, he shows that the lower things also suffer the same law, saying: Surveying all things round about, the spirit goeth forward. As if he were saying: If the force of nature does not suffer those things which are in heaven to stand, it is necessary that the same condition of mutability govern those things also which are under heaven. Indeed, just as to the sun? so also to the air he attributes an orbicular motion, so that its agitation may be shown to be perpetual. But that he subjoins in the plural: He returneth in his circuits — this can signify that the motion of the air is not always and everywhere the same, but that, since in one place it is stirred more vehemently, in another more moderately, its very fluctuation, 136Bpoured back into itself by a reversed turn, is moved unequally; and does not uniformly come to rest, so that we may not be forced to extend a motion once begun as far as the uttermost, but that the several motions and impulses, made as it were upon themselves; and gradually, the motion languishing over the space, come to rest. But that also which he says, Surveying, is aptly attributed to this element, in that by its mobility it cleanses and scatters all the filth sprinkled or gathered anywhere. Or because, penetrating all things by its subtlety, it pours itself out everywhere. Or else this word is coupled to the preceding sentiment thus: The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place; and there rising again he goeth about by the south, and turneth again to the north, surveying all things round about. And here, a distinction being made, then the following sentiment is brought in thus: 136CThe spirit goeth forward, etc. For the sun by its course surveys all things round about; because it touches all the parts of the world, rising or setting through the diverse signs. For in Cancer, rising and setting, it touches the north. In Capricorn, the south. In Libra and in Aries, it passes through the middle by the rising and the setting. There follows: The spirit goeth forward, and returneth in his circuits. According to the preceding exposition, we can now not incongruously incovenienter take the spirit to be that fiery power which, proceeding from the sun itself, pours itself out through all things, and, invisibly penetrating the universe, quickens and moves it. Whence the ancients also said that nature is. A craftsman fire, going forward into sensible things to be procreated. For of vital motion, and of sensible quickening, in all things that are born 136Dthe fiery power is the origin: which supplies increase to all things, and, feeding and cherishing them with an invisible nourishment, brings them at length to an invisible substance. And this hidden power of nature, moving and feeding all things, the poet also named a spirit: and his words are well known: First, the heaven and the lands, and the liquid plains, And the shining globe of the moon, and the Titanian stars, A spirit within doth nourish: and, poured through the limbs, Mind stirs the whole mass, and mingles itself with the great body. (Aeneid. VI, 688.) Although in these words he seems rather to approve that error which asserts that this sensible world is as it were a soul consisting of soul and body, and that its very soul is the spirit moving all things. But 137Ain whatever way the opinion of those who err be expounded, we with a sound understanding can take the spirit going forward into all things, and returning in his circuits, to be the hidden power of nature, which invisibly nourishes and quickens the universe, and leads each single thing to a certain end and lawful term. This spirit therefore, that is, the hidden power of nature, surveys all things; because, pouring itself out invisibly through all the parts of things, it distributes to each its proper quality according to the capacity of its nature. It goeth forward, and returneth, because it first advances by increase all things which rise in time, and then leads them back, as they grow old, to their origin. For it goeth forward, because it goes out in things being born, and in things growing it proceeds as far as a certain measure. It returneth, because in things growing old, and slipping backward through the failing 137Bof their nature, it is called back as far as the beginning of its own origin. Thus therefore we rightly take the courses and progressions of individual things to be as it were certain circles and orbs running back into themselves; because all things that have risen in time return at length by their setting thither whence they went out by the beginning of their birth. And each single thing indeed is proved to have, according to its own measure and the time in which it subsists, a course differing from another, that is, greater or less. But all things are known to have, as one origin, so also one end; because all things return by their setting to the earth, which at the beginning of their rising went out of the earth. Just as therefore the sun riseth and goeth down, and returneth to his place, so the spirit goeth forward, and returneth in his circuits. Because 137Cjust as in the body of the sun the fire, going forward locally, is led back to the beginning of its rising, so also naturally in all things that are born, the motion which it raised up through the increase of things, it leads back to its own origin through their failing and setting.

There follows a third clause in which is treated the element of water, which in the order of things is placed third after fire, in procreation is associated as second. For as much as pertains to the disposition and the order of things, fire possesses the first and highest place; air the second, next to fire. Afterwards water claims the third place; in the last and lowest place the earth settles. Among these four, fire and water, by nature indeed most opposed, yet friendly by an even confederation 137D, are the origin of all things that are born. And therefore if we attend to place or to nature, we discern these two to be separated from one another. If we look to their effect, we find them both nearest to one another and friendly. Therefore concerning the element of water, which affords to things being born the other vital fostering along with fire, as though third after fire and air, or second along with fire, silence was not to be kept among the natures of mutable things. And for that reason he describes this element's circuit also, and its running out into the procreating of sensible things, saying: All the rivers run into the sea, and the sea doth not overflow. And at once he adds the reason why the sea does not overflow when all the rivers have been received into it: namely, because again they return to the place from whence the rivers come, to flow again. For the channels of the waters, through the whole 138Abody of the earth, draw moisture inwardly and from without after the manner of veins, so that the watering may be evenly poured out into every part. But that this infusion may be able to be continual and perpetual, therefore the course of the waters has been disposed in an orb, and in that perennial circling, so that what is poured in from above may never fail; as much as flows downward in the one part, so much in the other part is called back to its rising through hidden passages. So also the food of the body is carried by a certain circuit, and first descending from the palate into the belly, and then passing over into the privy, and in that very passage of it, as by a certain instilling of nature, nourishment is supplied to what is failing; and when this has been evaporated and emptied out, it is necessary again that recourse be had to the help of eating for the repairing of the weakening limbs. As it were therefore a circle 138Bof ever-renewed need, running back into its own origin, is drawn; because, while without ceasing what has been taken passes away, it is always necessary that it be taken again, so that it may be able to furnish substance for the supplying of the defect. Such nourishment therefore as the substance of food supplies by assiduous repetition to the body it feeds, altogether such nourishment does the reflowing of the elements pour into the body of the earth for the procreating of its offspring and the quickening of its seeds. This fire, this water, this air cease not to do by continual approach and withdrawal without intermission, so that they may always replenish the things that befall and empty out the things that recede, so that, because the vigor of the past infusion cannot subsist, of necessity the watering for the repairing of fullness may be repeated anew. What confidence, therefore, of perpetual subsistence will the nourishments of things be able to afford, 138Cwhen in all things thus always without ceasing both the things that repair pass away, and the things repaired fail? For although a repeated infusion seems to afford some sort of consolation to this defect, yet it is a great misery always to receive for need, and never to be able to lack the need of receiving. Whence it is manifest that all transitory and falling things are vain, which continually grow empty of the solidity of their own state, either by passing away or by failing. A great spectacle therefore has here been prepared for holy minds, which know how to draw from visible things the knowledge of invisible ones. Which know how to say to their Creator: Thou hast made all things in wisdom, O Lord (Psal. CIII). Thou hast delighted me, O Lord, in thy making, and in the works of thy hands 138DI shall rejoice. How magnified are thy works, O Lord, exceeding deep are thy thoughts become (Psal. XCI).

For behold how all things transitory and subject to vanity are borne about in a circuit. And we know that a circle has no end. The things therefore which run in a circuit do indeed run, but they never arrive at an end. What rest, then, can be hoped for, where there can be no standing still? For where there is perpetual running, there is no standing. But where the way is a circuit, there is no place where the course could surely have an end. The things therefore which run in a circuit always run and never come to a standing. They always pass away, and never subsist. They are always being ended, and cannot find an end. When they have gone by, they are yet to come; when they have come upon us, 139Athey do not subsist. This is the way of all mutable things, and the way of all who love mutable things and who follow mutable things. For of the wicked also it is said: The wicked walk in a circuit (Psal. XI). And again: The head of their circuit (Psal. CXXXIX), and make them as a wheel, O Lord (Psal. LXXXII). The head too of all the wicked bears witness of himself, saying: I have gone round about the earth, and walked through it (Job I). And of him the Apostle says: He goeth about as a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (I Petr. V). You see therefore how the perverse always love the circuit, and do not withdraw from the circuit. Therefore the things which are perversely loved by the perverse, these themselves also all run in a circuit, for a testimony to them that they too follow a circuit. On the contrary the lover of eternal things says: My foot hath stood in the straight way 139B(Psal. XXVII). And again: Direct me in the path of thy commandments, for the same have I desired (Psal. CXVIII). And again: The path of the just is straight (Isai. XXVI). And elsewhere once more: They shall go, he says, straight, the things sent forth; and the Lord our God shall lead them to a sure place (Sap. V). O straight way, O circuit, whither dost thou lead. And thou, whither dost thou lead? Thou leadest, and leadest through. But thou leadest, and leadest astray; for those whom thou leadest, thou destroyest, thou dost not lead through. O circuit, how dost thou enwrap, how dost thou embrace thy followers? To those who run through thee thou grantest neither a going out from thee, nor an arrival within thee. Therefore all things transitory and falling are rolled through circuits while they pass away, so that we may not seek in them the good of eternity — things which we always behold both so to arrive that they pass away, and so to pass away that they do not subsist. Let us see 139Ctherefore yet further these circuits of vanity. For the wisdom of God, as has already been said, has wonderfully provided this: that the motion of all things should be driven round in a circle, so that bodily nature — which by flowing away might at some time have felt failure — always by running back into its own origin, while without interruption it receives what it has poured out, might pour out without failure what it receives, and that there might be a failing without failure; nor might that ever be wanting which is able to fail, so that it may always be failing. Whence in one and the same thing, both that which it is, is wretched, and that which has been made is wonderful, because in the same work both the matter is found frail, and the craftsman's design is to be admired. And corruptible nature indeed persuades to contempt of the world, but the mind sinks down in wonder at the contemplation of the design. 139DTo the beholding therefore of this design, after the course of mutable things has been unfolded, our Ecclesiastes turns himself, that in it he may exercise the mind's gaze through contemplation; because knowledge is not able sufficiently to comprehend it, he is eager to venerate it with worthy wonder. For, since he has unfolded the mutability of all things in three kinds of things — fire, air and water — according to the motion that moves, he shows thereafter how inexplicable that same mutability is according to the motion which is moved, through each several thing that rises and sets in the universe.

All things are hard: man cannot explain them by speech: the eye is not sated with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. When any thing whatever is discerned on its surface, not yet is either its hidden cause or 140Aits nature penetrated. For that which is, is seen; but of what sort that is which is seen, or what quality it keeps in the hidden place (whither bodily sense cannot come); why also it is so as it is seen, or whence it is so, or to what end it is — what man (I will not say in all things, but not even in any one thing whatever) is able to comprehend to the full? In how great darkness therefore is man enwrapped; by how great a blindness of ignorance is he hemmed in, whose sense can scarcely reach even so much as the surface of a few things? And even if he should discern all things that are according to their outward appearance, he would still not penetrate the hidden power of things and their invisible nature. Therefore the totality of things is in both ways incomprehensible to man: namely, both according to outward appearance, and according to inward 140Bquality. But some individual things come outwardly in part by their appearance to the sense, others are hidden altogether — either because they are remote in place, or because, though present in place, they exceed by their own subtlety the slowness of human sense. Scarcely therefore does human sense suffice to attain some few things among things; but of the whole it comprehends nothing perfectly as it is. Therefore all things are hard: hard according to the totality, namely, in that they cannot be attained, and hard according to each several thing, because they can be fully comprehended by no sense nor understanding. And if they cannot be perfectly searched out by reason, much less can they be explained by speech. For this very thing is more unspeakable than all things in things: that in so great a confusion of mutability nowhere is an evident and manifest 140Cdesign lacking to one who considers well; that even that which in things is not good is so well disposed, that in a certain manner the corruption of individual things is the beauty of the whole. Therefore human sense, sinking down in the consideration of these things, is sweetly refreshed out of its own failure; because in that which displeases according to corruption, in the most ordered beauty of the whole, even corruption itself is beautiful and pleases. Thus in a wondrous and unspeakable manner the Founder, in his creature, both punishes malice through the corruption of things and at once delights nature through beauty, so that man may recognize in his punishment what he has deserved through fault, and in his delight what he has lost. For how great an affluence of sweetness do we believe to be in the Creator of things, if 140Dwe find so wondrous a pleasantness in the beauty of creatures? Therefore, when he had spoken of the failure of human understanding in so manifold and perplexed and various a depth of things, he at once adds the delightfulness of nature in the beauty of those same things.

The eye is not sated with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. Since all the bodily senses find in created things their own delights, and each of them as it were certain proper dainties prepared for it — sight, namely, appearance; hearing, the sweetness of melody; smell, odor; taste, savor; and touch, smoothness. All the rest indeed serve bodily necessity, or even pleasure. But these two senses, that is sight and hearing, draw their nourishment rather toward spiritual delightfulness. Whence their refreshment also has no draining off of dregs, 141Abecause together with the perceiving of sweetness they draw no mass of corruption. For which reason their refreshment does not arrive at a satiety of sweetness; because no difficulty running through delays their appetite from perceiving sweetness, nor does any ensuing trouble restrain it. This nourishment therefore, pure and unmixed, without all bodily bulk, passes wholly into the refreshment of the soul; because although it flows forth from bodily appearance and passes through the sense of the body, it cannot nevertheless be retained by the body, since it has nothing bodily, nor does it bring in anything corpulent. For this reason therefore sight and hearing, as being more excellent than the rest and having nothing of depressing weight, have obtained a loftier seat in the body, so that they may freely and without obstacle flow out to their delights, or 141Badmit into themselves without difficulty those things that flow in. There are, to be sure, two things which enter to the mind from the appearance of things through sight. And two likewise which enter in through hearing from the perceiving of voices. For through sight there comes from things to the mind's knowledge substance and form. From voices through hearing, signification and melody. And substance from things works the same in the mind through sight as signification from voices does through hearing. And likewise form from things does the same in the mind through sight as melody from voices does through hearing. For there are two things by which the whole nature of the rational soul is ordered, namely knowledge and affection, that is, wisdom and love. And if the soul perfectly obtains these two and lawfully orders them, it is blessed. But if either it falls short in obtaining them so far as nature requires, 141Cor perverts them, once obtained, against nature, then in that part, without doubt, in which it suffers either the failure or the confusion of them, it must needs be made wretched. The whole substance therefore of the rational soul is governed by these two, that is by knowledge and affection, so that through wisdom it may find truth, and through love may embrace virtue. Therefore, that outward things also might serve the rational soul for the sake of blessedness, these two instruments of the senses were placed in the human body, so that through them the notions of visible things might enter in to the soul, and might produce in it wisdom or virtue, if it were not there at all, or increase it, if it were there in less measure. Therefore the essence of things entering in to the soul through sight, and the signification of voices through hearing, beget knowledge. But the form of things entering in through sight, 141Dand the melody of voices through hearing, kindle the mind to delightfulness. For as often as outwardly either sight is affected by the appearance of things, or hearing is soothed by the sweetness of voices, the mind awakes within with wondrous affections, answering to that by which it feels itself touched outwardly. And it comes to pass sometimes that, through the sweetness which it draws by bodily sense, it returns to the remembrance of invisible goods and, admonished in a certain manner from the likeness, begins to long with unspeakable desire for that whose shadow and image, as it were, it feels itself to have perceived in bodily affection.

Let Ecclesiastes therefore say: The eye is not sated with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. Because through these senses the beauty of visible things, while it affects the mind with delight in 142Athe contemplation of itself, kindles in it an unspeakable longing for invisible goods. Which longing, namely, thirsting after an ineffable sweetness, can rather be provoked than filled out by the bodily sight or hearing by which it is aroused, however great a delightfulness they may bring; and by human speech, however profuse or eloquent it may have been — though it is scarcely told even thinly — it is never perfectly explained. For from the appearance of visible things the rational mind conceives only, as it were, certain seeds of joys; but as desire soon grows out into immensity, it travails and does not contain itself in so great a delight. Let no one therefore think the sight of visible things harmful to chaste minds; because, if to see the works of God were altogether harmful, the use of seeing would by no means 142Bhave been created by him. For the work of God is as it were his word, through which he speaks to us, and the eyes themselves are as it were instruments by which the words of God are perceived through contemplation. Just as therefore the ear is an instrument for perceiving the word of man, so the eye is an instrument for perceiving the word of man, so the eye is an instrument for perceiving the word of the Creator. Therefore fittingly in the human body both the eyes are set in front and the ears placed at the side, as though by this it were signified to us that our intention ought to be directed secondarily to our neighbor, principally to God. Rightly therefore, that it might be shown how from the consideration of visible things the desire of eternal things is born in the mind, the eyes and ears alone are mentioned. Because by these alone, well nigh, does the way of wisdom 142Cand of virtue lie open to the mind, since, while beyond the other senses they perceive the beauty of visible things unmixed, they alone more purely kindle within the love of invisible goods. All things are hard: man cannot explain them by speech.

The eye is not sated with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. It is a marvel. The human heart does not suffice for the whole world, and the whole world does not suffice for the human heart. Why does the human heart not suffice for the whole world? Because all things are hard, and man cannot explain them by speech. Why does the whole world not suffice for the human heart? Because the eye is not sated with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. Therefore knowledge sinks down, affection transcends. Knowledge stretches itself as far as it can, and cannot take in the whole; but love drinks up the whole, 142Dand still cannot be satisfied. Why is this? Because charity rises high above knowledge, nor does the human heart say: It is enough — until it has come to him, and has found him by whom it was made that it might be, and for whom it was made that in him it might be blessed. Every delightfulness, every pleasantness, every beauty of created things can affect the human heart; satisfy it they cannot, save that sweetness alone for which it was made. For the appearances of visible things are only, as it were, certain veins through which the invisible beauty, manifesting itself, flows out even to us. And therefore, when these naturally provoke our sense and affection toward themselves, they do not indeed fill up desire, but goad it to seek out the appearance of the Founder and to long for his beauty. 143ATherefore all these things which are seen outwardly were made for provoking human affection, not for satisfying it, so that, aroused by them, it may rise up and, increased, may transcend them. Wherefore the eye is not sated with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. For that which we behold made beautiful does indeed delight, but it does not suffice, unless we find him who made it.

Or what he says can be understood thus: The eye is not sated with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. For because he had set down before that all things are hard, and that man cannot explain them by speech — lest perhaps it should be thought that they could be comprehended even by knowledge, he added: The eye is not sated with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. As if he were to say: It is no marvel if man cannot explain by speech the difficulty 143Bcultatem of things, who cannot even by sense take in or search out their depth. For whether he seek through himself the things to be found, or hear from another the things already found, everything that he can take in is beneath the satiety of fullness. For if he begins to contemplate through himself, the eye is not sated with seeing. If he seeks to be taught by another, the ear is not filled with hearing. For the narrownesses of the bodily instruments, if they pour themselves outward, do not suffice for the depth or the immensity of things to be unfolded. But if they pour themselves inward, they cannot fill the capacity of the human heart. For because the heart of man, blinded by the darkness of sin, has not an eye within by which it may fully see the light of truth, nor an ear by which it may perceive the word of God sounding inwardly, it is compelled to open bodily eyes and ears for the watering of the dryness 143Cof its ignorance, that outwardly it may draw at least some drop of truth in the appearance of things, whereby its thirst, though it cannot be altogether quenched, may at least a little be tempered. For this is what the Lord reproaches to his people through the prophet, saying: My people have done two sins. They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have digged for themselves cisterns broken apart, that cannot hold waters (Jer. II). For we know that a cistern is dug for this reason, that water gathered from without may flow down into it, and be drawn from it again to pass over into the uses of men. But because this has no living vein, however great it may seem and overflowing with a gathering of waters, it can at some time be drained out 143Dand dried up; because, when that which is poured in from elsewhere has been taken away and consumed, nothing of its own is left over to it whence it might be repaired. But the fountain which has a living vein, even if it is small, yet cannot altogether fail, nor does it ever feel a failure of its own outpouring, since to it an increase from its own comes always without failure. The bodily eyes and ears therefore, although they are the chief instruments by which the way is opened for the disciplines to the mind, yet, because the notions of visible things do not come from within from the fountain of truth, they lead them down to the heart of man through the narrow conduits of their own capacity and as it were like waters gathered here and there into a cistern. And because in the very things which they perceive they are able neither to comprehend the totality nor to penetrate the innermost parts, rightly is it now said: The eye is not satisfied 144Awith seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. Because the human mind, whether by living or by hearing, even if it perceives something, however little, of the truth, is nevertheless driven far from the fullness thereof by the condition of its own infirmity. It is no marvel therefore if the dryness of human speech does not suffice to explain the difficulty of things, since human sense also sinks down in the consideration of it. And therefore all things are hard, and man cannot explain them by speech: the eye is not sated with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.

What is it that hath been? The very thing that is to be. What is it that hath been done? The very thing that is to be done. Nothing new under the sun; nor is any man able to say: Behold, this is new. For it hath already gone before in the ages which were before us. Perhaps someone may reckon that that error is 144Bhere confirmed by which the philosophers of the Gentiles, concerning the revolution of the ages and the return of all things into the selfsame, attempted with marvelous madness to establish the eternity of times. For they said that the series of mutable things had run from eternity in the same order in which it is now beheld, and would run without end, by the same law, the world in its totality having neither beginning nor end, through certain ages succeeding one another. And that the great age consists of fifteen thousand years (which they call the year); and that when it is completed, all the heavenly bodies being called back to their own place whence each several one had gone forth from the beginning of the age, and again beginning their motion into the opening of another age by a like plan and manner, and likewise moving the nature subject to them by a like plan — that again absolutely the same 144Cthings all rise up anew, in the order in which they had gone before in the preceding ages, in the same order nonetheless, with the same essence, the same form, in altogether the same places and times, and accomplish their own course and a fate like to the former and the very same; that they suffer also the same law and undergo the same fortune, so that it befalls that the same men are born, that the same men likewise beget the same sons, live by the same fortune, die by the same lot: the same outcome of things, absolutely the same quality, and the same state and course of all things which the past times of the earlier age had held. And that such a revolution and repetition of all things into the selfsame always has been and always shall be without end, so that, just as by 144Dthe return of one star through each several year all these things are then renewed to their former state, so by the return of all the stars and of the whole of nature to their rising, through each several age and the great years, all things are restored to their first condition. But how great this error is, manifest reason will easily prove. For that times cannot be eternal is most evidently proved by this: that all time had a beginning; and it stands without contradiction that everything which had a beginning at some time was not. Further, all past time was at some time present. But all time which was at some time present, before it was present, was not yet. Otherwise, if it was always present, it was no longer time, but eternity. If therefore all past time at some time was 145Anot, there was [a time] when there was no time. And so times could not be eternal; but before times there was an eternity without time, which times neither increased when they began, nor will they consume when they shall be ended. It is clear therefore that the assertion of those is false who have proclaimed the eternity of the ages, and have testified that the beginning of mutability was without beginning. But lest perhaps in this place an error of this kind should seem to be confirmed, when it is said: Nothing new under the sun; nor is any man able to say: Behold, this is new. For it hath already gone before in the ages which were before us — in what understanding this is to be taken he shows at once in the words that follow, saying:

There is no remembrance of former things; nor indeed shall there be any recollection of those which are to be hereafter, with them that 145Bshall be in the last time. For if the former things and the last were absolutely the same as the present, he would by no means call men now present other than the former and other than those to come in the last time; nor would he say, with them that are to be after us in the last time, but he would say, with us who are to be in the last time. Unless perhaps someone should say that the first and the last are to be referred to the beginning and the end of the same age; otherwise those are neither first nor last who have been without beginning and are to be without end. But that the first and the last should be referred to the beginning and the end of the same age is forbidden by what he says: It hath already gone before in the ages which were before us. Because, while he speaks of some ages of those going before and others of those coming after, he shows that he has by no means meant the first and the last of the same age. 145CTherefore, since that sentiment shrinks back not only from Catholic truth but from reason as well, let us refer this saying to the likeness of things, which have been so established in their kinds from the beginning that each several one extends its offspring according to the likeness and the first form of its own origin, and there is nothing which exceeds the limit of the first disposition in its own kind. Thus in the very elements of the world, thus in those things which have been or are procreated out of them, nature keeps in all things the first disposition, so that nothing can be found under the sun other than the first, that is, diverse or unlike. As, for example, from the beginning heaven above, and earth below. From the beginning the lights in heaven — sun, moon and stars; birds in the air, fishes in the water, beasts on the earth. From the beginning flight for birds, swimming 145Dfor fishes, walking for men, and for certain beasts crawling, and dragging for serpents. And all these things, as they were, so they are, so they remain. And if at any time perchance, by some miracle happening beside the accustomed course of nature, they become other than they always are, yet they do not become so in the whole, nor do they always become so, so that that first establishment, although it may sometimes seem to be interrupted, may never nevertheless seem to be dissolved. Therefore the wisdom of God rules this confusion also. And what is confused to us is not so to him. And therefore nothing is new under the sun; because that which passes away in time has been ordained from eternity by him who is above the sun. And therefore each several thing, because they cannot stand in themselves by immutability, yet keep their standing in their own kind 146Athrough likeness, so that although individual things cannot always be what they are, yet the whole are never found to be other than the individuals. Therefore nothing new under the sun. How much more above the sun? For therefore also nothing is new under the sun, because that which is above the sun is eternal. Under the sun and moon there is nothing new; nor yet is there anything eternal. For nothing under the sun is eternal, because everything that is under the sun passes away in itself; yet it is not new, because it subsists in the likeness of its own kind. Therefore under the sun nothing is new, and nothing eternal. For because it hath gone before in the ages which were before us, therefore it is not new; and because there is no remembrance of things past, therefore it is not eternal. And therefore, because everything that comes passes away and does not subsist, nor does anything remain 146Bunder the sun, the eye is not sated with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing; because, while it enters it slips away, and everything flees while it is thought to be held; and the sentiment is fulfilled: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What then, since under the sun the eye is not sated with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing? Let it go above the sun, where not only is there nothing new, but nothing transitory either; where there is both the remembrance of former things and the presence of things to come — nay rather, where all things past and to come are present; because nothing there is either past or future, where everything that is, is present, and everything that is, is there. There therefore both the eye can be sated with seeing and the ear filled with hearing: where a consummate and full perfection is perceived, and, the fullness having been perceived, eternity is not emptied out. So therefore this whole sentiment, by which it is said that under the sun there is neither anything new 146Cnor anything eternal, seems to look to this: that man may recognize what he ought either to flee or to follow. For in this, that nothing under the sun is new, the eternal disposition is shown. But in this, that nothing under the sun can be abiding, it is demonstrated that in those things which are under the sun eternity is indeed signified, yet is not. In those very things therefore which are under the sun we recognize at once both: in that nothing is eternal, that what they are must be fled; and in that nothing is new, that what they are not must be followed. Wherefore let him run back to the highest sentiment, that, because in those things which are under the sun the eyes cannot be sated nor the ears filled by knowledge — since they do not comprehend the whole that is — nor can they be by desire, because, even if they should comprehend, the whole that is does not suffice, 146Dnor does that which is present remain as long as they are able. They know that everything which is under the sun is vanity, and that man can have nothing more out of all his labor wherewith he labors under the sun.

Let him say then: All things are hard, so as to be comprehended by human sense — things which can neither be numbered in their multitude, nor comprehended in their quantity, nor searched out in their depth. And therefore it is no marvel if speech fails where understanding sinks down; and on this account man cannot explain them by speech, so as to render an account of each several thing, because he does not know all things: For the eye is not sated with seeing, when it considers by itself; nor is the ear filled with hearing, when it is taught by another — so that either the intention going out to the search of things might comprehend the whole, as much as is without, 147Aor knowledge entering in might fill up the whole, as much as is within. Therefore the eye and the ear suffice neither for the whole world, so as to take in the whole, nor for the whole mind, so as to fill the whole. And yet through those things which are without they are admonished to go forward thither where life is, where they may find the whole and take in the whole, because all things in him were life, and the life was the light of men (Joan. I). Thither therefore let them go forward, where at once they may find the whole and take in the whole and possess the whole, where in the eternal disposition those things have already been made which are to be in time. For what is it that hath been? For the very same, and not another, is to be in time than that which was before times, in the eternal disposition of God. Nor is any other mutable thing unfolded thereafter in the order of things than that which was ever fixed and abiding 147Bin that ratified and unvarying divine disposition. And that it may manifestly appear that the subsequent effect of things accords with providence, therefore also in the very series of things the future does not disaccord with the past. For what is it that hath been done? The very thing that is to be done. Therefore what has always been in providence is at some time to be in fact; and what has already been done in fact is still to be done through likeness. But it seems to me that this ought not to be passed over, that he does not say. What is it that is to be, that he might then subjoin. The very thing that hath been — since past things are more certain than things to come, and because, even if they are not, yet they were at some time and were seen. But things to come never were.

And therefore that which is less certain would seem 147Crather to be put in the question; but in the answer, that which is agreed to be more known. But it is to be noted that the effect of things, according to cause, is later than providence; in our knowledge, earlier. Because until we behold a thing in its own act, we are utterly ignorant of what has been disposed concerning it in the eternal providence. And therefore rightly, when he asked, saying: What is it that hath been? (because providence in itself is hidden) he at once sends his hearers to the act of things for the understanding of it, saying: The very thing that is to be; because we cannot know what goes before in foreknowledge, until we have seen what follows after in the effect of things. But in the things themselves also we shall gather the quality of past things which we have not seen from the comparison of things to come 147Dwhen they shall have come upon us. Let him say then: What is it that hath been? The very thing that is to be. Because, as has been said, that which goes before in providence — this same and not another follows after in the effect of things. And thereafter: What is it that hath been done? The very thing that is to be done. Because the same nature of things in each several kind has exhibited in act, in things past, the same likeness which it will bring forth they shall have come upon in things to come. And therefore there is nothing new in the kinds of things under the sun whose likeness has not gone before. Nor is any man able to say: This is new — as far as concerns the likeness of its own kind. For it hath already gone before in the ages which were before us, in its own kind, of which it is. And yet all things flow, nor does anything remain under the sun. And the things which are fixed in the disposition of him who orders 148Athem, passing away in themselves, withdraw at once both from our presence and from our memory. For first they are withdrawn from our presence, so that they do not subsist by appearance; then they are also blotted out from memory by forgetfulness, so that they do not subsist even by recollection. And lest perchance the passing of things past should not suffice to draw the hard hearts of men to contempt of visible things, if, when those had been taken away, they who are present could have had confidence about their own standing. Therefore, after he said in recalling their passing: There is no remembrance of former things, he at once demonstrates the destruction of these also, saying: But neither of those who are to be after us. For if they are to be after us, they are surely others: it is plain that we who now subsist, when those shall have come who are to be after us, and we too taken away by the same 148Blot, shall then by no means come even into the recollection of the living. What then does it profit us that we have succeeded into this life those who were taken away by death, since we too, going down when our own time shall have come, shall leave other successors behind us. If therefore we wish to know of what sort we shall be with those who are to be after us, let us consider of what sort they now are with us who, long since taken away from this life, have gone before us. And that every hope of present things may be taken away from wicked minds, those also who are to be after us are said not to be about to remain, nor to be about to come into recollection with their own posterity — lest even this should come as a consolation to depraved minds, if he who cannot stand in himself might at least subsist in his heir or successor. Therefore 148Che shows one and the same destruction of all things past, present, and to come. There is no remembrance of former things; nor shall there be any recollection of those who are to be after us, with them that shall be in the last time — that he may subject all things to vanity, and turn the human mind from the love of those things which are seen under the sun to the desire of eternal things.

But if anyone should not be willing to be content with the simple exposition, he has something else which he may understand in these words that have been expounded above, fittingly enough and perhaps more manifestly. For because he had said that neither is the eye sated with seeing nor the ear filled with hearing, he immediately adds the cause why neither can sight fill the eye nor hearing the ear: namely, because 148Dthe appearances of transitory things, coming indeed through the sense, arouse longing, but, swiftly fleeing away, cheat desire by their passing. For concerning this passing he subjoins the sentiment, saying: What is it that hath been? It already is not: for it has passed away, and now is not. The very same shall that also be which is to be: for it too, when it shall have come, will pass through, and when it shall have passed through, it will be no more. What is it that hath been done? That too has already passed through, and is not itself. Therefore the same shall that also be which is to be done; because it too, when it shall have been done, will pass through, and will be no more. But it can be asked why he mentioned past things only and things to come, when he rather intends to persuade to contempt of present things? But this very thing pertains to a great contempt of those things which 149Aare seen: that he willed to mention in their number only those things which alone the sense of the flesh comprehends as present, as though he saw that those things alone are not, which alone seem to be — so that he cannot even say what it is that is. That which is, while it is, is well nigh nothing: for the moments of present things flee away with so hasty a course and so swift a slipping by that they cannot even wait for the words of those who speak about them. For even if it can sometimes be rightly said by the questioner, according to something, "it is," yet it is always more truly said by the answerer, "it was, and is not." Thus the question itself seeks an answer which as yet is not. But the answer, when it comes, does not find the question, which now is not. In a true consideration therefore he saw that this alone, as it were, is not, which alone seems to be. For since it at once both 149Bbegins to be out of that which is not yet, and ceases to be into that which now is not, that which is, is well nigh nothing. And therefore by no means ask: what is it that is? Because that very thing of the questioner, to the answerer however near at hand, has already been, and is not. Rightly therefore is it said: What is it that hath been? The very thing that is to be. What is it that hath been done? The very thing that is to be done. As if he were to say: From the consideration of things past weigh what you ought to expect concerning the things that come after; for both are the same. Both that which hath been, and that which is to be. That which hath been done, and that which is to be done. It is the same, not by essence, but by a like nature. For that which hath been (as far as concerns things) and that which hath been done (as far as concerns actions), both have passed through. And there is not now even that which hath been 149Cdone. Likewise that which is to be among things, and that which is to be done among actions, the whole will pass through, and there will be nothing perpetual under the sun. Whence is this? Because the condition of things past, and of those which are to be, is the same, and the nature alike. For nothing is new under the sun, nor is any man able to say: Behold, this is new. For it hath already gone before in the ages which were before us. And because the condition is alike, therefore as things past, so also things to come. And of what sort, thinkest thou, are those things past themselves? Hear of what sort: There is, he says, no remembrance of former things. Therefore not only has their presence been taken away by destruction, but their memory too has been blotted out by forgetfulness. A great ruin. Of such sort are also those things which are to be. For neither of those who are to be 149Dafter us shall there be any recollection with them that shall be in the last time. And the sentiment is true: Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.

HOMILIA III. Quomodo Ecclesiastes probet per sua opera omnia hominum opera vana, cum praedictorum epilogo.

Ego Ecclesiastes fui rex Israel in Hierusalem: et proposui in animo meo quaerere et investigare sapienter de omnibus quae fiunt sub sole. Sermones sapientium et aenigmata eorum scrutari, et eam quae intrinsecus abscondita est sapientiae dulcedinem ad gustum elicere, speciemque ejus in lucem proferre quis potens est? Scriba doctus in regno coelorum qui profert de thesauro suo nova et vetera (Matth. XIII), si nobis adveniat, ecce ille qui dedit Deus sapientiam 150Aet intelligentiam adaperire eam et manifestare, ut sciant homines, quoniam in ipsa est vita. Sed nos quid sumus? tenebrae ad lucem ut comprehendere cogitemus quod abscondit Deus ab oculis hominum, amicis suis revelare secretum sapientiae suae. Quid facimus nos? Ergo non meditabimur in mandatis ejus, neque investigabimus semitas illius, et requiescere poterit cor nostrum donec inveniat illam. Tantum ipsis sermonibus persequamur illam: et si forte inventio differatur, pascat interim nos inquisitio illius super omnia; si inventam non possumus, tamen quaesitam doceamus. Ecce Ecclesiastes noster hucusque de rerum mutabilium vanitate disputans brevi sermone tam multa complexus est, ut in illis ejus verbis hoc nobis mirabile appareat, quo pacto 150Btotum et de toto totum, ita dictum sit, ut ad brevitatem quidem nihil minus; ad evidentiam vero nihil amplius dicendum videatur. Sed hoc sapientia fecit quae in toto tota est, et in singulis tota. Nec in singulis tota contrahitur, nec in toto tota dilatatur; sed tanta in singulis quanta in toto, et in toto talis qualis tota in singulis, quia nec unitas minor se esse potest, nec immensitas major. Ipsa ergo sapientia in hoc brevi sermonis corpore totam universitatis effigiem expressit, ut parvi in parvo magnum videamus, quia in seipso totum non possumus. Et vidimus illic totum mundum, et agnovimus vere universorum nihil esse quod maneat, sed fluere ac pertransire omnia quae sub sole sunt, veramque constare sententiam, quod omnia vanitas. Nunc ergo 150Cpostquam nobis demonstravit qualia sint ea quae nobiscum facta sunt, transit ut doceat nos quid sentire debeamus, aut exspectare de iis quae a nobis fiunt. Quia si id quoque vanitati subjectum est quod Deus fecit, dubitari non potest omnino vanum esse, et multo magis vanum, quod homo vanitas facit. Hoc est quod modo ingreditur demonstrare omnia videlicet opera hominum quae sub sole fiunt vana esse, et nihil amplius habere hominem de universo labore suo quo laborat sub sole. Ut autem suae assertioni fidem faciat, seipsum in exemplum proponit omnium quae dicturus est, asserens se cuncta quae loquitur experimento didicisse ac probasse vera. Et idcirco talem proponit suam personam, 150Dut non incredibile videatur harum rerum omnium eum experimentum habere potuisse. Propterea potentiam et dignitatem suam demonstrat rex Israel in Hierusalem. Sapientiam quoque ostendit. Et praecessi sapientia omnes qui fuerunt ante me in Hierusalem. Divitias enumerat, domos, vineas, hortos, pomaria, piscinas, servos, ancillas, armenta, greges, aurum, argentum. Postremo ne quid defuisse putetur, luxum quoque et voluptatem adjungit. Cantores, cantatrices et delicias filiorum hominum: et omnia, inquit, quae desideraverunt oculi mei non negavi eis, nec prohibui cor meum quin omni voluntate sua frueretur in iis quae paraveram. Et in iis omnibus per omnia rerum experimenta cucurrisse, nihilque se praeter vanitatem et 151Aspiritus afflictionem curamque superfluam invenisse testatur in cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Quae autem sint illa quae fiunt sub sole, supra jam dictum est. Sed ut competentius sermo ad ea quae sunt dicenda transeat, breviter nunc et summatim repetemus quae dicta sunt.

Per solem namque tempus significari ostendimus, propterea quia per solem praecipue omnis temporum mutabilitas atque vicissitudo distinguitur, ut idem intelligatur per id quod dictum est, sub sole, ac si dictum fuisset sub tempore. Rursum, ut evidentius pateret quae essent illa quae sub tempore facta auctor vanitatis argueret, distinximus alia esse quae facta sunt cum tempore, alia quae facta sunt in tempore. Eorum item quae facta sunt in tempore, 151Balia facta sunt in tempore, non sub tempore, alia in tempore, et sub tempore. Et ea quidem quae facta sunt sub tempore, magis subjecta sunt tempori, et obnoxia mutabilitati, quia in tempore coeperunt et pariter finientur in tempore, atque ideo ne se ad aeternitatem aliquatenus extendant quodammodo tempore concluduntur; quia eorum tempus et praecessit initium, et subsequitur finem. Tamen in his ne prorsus vanitas dominetur, et non inveniat veritas sub sole ubi caput reclinet (Matth. VIII), excepimus quaedam ex his quae fiunt sub tempore, et eis si vanitatem prorsus non tollimus, servire tamen vanitati prohibemus. Eorum quippe quae fiunt sub tempore, alia fiunt pro tempore, alia fiunt pro aeternitate. Et ea quae sub tempore fiunt pro tempore, 151Cactu et fructu vana sunt. Ea vero quae sub tempore pro aeternitate fiunt, actu quodammodo vana sunt, sed fructu non sunt; quoniam et si transeant in opere, permanent tamen in retributione. Quapropter ejusmodi etsi plene vanitatem non evaserunt, non tamen vanitati sed veritati serviunt; neque in eis omnino vanum est quod sunt, quia vanitas non est pro quo sunt. Illa vero quae sub tempore et pro tempore fiunt, prorsus vanitati subjecta sunt; quia, et quod in illis est vanum est, et vanitas pariter quod ex illis est. Et haec sunt illa de quibus in praesenti agitur. In quibus sub sole nihil praeter vanitatem et afflictionem spiritus, vel cum fiunt, vel cum facta sunt: ab eis, qui transitoria diligunt, invenitur.

HOMILY III. How Ecclesiastes proves through his own works that all the works of men are vain, with an epilogue of the things aforesaid.

I Ecclesiastes was king of Israel in Jerusalem: and I proposed in my mind to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things that are done under the sun. To search out the words of the wise and their riddles, and to draw forth to the taste that sweetness of wisdom which is hidden within, and to bring its beauty forth into the light — who is able? A scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven, who bringeth forth out of his treasure new things and old (Matth. XIII), if he should come to us — behold, he who God gave wisdom 150Aand understanding to lay it open and to make it manifest, that men may know that in it is life. But what are we? Darkness before light, that we should think to comprehend what God has hidden from the eyes of men, to reveal the secret of his wisdom to his friends. What do we do? Therefore we shall not meditate on his commandments, nor shall we search out her paths, and our heart will be able to rest until it find her. Only let us pursue her with these very words; and if perhaps the finding be deferred, let the search for her meanwhile feed us above all things; if we cannot [teach] her as found, yet let us teach her as sought. Behold, our Ecclesiastes, disputing thus far concerning the vanity of mutable things, has embraced in a brief discourse so many things that in those words of his this appears wonderful to us: in what manner 150Bthe whole, and the whole concerning the whole, has been so said that for brevity indeed nothing less, but for evidence nothing more, seems needful to be said. But wisdom did this, which is whole in the whole and whole in each several thing. Nor is she, whole in individual things, contracted; nor is she, whole in the whole, expanded; but she is as great in individual things as in the whole, and in the whole such as she is whole in individual things, because neither can unity be less than itself, nor immensity greater. That same wisdom therefore has expressed in this brief body of discourse the whole image of the universe, that we, being small, may see the great in the small, since in itself we cannot [see] the whole. And we have seen there the whole world, and have recognized that truly there is nothing of all things that abides, but that all things which are under the sun flow and pass through, and that the sentiment stands true, that all is vanity. Now therefore, 150Cafter he has demonstrated to us of what sort those things are which were made along with us, he passes on to teach us what we ought to think or to expect concerning those things which are done by us. Because if that also which God made is subject to vanity, it cannot be doubted that what man, who is vanity, makes is altogether vain, and much more vain. This is what he now enters upon to demonstrate: namely, that all the works of men which are done under the sun are vain, and that man has nothing more out of all his labor wherewith he labors under the sun. But that he may win credence for his assertion, he sets himself forth as an example of all the things he is about to say, asserting that he has learned by trial all that he speaks and has proved it true. And therefore he sets forth his own person as of such a kind 150Dthat it may not seem incredible that he could have had trial of all these things. Therefore he demonstrates his power and dignity: king of Israel in Jerusalem. He shows his wisdom also: And I went before in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem. He enumerates his riches: houses, vineyards, gardens, orchards, fishponds, menservants, maidservants, herds, flocks, gold, silver. Lastly, lest anything should be thought to have been lacking, he adds luxury also and pleasure: singing men, singing women, and the delights of the sons of men; and all things, he says, which my eyes desired I denied them not, nor did I keep back my heart from enjoying every pleasure of its own in those things which I had prepared. And he testifies that in all these he ran through every trial of things, and found nothing beyond vanity and 151Aaffliction of spirit and superfluous care in all things that are done under the sun. But what those things are which are done under the sun has already been said above. But that the discourse may pass over more suitably to those things which are to be said, we shall now briefly and summarily repeat what has been said.

For we have shown that by the sun time is signified, for this reason: because chiefly by the sun is all the mutability and vicissitude of times distinguished, so that the same is understood by that which is said, under the sun, as if it had been said, under time. Again, that it might appear more evidently what those things were which, done under time, the author reproves of vanity, we distinguished that some things were made with time, others made in time. Likewise of those which were made in time, 151Bsome were made in time, not under time; others in time and under time. And those indeed which were made under time are more subject to time and liable to mutability, because they began in time and will likewise be ended in time; and therefore, lest they should extend themselves in any degree to eternity, they are in a certain manner shut in by time, since their time both went before their beginning and follows after their end. Yet, lest vanity should altogether rule in these, and truth should not find under the sun where to lay its head (Matth. VIII), we have excepted certain of those things which are done under time; and if we do not altogether take vanity away from them, yet we forbid them to serve vanity. For of those things which are done under time, some are done for time, others are done for eternity. And those which are done under time for time 151Care vain in act and in fruit. But those which are done under time for eternity are in a certain manner vain in act, but in fruit are not; because, even if they pass away in the work, yet they remain in the recompense. Wherefore such things, even if they have not fully escaped vanity, yet serve not vanity but truth; nor is that which they are altogether vain in them, because that for which they are is not vanity. But those which are done under time and for time are altogether subject to vanity; because both that which is in them is vain, and that which is from them is likewise vanity. And these are the things of which we treat at present. In which, under the sun, nothing beyond vanity and affliction of spirit — either when they are being done, or when they have been done — is found by those who love transitory things.

HOMILIA IV. De rerum vanitate, et hominum occupatione pessima.

151D

Et tamen in his ipsa vanitas quasi per quosdam gradus ad incrementum consurgit, et corruptio velut a modico excrescens, paulatim aucta semper in pejus procedit. Nam in eis prima origo vanitatis invenitur, curiositas, deinde cupiditas, postremo voluptas. Inter quas prima quidem ad concupiscentiam oculorum pertinet; secunda ad ambitionem saeculi; tertia ad concupiscentiam carnis. Per quas videlicet vanitates humanus animus a summa veritate defluens in tantum praecipitatur, ut carnalibus tandem desideriis pressus totusque voluptatum illecebris 152Adevinctus suae originis non solum per se reminisci non valeat, sed nec admonitus quidem velle possit aut non esse quod male est, aut esse quod male non est. Nam quod est, male est, et quod esse deberet, male non est. Et quod vult aut non esse, quod est, aut esse quod non est: hoc utroque pejus est. Hoc igitur noster Ecclesiastes exemplo sui demonstrare hic incipit, scilicet qualiter humanus animus per hos errorum gradus a summa veritate in vanitatem corruat, et ipso suo vitio se propellente semper in deterius eat. Veritati enim inhaerere, et ipsam propter se diligere veritatem, verum bonum ejus esse debuerat.
