Cum ergo veritatem deserit et se ab illa, adversionem mentis deflectit, hanc primum repulsus, erroris sui poenam patitur, ut 152Bipsam quam in se, et propter se amare noluit veritatem, jam pro vanitate quaerere incipiat, et quia desiit illud unum contemplari in quo omnia videret, modo non tam veritatem quam novitatem affectans, multa scire concupiscat. Quia enim illam in qua vera mentis refectio est internam contemplationem perdidit, in earum, quae foris sunt rerum cognitione quasi cibum intelligentiae esuriendo requirit. Sed quia in eis, quae extrinsecus apparent universis nequaquam perfecta cognitio veritatis inveniri potest, incipit miser defectus sui aerumna languens, quasi quodam fastidio de aliis semper ad alia appetenda discurrere, et priora abjiciens quasi vacua, et sterilia sperat se desiderii sui effectum in iis quae supersunt posse obtinere, tam stultus et caecus, ut cum 152Cse in iis semper frustrari videat, nec unquam ad desiderii finem pertingere, nequaquam tamen haec aliquando quasi vana et infructuosa cesset ambiri. Sed hujus tam impudentis desiderii et stultae curiositatis, qua se in cognitione visibilium rerum supervacue extendit, et sui Creatoris cognitionem in qua sola vera beatitudo constat, aut habitam negligit, aut non habitam quaerere dissimulat, justa tamen poena subsequitur; quoniam ibidem ubi perverse delectationem quaerit, nihil praeter dolorem et spiritus afflictionem invenit. In tanta enim occupatione majorem viribus difficultatem reperiens, quasi quodam pondere anxietatis suae opprimitur, quia dum eum ad quaerendam in hujusmodi sapientiam ubi inveniri non potest, desiderium impellit, multitudine pariter 152Ddistrahitur et profunditate reverberatur. Hic est ergo labor et afflictio spiritus, quo mens stulta et impudens merito pro sua temeritate atteritur, dum non solum Creatorem suum obliviscens, sed semetipsam quoque negligens, in rebus infimis, quae ad salutem non pertinent, investigandis occupatur. Et tamen aliquando scientia tali vanitate quaesita, tantoque labore ex parte quantulacunque inventa, animum per superbiam inflat, et de curiositate ad elationem quasi de vanitate ad vanitatem praecipitat. Quae videlicet elatio ambitionem saeculi inducens, dum laudis cupidum efficit, ad amorem pompae et gloriam divitiarum animum accendit, ut dum de boni interioris gloria ad appetitum exterioris labitur, semper 153Aad deteriorem vanitatem praecipitetur. Sed neque hic stare potest semel coepta corruptio. Nam bona carnis sicut prius dum non habentur, ut quaeri debeant, cupido blandiuntur per speciem; ita postea dum possidentur fractum enerviter, et emollitum usu illiciunt ad voluptatem. Sicque miser animus post amorem vanae laudis, post ardorem magis vanae cupiditatis, novissimae ad appetitum voluptatis inflammatur, ut jam etiam in carne vanitatem seminare incipiat, ut post de carne caro factus fructum vanitatis in corruptione metat. Hic est enim fructus vanitatis, ut mens misera tandem carnalibus desideriis obruta, et voluptate carnalium desideriorum sopita, intantum obdormiat ut jam nunc sapientiam non solum veritate, sed nec specie quidem requirat. 153BTantoque avidius totam se ad carnis voluptatem male dulcem experiendam effundat quanto magis interius fatigata, et ab inquisitionis suae intentione repulsa, de invenienda veritate desperat. Et quia supra se tendens per inquisitionem labore se atque difficultate nimia succubuisse considerat ad aliam se, et quae sine labore haberi valeat consolationem tota aviditate relaxat, sed, et ibi quoque vanitatem inveniens, requiescere non sinitur; quia in carnis voluptate fugientem delectationem nec cum praesens est retinere potest, nec cum praeterierit revocare. Sicque undique fatigata et dissipata procella vanitatis suae concutitur, ut per idipsum quo male delectata abiit, salubriter tandem afflicta redire compellatur. Et saepe gravis quaedam sit lucta in animo, ut dum 153Cse in infimis delectari pariter, et affligi considerat, magno desiderio amore libertatis dilecta etiam, si fieri possit, deserere concupiscat. Hanc igitur luctam, et tumultuationem humanae mentis per varia vitae mortalis studia, in verbis sequentibus omnium causam in se per sententiam transumens Ecclesiastes exprimet: et qualiter de vanitate curiositatis ad vanitatem pompae, et ambitionis, ac deinde ad vanitatem voluptatis corruat, ostendet sicut in serie libri ac ordine demonstratur. Sed quia, quae in praefatione dicenda erant, explevimus: nunc ad exponenda verba narrationis ejus revertamur.

HOMILY IV. On the vanity of things, and the worst occupation of men.

151D

And yet in these things vanity itself rises up to increase as though by certain steps, and corruption, growing out as it were from a little thing, increased by degrees, always proceeds to the worse. For in them is found the first origin of vanity, curiosity; then cupidity; lastly pleasure. Among which the first indeed pertains to the concupiscence of the eyes, the second to the ambition of the world, the third to the concupiscence of the flesh. Through which vanities, namely, the human mind, flowing down from the highest truth, is cast headlong so far that, pressed at last by carnal desires and wholly bound fast 152Aby the enticements of pleasures, it not only cannot of itself remember its own origin, but cannot even when admonished will either that what evilly is should not be, or that what evilly is not should be. For what is, is evilly; and what ought to be, evilly is not. And that it wills either that what is should not be, or that what is not should be: this is worse than both. This therefore our Ecclesiastes here begins to demonstrate by the example of himself: namely, in what manner the human mind falls down through these steps of errors from the highest truth into vanity, and, its own vice driving it on, always goes to the worse. For to cleave to truth, and to love truth itself for its own sake, ought to have been its true good. When therefore it forsakes truth and turns away from her the mind's attention, then first, repulsed from her, it suffers the punishment of its own error: that 152Bthe very truth which it would not love in itself and for its own sake it now begins to seek for the sake of vanity; and because it has ceased to contemplate that one thing in which it might see all things, now, aiming not so much at truth as at novelty, it longs to know many things. For because it has lost that inward contemplation in which is the true refreshment of the mind, it seeks hungrily, as it were the food of understanding, in the knowledge of those things which are without. But because in all those things which appear outwardly a perfect knowledge of the truth can by no means be found, the wretch, languishing in the misery of his own failing, begins, as with a certain loathing, to run about always from some things to the desiring of others; and, casting away the former as empty and barren, he hopes that he can obtain the effect of his desire in those that remain — so foolish and blind that, though 152Che sees himself always frustrated in them, and never reaching the end of his desire, yet these things by no means ever cease to be courted as vain and unfruitful. But a just punishment nevertheless follows upon this so shameless desire and foolish curiosity, by which it stretches itself out superfluously in the knowledge of visible things, and either neglects the knowledge of its Creator — in which alone true blessedness consists — when it is had, or dissembles to seek it when it is not had; since in the very place where it perversely seeks delight, it finds nothing beyond grief and affliction of spirit. For in so great an occupation, finding a difficulty greater than its strength, it is oppressed as by a certain weight of its own anxiety; because, while desire drives it to seek wisdom in things of this kind, where it cannot be found, it is at once distracted by their multitude 152Dand beaten back by their depth. This then is the labor and affliction of spirit by which the foolish and shameless mind is deservedly worn away for its own rashness, while, not only forgetting its Creator but also neglecting itself, it is occupied in searching out the lowest things, which do not pertain to salvation. And yet sometimes knowledge, sought with such vanity and found with so great labor in however small a part, puffs up the mind through pride, and casts it headlong from curiosity to elation, as from vanity to vanity. Which elation, namely, bringing in the ambition of the world, while it makes the mind greedy of praise, kindles it to the love of pomp and the glory of riches, so that, while it slips down from the glory of the inward good to the appetite of the outward, it is always 153Acast headlong into a worse vanity. But neither can corruption, once begun, stand still here. For as the goods of the flesh, while they are not yet had, flatter the greedy man by their appearance, so that they must needs be sought, so afterward, while they are possessed, they entice to pleasure one nervelessly broken and softened by use. And so the wretched mind, after the love of vain praise, after the ardor of a more vain cupidity, is lastly inflamed to the appetite of pleasure, so that now it begins even to sow vanity in the flesh, that afterward, made flesh out of flesh, it may reap the fruit of vanity in corruption. For this is the fruit of vanity: that the wretched mind, overwhelmed at last by carnal desires and lulled asleep by the pleasure of carnal desires, sleeps so deep that now it seeks wisdom not only not in truth, but not even in appearance. 153BAnd it pours itself out wholly to the trying of the evilly sweet pleasure of the flesh the more greedily, by how much the more, wearied within and repulsed from the intention of its own search, it despairs of finding the truth. And because, stretching above itself through search, it considers that it has sunk down under labor and excessive difficulty, it lets itself loose with all greediness to another consolation, and one that can be had without labor; but there too, finding vanity, it is not suffered to rest, because in the pleasure of the flesh it can neither keep hold of the fleeing delight when it is present, nor call it back when it has passed away. And thus, wearied and scattered on every side, it is shaken by the storm of its own vanity, so that through that very thing wherein it went away evilly delighted, it may at last, wholesomely afflicted, be compelled to return. And often there is a certain grievous struggle in the mind, so that, while 153Cit considers itself at once delighted and afflicted in the lowest things, with great desire, for love of liberty, it longs to forsake even the things it has loved, if it could be done. This struggle therefore and tumult of the human mind through the various pursuits of mortal life Ecclesiastes will express in the words that follow, taking upon himself in a sentiment the case of all; and he will show in what manner it falls down from the vanity of curiosity to the vanity of pomp and of ambition, and thereafter to the vanity of pleasure, as is demonstrated in the sequence and order of the book. But since we have completed those things which were to be said in the preface, let us now return to expounding the words of his narrative.

HOMILIA V. De dictorum verborum Ecclesiastae litterali et morali expositione.

153D

Ego Ecclesiastes fui rex Israel in Hierusalem. Primum mihi hoc nequaquam praetereundum videtur, quod quidam hunc librum Salomonem in poenitentia existimant conscripsisse: et quod idcirco in eo vanitatem mundanarum rerum, et maxime carnalis voluptatis tam studiose arguat; quoniam ipse experimento cuncta didicerit deliciarum luxu corruptus, et blandimentis seductus mulierum. Et quod idcirco noluit dicere: Rex sum Israel in Hierusalem; quia deposita regni purpura, de solio suo jam descenderat, contemptaque quam male tenuerat potestate, in habitu poenitentiae reatum suum plangebat, ideoque ait: rex fuit in Hierusalem. Atque utinam hoc verum esse constaret, et tam certum de 154Apoenitentia illius, quam non dubium de culpa testimonium haberemus! Nunc autem, quia dubia pro certis affirmare non possumus; illa quae dubia non sunt prosequamur. Ego Ecclesiastes. Seipsum, ut diximus, in exemplum proponit omnium, quae dicturus est, quatenus verbis illius eo citius auditores fidem adhibeant, quod cum non audiendo solum, sed experiendo intelligunt didicisse, quae docuit. Ac si diceret. Ego qui vos doceo expertus sum universa quae dico. Nam, quae sit vanitas in culmine terrenae potestatis, quis scire melius potuit? Ego quippe fui rex Israel in Hierusalem. Satis magna sublimitas in tanto populo, et in tam nobili ac famosa civitate regnare, seque in regni solio videre cunctis, et potestate Dominum, et honore praelatum. Et haec quorsum? 154BFui, inquit. Quasi dicat: Jam non sum; quia etsi sum, idipsum jam nihil esse agnosco quod sum. Et quomodo ad id pervenerit ut nihil se esse agnosceret, deinde prosequitur dicens:

Proposui in animo meo quaerere, et investigare prudenter de omnibus, quae fiunt sub sole. Quasi diceret: Ego exterius potestate tumidus et interius scientia inflatus, altiora me quaerere conatus sum. Sed ubi inaniter praesumendo supra me tumui, ibi deficiendo veraciter directionem mei agnovi. Proposui in animo meo quaerere et investigare sapienter de omnibus, quae fiunt sub sole. Magnum propositum si ad effectum venire potuisset, sed mens humana quomodo ad tanta sufficeret? Magna igitur superbia mortalem hominem de tam multis praesumere, et 154Crursum magna curiositas tam multa appetere. Proposui, inquit. Videte quomodo elationem sonant omnia. Non ait, cogitavi; sed proposui, ut saltem venialis fuisset, et humana tentatio si subito ac transitorie, sicut nonnunquam solet, tumida cogitatio animam tangeret: et tamen per consensum recepta, vel approbata non fuisset. Nunc vero non solum elata, verum etiam caeca mens, ad tantum erroris profundum corruit, ut non solum id quod inordinatum erat facere cogitaret, sed etiam id quod impossibile fuerat implere se posse praesumeret. Proposui in animo meo. Ingens conatus. Et quae? Quaerere, et investigare. Quaerere ignota, et investigare profunda. Quomodo? sapienter. O cor insipiens! 154DErgo sapientiam non quaeris, sed tantummodo per sapientiam, quaerere te profiteris: hoc enim dixisti: Proposui in animo meo quaerere, et investigare sapienter de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Si ergo sapienter quaeras, per sapientiam quaeres. Et dicis: Utique sic; per sapientiam quaeram. Male enim quaererem, si per sapientiam non quaererem. Nam si sine sapientia quaererem, etiamsi sapientiam quaererem, insipienter quaererem. Sapientiam vero insipienter quaerere, idipsum jam sapere non esset, sed desipere. Quapropter sapienter quaeram, et per sapientiam quaeram, et sapientiam quaeram. Dic ergo mihi sapientiam per quam quaeres, ubi quaeres? et per quam sapientiam quaeres sapientiam. Per quam quaeris? Jam, inquit, habeo sapientiam 155Aper quam quaeram et ideo per sapientiam quam habeo, quaeram; et sapientiam per quam quaeram, non quaeram. Quid quaeres? De cunctis, quae fiunt sub sole. Quid est de cunctis? Quare non dixisti cuncta quae fiunt sub sole? Quia, inquit, majus aliquid, et multo majus proposui. Nam ea quae fiunt sub sole cuncta visibilia sunt, et ideo si magnum est, summum tamen non est quaerere et investigare ea quae oculo comprehendi possunt. Idcirco illa non quaeram, sed de illis quaeram. Quaerere et investigare de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Non illa quae videntur, sed de illis quae videntur illa quae non videntur. Non illa, quae fiunt sub sole, quae videntur; sed de illis, quae fiunt sub sole, rationes et causas eorum, quae non videntur. Haec ergo proposui, 155Bquaerere, et investigare sapienter de cunctis, quae fiunt sub sole. Magnam profecto sapientiam habes. Quis tibi tantam sapientiam dedit? Homo es tu, et quaeres sapienter de cunctis, quae fiunt sub sole? Unde tibi talis sapientia: Deus, inquis, dedit. Videamus modo. Non enim indiscussus pertransibis. Volumus enim prius scire utrum possis de semetipso rationem reddere, qui cum tanto proposito advenisti, ut putes eorum, quae fiunt sub sole, omnium rationem investigare. Dic ergo in illa sapientia, per quam rationem omnium investigare proponis, tuam saltem possibilitatem adhuc agnoscere potuisti: ego, inquit, nisi sperassem me ipsam rem posse ad effectum perducere, quod omnino impossibile crederem, et si facere cogitarem, nequaquam 155Ctamen me facturum proponerem. O cor insipiens! Hoc est quod dixi; quia non cognovisti te, idcirco praesumpsisti appetere quod erat supra te, in altero caecum, in altero tumidum, in utroque stultum. Tu ergo investigabis sapienter de cunctis, quae fiunt sub sole. Investiga modo, satage, da operam. Quaere, et invenies. Quid invenies? Sapientiam invenies. Quam sapientiam? Ut cognoscas tuam stultitiam. Quaeres enim et non invenies quod quaeres; laborabis et non proficies, et sola vexatio dabit intellectum auditui.

Hanc enim occupationem pessimam dedit Deus filiis hominum ut [distendantur] occuparentur in ea. Recte et juste, ut quia in veritate stare noluerunt 155Dper multiplicitatem divisi distendantur et occupentur in vanitate. Propterea, inquit, vidi cuncta, quae fiunt sub sole, et ecce universa vanitas et afflictio spiritus, Deo gratias. Modo primum sapere coepisti. Modo video te sapientiam habere, per quam possis quaerere, et investigare sapienter de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Sapienter enim invenisti et sapienter intellexisti quod universa vanitas et afflictio spiritus. Velim tamen scire unde ista tibi poenitudo tam subita. Magnum quoddam exspectavimus, et illud propositum grande omnes non attentos et exspectantes jam fecerat. Quis enim de tanta promissione exiguum aliquid exire posse putaret? Quaerere, et investigare sapienter de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Et qui postea: Hanc occupationem pessimam 156Adedit Deus filiis hominum, ut distendantur in ea. Quam occupationem dicis? Hanc inquis, ut proponant in animo suo quaerere et investigare sapienter de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Quare ergo tu hanc occupationem pessimam dicis: Quaerere et investigare sapienter de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole? Tolle, ait, sapienter. Non enim occupatio pessima, esset sapienter, quaerere et investigare de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Sed quis hoc potest? Supra hominis sensum est causas investigare omnium et comprehendere rationem universorum quae fiunt sub sole. Ergo proponi potest, fieri non potest quaerere et investigare sapienter de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Multa enim latent et absconduntur plurima et cuncta reservantur in posterum, nec debet investigari 156Bquod fieri non licet. Ergo quod non potest sapienter fieri, non potest sapienter proponi, etiamsi proponitur sapienter fieri. Ego igitur insipienter proposui quod sapienter facere non potui, quaerere et investigare de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Utrobique insipiens, et dum proposui quod non potui, et dum feci quod non debui, tertia adjuncta insipientia: quod utrumque ignoravi. Quaesivi tamen et investigavi quod quaerere et investigare proposui, quaesivi, et non inveni quod quaesivi. Aliquid tamen inveni: scilicet non posse me quod credidi, et ibi agnovi quod hanc occupationem pessimam dedit Deus filiis hominum ut distendantur in ea. Ergo insipientem fuisse profuit; sed tamen insipientia, sapientia non fuit. Data est tamen insipientia, ut ad sapientiam 156Cerudiat filios hominum. Dimissi sunt sibi, ut agnoscant se, et agnoscentes damnent, et fugiant quod facti sunt ex se. Hanc ergo occupationem pessimam dedit Deus filiis hominum ut distendantur in ea. Quia enim mens hominis in illo uno bono stare noluit, in quo potuit feliciter requiescere, et sine distractione vel occupatione, summae veritatis plenitudinem possidere, projecta foras extra semetipsam in multiplicitatem rerum visibilium spargitur, et veritatem quam intus caecata a fonte haurire non potest, quasi per rivulos quosdam visibilium arescentibus praecordiis saltem fugere conatur. Sed quo magis se foras per intentionem ad visibilia fundit tanto magis intus ab invisibilium cognitione tenebrescit; 156Dquia dum amplius per exteriora spargitur, magis ab interioribus aversa caecatur. Unde bene Cain cum scelus suum detectum cerneret, et majori scelere reprobus, de venia sceleris desperaret, legitur dixisse ad Dominum. Ecce ejicies me hodie a facie terrae! et a facie tua abscondar: et ero vagus et profugus super terram (Gen. IV). Reproba etenim mens ejecta a facie Domini absconditur, dum se per exteriora spargens, tanto magis ab interni luminis aspectu tegitur, quanto magis in iis quae foris sunt, cogitandis semper occupata tenetur. Unde bene illic dicitur, vagus et profugus. Vagus enim per inordinatam concupiscentiam, et profugus per peccatricem conscientiam, dum se in concupiscentia per cogitationem dividit, et in conscientia per desperationem 157Aavertit, ipse sibi peccator ne redire valeat, ad se lumen veritatis abscondit. Ergo hanc occupationem pessimam dedit Deus filiis hominum ut distendantur in ea. Quare dedit, ut distendantur in ea? Ut se tendant et distendant, laborent et deficiant, et revertantur et sanet eos. Si enim in occupatione sua non distenderentur neque laborarent, dulcis fieret nimis ipsa occupatio, et nollent illam deserere, neque redire amplius, concupiscerent ubi veritas est. Propterea dedit illis occupationem pessimam Deus, ut distendantur in ea. Agamus pietati ejus gratias, quia laborare nos fecit in malo nostro, in aversione nostra; quia sepivit spinis viam nostram ut revertamur et convertamur ad ipsum virum et sponsum et amicum animae nostrae, quia bene erat nobis tunc 157Bmagis quam nunc. Hoc autem non intelleximus nos et putavimus nobis bene esse cum male erat. Et ideo aspersit ipse amaritudinem et absinthium, et fel in poculum dedit super male dulcem et blandientem ad mortem aversionem nostram et occupationem pessimam. Et dedit hanc occupationem pessimam filiis hominum ut distendantur in ea. Occupatio enim est distractio et illigatio mentium quae avertit et dissipat et illaqueat animas ne cogitare pervaleant ea quae salutis sunt, et ideo occupatio. Quare pessima? Quia est et alia mala occupatio, sed non pessima; et ipsa est quae circa necessitates vitae mortalis versatur, et sollicita est erga plurima; et ipsa occupatio mala est; et ut amplius aliquid dicamus, ipsa malitia est, ut de illa recte dictum intelligatur: Sufficit diei malitia 157Csua. (Matth. VI). Haec ergo occupatio miseriae vitae mortalis necessaria est; postea a gloria vitae immortalis absorbenda: et ideo mala est ad miseriam, sed mala non ad culpam; quoniam si poenam habent a beatitudine alienam, culpam non habet justitiae ac veritati contrariam. Occupatio autem curiositatis qua se mens ad illicita extendit, et instat scrutari et investigare quod ei scire aut non convenit, aut noxium est: ipsa est pessima occupatio, quia, dum se dilatat ultra mensuram, aut affectum capit, et animum per inanem scientiam inflat; aut si apprehendere non valet per dilationem et desperationem fatigat.

HOMILY V. On the literal and moral exposition of the words of Ecclesiastes already spoken.

153D

I Ecclesiastes was king of Israel in Jerusalem. First this seems to me by no means to be passed over: that some judge that Solomon wrote this book in penitence, and that he therefore so studiously reproves in it the vanity of worldly things, and most of all of carnal pleasure, because he himself had learned all things by experience, corrupted by the luxury of delights and seduced by the blandishments of women. And that therefore he was unwilling to say: I am king of Israel in Jerusalem; because, the purple of the kingdom laid aside, he had already come down from his throne, and, despising the power which he had ill held, he was bewailing his guilt in the habit of penitence — and therefore he says: he was king in Jerusalem. And would that it stood established that this is true, and that we had as certain a testimony concerning 154Ahis penitence as we have an undoubted one concerning his fault! But now, since we cannot affirm doubtful things for certain, let us pursue those which are not doubtful. I Ecclesiastes. He sets himself forth, as we have said, as an example of all the things he is about to say, so that hearers may the sooner give credence to his words, in that they understand that he learned what he taught not by hearing only, but by experiencing. As if he were to say. I who teach you have made trial of all the things I say. For who could better know what vanity there is in the summit of earthly power? For I was king of Israel in Jerusalem. A loftiness great enough: to reign over so great a people and in so noble and famous a city, and to see oneself upon the throne of the kingdom, lord over all in power and set above all in honor. And to what end these things? 154BI was, he says. As though he should say: Now I am not; because even if I am, I now recognize that that very thing which I am is nothing. And how he came to this, that he should recognize himself to be nothing, he then pursues, saying:

I proposed in my mind to seek and to search out prudently concerning all things which are done under the sun. As though he should say: I, outwardly swollen with power and inwardly puffed up with knowledge, attempted to seek things higher than myself. But where by vainly presuming I swelled above myself, there by failing I truly recognized the direction of myself. I proposed in my mind to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun. A great purpose, if it could have come to effect; but how should the human mind suffice for so great things? Great pride therefore it is that mortal man should presume concerning so many things, and 154Cagain great curiosity to desire so many. I proposed, he says. See how all things sound of elation. He does not say, I thought; but, I proposed — whereas the temptation would at least have been venial and human if a swollen thought had touched the soul suddenly and in passing, as it is sometimes wont to do, and yet had not been received or approved by consent. But now the mind, not only lifted up but also blind, fell down into so great a depth of error that it not only thought to do that which was disordered, but even presumed that it could fulfil that which had been impossible. I proposed in my mind. A huge attempt. And what things? To seek, and to search out. To seek things unknown, and to search out things deep. How? Wisely. O foolish heart! 154DTherefore thou dost not seek wisdom, but professest only to seek by wisdom: for this thou hast said: I proposed in my mind to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun. If therefore thou seekest wisely, thou wilt seek by wisdom. And thou sayest: Just so; I will seek by wisdom. For I should seek ill, if I did not seek by wisdom. For if I should seek without wisdom, even if I sought wisdom, I should seek foolishly. But to seek wisdom foolishly — that very thing would now be not to be wise, but to be without sense. Wherefore I will seek wisely, and I will seek by wisdom, and I will seek wisdom. Tell me then the wisdom by which thou wilt seek: where wilt thou seek? and by what wisdom wilt thou seek wisdom. By which dost thou seek? Already, he says, I have the wisdom 155Aby which I may seek; and therefore by the wisdom which I have I will seek; and the wisdom by which I may seek, I will not seek. What wilt thou seek? Concerning all things which are done under the sun. What is "concerning all things"? Why didst thou not say, all things which are done under the sun? Because, he says, I proposed something greater, and much greater. For the things which are done under the sun are all visible, and therefore, though it be a great thing, yet it is not the highest, to seek and to search out those things which can be comprehended by the eye. Therefore I will not seek those things, but I will seek concerning those things. To seek and to search out concerning all things which are done under the sun. Not those things which are seen, but, concerning those which are seen, those things which are not seen. Not those things which are done under the sun, which are seen; but, concerning those which are done under the sun, the reasons and causes of those things which are not seen. These things therefore I proposed: 155Bto seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun. Surely thou hast great wisdom. Who gave thee so great wisdom? Art thou a man, and wilt thou seek wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun? Whence hast thou such wisdom: God, thou sayest, gave it. Let us now see. For thou shalt not pass by unexamined. For we wish first to know whether thou canst render an account of thyself, thou who hast come with so great a purpose that thou thinkest to search out the reason of all the things which are done under the sun. Say then: in that wisdom by which thou proposest to search out the reason of all things, hast thou been able as yet to recognize at least thine own possibility: I, he says, unless I had hoped that I could bring the thing itself to effect — what I should believe altogether impossible, even if I thought to do it, yet I should by no means 155Cpropose that I would do it. O foolish heart! This is what I said: because thou hast not known thyself, therefore thou hast presumed to desire what was above thee — in the one blind, in the other swollen, in both foolish. Thou therefore wilt search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun. Search now, bestir thyself, give effort. Seek, and thou shalt find. What wilt thou find? Thou wilt find wisdom. What wisdom? That thou mayest know thine own folly. For thou shalt seek and shalt not find what thou seekest; thou shalt labor and shalt not profit, and vexation alone shall give understanding to the hearing.

For God hath given this worst occupation to the sons of men, that [they may be distended] they might be occupied therein. Rightly and justly: that because they would not stand in truth, 155Dthey should, divided through multiplicity, be distended and occupied in vanity. Therefore, he says, I saw all things which are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit. Thanks be to God. Now for the first time thou hast begun to be wise. Now I see that thou hast the wisdom by which thou canst seek and search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun. For wisely hast thou found, and wisely hast thou understood, that all is vanity and affliction of spirit. Yet I should like to know whence comes to thee this so sudden repentance. We expected something great, and that grand purpose had already made all men not attentive and expectant. For who would think that anything scanty could come forth out of so great a promise? To seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun. And how afterward: God hath given this worst occupation 156Ato the sons of men, that they may be distended therein. What occupation dost thou mean? This, thou sayest: that they propose in their mind to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun. Why then dost thou call this the worst occupation: To seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun? Take away, he says, "wisely." For it would not be the worst occupation, wisely to seek and to search out concerning all things which are done under the sun. But who can do this? It is above the sense of man to search out the causes of all things and to comprehend the reason of all that is done under the sun. Therefore it can be proposed, but it cannot be done, to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun. For many things lie hid, and very many are hidden away, and all are reserved for hereafter; nor ought that to be searched out 156Bwhich is not lawful to be done. Therefore what cannot wisely be done cannot wisely be proposed, even if it is proposed to be done wisely. I therefore foolishly proposed what I could not wisely do: to seek and to search out concerning all things which are done under the sun. Foolish on both sides — both when I proposed what I could not, and when I did what I ought not — with a third folly added: that I knew neither of the two. Yet I sought and searched out what I proposed to seek and to search out; I sought, and I did not find what I sought. Yet I found something: namely, that I could not do what I had believed; and there I recognized that God hath given this worst occupation to the sons of men, that they may be distended therein. Therefore it profited to have been foolish; but yet folly was not wisdom. Yet folly was given, that it might train 156Cthe sons of men unto wisdom. They have been left to themselves, that they may know themselves, and knowing may condemn and flee what they have become of themselves. This worst occupation therefore God hath given to the sons of men, that they may be distended therein. For because the mind of man would not stand in that one good in which it could happily rest, and without distraction or occupation possess the fullness of the highest truth, it is cast forth outside itself and scattered into the multiplicity of visible things; and the truth which, blinded within, it cannot draw from the fountain, it attempts at least to flee, with parched inward parts, as it were through certain rivulets of visible things. But the more it pours itself outward by intention toward visible things, so much the more does it grow dark within from the knowledge of invisible things; 156Dbecause, while it is scattered more widely through outward things, it is the more blinded, being turned away from inward things. Whence fittingly Cain, when he beheld his own crime uncovered, and, reprobate by a greater crime, despaired of pardon for his crime, is read to have said to the Lord. Behold, thou dost cast me out this day from the face of the earth! and from thy face I shall be hid: and I shall be a vagabond and a fugitive upon the earth (Gen. IV). For the reprobate mind, cast out from the face of the Lord, is hidden, while, scattering itself through outward things, it is so much the more covered from the sight of the inward light, by how much the more it is held always occupied in thinking upon those things which are without. Whence fittingly it is there said, a vagabond and a fugitive. A vagabond, namely, through disordered concupiscence, and a fugitive through a sinful conscience: while he divides himself in concupiscence through thought, and in conscience through despair 157Aturns himself away, the sinner himself hides from himself the light of truth, that he may not be able to return. Therefore God hath given this worst occupation to the sons of men, that they may be distended therein. Why did he give it, that they may be distended therein? That they may stretch and distend themselves, may labor and fail, and may return, and he may heal them. For if they were not distended in their occupation, nor labored, that occupation itself would become exceedingly sweet, and they would not be willing to forsake it, nor would they long any more to return where truth is. Therefore God gave them the worst occupation, that they may be distended therein. Let us give thanks to his mercy, because he has made us labor in our evil, in our turning away; because he has hedged our way with thorns, that we may return and be converted to him, the husband and spouse and friend of our soul, because it was well with us then 157Bmore than now. But this we did not understand, and we thought it was well with us when it was ill. And therefore he himself sprinkled bitterness and wormwood, and gave gall into the cup, upon our evilly sweet turning-away, which flatters unto death, and upon the worst occupation. And he gave this worst occupation to the sons of men, that they may be distended therein. For occupation is the distraction and the binding of minds, which turns aside and scatters and ensnares souls, that they may not be strong enough to think upon those things which are of salvation — and therefore, occupation. Why the worst? Because there is another evil occupation also, but not the worst; and it is that which is busied about the necessities of mortal life, and is anxious about very many things; and that occupation is evil; and, to say something further, it is malice itself, so that of it that word is rightly understood: Sufficient for the day is its own malice. 157C(Matth. VI). This occupation therefore is necessary to the misery of mortal life, to be swallowed up afterward by the glory of immortal life; and therefore it is evil unto misery, but not evil unto fault; since, if they have a punishment alien from blessedness, it has not a fault contrary to justice and truth. But the occupation of curiosity, by which the mind stretches itself out to unlawful things, and presses on to search and to investigate what it either does not befit it to know, or is harmful to it — that is the worst occupation; because, while it spreads itself beyond measure, either it takes hold of what it has set its affection upon, and puffs up the mind through empty knowledge, or, if it is not able to lay hold of it, it wearies the mind through delay and despair.

HOMILIA VI. Quid sit distendi in occupatione pessima.

157DHanc ergo occupationem pessimam dedit Deus filiis hominum ut distendantur in ea. Quid est distendantur? Exterius intumescant, interius inanes fiant. Nam quod distenditur foris quidem majus apparet; sed unde extrinsecus incrementum accepisse cernitur, inde veraciter interius soliditatem amisisse comprobatur. Dum enim ultra se pertingere nititur in id quod non est, in semetipso deficere incipit, et inanescere ab eo quod est. Sic nimirum mens humana dum per curiositatem ad inquirenda ea quae extra ipsam sunt, tenditur ne semetipsam considerare valeat, ipsa suae inquisitionis occupatione praepeditur. Hanc ergo occupationem pessimam dedit Deus filiis hominum ut distendantur in ea. O pessima 158Aoccupatio! o distentio perniciosa! quo trahis animum? Quantum promittis, et quantum tollis? Promittis homini totum quod ipse non est, et tollis totum quod ipse est. Quid si totum dares quod promittis, et totum tolleres, quod tollis? Quid enim prodest homini si universum mundum lucretur, animae vero suae detrimentum patiatur? (Matth. VI.) Quanto magis modo, quia fallaciter totum promittis, et veraciter totum tollis? Pessima es distendens et dissipans, affligens et crucians animos: quibus dominaris illa semper appetenda suggerens, quorum inquisitio aut noxia sit, aut vana; inventio vero multo magis aut inutilis, aut perniciosa. Si ergo dulcis esses, et sine labore animos possidere valeres, quis malitiam tuam unquam deprehenderet? Nunc autem 158Bipse labor et afflictio quam mentibus ingeris odiosam te faciunt, et facilius quod promittis vanum esse agnoscitur, dum id quod infers durum esse sentitur. Sic multos erudis ad sapientiam, qui tunc demum plene deprehendunt, quanta post te sequatur vanitas, cum sentire coeperint experiendo quanta in te lateat laborantibus difficultas. Propterea iste adjunxit et ait: Vidi quae fiunt cuncta sub sole, et ecce universa vanitas et afflictio spiritus (Eccle. I). Vidi, inquit, ubi, vidisti? Quis te docuit? Faciendo, inquit, vidi; experiendo cognovi. Quid fecisti? Preposui, ait, in animo meo quaerere et investigare sapienter de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole (Ibid.). Et ecce quaerere coeperam et investigare, et existimavi me in tam operoso studio exitum aliquem invenire. Extendi 158Cergo animum meum quantum potui; cogitationem meam in omnia circumlustranda diffudi. Abstuli somnum ab oculis meis, nec dedi requiem cordi meo nocte ac die donec invenirem quod quaerebat anima mea, ut invenirem rationem de omnibus quae fiunt sub sole. Sed quis finis in tantis conatibus esse potuisset? Feci et defeci, conabar et repellebar, donec contabuit anima mea et sensus contenebrati sunt, quoniam in tanta rerum multitudine et veri latentis profunditate, dum intellectus et spargi inciperet et reverberari, pondus laboris et inextricabilis luctae angustiam ultra sustinere non valui. Tunc in memetipsum reversus et quasi repulsus ab illo cui obniti conabar denso ac immeabili latentis naturae invio; cogitare coepi stultum 158Desse et vanum illarum rerum scientiam tam pertinaci studio hominem mortalem quaerere, quae non solum extra ejus naturam factae sunt, sed nec saluti ejus sive sciantur adjicere quidquam possunt, sive nesciantur auferre. Ibi ergo vidi quod hanc occupationem pessimam dedit Deus filiis hominum; ut distendantur in ea, quia cuncta quae fiunt sub sole, universa vanitas et afflictio spiritus. Nam quia fructum non habent, vana sunt, et quia affligunt, noxia. Possidentes quippe non adjuvant, et quaerentes se affligunt. Sine labore enim quaeri non possunt, sed possunt sine utilitate possideri. Animus namque statim ut cura ac desiderio quaerendi atque inveniendi ea occupatus fuerit, et se per curiositatis 159Astudium ac sollicitudinem cupiditatis in ea diffuderit digna temeritatis suae poena affligendus; et multiplicitate spargitur, et difficultate reverberatur. Vidi ergo cuncta quae sub sole fiunt, et ecce universa vanitas et afflictio spiritus. Vidi et hoc ipsum vanum fuisse quod proposui in animo meo, quaerere et investigare sapienter de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Vidi vanum esse quod occupantur filii hominum occupatione pessima ut distendantur in ea: et hoc totum vidi cum expertus sum, et vidi quantus labor et afflictio spiritus esset in eo quod proposui in animo meo, quaerere et investigare sapienter de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole. Et vidi quia universa vanitas et afflictio spiritus in omnibus quae fiunt sub sole. Haec ergo vidi. Quare autem similiter 159Bnon vident omnes filii hominum occupationem pessimam, quam dedit eis Deus ut distendantur in ea, ut intelligant et videant vanitatem et afflictionem spiritus, in omnibus quae fiunt sole? Quare laborant et non sentiunt; affliguntur ac dissipantur; et distenduntur in occupatione pessima, et non intelligunt vanitatem suam et afflictionem spiritus in omnibus quae fiunt sub sole? Quia, inquit, perversi difficile corriguntur. De quo dicamus latius.

HOMILY VI. What it is to be distended in the worst occupation.

157DThis worst occupation therefore God hath given to the sons of men, that they may be distended therein. What is, that they may be distended? That outwardly they swell, inwardly they become empty. For what is distended appears indeed greater without; but whence it is seen to have taken increase from without, thence it is truly proved to have lost solidity within. For while it strives to reach beyond itself into that which is not, it begins to fail in itself and to grow empty of that which is. So indeed the human mind, while through curiosity it is stretched toward searching out those things which are outside itself, is hindered by the very occupation of its own searching, so that it cannot consider itself. This worst occupation therefore God hath given to the sons of men, that they may be distended therein. O worst 158Aoccupation! O ruinous distension! whither dost thou drag the mind? How much dost thou promise, and how much dost thou take away? Thou promisest to man the whole of what he himself is not, and thou takest away the whole of what he himself is. What if thou didst give the whole that thou promisest, and take away the whole that thou takest away? For what doth it profit a man if he gain the whole world, but suffer the loss of his own soul? (Matth. VI.) How much more now, since falsely thou promisest the whole, and truly thou takest away the whole? Thou art worst, distending and scattering, afflicting and torturing minds; suggesting to those whom thou rulest that those things are always to be desired whose searching out is either harmful or vain, and whose finding is much more either useless or ruinous. If therefore thou wert sweet, and couldst possess minds without labor, who would ever detect thy malice? But now 158Bthe very labor and affliction which thou bringest upon minds make thee hateful, and what thou promisest is the more easily recognized to be vain, while what thou bringest in is felt to be hard. Thus thou trainest many unto wisdom, who then at last fully detect how great a vanity follows after thee, when they have begun to feel by experience how great a difficulty lies hid in thee for those who labor. Therefore he added and said: I saw all things that are done under the sun, and behold all is vanity and affliction of spirit (Eccle. I). I saw, he says, where, didst thou see? Who taught thee? By doing, he says, I saw; by experiencing I came to know. What didst thou do? I set before, he says, in my mind to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun (Ibid.). And behold, I had begun to seek and to search out, and I thought that in so laborious a study I should find some issue. I stretched out 158Ctherefore my mind as far as I could; I poured out my thought upon surveying all things. I took sleep away from my eyes, nor did I give rest to my heart night and day, until I might find what my soul was seeking, that I might find the reason concerning all things which are done under the sun. But what end could there have been in such attempts? I did and I failed, I strove and I was driven back, until my soul wasted away and my senses were darkened; since, in so great a multitude of things and in the depth of hidden truth, while the understanding began both to be scattered and to be beaten back, I was no longer able to bear the weight of labor and the straitness of an inextricable struggle. Then, returned into myself and as it were driven back from that dense and impassable pathlessness of hidden nature against which I was striving to press, I began to think that it is foolish 158Dand vain that mortal man should seek with so obstinate a zeal the knowledge of those things which not only were made outside his nature, but also can neither add anything to his salvation if they be known, nor take anything away if they be not known. There therefore I saw that God hath given this worst occupation to the sons of men; that they may be distended therein, because all things which are done under the sun are all vanity and affliction of spirit. For because they have no fruit, they are vain; and because they afflict, they are harmful. For they do not help those who possess them, and they afflict those who seek them. For they cannot be sought without labor, but they can be possessed without profit. For the mind, as soon as it has been occupied with the care and desire of seeking and of finding them, and has poured itself out into them through the zeal of curiosity 159Aand the solicitude of cupidity — to be afflicted with a punishment worthy of its own rashness — is both scattered by their multiplicity and beaten back by their difficulty. I saw therefore all things which are done under the sun, and behold all is vanity and affliction of spirit. I saw that this very thing also had been vain, that I proposed in my mind to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun. I saw that it is vain that the sons of men are occupied with the worst occupation, that they may be distended therein; and all this I saw when I had made trial of it, and I saw how great labor and affliction of spirit there was in this, that I proposed in my mind to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun. And I saw that all is vanity and affliction of spirit in all things which are done under the sun. These things therefore I saw. But why do not all the sons of men likewise 159Bsee the worst occupation which God hath given them, that they may be distended therein, so as to understand and see the vanity and affliction of spirit in all things which are done under the sun sole? Why do they labor and not feel it; are afflicted and scattered; and are distended in the worst occupation, and do not understand their own vanity and the affliction of spirit in all things which are done under the sun? Because, he says, the perverse are corrected with difficulty. Of which let us speak more at large.

HOMILIA VII. Quod perversi difficile corrigantur, etc.

Perversi difficile corriguntur. Idcirco non possunt intelligere, quia perversi sunt, et ideo laborant et non sentiunt, et delectantur in afflictione sui (Job 159CXXX), et putant bene sibi esse, dum male est. In tantum enim perversi sunt, ut judicium veritatis non sit in eis; putantes bonum esse quod malum est, et quod bonum est malum ponentes tenebras lucem, et lucem tenebras; existimantesque amarum dulce; et dulce amarum (Isa. V). Delicias enim esse computant sub sensibus; et idcirco amant dolores suos, et se voluntarios ingerunt ad occupationem pessimam et distenduntur in ea; quia dum caeca mente quod falso delectare videtur, appetunt, quod vere cruciat et affligit, non attendunt. Propterea ergo non vident vanitatem suam et afflictionem spiritus in omnibus quae fiunt sub sole; quia perversi sunt et difficile corriguntur. Et stultorum infinitus est numerus. Non solum enim aversi sunt, sed etiam 159Dperversi. Aversi a Deo; in semetipsis perversi. Et aversi non facile convertuntur, quia perversi difficile corriguntur. Nam si in semetipsis corrigerentur, per semetipsos converterentur. Quia si prius judicium veritatis in semetipsis reciperent, suo postmodum judicio vanitatem fugiendam et veritatem sequendam esse viderent. Nunc autem nec aversi lumen veritatis vident, nec perversi per lumen veritatis vident, et ideo difficile corriguntur, quia rectitudinem et veritatem nec absentem quaerere sciunt, nec praesentem approbare. Ideo perversi difficile corriguntur, et stultorum infinitus est numerus. Tam multi enim non essent si facile corrigi potuissent. Et in hoc manifeste ostenditur quam difficilis sit perversorum correctio quod infinita est 160Astultorum multitudo Nunc ergo perversi et stultitam sunt ad correctionem perversitate difficiles, quam multitudine contra veritatem audaces; et ideo perversi difficile corriguntur, et stultorum infinitus est numerus. Vis, inquit, scire quam difficile perversi corrigantur? Cape me. Ego hodie tibi omnium exemplum fiam. Nam et ego aliquando perversus fui et non intellexi ipse perversitatem meam; sed putavi me rectum esse, et recte agere quando proposui in animo meo quaerere et investigare sapienter de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole; nec erat tunc aliqua consideratio veritatis in me, quae me corrigeret et cohiberet; ne excedere tentarem mensuram meam, neque appetere praesumerem quae non sunt data hominibus scire et investigare. Descendi ergo in 160Boccupationem pessimam quam dedit Deus filiis hominum, ut distendantur in ea, et dispersi animum meum in omnia, et cogitatione coepi per cuncta discurrere, ut quaererem et investigarem de cunctis quae fiunt sub sole: at non valui. Et coepi laborare et taedio vehementer affligi; et vidi quod mens mea quocunque se vertebat, dolore et amaritudine et sollicitudine replebatur, et erat labor quaerendi immensus, et inventionis fructus exiguus. Fiebat ergo ut tandem aliquando poena ipsa et afflictio magna, prudentem me facerent. Et vidi cuncta quae sub sole fiunt et ecce universa vanitas et afflictio spiritus. Cognovi ergo veritatem, et reprobavi vanitatem, quia sensi afflictionem. Et videbar jam in totum correctus de perversitate mea; sed erat adhuc aliud involumentum; 160Cet nescivi quod perversi difficile corriguntur. Eram jam tunc correctus, ut de vanitate veritatem cognoscerem, et non eram correctus adhuc ne de veritatis cognitione superbirem. Excussa jam fuerat una erroris palea et restabat adhuc alia magis tenax atque inhaerens palea elationis. Tam difficile enim perversi corriguntur, ut correctionem et purgationem aut non admittant omnino, aut ad perfectum non recipiant. Propterea ego jam corrigi coeperam; sed nondum adhuc perfecte correctus eram; et ideo cognovi laborem praesumptionis meae, sed inventionis meae usum non cognovi. Cognovi vanam esse afflictionem, non profutura saluti quaerere; sed nondum cognovi vanam esse elationem 160Dde inventis superbire.

Propterea locutus sum in corde meo dicens: Ecce magnus effectus sum. Nescivi enim, quoniam inflatione tumueram, et ideo magnus mihi videbar, et dixi in corde meo: Ecce magnus effectus sum. In corde dixi: De corde enim tumui, et ideo in corde dixi; quia in corde vidi unde tumui, ut ibi esset elatio, ubi erat causa elationis. Locutus sum in corde meo: Ecce magnus effectus sum. Quam magnus!

Praecessi, ait, sapientia omnes qui fuerunt ante me in Hierusalem. Paulatim pergitur in corruptionem, et mens prava excrescente tumore in deterius semper praecipitatur. Primum de se plusquam debuit, sensit; deinde usque ad aliorum contemptum 161Avenit. Praecessi sapientia omnes qui fuerant ante me in Hierusalem. Propterea ergo tumuisti et inflatus eras; quia praecessisti sapientia omnes qui fuerunt ante te in Hierusalem. Et quantum hoc fuit ut ideo cervicem erigeres; quia praecessisti sapientia omnes qui fuerunt ante te in Hierusalem? Ne mireris, inquit. Saepe superbia singularitate magis gaudet quam comparatione. Neque enim semper attendere curat elatio quales illi sint, quos in comparatione praecedit; quia hoc solum nonnunquam illi ad exaltationem abundat, quod inter omnes qui fuerunt ante eum in Hierusalem, nullum sibi aequalem agnoscit. Propter hoc igitur et ego videns quod praecessi sapientia omnes qui fuerunt ante me in Hierusalem; et si paucos cernerem fuisse ante me in Hierusalem 161Bsapientes, vehementer tamen gloriatus sum illis me superiorem in sapientia considerans; quoniam licet nec plurimi, nec magni illi fuerunt ante me, quibus factus sum comparatione praecipuus: vidi tamen multos post me venire posse sapientes in Hierusalem quibus fierem exemplo sapientiae primus. Quod ergo me sapientia praetuli in comparatione praecedentium: ad hoc quoque spectabat quod gloriabar exemplo praecipuo in auctoritatem constitui futurorum, ut praecedentibus quidem summus, subsequentibus vero primus sapientiae auctor invenirer. Et ideo locutus sum in corde meo, dicens: Ecce magnus effectus sum et praecessi sapientia omnes qui fuerunt ante me in Hierusalem.

Et mens mea contemplata est multa sapienter et 161Cdidici. Ergo aliquantulum jam correctus eras, quia non dixisti, mens mea contemplata est omnia sapienter, sicut superius proposueras quaerere et investigare sapienter de omnibus quae fiunt sub sole; sed moderatius aliquid intulisti, dicens: Mens mea contemplata est multa sapienter, ut ostenderes te eruditum occupatione pessima, et vidisse vanitatem et afflictionem spiritus, ne amplius de universis praesumeres, sed tamen nondum plene correctum ut de plurimis non superbires. Quaerendo igitur omnia invenisti plurima, non omnia, et deficiendo ad omnia intellexisti non debere hominem de omnibus praesumere; sed inveniendo plurima non considerasti non debere hominem etiam de plurimis superbire. Ergo secundum aliquid correctus fuisti, et 161Dsecundum aliquid incorrectus, cum dixisti: Mens mea contemplata est multa sapienter et didici; quia licet multa fuerint ad pauca, et ipsa tamen pauca fuerunt ad omnia. Hoc vero ad humilitatem magis spectabat, ut qui jam defectum tuum expertus fueras erga omnia; inventa tua plurima non ad pauca aliorum plurima; sed pauca potius vocares ad ea, quae non potuisti, omnia. Sed quia temeritas curiositatis jam repressa erat per defectum et afflictionem sui in investigatione omnium; sed tumor elationis creverat in contemplatione plurimorum; ideo adhuc tumuisti et dixisti: Ecce magnus effectus sum, et praecessi sapientia omnes qui fuerunt ante me in Hierusalem et mens mea contemplata est multa sapienter 162Aet didici. Sed, quaeso te, si praecessisti sapientia omnes qui fuerunt ante te in Hierusalem, a quo didicisti ut diceres: Mens mea contemplata est multa sapienter et didici? Si sapientior omnibus fuisti, a quo discere potuisti quod ipse non noveris? An propterea etiam sapientior omnibus fuisti; quia ab omnibus didicisti et omnium sapientia in te uno collecta est, ut inde praecederes sapientia de universis singulos, quod dicens a singulis doctores habuisti universos? An forte non ab hominibus didicisti; sed experimenta rerum te docuerunt quae mens tua contemplata est sapienter, ut inde contemplatio sapientiae rationi certior fieret quod hanc ipse rerum effectus experienti manifeste comprobaret? Neque enim congruere videtur typo tuo ut ab hominibus 162Bdisceres, qui in tantum supra homines aestimatione elevatus fueras, ut non solum multa sapienter, sed et universa quae sub sole fiunt quaerere et investigare putares: ergo contemplatus es et didicisti; quia cogitasti et probasti, quatenus eo majorem vim atque potentiam intelligentiae tuae demonstrares quo cuncta argumenta rationis tuae ad visibilia rerum experimenta evidentius produceres. Et forsitan iste voluntarie in sapientia sua stultus factus est, ut stultos sapientiam doceat. Non enim vias erroris sui tam diligenter nobis exponeret nisi in eodem suo errore nostri eruditionem cogitaret. Propterea ingeminat adhuc et commendat malam illam diligentiam suam, atque eam de qua tumuit, sapientiam qualiter adeptus sit, subjungit, 162Cdicens:

Dedique cor meum ut scirem prudentiam atque doctrinam, erroresque et stultitiam. Quae verba sub eodem sensu duobus modis superioribus conjungi possunt; quia enim primum hanc elationem ostensurus, sic coeperat. Locutus sum in corde meo; ac deinde quid locutus sit subjungit. Ecce magnus effectus sum, et praecessi sapientia omnes, qui fuerunt ante me in Hierusalem; et mens mea contemplata est multa sapienter et didici; et postea id quod modo proposuimus intulit. Dedique cor meum ut scirem prudentiam atque doctrinam, errores et stultitiam. Potest haec tota series sub una continuatione comprehendi, ut totum hoc in corde suo dixisse intelligatur scilicet quod magnus effectus sit; et quod 162Domnes qui ante eum fuerunt in Hierusalem sapientia praecesserit; et quod mens ejus multa sapienter contemplata sit multaque didicerit; et quod cor suum dederit ut sciret prudentiam atque doctrinam, erroresque et stultitiam; et quod post haec omnia cum ita locutus esset in corde suo, et se extulisset de investigatione et consideratione tantarum rerum; tandem resipiscens agnoverit hanc quoque gloriationem vanam, et propter hoc subjungat:

Et agnovi quod in his esset quoque vanitas et afflictio spiritus: eo quod in multa sapientia multa sit indignatio; et qui addit scientiam, addit et laborem. Si quis autem distinguere velit sententiam, et hoc quod postremo intulimus seorsum a supradictis partiri, 163Apotest sic a praecedentibus inferre, ut quasi ea quae supra dicta sunt, omnia locutus sit in corde suo, scilicet quod magnus effectus est, quod praecessit sapientia omnes qui fuerunt ante eum in Hierusalem, quod mens sua contemplata est multa sapienter et didicit; et cum haec omnia dixisset in corde suo, deinde altiora adhuc investiganda testatur; ac si diceret: Haec omnia quae supra dicta sunt locutus sum in corde meo, et cum haec universa locutus essem in corde meo, tunc demum ex praecedenti contemplatione fiduciam sumens dedi cor meum, ut adhuc altiora quaererem, et profundiora investigarem; ut scilicet scirem prudentiam atque doctrinam, erroresque et stultitiam. Quod autem dicit dedisse se cor suum sic intelligendum est, quod liberum illud 163Bfecit et expeditum ut non per illa aut illa divideretur, sed totum propositae considerationi intenderet. In quo verbo etiam typum superbiae et tumorem elationis exprimit: quod cor suum contemplationi sapientiae dedisse se dicit; quasi illi possibilitas inveniendi verum protinus subesset, si tantum voluntas quaerendi non deesset. Ad quid autem dederit cor suum, exponit dicens: Ut scirem prudentiam atque doctrinam, erroresque et stultitiam. Superius multa se sapienter contemplatum fuisse et didicisse testatus est; nunc autem post haec omnia investigare disponit, ut sciat prudentiam, atque doctrinam, erroresque et stultitiam. Unde patet quod superiora ad rerum naturam referenda sunt; haec vero quae subjungit ad mores hominum, praepostero quidem ordine 163Cusus; quia prius vita propria corrigenda erat per circumspectionem morum; ac deinde caeteris quae extra propriam naturam fuerunt, studium adhibendum, ut primum interiores cordis oculi mundarentur a vitiis, et postea aperirentur in contemplatione veritatis. Sed elatio quae foris magna apparere voluit, primum exteriora quaesivit, ut prius per exteriorem scientiam viam jactantiae aperiret, deinde etiam interiora sua scrutando ad ostentationem foras projiceret. Unde recte cum dixisset prudentiam se quaesisse, pariter adjunxit etiam doctrinam; quia mens gloriae et ostentationis cupida, nequaquam prudentiam circumspectionis ad bene vivendum, sed ad docendum habere voluit; et ideo scientiam prudentiae sine scientia doctrinae inutilem, sibi et infructuosam 163Dfore reputavit. Quod autem etiam errores et stultitiam scire se voluisse fatetur: nequaquam ad hoc mala cognoscere voluit, ut cognita vitaret; sed ut et se de malorum cognitione extolleret, et alios de opere damnaret. Error vero est cum per ignorantiam malum committitur, stultitia autem cum malum cognitum non vitatur. Ergo et bona pariter et mala scire voluit, et cum scientia utrorumque doctrinam simul concupivit, ut totum quod mens per scientiam comprehenderet, per doctrinam ad ostentationem manifestare valeret. Sed perversus animus ubique nequitiae suae poenam inveniens, totum quod inordinate propter elationem appetiit, propter laborem et afflictionem spiritus refugit. 164ANam quia hunc pariter, et curiositas ad inquisitionem impellebat, et superbia ad ostentationem; dignum erat ut et tumidum labor premeret, et curiosum occupatio dissiparet, quatenus in poena saltem vitium suum agnosceret, eumque etsi non amor virtutis, vel dolor afflictionis ad mensuram cohiberet. Propterea superius curiosus occupationem invenit; hic vero elatus laborem et afflictionem; quoniam dum mala et bona non ad aedificationem, sed ad elationem scire quaerit: ipsa ei cognitio testimonium fit pravitatis suae, ut ipsa iniquum per conscientiam arguat, quam elatus ad ostentationem quaerebat. Inde enim semetipsum despicere cogitur, unde in oculis aliorum magnus fieri conatur; quia dum amplius scire quaerit quod de veritate aliis insinuet, 164Bmagis in semetipso videt de pravitate quod damnet. Hinc ergo sibi ipsi animus indignatur et rixam quamdam ac luctam sumit contra se, quia turpitudinem vitiorum quam superbia despicit, pravitas defendit. In hac ergo hujusmodi conflictatione grandis superbiae labor nascitur et indignatio; quia, dum subjacere vitiis dedignatur, atque ea a se propellere nititur, ne perficere valeat quod vult, pravis suis desideriis superatur. Inde ergo jam ipsam etiam cognitionem veritatis abominari incipit, ut quia id quod in semetipsa odit, propter infirmitatem, non potest tollere, possit saltem per ignorantiam non videre. Propterea cum dixisset in sua scientia laborem et afflictionem invenisse, atque eadem afflictio et labor unde esset, exposuisset, dicens: Eo quod 164Cin multa sapientia multa sit indignatio, et qui addit scientiam, addit et laborem, protinus qualiter per eamdem afflictionem spiritus et laborem et indignationem attritus et accidiatus ipsam scientiam superaverit; et animum suum ab inquisitione sapientiae ubi affligebatur ad delicias et voluptatem converterit, subjungit, dicens:

HOMILY VII. That the perverse are corrected with difficulty, etc.

The perverse are corrected with difficulty. Therefore they cannot understand, because they are perverse; and therefore they labor and do not feel it, and they take delight in their own affliction (Job 159CXXX), and think it is well with them while it is ill. For they are perverse to such a degree that the judgment of truth is not in them, thinking good to be what is evil, and what is good to be evil, putting darkness light, and light darkness; and esteeming bitter sweet, and sweet bitter (Isa. V). For they reckon that there are delights beneath the senses; and therefore they love their own griefs, and thrust themselves willingly upon the worst occupation, and are distended therein; because, while with blinded mind they desire what falsely seems to delight, they do not attend to what truly tortures and afflicts. Therefore then they do not see their own vanity and the affliction of spirit in all things which are done under the sun, because they are perverse and are corrected with difficulty. And the number of fools is infinite. For they are not only turned away, but also 159Dperverse. Turned away from God; in themselves perverse. And being turned away they are not easily converted, because being perverse they are corrected with difficulty. For if they were corrected in themselves, they would be converted through themselves. Because if they first received the judgment of truth in themselves, they would afterward see by their own judgment that vanity must be fled and truth followed. But now, being turned away, they do not see the light of truth; nor, being perverse, do they see by the light of truth; and therefore they are corrected with difficulty, because they know neither how to seek rightness and truth when absent, nor how to approve them when present. Therefore the perverse are corrected with difficulty, and the number of fools is infinite. For they would not be so many if they could easily be corrected. And in this it is manifestly shown how difficult the correction of the perverse is, that the multitude of fools 160Ais infinite Now therefore the perverse and stultitam are as hard to correction by their perversity as they are bold against truth by their multitude; and therefore the perverse are corrected with difficulty, and the number of fools is infinite. Wilt thou know, he says, how hard it is for the perverse to be corrected? Take me. I will this day become for thee an example of all. For I too was once perverse, and I myself did not understand my own perversity; but I thought myself to be upright, and to be acting rightly, when I proposed in my mind to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun; nor was there then any consideration of truth in me which might correct and restrain me, lest I should attempt to exceed my own measure, nor presume to desire those things which have not been given to men to know and to search out. I went down therefore into 160Bthe worst occupation which God hath given to the sons of men, that they may be distended therein, and I scattered my mind upon all things, and began to run through all things with thought, that I might seek and search out concerning all things which are done under the sun: but I was not able. And I began to labor and to be vehemently afflicted with weariness; and I saw that my mind, whithersoever it turned itself, was filled with grief and bitterness and anxiety, and the labor of seeking was immense, and the fruit of finding scanty. It came to pass therefore that at length the punishment itself and the great affliction made me prudent. And I saw all things which are done under the sun, and behold all is vanity and affliction of spirit. I knew therefore the truth, and I rejected vanity, because I felt the affliction. And I seemed already wholly corrected of my perversity; but there was still another entanglement; 160Cand I did not know that the perverse are corrected with difficulty. I was then already corrected, so that I might know truth out of vanity, and I was not yet corrected so that I should not be proud of the knowledge of truth. One chaff of error had already been shaken off, and there still remained another, more tenacious and clinging, the chaff of elation. For the perverse are corrected with such difficulty that they either do not admit correction and purgation at all, or do not receive it to perfection. Therefore I had already begun to be corrected, but I was not yet perfectly corrected; and therefore I knew the labor of my presumption, but I did not know the use of my finding. I knew that it is a vain affliction to seek things not profitable to salvation; but I did not yet know that it is a vain elation 160Dto be proud of things found.

Therefore I spoke in my heart, saying: Behold, I am become great. For I knew not that I had swollen with puffing up, and therefore I seemed great to myself, and I said in my heart: Behold, I am become great. In my heart I said: for out of the heart I swelled, and therefore in the heart I said it; because in the heart I saw whence I swelled, so that the elation might be there where the cause of the elation was. I spoke in my heart: Behold, I am become great. How great!

I went before, he says, in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem. Little by little one proceeds into corruption, and the depraved mind, as the swelling grows, is always cast headlong into the worse. First it thought of itself more than it ought; then it came even to the contempt of others. 161AI went before in wisdom all who had been before me in Jerusalem. Therefore then thou didst swell and wast puffed up, because thou didst go before in wisdom all who were before thee in Jerusalem. And how great a thing was this, that thou shouldst therefore lift up thy neck, because thou didst go before in wisdom all who were before thee in Jerusalem? Do not wonder, he says. Often pride rejoices more in singularity than in comparison. For elation does not always care to attend to what sort those are whom it goes before in the comparison; because sometimes this alone abounds for its exaltation, that among all who were before it in Jerusalem it recognizes none equal to itself. For this reason therefore I too, seeing that I went before in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem — even if I discerned that there had been few wise men before me in Jerusalem, 161Byet I gloried vehemently, considering myself superior to them in wisdom; since, although those before me, in comparison with whom I was made pre-eminent, were neither very many nor great, yet I saw that many wise men could come after me in Jerusalem, to whom I should become the first by the example of wisdom. That therefore I preferred myself in wisdom in comparison with those who went before looked also to this, that I gloried that I was established by a pre-eminent example into an authority for those to come, so that to those who went before I might be found the highest, but to those who came after the first author of wisdom. And therefore I spoke in my heart, saying: Behold, I am become great, and I went before in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem.

And my mind hath contemplated many things wisely, and 161CI have learned. Therefore thou wast already somewhat corrected, because thou didst not say, my mind hath contemplated all things wisely, as thou hadst above proposed to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things which are done under the sun; but thou didst bring in something more moderate, saying: My mind hath contemplated many things wisely — that thou mightest show thyself taught by the worst occupation, and to have seen the vanity and affliction of spirit, so as not to presume any further concerning all things; but yet not fully corrected, so as not to be proud concerning very many. By seeking all things therefore thou didst find very many, not all; and by failing toward all thou didst understand that man ought not to presume concerning all things; but by finding very many thou didst not consider that man ought not to be proud even concerning very many. Therefore in some respect thou wast corrected, and 161Din some respect uncorrected, when thou didst say: My mind hath contemplated many things wisely and I have learned; because, although they were many in comparison with few, yet those very things were few in comparison with all. But this looked rather to humility: that thou, who hadst already made trial of thine own failing with regard to all things, shouldst call the very many things thou hadst found not many in comparison with the few of others, but rather few in comparison with those things, all of them, which thou couldst not attain. But because the rashness of curiosity had already been repressed through its own failure and affliction in the searching out of all things, but the swelling of elation had grown in the contemplation of very many things, therefore thou didst still swell and say: Behold, I am become great, and I went before in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem, and my mind hath contemplated many things wisely 162Aand I have learned. But, I ask thee, if thou didst go before in wisdom all who were before thee in Jerusalem, from whom didst thou learn, that thou shouldst say: My mind hath contemplated many things wisely and I have learned? If thou wast wiser than all, from whom couldst thou learn what thou thyself didst not know? Or wast thou therefore also wiser than all, because thou didst learn from all, and the wisdom of all was gathered in thee alone, so that thence thou mightest go before in wisdom, out of all men, each one severally — in saying which thou hadst all men as teachers, from each severally? Or perhaps thou didst not learn from men, but the trials of things taught thee what thy mind contemplated wisely, so that thence the contemplation of wisdom might become more certain to reason, in that the very outcome of things manifestly proved it to one making trial? For it does not seem to accord with thy character that thou shouldst learn from men, 162Bthou who hadst been raised in esteem so far above men that thou didst think to seek and to search out not only many things wisely, but even all things which are done under the sun: therefore thou didst contemplate and learn, because thou didst think and prove, so that thou mightest demonstrate the force and power of thy understanding to be so much the greater, the more evidently thou didst bring forth all the arguments of thy reason to the visible trials of things. And perhaps this man willingly became a fool in his own wisdom, that he might teach fools wisdom. For he would not so diligently set forth to us the ways of his own error, unless in that same error of his he were thinking of our instruction. Therefore he still redoubles and commends that evil diligence of his, and subjoins how he obtained that wisdom of which he swelled, 162Csaying:

And I gave my heart that I might know prudence and doctrine, and errors and folly. Which words can be joined to those above in two ways under the same sense; for, being about first to show this elation, he had thus begun. I spoke in my heart; and then he subjoins what he spoke. Behold, I am become great, and I went before in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem; and my mind hath contemplated many things wisely and I have learned; and afterward he brought in that which we have just now set forth. And I gave my heart that I might know prudence and doctrine, errors and folly. This whole series can be comprehended under one continuation, so that he is understood to have said all this in his heart: namely, that he was made great; and that 162Dhe went before in wisdom all who were before him in Jerusalem; and that his mind contemplated many things wisely and learned many things; and that he gave his heart that he might know prudence and doctrine, and errors and folly; and that after all these things, when he had thus spoken in his heart and had exalted himself concerning the searching out and the consideration of so great things, at last, coming to his senses, he recognized that this glorying also was vain, and on this account subjoins:

And I knew that in these also there was vanity and affliction of spirit: in that in much wisdom there is much indignation; and he who adds knowledge, adds also labor. But if anyone wishes to distinguish the sentiment, and to divide off what we have brought forward last from the things said above, 163Ahe can draw it from what precedes in this way: that all the things which have been said above he spoke, as it were, in his heart — namely, that he was made great, that he surpassed in wisdom all who were before him in Jerusalem, that his mind contemplated many things wisely and learned them; and when he had said all these things in his heart, he then testifies that things higher still are to be investigated. As if he were saying: All these things which have been said above I spoke in my heart, and when I had spoken all these things together in my heart, then at last, taking confidence from the preceding contemplation, I gave my heart, that I might seek things higher still and investigate things deeper; namely, that I might know prudence and doctrine, and errors and folly. But that he says he gave his heart is to be understood thus: that he made it free 163Band unencumbered, so that it should not be divided among this thing or that, but should stretch itself wholly toward the consideration set before it. In this word he also expresses the type of pride and the swelling of elation: that he says he gave his heart to the contemplation of wisdom, as though the possibility of finding the truth lay ready at hand for him, if only the will to seek were not lacking. But to what end he gave his heart he sets forth, saying: That I might know prudence and doctrine, and errors and folly. Above he testified that he had contemplated and learned many things wisely; but now, after all these things, he disposes himself to investigate, that he may know prudence and doctrine, and errors and folly. Whence it is plain that the things above are to be referred to the nature of things, but these which he subjoins to the morals of men — using indeed a preposterous order, 163Csince first his own life ought to have been corrected by circumspection of morals, and then study applied to the other things which lay outside his own nature, so that first the inner eyes of the heart might be cleansed from vices, and afterward opened in the contemplation of truth. But elation, which wished to appear great without, sought first the outward things, so that first, through outward knowledge, it might open a way for boasting, and then, by searching its own inward things as well, might cast them forth without for display. Whence rightly, when he had said that he had sought prudence, he added doctrine equally; because a mind greedy of glory and display wished by no means to have the prudence of circumspection for living well, but for teaching; and therefore it reckoned that the knowledge of prudence, without the knowledge of doctrine, would be useless to it and unfruitful. 163DBut as for his confessing that he wished to know errors and folly also: by no means did he wish to know evils for this, that once known he might avoid them; but that he might both exalt himself over the knowledge of evils, and condemn others for their work. Now error is when evil is committed through ignorance, but folly is when evil that is known is not avoided. Therefore he wished to know both goods and evils alike, and along with the knowledge of both he coveted doctrine at the same time, so that all that the mind might comprehend through knowledge, it might be able to manifest for display through doctrine.
