Ita Deus descendit ad unum, et homo ascendit ad unum: et in uno duo inventa sunt, alterum ex nostro, alterum ex suo: erant quippe tria quaedam. Deus erat, justus et beatus, et homo erat miser et injustus: et quia haec convenire 181Bnon potuerunt, posuit se in medio homo Deus conjungens miserum et justum, ut per justitiam miseriam vinceret, et justitiam ad beatitudinem repararet. Igitur cum esset nobiscum Emmanuel per justitiam quam ad nos attulerat, et per miseriam quam a nobis assumpserat, redire coepit unde venerat. Ut in homine per justitiam miseriam vinceret, et hominem cum justitia per miseriam ad beatitudinem revocaret. Tenuit igitur justitiam, et sustinuit miseriam quousque miseriam vinceret, et justitiam coronaret. Et cucurrit, et praecessit nos. Passus pro nobis, et exemplum relinquens nobis, ut sequamur vestigia ejus (I Petr. II). Liberans nos a servitute peccati, ut et nos in miseria justitiam habeamus, 181Cet per miseriam cum justitia ad beatitudinem transeamus. Promittens nobis quod accepit, si patimur quod sustinuit; ut regnemus cum ipso, si patimur pro ipso. Ita igitur Verbum incarnatum factor et rex noster, quia sequi ipsum non potuimus in sua majestate, praecessit nos in nostra humilitate, et de nostro viam statuit ut ad sua perveniamus. Sed nec sic quidem sequi eum posset homo, nisi adjutus esset ab ipso; quia nec justus homo per mortem ad vitam curreret, nisi ille qui peccatori dedit justitiam etiam patienti constantiam daret. Recte igitur, qui sapientiam contemplatus fuerat, et quam per se nihil homo agnoverat, dixit: Quid est homo, ut sequatur regem factorem suum? Vere enim iste ad contemplandam sapientiam transiverat, et 181Dvere a sapientia illuminatus erat: multo magis nunc sapiendo veraciter hominis infirmitatem agnoscens, quam prius inaniter se ultra hominis possibilitatem extendens. Ibi enim elatus est ut deficeret, hic ut proficeret humiliatus. Illic extra se per elationem tumuit, ut in se evacuaretur, hic se per humilitatem ad se collegit, ut soli daretur. Et hoc totum sapientia fecit postquam eam contemplatus est, ostendens illi in luce sua prius tenebras ejus: postea, et lucem suam, et totum in luce sua, et per lucem suam. Et non erant tenebrae lux, nec in luce tenebrae erant; sed per lucem tenebrae videbantur, et a luce dividebantur, et ait:

Et vidi quia tantum praecederet sapientia stultitiam quantum differt lux a tenebris. Quomodo hoc videbatur? 182AQuia sapientia illuminat, stultitia excaecat. Et unde hoc probari potest, quod sapientia illuminat, stultitia excaecat? Intendite:

Sapientis oculi in capite ejus; stultus in tenebris ambulat. Modo probatum est quod sapientia illuminat, stultitia excaecat. In quo probatum est? Quia sapiens oculos illuminatos habet, stultus nihil videt. Si enim sapiens oculos illuminatos habet, ergo sapientia illuminat. Et sit stultus nihil videt, ergo stultitia excaecat. Nam sapientia lux est, et illuminat. Si habueris oculos quo illa attingit; si autem oculos habes ubi lux non est, oculos habes, sed nihil vides. Et quid prodest hoc? Sint ergo oculi tui ubi lux est, ne efficiaris quasi oculos non habens, si lucem non habes. Ubi autem est lux? Sursum est 182Blux ubi est sapientia. Nam sapientia sursum est; et lux sursum, et omnis lux de sursum venit. Et sicut deorsum tenebrae sunt sine luce, ita sursum lux sine tenebris. In medio vero post lucem tenebrae, et post tenebras lux. Propterea sunt dies coeli quos tenebrae non dividunt, neque obscurum interpolat. Et dies terrae sunt quibus tenebrae succedunt. Quia ubi sapientia semper est, semper lux est; et ubi sapientia non semper est, tantum lux est, quantum sapientia est. Et ubi sapientia nunquam est, nunquam lux est. Ergo lux est quo attingit sapientia, et quo non attingit sapientia, lux non est. Et quo non attingit sapientia, si attingit a fine usque ad finem, quid relinquitur extra quo attingere non 182Cpossit, quae totum penetrat et complectitur totum? Gyrum coeli circuivi sola, et profundum abyssi penetravi, et in fluctibus maris ambulavi (Eccli. XXIV): attingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponens omnia suaviter (Sap. VIII). Magna igitur quaestio est quidnam sit quo non attingit sapientia. Ubi oculi stultorum sunt, qui ambulant in tenebris et non vident. Aliam itaque Scripturam interrogemus, ubi sunt oculi stultorum, qui in tenebris ambulant et non vident. Dicit enim: Oculi sapientis in capite ejus; oculi autem stultorum in finibus terrae. Ergo in finibus terrae tenebrae sunt, et propterea non vident stulti qui ambulant in tenebris, quia oculos habent in finibus terrae. Nam si lumen ibi est ubi oculos habet, non ambulant in tenebris stulti; sed 182Dilluminatos habent oculos et vident. Si vero stultus in tenebris ambulat, et oculi stultorum sunt in finibus terrae, ibi procul dubio tenebrae sunt, ubi oculi videre non possunt. Et ubi est hoc? In finibus terrae. Ergo procul sunt tenebrae, et lumen prope est. Quare ergo facilius tenebras invenimus quam lumen? Forte, quia nos longe non sumus a finibus terrae et habitamus juxta populum tenebrarum, neque perreximus adhuc a finibus terrae ad audiendam sapientiam Salomonis (III Reg. X), ubi lumen est: idcirco impingimus in tenebras et caligamus a luce. Ipsa tamen lux prope est et ingerit se; sed lippientes oculi fuscum amant, et converterunt in tenebras. Ergo prope est lux, nos autem longe sumus; et tenebrae longe sunt, et nos propinquamus ad illas.

HOMILY X. On the remaining vanities, as far as that place: « The fool walketh in darkness. »

172C

And when I had turned myself to all the works which my hands had made, and to the labors in which I had sweated in vain, I saw in all things vanity and affliction of mind, and that nothing remains under the sun. We have heard above with how great zeal this man toiled at gathering riches and increasing his goods; and then, on his own testimony, we have learned how he poured out his soul upon wantonness and upon the trying of pleasure, in those affluences of things which he had prepared; but now let us hear what he subjoins after all these things. When, he says, I had turned myself to all the works which my hands had made, and to the labors in which I had sweated in vain, I saw in 172Dall things vanity, and affliction of mind, and that nothing remains under the sun. And so at the outset this presses a question upon us: how does this man now for the first time say that he has turned himself to seeing his own works, when hitherto he seems to have done nothing else than to have applied his intention and his zeal to these things? When he made his works great, built houses, planted vineyards, and made gardens and orchards, and built pools, had menservants and maidservants, herds and flocks, silver and gold, the substance of kings and of provinces, and the delights of the sons of men. When, in short, not only in deed but also in mind he had so plunged himself into the love of his own things and into pleasure that he reckoned this his own portion, and in a manner believed himself to have been made for nothing else than that 173Ahe might delight himself in all these things which he had prepared: did he not see what he was doing? But he saw the appearance; he did not foresee the corruption. He saw what those things seemed to be which stood, but he did not attend to what those had become which had perished. For the love of present things, while it turned the whole intention of the mind upon itself, and, having entered through the gaze of the flesh into the deceptive appearance of the things that were seen, occupied the eyes of the heart as well, at one and the same time both took away the memory of things past and hid the foresight of things to come. Whence it came about that, while he looked to those things alone which were seen, he could not recognize the truth in them either; and at the same time, in his own works, being turned toward them, he saw the appearance which was coveted, and being turned away, he did not recognize the vanity which was to be guarded against. But it sometimes happens that 173Btemporal goods are the more quickly detected to be vain when they have begun to abound the more — goods which often, when they are not had, are reckoned to have been able to profit, had they been at hand. But when, once had, they cannot, even in their own affluence, drive out the poverty of the mind, then for the first time they make manifest to him who tries them how scant a fruit they confer for those who labor. Whence fittingly this man, after so great an affluence of all things and the use of pleasures, says that he turned himself, that he might understand his own vanity. Because when he began to learn by experience that the things he possessed could not make him happy, then he recognized that the things sought with empty labor had made him far more wretched. When, he says, I had turned myself to all the works which my hands had made — namely, looking back to what sort of fruit could have followed such great labors — then, he says, I found 173Cthat the fruit of my labors was not repaid me in an equal balance, and therefore I judged that I had labored in vain, looking back on the labors in which I had sweated in vain. For in all things there is vanity and affliction of mind. First affliction, afterward vanity; but also after vanity, affliction; and before vanity, affliction; and in vanity, affliction; and the whole is vanity, and the whole is affliction. For all things are vain which, even while they are, do not show forth to their lovers what they promise; and when they are thought to be held fast, they pass away. But it could perhaps have seemed tolerable, if there were vanity alone and there were not affliction. But as it is, there is both affliction before vanity, and affliction in vanity, and affliction after vanity, since the things that were possessed with love can neither be acquired without labor, nor kept without anxiety, 173Dnor lost without grief. And therefore both the whole is vanity and the whole is affliction, because both in affliction there is vanity and in vanity affliction. And on this account, being turned, he rightly says: I saw in all things vanity and affliction of mind: and that nothing remains under the sun. For, instructed in his own affairs, he began to judge the affairs of others also; and what he had come to know in part, he truly pronounced of the whole, saying: Nothing remains under the sun. And from this it can be gathered how much, in other matters, whether toward good or toward evil, it avails a man to know what sort of man he himself has been to himself. For in some measure all things begin to be to you that which you yourself have been to yourself. If you do not see yourself, you see nothing well. If you are not deceived in the judgment of yourself, you are easily directed in the judgment of another. As here too, 174Abeing turned and directed, when he had subjoined concerning his own works: He saw in all things vanity and affliction of mind — at once, as one instructed in his own affairs, he begins to judge the affairs of others, and from the judgment of his own works he forms a sentiment about all things, saying: And that nothing remains under the sun. But because for perfection it does not suffice to reprove evils unless a man know also how to choose goods, he subjoined and said:

I passed over to contemplate wisdom. "Hebrew" is interpreted one passing over. This man, therefore, was made a Hebrew in order to contemplate wisdom. And indeed he himself was a Hebrew before too according to the flesh, but he was not a Hebrew according to the truth, until he began to pass over to contemplate wisdom. Just as one is called a Jew according to the flesh, and a Jew 174Baccording to the truth, so one is a Hebrew according to the flesh and another a Hebrew according to the truth. But he who is openly a Jew according to the flesh, and he who is openly a Hebrew according to the flesh, is not truly a Jew, and is not a true Hebrew. But he who in secret is a Jew according to the spirit, and according to the spirit is a Hebrew, is truly a Jew and truly a Hebrew. For many pass over according to the flesh and do not pass over according to the truth, because they do not pass over in order to arrive at the truth. They would more easily cross the seas and traverse far-off regions than reach the truth — and she is near. Near is, says Scripture, the word in thy mouth (Rom. X); and the truth of the word is in the heart, and the word itself is truth, because the truth is the word. 174CAnd though the truth herself is so near, yet nothing is farther from those who love folly. But what is more foolish than always to look upon the lowest things, and to have countenances bent down to the earth? For this was given to the beasts, to whom it is granted to desire nothing beyond. But wisdom dwells in the things above; and to her they are unwilling to be lifted up, who are compared to the beasts and gaze upon the earth. This is that very folly out of which this man passed over to contemplate wisdom, when he despised the false goods which he had loved on earth, and lifted himself up to contemplate and to love the true goods which are above; because in all these things which are below under the sun he beheld vanity. Therefore, when he had seen in all things vanity and affliction of mind, and that nothing remains under 174Dthe sun, he passed over to contemplate wisdom above the sun. O how difficult a passage, and a way of how many days, for those who have weak steps! And I know not whether the whole life of a man can suffice to accomplish this journey. For who, living in this mortal life, will be able to lay hold of wisdom fully? For wisdom is drawn from hidden things and is found in hidden things; and wisdom always loves the secret place, nor does she offer herself to be contemplated save to those who enter in to her. But this is very grievous to weak souls: that they should leave what they have loved and forsake what is beloved, and pass over to the desiring of things which they do not know unless they be instructed by their own griefs, and that things which before were sweet should begin to be bitter; and thus in a certain manner many are drawn back, and are compelled to enter and to pass over to contemplate 175Awisdom. For when they have begun to taste and to understand the sweetness and pleasantness of wisdom, then they have no more need to be compelled, but follow willingly; and they gladly despise all things and leave all things, that they may pass over to contemplate wisdom; and then they arrive quickly, because they run swiftly and seek ardently, and wisdom begins to be near to them, because they themselves draw near to her and do not go far off from her into alien desires. So when Moses was in the desert a shepherd of animals, and had an Ethiopian woman for a wife, he did not yet know any fire but a consuming one; therefore he wondered that the bush was burning and was not burned up (Exod. III). For as long as the soul feeds its own desires upon the lowest pleasures, and, bound by carnal concupiscence, has not yet come to the embraces 175Bof wisdom, it is in a fire consuming and devouring, even to perdition. For the flame of lust and the love of the flesh consume those whom they kindle. But the love of wisdom has light, and has no consuming; and if it kindles the cold, yet it does not burn up those who are burning. Therefore Moses wondered how the bush was burning and was not burned up. For he too was burning, because he had an Ethiopian wife; nor was this a miracle to him, but to burn and not be burned up: what he had not experienced, this was a miracle to him. And the miracle itself drew him and urged him to pass over and see the greatest vision — how the bush was burning and was not burned up; and he began to run into a sweeter desire, and to forget the old longings where he was burning and was burned up, 175Cand to loathe the love of his Ethiopian wife, because she was black and was not beautiful, nor like that Shunamite woman who warms old men and does not burn the young. For that fire, by which the bush was burning and was not burned up, did not signify the love of this Shunamite, that is, of wisdom; and therefore Moses, after he had passed over to see the vision, and had begun to feel how sweetly her flame burned, could no longer be held by the love of his Ethiopian wife, but, his heart kindled with a better fire, came even to converse with the Most High, and was sent for the salvation of the people. For in fire God spoke to him, and out of the fire he was heard, and through fire he was understood. And there was within a flame which had set his heart alight, by which, like the bush, he was burning and was not burned up. The mind itself had conceived God in fire, 175Dand through fire it knew God. For unless it had burned, it would not have seen nor known; because fire itself is love, and love itself is knowledge. He knew, therefore, and loved; he saw and burned; he tasted and loved; and fire conquered fire, love overcame delight. The Ethiopian woman was despised, deformed and black, whom her own flame had darkened, and her very love made her not lovable. She was despised in comparison with the fairer one; nor did he wish to serve any longer for her, who recognized that with her he would always be a slave. For the carnal life and the concupiscence of the flesh is not from God the Father, but from the devil the father; and it consigns its own lovers to the servitude of its father and subjects them to his domination. And Moses serves and feeds 176Athe cattle, and buys the love of a foul wife with base attendance; nor can he be free until God comes in fire and appears in love. For then he easily despises what he had loved wickedly, when he has begun to taste what he may desire more sweetly. And now Moses does not deign to serve for the Ethiopian woman; and although he does not cast her off afterward when she follows, yet he does not receive her into love. For, made a lover of wisdom, he ought so to have admitted the care of the flesh as not to subject himself by affection to it when it wantoned shamelessly, but yet to condescend by compassion to it when it was weak and compliant. For it is one thing to love for joy, another to endure for use. It is one thing to receive into the fellowship of love, and another to endure in the part of compassion. The life of the flesh is to be borne in necessity; wisdom 176Bis to be joined to us in love. That one is to be sought after for her own sake; this one is to be fled for its own sake to be endured for our sake. Therefore Moses after the vision does not serve in Midian the father of the Ethiopian woman, nor does she any more bear sons, as one driven back from the bed, where the place of love and of affection is; and another fairer and more lovable having been received, from whose fellowship the face of Moses would be made not dark but luminous, whose love was shown in that fire, when the bush was burning and was not burned up. But Moses ran that he might pass over and contemplate the vision, because he had not yet conceived the fire of wisdom nor felt its sweetness. Therefore he wondered, and by that very wonder was drawn, so that drawing near he might grow warm and burn. And the fire itself, which enlightened him while absent, kindled him as he drew near. Therefore, drawing near, 176Che loosed his shoe, gladly renouncing now the carnal desires, the sweetness of that love having been tasted and its pleasantness recognized. For what could the concupiscence of the flesh have availed, compared with the love of wisdom? Therefore Moses hastened to run and to see the vision, and to pass over to contemplate wisdom. And it has been made manifest how he passed over, and how he arrived at contemplating wisdom. How much he saw in her, and how much he came to know of him, and how he was made a friend of wisdom, penetrating even into her depths and privy to her secrets. And how many are there from the beginning who wished thus to pass over to contemplate wisdom? First Abraham, that great father, went out from the fire of the Chaldeans, and passed over to contemplate 176Dwisdom, and came into the land of vision which God showed him, and saw the brightness of wisdom and rejoiced. And Isaac had gone out to meditate, and passed over to contemplate wisdom; and God spoke with him. Jacob too, going on to contemplate wisdom, passed over as he came from Mesopotamia, and saw the Lord face to face, and his soul was made safe (Gen. XXXII). After these, all the patriarchs and all the prophets passed over, and all wished to contemplate wisdom. And last of all wisdom herself came, and passed over, and her friends contemplated her; since she had come for this, that she might be seen, lest she should be sought in vain if she were never seen; and she said to those who had passed over, that they might contemplate 177Aher. Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. Many kings and many prophets have wished to see what you see, and have not seen; and to hear what you hear, and have not heard (Matth. XIII). This she said, and passed over, that after her those might pass over who desired to contemplate her, lest perchance she should now not be sought, if she were always seen. And many others followed after her, and very many passed through, and wisdom was made manifold. And many wished to pass over and could not arrive, because they did not hold the way. Others passed over and arrived. Others wished to pass over and could not pass through, because they thought to go by themselves. For the philosophers of the nations also, they too wished to pass over to contemplate wisdom, but they went astray and became vain, because they thought to lead 177Bthemselves. And yet they had begun to pass over, and had arrived as far as something, and came up to the way; but they did not enter the way, because they did not believe in Christ. Do you wish to know how far they had come? They were on earth in body, and they ascended in mind and passed over all earthly things, searching out the heavenly. Even to the moon and even to the sun, even to the stars of heaven, finally even to heaven itself and even to the firmament itself they ascended by their own wit, and arrived by their understanding. And what was there beyond, whither they could have gone? But wisdom is above all things, nor can she be found within all things, she through whom all things were made. He is none of these things, from whom is everything that is. But where could they have found that? It was not seen, and yet it was sought; nor could it lie hid so as not to speak, 177Cnor be searched out so as to be found. Wisdom was within, and they were without; and they entered in mind after her, that they might pass over to contemplate wisdom. And they investigated and searched through wisely, and comprehended the secrets of nature, and found many hidden things; and none of these was wisdom, because all this was made through wisdom. Above all things, whither they ascended; within all things, whither they entered; and there was nothing beyond where they could have sought wisdom. And they fell and failed, searching out searchings; and it seemed to them that there was something divine above all things, and yet they did not know it nor understand it; but seeing, they grew the more dim, because with weak eyes they struck against a splendid light. And they began to reckon many false things concerning the true, and to liken God 177Dby their own perverse heart, not to what he was, but to what seemed to them, who could not see what he was. But they reckoned that they saw well, and became vain in their own thoughts; and they were the worse blinded, and were found to wander the more deeply the more subtly they searched. But others thought that wisdom was to be sought more subtly by morals; and very many became despisers of their own goods, but not correctors of their own vices. And these too arrived as far as something, because they had the appearance of truth, but did not hold the truth. They cast away money, but retained malice. What was without they cleansed, and what was within they kept polluted. But this was not wisdom, because it was not truth, 178Abut a false image alone. But they thought that they were walking along the road of the virtues; yet whither they were tending they did not know, because they did not know their own direction and end. And there were yet others who had certain virtues and were borne into them by a natural leading; and they passed over and arrived as far as something; and from a certain part of nature, by which she did not lie wholly subject to corruption, they saw the good and desired it. And it was given them to be capable of much in the pursuit of the virtues, and with an upright disposition inclined to goodness. Who does not know this — how many men of virtues they too had, and how great things, wonderful and worthy of imitation, they did: pursuing justice, cultivating piety, keeping chastity, confirmed in patience, steadfast in fidelity, circumspect in prudence — and what shall we say? Were not all these things 178Bgood? They were indeed, but of nature, not of grace; of creation, not of restoration: goods which nature had kept, lest she should be wholly corrupted; not goods which grace had given, that nature might be freed from corruption. Goods which grace had indeed given to nature when she was first created, and afterward had left to her when she was corrupted; but had not added over and above to her when she was to be purged from corruption. Goods by which the beauty of a nature well created might be proved; not by which the loftiness of a nature to be glorified might be acquired. All these, therefore, were goods for their own part, but they were not true goods, because they did not direct the mind by intention to the highest good. And by all these wisdom was not found, because she was not sought in truth; and she drew near neither to those, that she might enlighten their eyes to the truth, nor 178Cto these, that she might direct their steps to virtue. And therefore neither could the blind find her, nor the lame arrive at her. But let this our Hebrew say what he has done, and how much he has profited by his passing over; since he too testifies that he passes over with the rest to contemplate wisdom, saying: I passed over to contemplate wisdom. This, therefore, is what you ought to consider. For he who passes over to wisdom leaves folly behind. And what is it that follows?

Errors also, and folly. If he passes over to wisdom who passes over to contemplate wisdom, how does he withdraw from folly, or leave error behind, who passes over to contemplate errors and folly? But wisdom is light; error, however, and folly are darkness. And he who is in darkness sees neither the darkness 178Dnor the light. But he who is in the light sees both the darkness and the light, because all things that are reproved are reproved by the light. Since therefore he cannot see his own darkness, because he himself is still in darkness, but comes from the darkness to the light, that he may see through the light both the darkness and the light — not the darkness through darkness and the light through light, but darkness and light through the light alone. No one goes to darkness that he may see darkness, but comes to the light that he may see through the light not only light, but both darkness and light. He, therefore, who wishes to see his own darkness withdraws from it, lest he himself be in darkness and see nothing; and he passes over to the light, that through the light he may see darkness and light alike. Rightly therefore Ecclesiastes, when he passes 179Aover to contemplate wisdom, comes to her — about to contemplate errors and folly also — as to a light, that in her he may see both the darkness and the light. That is, that in her he may see also that she is wisdom; and that through her he may see errors and folly, which is not wisdom. For he who sees wisdom sees that she is wisdom; and he who sees errors and folly sees that this is not wisdom; and yet he can see wisdom, and can see errors and folly, only through her — and she is wisdom. He, therefore, who passes over to contemplate errors and to contemplate folly passes over to wisdom, just as he who passes over to contemplate wisdom passes over to wisdom. Yet the one — that is, errors and folly — he contemplates in order to flee it; but to the other, that 179Bis, to wisdom, he draws near in order to contemplate her; because neither of the two is wisdom, but to contemplate both is wisdom; and he who passes over to contemplate both passes over to nothing other than wisdom, nor does he leave behind anything other than errors and folly. Let him say, therefore: He passed over to contemplate wisdom, and errors and folly. What is error: not to know what is right. What is folly? To know and not to follow. What is wisdom? To know cognocere and to love the good. But to know evil and to hate it — this too is wisdom, and the first wisdom; because to have hated evil is to have loved the good, and to have known evil is to have understood the right. Wherefore to know and to love the good is wisdom, and this same is to hate and to have known evil. And all this is known in wisdom, 179Cwhen wisdom is seen, and what she is, that it may be loved; and what she is not, but is made manifest through her, that it may be hated. O how good this passing over is, and how happily he removes who removes to contemplate wisdom! What wonder is it if the God of the Hebrews is the Lord God, who makes such passers-over, and makes them pass over to such things? Pass over to me, says Wisdom, all you who desire me, and be filled with my generations. For my spirit is sweet above honey, and my inheritance above honey and the honeycomb. They that eat me shall yet hunger, and they that drink me shall yet thirst; they that make me clear shall have eternal life (Eccli. XXIV). Since I give light of doctrine to all as it were before the dawn; and I will enlighten all 179Dwho hope in the Lord. For do you wish to know how wisdom enlightens those who have passed over to contemplate her? Question this very man, who passed over to contemplate wisdom; and consider how he has been enlightened from the time that he began to see her. For how blind he was before he had passed over to contemplate her, you have heard sufficiently above, when he thought to go where there was no way for man: to seek out and to investigate all things that were under the sun; and believed it to be something great to investigate the nature of those things which stand outside the nature of man — things which, even if they be known, so far as lies in them, cannot confer salvation, nor, if they be unknown, take it away. There, therefore, he was blind, in not seeing nor knowing in himself what he could, nor desiring for himself what he ought. But 180Anow, enlightened by wisdom, attend to what he says.

What is man, I say? What is he, I say? I do not ask what he is as though admiring his dignity, but as knowing his infirmity. What is man? Man is nothing. Man is not anything such that he may be found sufficient for this. For what?

That he may be able to follow the king, his maker. For if he cannot attain the thing made, much more can he not follow the maker. If he cannot investigate what has been made, how can he comprehend him who made it? What is man, that he may be able to follow the king, his maker? His king and his maker. The very same who is king is maker. He is maker because he created; king, because he governs in that which he created, and directs it 180Bto that for which he created it. For he created in a great good, and directs to the highest good. Who is he that follows his maker? He who lives as he was made. Who walks according to that for which he was instituted? He who keeps the good which he received when created, and guards unpolluted what nature conferred. This man follows his maker. And who is he that follows his king also? He who tends toward that to which he is directed; who hastens to arrive whither he is invited; who obeys the laws of one who presides well; who at the command of him who orders bends himself to all things with a spontaneous will. This man follows his king. But who is the man who can answer God? Who will be found sufficient to render a return to God? If he himself goes before, and so that you may follow: then one thing is his, another yours. Nay, if he himself begins the good and you complete it, what is less 180Cis his, and what is greater is yours. If God goes before by beginning the good, and you follow after by perfecting it, you are now found not only equal to God, but greater. But perhaps he goes before by showing, so that you may follow by imitating. And where then is what is said: His mercy shall go before me and shall follow after? (Psal. LVIII.) Where is: Of him, and through him, and in him are all things? (Rom. XI.) Where is: What hast thou that thou hast not received? And if thou hast received, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received? (II Cor. IV.) For if to show is his and to follow is yours, then you have something which you have not received; nor are all things of him and through him and in him, but certain things are man's which are not of him, if a man can of himself do some things which are not 180Dthrough him. But wisdom does not enlighten for this, that a man should think thus; or that he should say that a man can have anything as it were from himself, who could not have even this from himself, that he is a man. What, then, does he say? What is man, that he may be able to follow the king, his maker? For how far do you think man is from God, that he should reach where he is? For what is it to reach where he is, unless it be to be what he is? And what is God? Or what is man? See how far apart they are. God is just and blessed; man unjust and wretched. See how greatly the just and the unjust, the wretched and the blessed, stand apart. But misery cannot be together with blessedness, nor can injustice arrive at blessedness. Justice is the way, blessedness the fatherland. But the servant of sin cannot be just, unless he has been freed from sin. See 181Atherefore that man cannot follow the king, his maker, unless he be first visited by the king, his maker. Man cannot go to him; but he can, if he will, come to man. Therefore the king and maker of man came to man. He came to that which man was, and he himself was made what he was not. He was made man for man, taking on our misery, retaining his own justice. And there appeared between God and men, as the mediator of God and men, the man God: as God drawing near to men through misery, and as man not withdrawing from God through justice. Thus God descended to one, and man ascended to one; and in the one, two were found, the one from what is ours, the other from what is his: for there were, as it were, three things. God was just and blessed, and man was wretched and unjust; and because these could not come together, 181Bthe man God set himself in the midst, joining the wretched and the just, that through justice he might conquer misery, and might restore justice to blessedness. Therefore, when Emmanuel was with us through the justice which he had brought to us, and through the misery which he had taken up from us, he began to return whence he had come. That in man he might conquer misery through justice, and might call man back, with justice, through misery to blessedness. He held justice, therefore, and endured misery, until he should conquer misery and crown justice. And he ran, and went before us. Suffering for us, and leaving us an example, that we may follow his steps (I Petr. II). Freeing us from the servitude of sin, that we too may have justice in misery, 181Cand through misery, with justice, may pass over to blessedness. Promising us what he received, if we suffer what he endured; that we may reign with him, if we suffer for him. Thus, therefore, the incarnate Word, our maker and king, because we could not follow him in his own majesty, went before us in our humility, and out of what is ours established a way, that we might come to what is his. But not even so could man follow him, unless he were helped by him; because not even a just man would run through death to life, unless he who gave justice to the sinner should also give constancy to him who suffers. Rightly therefore he who had contemplated wisdom, and had recognized how utterly nothing man is by himself, said: What is man, that he should follow the king, his maker? For truly this man had passed over to contemplate wisdom, and 181Dtruly had been enlightened by wisdom: much more now, in being wise, truly recognizing the infirmity of man, than before, vainly stretching himself beyond the possibility of man. For there he was lifted up so as to fail; here he was humbled so as to advance. There he swelled outside himself through elation, so as to be emptied within himself; here through humility he gathered himself to himself, that he might be given to the One alone. And wisdom did all this after he had contemplated her, showing him in her own light first his darkness, and afterward her own light also — and the whole in her light and through her light. And the darkness was not light, nor was there darkness in the light; but through the light the darkness was seen, and was divided from the light. And he says:

And I saw that wisdom excelled folly as much as light differs from darkness. How was this seen? 182ABecause wisdom enlightens, folly blinds. And whence can this be proved, that wisdom enlightens and folly blinds? Attend:

The eyes of a wise man are in his head; the fool walketh in darkness. Just now it has been proved that wisdom enlightens, folly blinds. In what has it been proved? Because the wise man has enlightened eyes, the fool sees nothing. For if the wise man has enlightened eyes, then wisdom enlightens. And if sit the fool sees nothing, then folly blinds. For wisdom is light, and enlightens. If you have eyes where she reaches; but if you have eyes where the light is not, you have eyes, but see nothing. And what does this profit? Let your eyes therefore be where the light is, lest you be made as one not having eyes, if you have not the light. But where is the light? Above is 182Bthe light, where wisdom is. For wisdom is above, and light is above, and all light comes from above. And as below there is darkness without light, so above there is light without darkness. But in the middle, after light there is darkness, and after darkness light. Therefore there are days of heaven which darkness does not divide, nor does obscurity break in upon them. And there are days of earth upon which darkness follows. Because where wisdom always is, there is always light; and where wisdom is not always, there is as much light as there is wisdom. And where wisdom never is, there is never light. Therefore there is light where wisdom reaches, and where wisdom does not reach, there is no light. And where does wisdom not reach, if she reaches from end to end — what is left outside, where she cannot 182Creach, she who penetrates the whole and embraces the whole? I alone have compassed the circuit of heaven, and have penetrated the depth of the abyss, and have walked in the waves of the sea (Eccli. XXIV): reaching from end to end mightily, and ordering all things sweetly (Sap. VIII). It is a great question, therefore, what that may be where wisdom does not reach. Where the eyes of fools are, who walk in darkness and do not see. Let us therefore question another Scripture, where the eyes of fools are, who walk in darkness and do not see. For it says: The eyes of a wise man are in his head; but the eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth. Therefore in the ends of the earth there is darkness, and for that reason the fools who walk in darkness do not see, because they have their eyes in the ends of the earth. For if the light is there where he has his eyes, fools do not walk in darkness, but 182Dhave enlightened eyes and see. But if the fool walketh in darkness, and the eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth, then beyond doubt there is darkness there, where the eyes cannot see. And where is this? In the ends of the earth. Therefore the darkness is far off, and the light is near. Why then do we find darkness more easily than light? Perhaps because we are not far from the ends of the earth, and dwell beside the people of darkness, nor have we yet gone from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon (III Reg. X), where the light is: therefore we strike against the darkness and are dimmed away from the light. Yet the light itself is near and presses itself upon us; but bleary eyes love the dark, and have turned themselves into darkness. Therefore the light is near, but we are far off; and the darkness is far off, and we draw near to it.

HOMILIA XI. Qui sint fines terrae in quibus sunt oculi stultorum: et quomodo sapientia attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter, etc.

183A

Ubi tamen sunt tenebrae, et ubi est lux? Et quis est finis? et finis quo attingit sapientia. Et qui sunt fines terrae, ubi sunt oculi stultorum qui ambulant in tenebris, et non vident. Et quod est caput sapientis ubi sunt oculi ejus qui non ambulat in tenebris sicut stultus, sed illuminatos habet oculos? Ne forte ergo et nos in tenebris remaneamus, inquiramus lucem sapientiae, ut intelligamus, ubi ipsa maneat sapientia, et divisionem lucis et tenebrarum. Ubi finiuntur lux et tenebrae, et terminum uniuscujusque. Usquequo ipsa sapientia, et quid ipsa, et quid 183Bextra ipsam, et quid sine ipsa. Primum, quia duos fines audivimus, alterum a quo et alterum usque ad quem se extendit Sapientia, attingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponens omnia suaviter (Sap. VIII). Et nondum adhuc cognovimus qui sunt isti duo fines, et ubi sunt, et an finem habeant isti fines, et an ultra istos aliud aliquid sit, quo non attingit sapientia. Et si est, quomodo fines sunt qui non perveniunt ad finem? Si autem non est, quomodo fines terrae ubi tenebrae sunt, intra istos fines continentur, et tenebrae esse possunt in luce, quia Sapientia attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter et disponit omnia suaviter. Primum ergo duo sunt fines rerum omnium. Alter est finis supra quem nihil, et alter sub quo nihil. Finis supra quem nihil, summum 183Comnium est. Finis sub quo nihil, infimum. Itaque duo sunt fines omnium, summum et infimum. Et quidquid in universitate est praeter summum et infimum, medium est inter summum et infimum. Et unumquodque quando magis discedit ab altero, tanto magis accedit ad alterum, sive a summo ad infimum, sive ab infimo ad summum. Vis nosse si forte Scriptura manifestius alicubi fines istos commemoret? Si ascendero, inquit Psalmista, in coelum, tu illic es; si descendero ad infernum, ades (Psal. CXXXVIII). Ergo coelum et infernum duos fines constituit excursus sui. Nihil autem altius est coelo, et nihil profundius inferno. Itaque coelum summum omnium est; infernus infimum, supra 183Dquod nihil et sub quo nihil, et pertingit Sapientia a fine usque ad finem, et implet totum ac penetrat. Si ascendo in coelum, inquit, tu illic es; si descendero ad infernum, ades. Non dixit, in coelo ades. Neque in inferno, illic es. Sed, si ascendero in coelum, illic es; si descendero ad infernum, ades. Ergo in coelo est, in inferno adest; in coelo manens, in infernum adveniens, in coelo exspectat advenientes, in inferno sequitur fugientes. Ascendentes in coelum illic eum inveniunt, descendentes ad infernum illic eum non effugiunt. Si ascendero in coelum, inquit, tu illic es; si descendero ad infernum, ades. Et tamen utrobique es, et ubi es, et ubi ades, pertingens a fine usque ad finem. A fine ubi es, usque ad finem ubi ades, fortiter, et disponens omnia suaviter. Ecce 184Amodo distinximus duos fines ad quos pertingit sapientia, summum et infimum, quorum alter quasi locus est sapientiae ubi consistit; alter vero velut excursus quidam et, ut ita dicatur, meta porrectionis qua se extendit. Finis ille a quo exit sapientia, caput est, ante quem nihil. Finis vero in quem excurrit, finis ultra quem nihil. Finis ille caput est et finis. Finis iste non caput, sed tantum finis. Caput est ille finis, quia ab ipso, et non supra; finis est, quia usque ad ipsum, et non ultra. Alter autem finis, caput non est; quia ab ipso nihil: sed tamen finis, quia quidquid usque ad ipsum, non ultra ipsum. Ille igitur finis qui sursum est, quasi principium et origo est, supra quem nihil. Finis vero qui deorsum est, quasi meta et terminus ultra quem nihil. Omnium 184Benim rerum origo et principium a summo est; terminus autem et finis in infimo. Quapropter finis deorsum finis est, et tantum finis. Finis vero sursum, non solum finis, sed et caput et finis. Si ergo coelum sursum est et infernus deorsum, et nihil altius coelo, et nihil profundius inferno inveniri potest: principium est coelum, et infernus finis. O quam bonum principium, et quam malus finis.

Ideo fortassis oculi sapientis in capite ejus sunt, quia in medio constitutus respicit principium suum, ut ibi finem faciat ubi accepit originem. Non est enim bonum in alium finem finiri, ubi finis est consumptionis non consummationis. Propterea homo qui ad aeternitatem creatus est, solus inter omnia animalia vultum erectum habet, ut coelum contempletur; 184Cet in finem consummationis tendat; et non solum visibile hoc coelum oculis corporeis suspiciendum existimet, sed mente quoque et cordis visione supra coelum usque ad invisibilia coeli, et spiritalia virtutum, oculos interiores clariore atque perspicaciore intuitu attollens, usque ad finem, qui non habet finem, in lumine aeternitatis contemplatione conscendat. Illud est verum coelum supra omne coelum: quod non solum coelum coeli est, sed coelum coelorum. Non primo secundum; sed primo, et secundo tertium. Propter hoc Paulus usque ad tertium coelum raptum se gloriatur (II Cor. XII), qui ad summum omnium mente pervenerat: et non solum visibile coelum, quod et humana cogitatio superare 184Dpotest transierat, sed ea quoque, quae invisibilia super hoc visibile totum creata sunt omnia transgressus ad primum principium, et aeternitatis caput inspiciendum elevatus erat. Hoc est coelum tertium. Primum enim coelum visibile est coelum. Secundum coelum est visibilis coeli invisibile coelum. Tertium coelum est coeli visibilis et coeli invisibilis invisibile coelum. Primum coelum tantum est coelum, et terrae coelum. Secundum coelum, coeli coelum. Tertium coelum, coelorum coelum. Et hoc coelum supra se non habet coelum. Primum coelum est supremus status conditionis. Secundum coelum est supra conditionem provectus virtutis. Tertium coelum est sublime contemplationis. Primus infernus est infimus status conditionis. Secundus infernus est 185Asub conditione defectus iniquitatis. Tertius infernus est profundum damnationis. Primum coelum et primus infernus, finis et finis. Secundum coelum et secundus infernus, finis et finis. Tertium coelum et tertius infernus, finis et finis. Et ubique Sapientia: Pertingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponit omnia suaviter. A primo coelo usque ad primum infernum, primus est excursus sapientiae. Incipiens enim a summo deorsum, et a supremo usque ad fundum rerum descendens, comitatur ac fovet cuncta quae operata est, ut non subsistant sine ipsa quae facta et creata sunt ab ipsa. A supremo autem usque ad infimum in universis quae subsistunt, singula quaeque quanto magis a perfecta pulchritudine consummatoque decore summorum degenerant, 185Btanto magis quasi fugientia quodammodo a sapientia elongant. Sed ipsa Sapientia fugam rerum a fine usque ad finem sequitur; quia in universis, quae fecit nihil ex toto deserens, singula quaeque a summis usque ad infima proprio convenientique suo generi decore moderando: his quoque se praesentem esse testatur. Eadem enim ipsa quae excellentissima creaturarum in summa et supereminenti pulchritudine disposuit; inferiora quoque consequenter coaptans et dispositione prosequens, usque ad fundum rerum nihil inordinatum relinquit. Pertingit itaque Sapientia ad finem usque ad ea quae in rebus omnibus infima sunt; quia in his etiam aliquid ejus invenitur, quae per infirmitatem conditionis et defectum naturae a summis longe recesserunt. Sed tamen ipsa 185CSapientia in summis quasi permanendo consistit; ad infima vero quasi excurrendo pertingit, quia illa in perfecto decore suo immutabiliter subsistentia nusquam ab ejus similitudine defluunt. Ista vero per defectum fugientia per idipsum tamen, quod in suo genere retinent pulchritudinis, sibi quoque sapientiam adesse ostendunt. Pertingit ergo ubique sapientia, quia in omni quod est, pulchrum aliquid est, et omne quod pulchrum est, sapientiae opus est. Quod vero in eo, quod est, pulchrum non est, Sapientiae opus non est; quia quod pulchrum est in omni quod est, ipsa fecit: quod autem pulchrum non est, ipsa non fecit, sed permisit in eo quod pulchrum fecit. Quare ergo non totum pulchrum fecit in eo quod fecit: et quare non fecit, ut non pulchrum 185Dnusquam esset in eo, quod fecit? Fortassis fatigata erat priora illa faciendo in quibus summam quamdam perfectamque pulchritudinem effecerat. Et idcirco caetera quomodo potuit, postea prosecuta est, faciendo quidem ut totum pulchrum esset quod in eis fecit, sed non faciendo, ut non pulchrum in eis non esset, quod non fecit sed permisit; quia ut omnino non esset, facere non potuit. Deinde itaque ad alia post alia descendendo, et alia post alia faciendo, tanto minus semper posterioribus operum suorum pulchritudinis ac decoris contulit, quando magis priora faciendo, et vires fortitudinis suae qua amplius posset, et qua sciret amplius, prudentiae suae vim ingeniumque consumpsit. Propterea rerum 186Aordo deorsum degeneravit ad infima descendens. Et nisi sapientia sibi prospexisset, ut in his tandem faciendi finem constitueret, non erat fortasse ultra pulchritudinis aliquid quod faciendis conferre potuisset.

Quid dicimus? Ergo in faciendo minorata est sapientia Dei? et debilis prosecuta opus suum in finem? Et ubi est pertingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter? Si fortiter pertingit Sapientia a fine usque ad finem: ergo non est defectu opificis, differens pulchritudo conditionis. Quare ergo non aeque pulchra sunt omnia, nisi ut magis pulchra sint simul universa? Nam si non essent differenter pulchra singula, non essent incomparabiliter pulchra universa; quia summa esset pulchritudo in singulis 186Bquaelibet excellens illa foret, et caeteris omnibus eminentior, non esset omnis pulchritudo in universis. Ergo Sapientia a fine usque ad finem fortiter pertingit; quia sic opera sua usque ad fundum rerum persequitur, ut etiam defectum inferiorum ad universorum pulchritudinem moderetur, ut inde universitas magis pulchra sit, quod in universitate quaedam aliorum comparatione et respectu defectum patiuntur. Nam hoc ipsum, quod in quibusdam ejus operibus pulchris non pulchrum videtur, turpe tamen non est, ubi est; sed minus in parte pulchritudinis habet, quia hoc in toto pulchrum est ad quod est. Ergo in nulla parte turpitudo, sed tamen in quibusdam partibus major, in quibusdam minor pulchritudo est; quia ex eo in toto partium maxima 186Cest, quod in partibus differens, et multipliciter variata distinctaque omnifariam pulchritudo est. Deinde sequitur, et dicit: Disponens omnia suaviter. Suaviter enim omnia disponit, quia in tam multis tamque diversis rerum generibus singula quaeque ad terminum suum promonens, nihil universitatis concordiam pacemque turbare permittit; sed sic unicuique quod suum est tribuit, ut dissimiliter currentia ad unum finem conducat, et ut unius operatio vim effectumque alterius non impediat. O Sapientia, quam late diffunderis, et tamen non dissiparis. Quam in longinquum porrigis te, et defectum non pateris! Quantus est excursus tuus, a summo usque in infimum! Quantum coelum distat a terra, et infernus 186Dsub terra ubi est finis terrae, et ultra non est terra; quantum distat summum ab infimo, totum penetrat Sapientia. Et brevis est tamen via haec Sapientiae, et compendiosa porrectio, et modicum putat sibi omne quod est, ut transeat et apprehendat, et penetret; nec longe esse quidquid spatio porrigitur, quod bonitate proximum sit. Multo vero amplius distare a justitia iniquitatem et longinquius duobus, coelo a terra, et inferno sub terra. Justitia enim altior coelo est, et non solum coelo, sed etiam iis qui sunt in coelo. Angeli in coelo sunt, et a principio in coelo sunt; et inde supra id quod facti fuerant per justitiam ascenderunt. Et justitia altior coelo est, iniquitas profundior inferno. Profundior enim est omni, quod in creatura imum est, quia quod per iniquitatem 187Alapsum est sub omni creatura est; nec potest esse profundius quidquam eo quo nihil est pejus. Quantum igitur ascendit qui in coelum ascendit; tantum ascendit, qui ad justitiam proficit. Et quantum descendit, qui ad infernum descendit, tantum descendit qui ad iniquitatem cadit. Quantum autem ascendit, qui de inferno ad coelum ascendit, tantum ascendit qui de iniquitate ad justitiam redit. Quantum vero descendit qui de coelo ad infernum descendit, tantum descendit qui de justitia ad iniquitatem ruit.

Et in his omnibus ascendunt usque ad coelos, et descendunt usque ad abyssos, et anima eorum in malis tabescat (Psal. CVI). Ergo coelum est justitiae, et infernus iniquitatis; et rapiuntur motus animorum 187Balterna fluctuatione incessanter quasi contrariis flatibus acti ascendentes, et descendentes; et fiunt exaltationes, et depressiones, et commotiones magnae in illo invisibili salo fluctuantium desideriorum. Venit spiritus bonus, et sursum impellit. Venit spiritus malus, et impellit deorsum: et ascendunt usque ad coelos, et descendunt usque ab abyssos, anima illorum tabescente in incerto malorum suorum. Et quid dicit? Si ascendero in coelum, tu illic es; si descendero ad infernum, ades. Si enim ascendis in coelum justitiae, habes illic tecum sapientiam continentem te ne cadas; si autem descendis ad infernum culpae, adest illic sapientia apprehendens te ne effugias. Sursum dexteram habet, et deorsum 187Csinistram, pertingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponens omnia suaviter. Sursum fortis, deorsum fortis, ubique invincibilis. Sursum fortis est ut eos, qui in ipsa confidunt a malo conservet, et eos qui de se praesumunt in malum deserendo praecipitet. Deorsum fortis est, ut contemnentes pro malo condemnet, poenitentes a malo justificet. Ecce quantos in summo conservavit, quantos de summo praecipitavit, quantos de imo erexit, quantos in imo deseruit. Manifesta sunt judicia ejus: et qui seipsum novit, novit quomodo haec omnia quotidie Sapientia operatur in secreto cordis humani semper judicio praesidens: et occulta retributione ac dispensatione invisibili, merita examinando, nunc per gratiam assumit, nunc per justitiam deserit, nunc per lenitatem 187Dparcit, nunc per districtionem punit. Et cum deseruerit iterum assumit, et cum assumpserit iterum derelinquit, ut nesciat homo finem suum, et sollicitus ambulet omni tempore vitae suae, ut qui jacent non desperent, et qui stant non praesumant. Si in coelo justitiae sunt, timeant ruinam. Si in inferno culpae, quaerant misericordiam. Ideo ipsa justitia primum descendit ad infernum; postea ascendit ad coelum, ut descendens, spem daret liberandis, ascendens viam ostenderet glorificandis. Attingit ergo sapientia a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponit omnia suaviter. Finem enim utriusque comprehendit, et boni videlicet quod est in ipsa; et mali pariter, quod in ipsa non est. Sed in eo quod est ex ipsa defluit ab ipsa, nec tamen omnino sine 188Aipsa, quia quod natura non gignit ex suo, coercet potestate in suo. Malum enim propriam sedem non habet, sed natura peregrinum a suo, in alieno commoratur, ut constet quod non est in suo; quia si bona non essent in quibus mala essent, mala omnino non essent. Cum enim malum aliud non sit, quam boni corruptio, et omne quod corrumpitur bonum, aliud est a quo deficit, aliud in quo consistit. Et in quo consistit bonum est, quod deficit autem a quo deficit a bono, malum est: defectus a bono alibi omnino esse non potest, nisi in eo, quod constat in aliquo bono. Igitur si nullum bonum esset, nullum omnino malum esset; quia non esset ubi esse posset malitiam, si non eam in suo pateretur, quae eam non fecit, Sapientia. Non enim Sapientia 188Bmalitiam fecit; sed in eo quod fecit, malitiam esse permisit, ut collata malitiae Sapientia vinceret, et comparata pulchrior appareret. Confert enim se, et commetitur Sapientia malitiae in operibus suis, et vincit eam utrinque, ut attingat a fine usque ad finem; quia Sapientiam malitia ad defectum currens non evadit, sed Sapientia malitiam ad provectum surgens transcendit. Ideo enim malitia ad defectum currens Sapientiam non evadit, quia non potest malitia ipsa, quae corrumpat invenire, nisi in iis quae Sapientia creavit. Sapientia vero propterea malitiam ad provectum surgens transcendit; quia non potest totum malitia corrumpere, quod Sapientia potuit creare. Ut ergo malitia comparetur, nihil per malitiam 188Cad non esse deduci potest, quod a Sapientia esse non acceperit; ut autem malitia superetur non totum quod a sapientia factum est, malitia corrumpit.

Currit ergo sapientia, ut attingat a fine usque ad finem transcendens malitiam in incorruptis bonis, quo malitia non accedit: et consequens malitiam in iis, quae corrupta sunt, quo malitia non praecedit. Non enim malitia Sapientiam praecedere potest, ut vel ante illius exortum prior inveniatur, vel post illius defectum, posterior quia et prius corruptione invenitur, quod aliquando corruptionem admisit, et posterius corruptione quod totum corrumpi non potuit, et supra corruptionem quo corruptio non accessit. Et propterea Sapientia malitiam vincit, et stultitiam praecedit; quia attingit a fine usque ad 188Dfinem, id est ab exortu omnis boni, ut malitiam transcendat ultra defectum cujusdam boni ut malitiam concludat. In quo enim omne bonum aliquando sine corruptione exstitit prior Sapientia agnoscitur. In quo autem etiam bono quod corrumpitur, post corruptionem aliquid superest boni, quod omnino corrumpi non potest, posterior Sapientia invenitur. Vincit ergo Sapientia malitiam; quia attingit a fine in quo omne bonum, initium accepit, usque ad finem, in quo etiam corruptum bonum post defectum boni in aliquo bono subsistit. Attingit autem a fine usque ad finem fortiter, ut ipsam malitiam potestate ad mensuram cohibeat, et ratione ad ordinem restringat, ne vel in finem se porrigat totum perimens corruptio, vel ad extrema se diffundat, 189Atotum deformans confusio. Propterea ergo fortiter ubique pertingit subjiciens malitiam dominationi suae: et quidquid illa corruptionis ad confusionem ingerit, haec lege mirabili secretaque dispositione ad decorem operum suorum convertit, ex non pulchro efficiens, ut pulcherrimum fiat quod pulchrum est, et quod bonum per se constat, ex eo quod bonum non est, in consummationem bonitatis consurgat. Attingit ergo a fine usque ad finem fortiter et disponit omnia suaviter. Nihil excipitur a suavitate ejus. Omnia disponit suaviter. Quae omnia? Prava et recta, bona et mala, obnoxia et adversa, omnia disponit suaviter: non solum bona, sed etiam mala; non solum recta, sed etiam prava; non solum obnoxia, sed etiam adversa. Omnia 189Bdisponit suaviter. Quam suaviter? Vultis scire quam suaviter disponit omnia? Sine violentia adversa subjicit; sine tumultuatione prava dirigit, et in pacatissimo regno suo, quod justitia intus tenet, mala quoque et adversantium vitiorum motus, sine coactione secreto ordine sapientissimaque dispositione servire facit. Tam suaviter enim omnia etiam non suavia disponit, ut omnia quae contra ejus voluntatem se erigunt, neque potenter exstinguat, ut nihil sint neque violenter compellat, ut nihil possint; sed esse sinens et posse annuens, currentia contra suam voluntatem manifeste permittit, et occulte conducit ad implendam suam voluntatem. Et cum mali volunt illa contra ipsam, sine ipsa volunt; cum autem possunt quod volunt, ab ipsa possunt. Cum vero faciunt 189Cquod possunt, putant quidem et volunt facere se quod ipsa non vult; et tamen non aliud faciunt, nec facere queunt quam quod ipsa vult. Manifeste enim permittuntur et occulte conducuntur, ut suaviter disponantur; et pertingit usque ad eos Sapientia fortiter, ut ipsos ad suam dispositionem restringat; et disponit suaviter, ne ipsos contra eorum voluntatem compellat. Sed et si quando exterius violentiam pravis voluntatibus adhibendis, sive plectendis adhibet; nunquam tamen suavitatem suae dispositionis deserit; quia in se tranquilla permanens, unde adversantium pacem male quietam turbat: inde regnum justitiae suae solidius ad pacem componit. Propterea ergo pertingit a fine usque ad 189Dfinem fortiter et disponit omnia suaviter.

Restat nunc maximus ille et supremus Sapientiae excursus, a fine usque ad finem: qui nullum habent finem. Sursum sublime contemplationis, et deorsum profundum damnationis. Isti enim fines non habent ultra alios fines, quibus ipsi finiri possint; sed omnia usque ad ipsos, quae facta sunt ad ipsos, et ultra ipsos nihil. Ad istos duos fines universorum cursum, incipiens a medio sapientia hinc inde sive promovende, sive deserendo disponens conducit; sursum ascendentibus viam sternens justitiam; deorsum descendentibus viam relinquens iniquitatem, ut per justitiam eatur ab beatitudinem, per iniquitatem vero et injustitiam perveniatur ad damnationem. Quo cum ventum fuerit, sistet universa in finibus 190Asuis; et fines ipsi nunquam habebunt finem. Et tunc quoque ipsa Sapientia pertinget a fine usque ad finem fortiter, ut amplius nunquam vel a retributione justorum deficiat, vel a poena iniquorum desistat: disponens omnia suaviter hinc ad gaudium, illinc ad supplicium aeternum. Sed, quaeso, quae suavitas in inferis erit? quae suavitas in tormentis aeternis esse poterit, ut dicatur disponens omnia suaviter? An ideo suaviter, quia ipsa suavis permanet quae disponit, licet illi suaves non sint quos disponit, nec illud suave sit in quo disponit? Quomodo tamen suaviter disponit? An ideo suaviter disponit, quia ipsa dispositio suavis est, etiamsi illa suavia non sunt quae disponit: et sicut mala non male, sed bene disponit, ita insuavia et amara suaviter disponit? 190BPropterea enim mala sunt, et ab omnipotenti bona mala esse permissa sunt, non ut mala dona fiant; sed ut de malis bonum fiat, et bona ipsa malorum comparatione pulchrius elucescant; non ut bona malis augeantur adjunctis, sed commendentur comparatis. Quis autem sapiens est, ut intelligat haec, quid mala faciant in regno boni: et tamen si nihil facerent in regno sapientiae omnino mala non essent? Ergo aliqui faciunt mala propter quod esse permissa sunt: et bonum faciunt ipsa et mala et non ipsa mala faciunt bonum, sed ex ipsis malis facit bonum: qui et bonis et malis uti novit ad bonum. Hoc autem Sapientia est, quae pertingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponit omnia suaviter.

HOMILY XI. What the ends of the earth are in which the eyes of fools are: and how wisdom reacheth from end to end mightily, etc.

183A

Yet where is the darkness, and where is the light? And which is the end? And the end where wisdom reaches. And which are the ends of the earth, where the eyes of fools are, who walk in darkness and do not see. And what is the head of the wise man, where his eyes are, who does not walk in darkness like the fool, but has enlightened eyes? Lest, therefore, we too perchance remain in darkness, let us seek out the light of wisdom, that we may understand where wisdom herself abides, and the division of light and darkness. Where light and darkness are bounded, and the limit of each. How far wisdom herself reaches, and what she is, and what is 183Boutside her, and what is without her. First, because we have heard of two ends — the one from which and the other to which Wisdom extends herself, reaching from end to end mightily, and ordering all things sweetly (Sap. VIII). And we have not yet come to know which these two ends are, and where they are, and whether these ends have an end, and whether beyond them there is anything else where wisdom does not reach. And if there is, how are they ends which do not arrive at an end? But if there is not, how are the ends of the earth, where the darkness is, contained within these ends, and how can there be darkness in the light, since Wisdom reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly. First, therefore, there are two ends of all things. The one is an end above which is nothing, and the other one below which is nothing. The end above which is nothing is the highest 183Cof all. The end below which is nothing, the lowest. And so there are two ends of all things, the highest and the lowest. And whatever is in the universe besides the highest and the lowest is a middle between the highest and the lowest. And each single thing, the more it departs from the one, so much the more does it approach the other, whether from the highest to the lowest or from the lowest to the highest. Do you wish to know whether Scripture perchance somewhere mentions these ends more manifestly? If I shall ascend, says the Psalmist, into heaven, thou art there; if I shall descend into hell, thou art present (Psal. CXXXVIII). Therefore he has established heaven and hell as the two ends of his own course. But nothing is higher than heaven, and nothing deeper than hell. And so heaven is the highest of all, hell the lowest — above 183Dwhich is nothing and below which is nothing — and Wisdom reaches from end to end, and fills the whole and penetrates it. If I ascend into heaven, he says, thou art there; if I shall descend into hell, thou art present. He did not say, In heaven thou art present. Nor, In hell thou art there. But, if I shall ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I shall descend into hell, thou art present. Therefore in heaven he is, in hell he is present; abiding in heaven, coming into hell; in heaven he awaits those who come, in hell he follows those who flee. Those who ascend into heaven find him there; those who descend into hell do not escape him there. If I shall ascend into heaven, he says, thou art there; if I shall descend into hell, thou art present. And yet in both places thou art — both where thou art and where thou art present — reaching from end to end. From the end where thou art, to the end where thou art present, mightily, and ordering all things sweetly. Behold, 184Awe have now distinguished the two ends to which wisdom reaches, the highest and the lowest, of which the one is as it were the place of wisdom where she abides, but the other is like a certain running-out and, so to speak, the goal of the stretching by which she extends herself. That end from which wisdom goes forth is the head, before which is nothing. But the end into which she runs out is the end beyond which is nothing. That end is both head and end. This end is not head, but only end. That end is head, because from it, and not above it; it is end, because up to it, and not beyond. But the other end is not head, because from it is nothing; yet it is an end, because whatever there is, is up to it, not beyond it. That end, therefore, which is above, is as it were a beginning and origin, above which is nothing. But the end which is below is as it were a goal and limit beyond which is nothing. For the origin and beginning 184Bof all things is from the highest; but the limit and end is in the lowest. Wherefore the end below is an end, and only an end. But the end above is not only an end, but both head and end. If, therefore, heaven is above and hell below, and nothing higher than heaven and nothing deeper than hell can be found: heaven is the beginning, and hell the end. O how good a beginning, and how evil an end.

Therefore perhaps the eyes of the wise man are in his head, because, set in the middle, he looks back to his own beginning, that he may make his end there where he received his origin. For it is not good to be ended in the other end, where the end is one of consuming, not of consummation. Therefore man, who was created for eternity, alone among all animals has an upright countenance, that he may contemplate heaven 184Cand may tend toward the end of consummation; and that he may reckon that not only is this visible heaven to be looked up to with bodily eyes, but that also with the mind and with the vision of the heart, lifting the inner eyes with a clearer and more piercing gaze above heaven even to the invisible things of heaven and the spiritual things of the virtues, he may climb up by contemplation, in the light of eternity, even to the end which has no end. That is the true heaven above every heaven, which is not only the heaven of heaven, but the heaven of heavens. Not second to the first, but third to the first and to the second. On this account Paul glories that he was caught up even to the third heaven (II Cor. XII), who had come in mind to the highest of all; and he had passed over not only the visible heaven, which human thought too can surpass, 184Dbut, having passed over also all those invisible things which were created above all this visible whole, he had been lifted up to behold the first beginning and the head of eternity. This is the third heaven. For the first heaven is the visible heaven. The second heaven is the invisible heaven of the visible heaven. The third heaven is the invisible heaven of the visible heaven and of the invisible heaven. The first heaven is only heaven, and the heaven of the earth. The second heaven, the heaven of heaven. The third heaven, the heaven of heavens. And this heaven has no heaven above itself. The first heaven is the supreme state of creation. The second heaven is the advancement of virtue above creation. The third heaven is the sublimity of contemplation. The first hell is the lowest state of creation. The second hell is 185Athe failing of iniquity below creation. The third hell is the depth of damnation. The first heaven and the first hell, end and end. The second heaven and the second hell, end and end. The third heaven and the third hell, end and end. And everywhere Wisdom: She reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly. From the first heaven to the first hell is the first course of wisdom. For beginning from the highest downward, and descending from the topmost even to the bottom of things, she accompanies and cherishes all things which she has wrought, so that the things which have been made and created by her may not subsist without her. But from the topmost even to the lowest, among all the things that subsist, each single thing, the more it degenerates from the perfect beauty and consummate comeliness of the highest things, 185Bso much the more, as if fleeing, does it in a certain manner go far off from wisdom. But Wisdom herself follows the flight of things from end to end; because, deserting nothing wholly among all the things which she made, and tempering each single thing from the highest to the lowest with a comeliness proper and fitting to its own kind, she testifies that she is present to these also. For she herself, the very same who disposed the most excellent of creatures in a highest and supereminent beauty, fitting the lower things also in due sequence and following them up with her disposition, leaves nothing disordered even to the bottom of things. And so Wisdom reaches to the end, even to those things which in all things are lowest; because in these too something of her is found, which through the infirmity of their creation and the defect of their nature have withdrawn far from the highest. But yet 185CWisdom herself abides in the highest things as it were by remaining, but reaches the lowest as it were by running out; because those things, subsisting unchangeably in their own perfect comeliness, nowhere flow away from her likeness. But these, fleeing through defect, yet by that very thing which they retain of beauty in their own kind, show that wisdom is present to them also. Wisdom therefore reaches everywhere, because in everything that is there is something beautiful, and everything that is beautiful is the work of wisdom. But what, in that which is, is not beautiful, is not the work of Wisdom; because what is beautiful in everything that is, she herself made; but what is not beautiful, she did not make, but permitted in that which she made beautiful. Why then did she not make the whole beautiful in that which she made; and why did she not bring it about that what is not beautiful 185Dshould nowhere be in that which she made? Perhaps she had been wearied in making those former things, in which she had wrought a certain highest and perfect beauty. And therefore she pursued the rest afterward as she could, bringing it about indeed that the whole should be beautiful which she made in them, but not bringing it about that what is not beautiful should not be in them — which she did not make, but permitted; because she could not bring it about that it should not be at all. And so thereafter, descending to one thing after another and making one thing after another, she conferred always so much the less of beauty and comeliness upon the later of her works, as she the more, in making the former, consumed the strength of her might, by which she could do more, and the force and ingenuity of her prudence, by which she might know more. Therefore the order 186Aof things degenerated downward, descending to the lowest. And unless wisdom had looked out for herself, so as at last to set in these an end of making, there was perhaps nothing further of beauty which she could have conferred on the things to be made.

What do we say? Was the wisdom of God, then, diminished in the making? and did it pursue its work feebly to the end? And where is that which reaches from end to end mightily? If Wisdom mightily reaches from end to end, then the difference of beauty in the creation is not from a failing in the maker. Why then are not all things equally beautiful, unless it be that all things together may be more beautiful? For if individual things were not beautiful in differing degrees, all things together would not be incomparably beautiful; because the highest beauty would be in individual things — whatever one there were would be surpassing that one, and more eminent than all the rest — 186Bnot every beauty would be in all things together. Therefore Wisdom mightily reaches from end to end; because she so pursues her works down to the very bottom of things that she even orders the defect of lower things toward the beauty of the whole, so that the universe is the more beautiful for this, that in the universe certain things suffer defect by comparison with others and in respect of them. For this very thing, which in certain of her beautiful works seems not beautiful, is nevertheless not ugly where it is; but it has less of beauty in the part, because in the whole it is beautiful for that to which it is ordered. Therefore in no part is there ugliness, but nevertheless in certain parts there is greater and in certain parts lesser beauty; because the beauty in the whole of the parts is greatest 186Cfor this reason, that in the parts it is differing, and manifoldly varied and distinguished in every way. Then follows, and he says: Ordering all things sweetly. For she orders all things sweetly, because in kinds of things so many and so diverse, advancing each single one promonens to its own term, she permits nothing to disturb the concord and peace of the universe; but she so assigns to each what is its own that she leads things running unlike to one end, and so that the working of one does not hinder the force and effect of another. O Wisdom, how widely thou art poured out, and yet thou art not scattered! How far into the distance thou stretchest thyself, and sufferest no failing! How great is thy course, from the highest even to the lowest! By as much as heaven is distant from earth, and hell 186Dbeneath the earth where the end of the earth is, and beyond there is no earth; by as much as the highest is distant from the lowest, so much does Wisdom penetrate through. And yet this way of Wisdom is short, and her stretching-forth is compendious, and she counts all that is a small thing for her to pass over and to lay hold of and to penetrate; nor is anything far off that is stretched out in space, if it be near in goodness. But iniquity is far more distant from justice, and farther than the two, heaven from earth, and hell beneath the earth. For justice is higher than heaven, and not only than heaven, but even than those who are in heaven. The angels are in heaven, and from the beginning they are in heaven; and from thence they ascended, through justice, above that which they had been made. And justice is higher than heaven, iniquity deeper than hell. For it is deeper than everything that is lowest in creation, because that which has fallen through iniquity 187Ais beneath every creature; nor can anything be deeper than that than which nothing is worse. By as much, therefore, as he ascends who ascends into heaven, by so much does he ascend who advances toward justice. And by as much as he descends who descends to hell, by so much does he descend who falls to iniquity. And by as much as he ascends who ascends from hell to heaven, by so much does he ascend who returns from iniquity to justice. But by as much as he descends who descends from heaven to hell, by so much does he descend who rushes down from justice to iniquity.

And in all these things they ascend even to the heavens, and they descend even to the depths, and their soul amid evils wastes away (Psal. CVI). Therefore heaven belongs to justice, and hell to iniquity; and the motions of souls are snatched along 187Bby an alternating surge without ceasing, as though driven by contrary blasts, ascending and descending; and there come to be liftings up, and pressings down, and great commotions in that invisible sea of billowing desires. The good spirit comes, and drives upward. The evil spirit comes, and drives downward: and they ascend even to the heavens, and they descend even from the depths, their soul wasting away in the uncertainty of its own evils. And what does he say? If I shall ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I shall descend to hell, thou art at hand. For if you ascend into the heaven of justice, you have there with you wisdom holding you fast lest you fall; but if you descend to the hell of guilt, wisdom is there laying hold of you lest you escape. Above she has her right hand, and below 187Cher left, reaching from end to end mightily, and ordering all things sweetly. Above she is strong, below she is strong, everywhere unconquerable. Above she is strong, so as to keep from evil those who trust in her, and to cast headlong into evil, by forsaking them, those who presume upon themselves. Below she is strong, so as to condemn for evil those who despise, and to justify from evil those who repent. Behold how many she has kept safe at the summit, how many she has cast down from the summit, how many she has raised from the depth, how many she has forsaken in the depth. Manifest are her judgments: and he who knows himself knows how Wisdom works all these things daily in the secret of the human heart, always presiding at judgment: and by hidden requital and invisible dispensation, weighing merits, now she takes up through grace, now she forsakes through justice, now through gentleness 187Dshe spares, now through severity she punishes.
