And when she has forsaken she takes up again, and when she has taken up she again abandons, that a man may not know his own end, and may walk anxiously all the time of his life, so that those who lie prostrate may not despair, and those who stand may not presume. If they are in the heaven of justice, let them fear a fall. If in the hell of guilt, let them seek mercy. Therefore justice herself first descended to hell; afterward she ascended to heaven, that in descending she might give hope to those to be set free, and in ascending might show the way to those to be glorified. Wisdom, then, reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly. For she comprehends the end of both — of the good, namely, which is in her; and equally of the evil, which is not in her. But in that which is from her it flows away from her, yet not altogether without 188Aher, because what nature does not beget out of her own, she restrains by power within her own. For evil has no proper seat of its own, but by nature a stranger to what is its own, it lodges in what belongs to another, so that it is plain that it is not in its own; because if there were not good things in which evils were, evils would not be at all. For since evil is nothing other than the corruption of a good, and everything that is corrupted is good, that from which it falls away is one thing, that in which it subsists another. And that in which it subsists is good; but that which falls away, from which it falls away from the good, is evil: a falling-away from good can be nowhere else at all except in that which subsists in some good. Therefore if there were no good, there would be no evil at all; because there would be nowhere that malice could be, if Wisdom, which did not make it, did not suffer it within her own. For Wisdom did not make 188Bmalice; but in that which she made she permitted malice to be, so that Wisdom, set against malice, might conquer, and being compared might appear the more beautiful. For Wisdom sets herself against malice and measures herself with it in her works, and conquers it on both sides, so that she may reach from end to end; because malice, running toward defect, does not escape Wisdom, but Wisdom, rising toward advancement, transcends malice. For malice running toward defect does not escape Wisdom for this reason, that malice cannot find what it may corrupt except in those things which Wisdom created. But Wisdom, rising toward advancement, transcends malice for this reason: that malice cannot corrupt the whole of what Wisdom was able to create. So that malice may be compared, then, nothing can be brought through malice 188Cto non-being which has not received being from Wisdom; but that malice may be overcome, malice does not corrupt the whole of what has been made by wisdom.

Wisdom runs, therefore, that she may reach from end to end, transcending malice in the incorrupt goods, whither malice does not come; and following after malice in those things which have been corrupted, whither malice does not go before her. For malice cannot go before Wisdom, so as to be found either prior, before her rising, or posterior, after her failing; because that also is found prior to corruption which at some time admitted corruption, and posterior to corruption that which could not be wholly corrupted, and above corruption that to which corruption did not come. And for this reason Wisdom conquers malice, and goes before folly; because she reaches from end even to 188Dend, that is, from the rising of every good, that she may transcend malice, beyond the failing of a certain good, that she may shut malice in. For in that in which every good at some time stood without corruption, Wisdom is acknowledged as prior. But in that good also which is corrupted, in which after the corruption something of good remains over which cannot be corrupted at all, Wisdom is found posterior. Wisdom therefore conquers malice; because she reaches from the end in which every good received its beginning, even to the end in which even a corrupted good, after the failing of the good, subsists in some good. And she reaches from end to end mightily, so as to hold malice itself within measure by her power, and to restrain it to order by her reason, lest either corruption, destroying the whole, stretch itself unto the end, or confusion, deforming the whole, 189Apour itself out to the uttermost parts. For this reason, therefore, she reaches mightily everywhere, subjecting malice to her dominion: and whatever of corruption malice brings in toward confusion, this Wisdom, by a wondrous law and a secret disposition, turns to the beauty of her own works, bringing it about out of what is not beautiful, that what is beautiful becomes most beautiful, and that what stands as good in itself rises up, out of that which is not good, into the consummation of goodness. She reaches, then, from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly. Nothing is excepted from her sweetness. She orders all things sweetly. What things all? Crooked and straight, good and evil, the subject and the adverse — she orders all things sweetly: not only good things, but evil ones too; not only straight things, but crooked ones too; not only subject things, but adverse ones too. She orders all things 189Bsweetly. How sweetly? Do you wish to know how sweetly she orders all things? Without violence she subjects adverse things; without tumult she sets crooked things straight, and in her most peaceable kingdom, which justice holds within, she makes even evils and the motions of the vices that oppose her to serve, without compulsion, by a secret order and a most wise disposition. For she orders all things, even things not sweet, so sweetly that all the things which raise themselves against her will she neither powerfully extinguishes, so that they are nothing, nor violently compels, so that they can do nothing; but, allowing them to be and granting them to be able, she manifestly permits things running against her will, and secretly leads them to the fulfilling of her will. And when the wicked will those things against her, they will them without her; but when they can do what they will, they can do it from her. And when they do 189Cwhat they can, they think indeed and wish to do what she does not will; and yet they do not do otherwise, nor are they able to do otherwise, than what she wills. For they are manifestly permitted and secretly led, that they may be sweetly ordered; and Wisdom reaches even to them mightily, so as to restrain them to her own disposition; and she orders sweetly, so as not to compel them against their own will. But even if at times she outwardly applies violence to crooked wills to be applied to, or to be chastised; nevertheless she never forsakes the sweetness of her disposition; because, remaining tranquil in herself, from that very source whence she disturbs the ill-quiet peace of those who oppose her, she thence composes the kingdom of her justice the more solidly unto peace. For this reason, therefore, she reaches from end even to 189Dend mightily, and orders all things sweetly.

There remains now that greatest and highest course of Wisdom, from end to end: which ends have no end. Above, the sublimity of contemplation, and below, the depth of damnation. For these ends have no other ends beyond them by which they themselves might be bounded; but all things reach as far as these, which were made for these, and beyond them nothing. To these two ends wisdom, beginning from the middle, ordering on this side and on that, whether by advancing promovende or by forsaking, leads the course of all things; strewing justice as a way for those ascending above; leaving iniquity as a way for those descending below, so that through justice one may go to blessedness ab beatitudinem, but through iniquity and injustice one may come to damnation. And when it has come thither, she will set all things in their own ends; 190Aand the ends themselves will never have an end. And then too Wisdom herself will reach from end to end mightily, so that never more will she either fail in the requital of the just, or desist from the punishment of the iniquitous: ordering all things sweetly, on this side to joy, on that to eternal torment. But, I ask, what sweetness will there be in the regions below? what sweetness will there be able to be in eternal torments, that it should be said, ordering all things sweetly? Is it sweetly for this reason, that she who orders remains sweet herself, although those whom she orders are not sweet, nor is that sweet in which she orders? Yet how does she order sweetly? Is it sweetly for this reason that she orders, because the ordering itself is sweet, even if those things are not sweet which she orders: and, just as she orders evils not evilly but well, so she orders unsweet and bitter things sweetly? 190BFor therefore evils exist, and good things have been permitted by the Omnipotent to be evils, not that evils may become gifts; but that out of evils good may come to be, and that the good things themselves may shine out more beautifully by comparison with evils; not that good things may be increased by evils joined to them, but that they may be commended by things compared with them. But who is wise, that he may understand these things — what evils do in the kingdom of the good: and yet, if they did nothing in the kingdom of wisdom, they would not be evils at all? Therefore some do evils on account of which they have been permitted to be: and both they themselves and evils do good, and evils themselves do not make good, but he makes good out of the evils themselves: he who knows how to use both good things and evil for good. And this is Wisdom, which reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly.

HOMILIA XII. In illud, secundum aliam translationem: Oculi stultorum in finibus terrae; ubi nostra habet: Stultus in tenebris ambulat, et in reliqua capitis secundi.

190C

Diutius fortassis quam tractatus brevitas postularet in his discutiendis immorati sumus; sed non plane quam rei difficultas exigeret. Nunc igitur quia invenimus finem, et finem de quibus Scriptura locuta est, cum diceret Sapientiam pertingere a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponere omnia suaviter; et istos fines quaerere propositum erat propter fines terrae, ubi sunt oculi stultorum, qui ambulant in tenebris, ne forte pertingat Sapientia ad fines 190Dterrae quae a fine pertingit usque ad finem, et lux in tenebris luceat in finibus terrae, si Sapientia pertingit ad fines terrae, quae pertingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponit omnia suaviter. Quia igitur istos fines invenimus. Si tamen ea quae de finibus istis diximus, interpretationi Scripturae suam veritatem digne accommodare valeant, et non sit alia excellentior interpretatio cui ista jure concedat, nunc restat inquirere qui sint isti fines terrae, qui commemorati sunt, et ubi sunt, sed et quae sit terra ipsa, et ubi sit, in cujus finibus sunt oculi stultorum, qui non respiciunt ad caput suum ut videant, et non ambulent in tenebris. Primum ergo quaeramus, quae sit terra ista, et ubi sit terra ista. Scimus autem quod in hoc mundo terra est et coelum est, 191Aet inter terram, et coelum est quidquid in hoc mundo est. Nam in hujus mundi corpore coelum supremum est, et terra infima et sicut supra coelum nihil hujusmodi est, quod in ipso coelo non est, ita sub terra nihil est, nisi forte quod in terra est. Et si dicimus de terra ista, quod in finibus ejus oculi stultorum sunt quomodo hoc stare non poterit. Magis enim perspicaces quam caecos oculos praedicamus, quos usque ad fines terrae visione sua porrectos asserimus. Quis justorum hoc potuit, ut ambitum terrae oculis lustraret, et tam longinqua spatia, quae multorum labore annorum vix confici potuissent, una visione percurreret? Ridiculum est vel hoc cogitare, quod Scriptura de visione corporali dixerit. De terra ista visibili: Oculi stultorum 191Bin finibus terrae, nisi forte quis in his verbis hoc significare credat, quod stulti quique et carnalis vitae amatores, qui a terrena bona tota, mentis intentione semper ambiunt, pro eis adipiscendis ac quaerendis usque ad exteras nationes, et saepe usque ad ultimos fines terrarum discurrunt: et propterea illic oculos habere dicuntur, quod cogitatione ac desiderio semper illuc intendunt. Sapiens autem qui ad ea, quae sursum sunt mentem erexit et intentionem dirigit, ipse oculos in capite suo habeat, pro eo quod ad id quod summum omnium ac principale est adipiscendum intendat. Posset hoc, quantum ad veritatem interpretationis pertinet, satis convenienter induci; si Sapientia nos ad altiorem intelligentiam, et terram aliam, aliosque fines, et oculos alios 191Ccogitandos non vocaret. Nam, si caput sapientis recte spiritualiter intelligitur, necesse est ut terram quoque et fines ejus propter oculos stultorum mystice et non corporaliter interpretemur. Sicut ergo hic mundus visibilis habet terram suam et coelum suum, sic homo habet terram suam, et coelum suum. Nam et ipse homo mundus est et minor mundus dictus est homo. Hujus terra est caro ejus, et coelum ejus anima ejus. Sed in hoc mundo majore intra coelum terra est, in mundo autem minore coelum intra terram. Et tamen mundi minoris coelum majus est, quam coelum mundi majoris. Terra vero ejus quid est ad terram illius? Quam parva est? et tamen coelum ejus in terra ejus. Quid est coelum in 191Dterra? Anima in corpore. Anima coelum, corpus terra. Anima in corpore; coelum in terra. Et tamen semper coelum sursum, terra deorsum. Nam, sicut coelum hoc terra suo loco excelsius est, ita coelum illud terra sua natura sublimius. Propterea in mundo majore, quae in terra sunt, sub terra sunt; quae extra terram sunt, supra terram sunt. In mundo minore, quae intus sunt supra sunt, quae foris sunt subtus sunt. Quae sunt intus, et quae sunt foris? Invisibilia intus sunt, visibilia foris sunt. Ergo invisibilia supra sunt, visibilia subtus; et invisibilia supra coelum nostrum, invisibilia sub terra nostra. Omnia terrena sub terra nostra sunt, quia ad ejus servitutem facta sunt, et ad ejus obsequium ordinata. Ergo supra terram terra nostra. Et quid dicam? 192ANonne et supra coelum est terra nostra? Nonne illuc portavit eam, et illic collocavit eam sumptam de nobis, qui eam sumpsit pro nobis? Ergo supra coelum est terra nostra. Facta erat primum per naturam supra terram terra nostra, postea ivit per culpam in terram, et sub terram, terra nostra; sed nunc per gratiam elevata est supra coelum terra nostra. Ergo terrena omnia sub terra nostra sunt. Et est tamen ipsa terra terrenis juncta et quadam amicitia copulata, sicut coelum coelestibus junctum est et foederatum, et terra usque ad terrena, et coelum usque ad coelestia. Ergo terrena fines sunt terrae, et coelestia fines coeli; quia terra usque ad terrena et non ultra, et coelum usque ad coelestia et non ultra. Terra per concupiscentiam tendit se usque ad terrena, et 192Bcoelum per sapientiam tendit se usque ad coelestia. Caro enim, ut ait Apostolus, concupiscit adversus spiritum; et spiritus adversus carnem (Galat. V). Spiritus enim concupiscit sursum et caro concupiscit deorsum: et ideo in contrarium alteri utrumque se tendit. Et utrumque cum pervenerit quo tendit, ibi finem facit et non ultra se tendit. Ergo fines terrae terrena sunt, quo terra carnis per desiderium carnale tenditur. Et habet quidem terra nostra alium finem, judicii, sed desiderii alium finem non habet. Hucusque per desiderium tenditur, sed per judicium ultra ducitur. Per desiderium quidem concupiscentia tenditur ad terrena; sed per judicium post terrena in terram ducitur post terram ad gehennam. Per concupiscentiam ad voluptatem, post 192Cvoluptatem ad iniquitatem, post iniquitatem ad mortem, post mortem ad damnationem. Unusquisque, ait Scriptura, tentatur a propria concupiscentia abstractus, et illectus. Concupiscentia enim, cum conceperit, parit peccatum; peccatum autem, cum consummatum fuerit, generat mortem (Jac. I). Concepit dolorem, et peperit iniquitatem. Convertetur dolor in caput ejus, et in verticem ipsius iniquitas ejus descendet (Psal. VII).

Itaque carnalium voluptatum delectationes fines terrae sunt, et delectationes quidem carnis sequitur mors carnis. Mortem vero carnis sequitur ultio damnationis. Igitur fines terrae unum finem habent mortem quo excipiuntur, et consumuntur; mors 192Dautem finem habet damnationem, quo excipitur et consummatur. Delectationes enim carnales morte consumuntur, ut amplius non sint; mors vero carnis damnatione consummatur, ut semper sit. Istos fines stulti considerare nolunt, qui oculos habent in finibus terrae. Tantummodo enim primos fines terrae intuentur circa terram, ubi terra ipsa finitur; non ultra alium finem, ubi isti fines finiuntur. Intendunt ad fines desiderii sui, non ad fines judicii sui. Ad delectationem carnis suae, et ad voluptatum suarum illecebras oculos aperiunt, et quid ultra postea futurum sit non attendunt. Ideo stulti sunt qui in media via finem faciunt, ubi non est finis: et non prospiciunt finem ubi est finis. Cor stultorum ubi laetitia est et cor sapientium ubi tristitia (Eccle. 193AVII) Et alia Scriptura dicit. In omnibus operibus tuis omnis diebus vitae tuae, memorare novissima tua, et in aeternum non peccabis (Eccli. VII). Propterea stulti peccare non timent, quia ad solam respiciunt peccati delectationem, non autem respiciunt quae deinde sequitur, delectationis damnationem. Oculi stultorum in finibus terrae; oculi sapientis in capite ejus. Quod est caput sapientis? Quod cuique summum est, hoc caput est illi. Caput enim summum hominis est. Caput ergo sapientis, hoc est quod sapienti summum est. Quid autem sapienti summum est, nisi quod summum omnium est. Neque enim sapiens esset, qui pro summo haberet, quod summum non esset. Itaque summum omnium caput sapientis est: et fortasse ipsa sapientia, hoc caput est, quam 193Bqui sapiens est, cunctis praeponit, quae concupiscendum aliquid habere videntur, et in ejus comparatione despicit universa. Et recte, quia Sapientia summum omnium est; caput sapientis ipsa est, quoniam et hoc ipsum quod sapiens est, ab ipsa Sapientia est, et quod esse cupit, sapiens totum in ipsa est. Quapropter caput sapientis non aliud rectius accipitur, quam ipsa Sapientia; quoniam ab ipsa est bonitatis origo, et in ipsa consistit omnis boni consummatio.

Itaque summum omnium caput sapientis est, et hoc caput non aliud quam ipsa Sapientia est; quoniam Sapientia summa omnium est. Summum ergo bonum caput est, et summum malum finis. Duo enim sunt summum bonum, et summum malum, 193Caltrinsecus ex adverso constituta, et de medio universa bona, et mala ad istos duos fines recurrunt. Omne bonum ad summum bonum, et omne malum ad summum malum. Non enim est verum bonum, nisi conducat ad summum bonum, nec verum malum nisi recurrat ad summum malum. Ergo similiter omne malum ad summum malum, sicut omne bonum ad summum. Sed non similiter omne malum a summo malo, quemadmodum omne bonum a summo bono. Omne enim datum optimum, et omne donum perfectum desursum est descendens a patre luminum (Jac. I). Et de malis quid? Initia, inquit, dolorum sunt haec (Matth. XXIV). Ergo a summo bono omne bonum, et ad summum bonum omne bonum. Similiter 193Dad summum malum omne malum, sed non a summo malo omne malum. Ergo summum bonum omnium bonorum, et caput est, et finis. Summum omnium malorum caput non est, sed tantum finis. Igitur omne bonum praeter summum bonum, in tantum bonum est, quantum conducit ad summum bonum; et omne malum, praeter summum malum, in tantum malum est, quantum conducit ad summum malum. Multi enim fuerunt qui media ista bona habuerunt, et vera bona eis non fuerunt, quia per ea ad summum bonum non pervenerunt. Et multi fuerunt qui media mala gravia sustinuerunt, et mala eis non fuerunt, quia per ea ad summum malum non descenderunt. Illi itaque falsis bonis elati ad summum malum corruerunt; isti falsis 194Amalis exercitati, et humiliati ad summum bonum profecerunt. Propterea sapiens usque ad caput suum oculos levat, et non sufficit ei aliquid, quod infra est, donec perveniat ad id quod summum est. Quidam enim oculos sursum habuerunt et usque ad caput oculos non erexerunt, sed in corpore medio remanserunt. Sed quid facerent membra sine capite? Nunquid vivere possent membra a capite praecisa? ita omne bonum, sine summo bono non est verum bonum. Vidistis hominem abstinentem ab his quae lege prohibentur, non homicidium facientem, non adulterantem, non rapientem, non falsum testimonium perhibentem, non concupiscentem rem proximi sui, et dixistis hominem bonum, bonae vitae, bonae conversationis, dignum laude, dignum retributione. 194BEt quam multi fecerunt haec, et Deo non placuerunt; quia propter Deum non fecerunt, quod fecerunt: et ideo nec bene fecerunt, quia propter summum bonum non fecerunt. Vidistis alium adhuc altius ascendentem et majora bona facientem, non solum a malo abstinentem, sed etiam in bono se exercentem, jejunantem, orantem, elemosynas multas tribuentem, compatientem miseris, subvenientem in angustia, et tribulatione constitutis, et praedicastis magnum et imitatione dignum, quasi Deo proximum et delectum. Et tamen multi omnia ista fecerunt, et nihil profecerunt; quoniam Deum in causa non posuerunt. Non habuerunt oculos in capite suo sicut sapiens, sed in tentationem suam deorsum curvantes, vel sibi, vel aliis placere cupientes 194Cet de bono suo sine Deo gloriantes, bonum suum perdiderunt, et ad summum bonum non pervenerunt. Merito enim membra viva tenere non potuerunt, qui caput a corpore praeciderunt. Ideo oculi sapientis in capite ejus, ut ad summum bonum prius mentis intentione ac desiderio praecedat, postea studio et actione subsequatur, deinde retributione perveniat. Praecedat intentione, ut omne quod facit, pro illo adipiscendo faciat; subsequatur studio, ut in illo perseveret; perveniat retributione, ut illud in praemium accipiat. Tali modo igitur oculi sapientis sunt in capite ejus.

Propterea namque caput nostrum cum esset deorsum, nobiscum ne forte nostra quoque intentio deorsum 194Dremaneret, ascendit sursum caput ad caput, ut nos traheret post se: et ecce sursum sunt non duo capita, sed unum caput. Caput enim deorsum fuit Christus homo in mundo, et caput sursum fuit Deus Pater in coelo. Vis scire quod Christus caput est? Caput mulieris vir, caput viri Christus (I Cor. XI). Et caput omnis Ecclesiae Christus constitutus est a Deo. Et ipsa Ecclesia sponsa Christi, et corpus Christi, quid dicit de sponso suo Christo? et de capite suo Christo? Ipsa namque sponsa est, quae in canticorum dilectum suum commendans, post multa talia et alia multa, hoc in ejus laudem addit, dicens: Caput ejus aurum optimum (Cant. V). Ergo caput est Christus, et caput habet Christus. Et quod est caput Christi? Audi Apostolum: Caput mulieris vir; caput 195Aviri Christus: Caput Christi Deus (I Cor. XI). Itaque caput Christi est Deus: et ipse Christus ascensurus in coelum dixit: Ascendo ad Patrem meum, et Patrem vestrum: Deum meum et Deum vestrum (Joan. XX). Si ergo ad Deum ascendit, ad caput suum ascendit; quia caput Christi Deus. Et hoc caput est aurum illud optimum quod nulla rubigo consumit, nulla vetustas conficit; quia immortalis divinitas corruptionem non recipit. Ecce igitur caput nostrum sursum est Christus, et caput nostrum sursum est Deus, et unum caput nostrum Christus et Deus; quia et Christus Deus, et unus Deus Christus: et caput Christi Deus et unum caput Christus, et caput Christi Deus; sicut unum principium Christus, et caput Christi Deus: Ego, inquit, 195Bprincipium, qui et loquor vobis (Joan. VIII). Hoc enim principium ipsum est caput nostrum: ad quod sapiens oculos suos erexit, nunc ad illum intendendo per fidem, ut postmodum in illud oculos suos habere possit, illud contemplando per speciem. Ad hoc principium et ad caput istud, ut oculos levemus Scriptura nos admonet, dicens: Si consurrexistis cum Christo, quae sursum sunt sapite, ubi Christus est in dextera Dei sedens; quae sursum sunt quaerite, non quae super terram. Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo (Coloss. III). Nam ubi mortui sumus, ibi sapere non debemus; sed ibi sapere debemus, ubi vitam habemus. Si mortui sumus super terram, quomodo sapimus super terram? Quis enim mortuus sentit? Ibi 195Citaque sentire debemus, ubi vitam habemus; ibi sapere, ubi vita nostra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo, ubi Christus est ad dexteram Dei sedens. Quid est sapere? amare ipsum, est sapere. Amor enim ipse sapor est, et dilectio ipsa sapientia est. Amare itaque quae sursum sunt, hoc est sapere ea, quae sursum sunt; quia ipsa dilectio illuc trahit, ubi est quod diligitur: et habet interim saporem suum quo reficitur, donec perveniatur ad id quod diligitur. Quia ergo quod per sapientiam diligitur, sursum est; idcirco sursum trahit ipsa Sapientia. Et quia quod per concupiscentiam diligitur, deorsum quoque trahat necesse est ipsa concupiscentia. Ab eo autem quo Sapientia sursum trahit, et concupiscentia deorsum, quasi divisio est tenebrarum a luce: et quae corda 195Ddeorsum descendunt a luce deficiunt; quae vero ascendunt in luce sunt. Qui enim ad vanitatem descendunt, a veritate deficiunt, et qui a veritate deficiunt, deficiunt a luce; quia veritas lux est. Et non deficit ipsa lux, sed ipsi a luce deficiunt, quando tenebrae fiunt; quia tenebrae non sunt lux, nec illuminantur a luce ut luceant. Tamen ipsa lux lucet etiam in tenebris, sed tenebrae eam non comprehendunt (Joan. I), ut eam in se suscipiant, et participes ejus fiant, quoniam tenebrae luci communicare non possunt. Istae ergo sunt tenebrae in quibus ambulant stulti: qui terrena sapiunt et non intelligentes honorem suum, comparati sunt jumentis insipientibus et similes facti sunt illis (Psal. XLVIII). Nam 196Aquia more jumentorum sola terrena appetunt, et coelestia nullo mentis affectu requirunt; ita tandem carnis delectatione caecantur, et voluptatum illecebris sopiuntur, ut nec cogitare valcant a quibus bonis ceciderint, neque ad quae mala sint perventuri prospicere. Quid igitur isti, nisi in tenebris ambulant, qui ita prava delectatione caecati sunt, ut nec vera bona possint cognoscere, nec vera mala praevidere? Quas tenebras intus patiuntur qui lucem praesentem non vident, et illud bonum non possunt agnoscere, cujus praesentiam nulla valent aversione declinare? Quare hoc? nisi quia stultitia excaecavit oculos eorum: quam in finibus terrae illos defixerunt, statuentes apud se oculos suos declinare in terram.

196BSed ne forte contrarium quis putet quod hic stultus in tenebris ambulare dicitur, et quod illic, ut commemoratum est, oculi stultorum in finibus terrae esse perhibentur. Videtur enim quasi utrumque affirmatum, quod videant et non videant, cum utrumque tamen verum simul esse possit, quod videant et non videant. Nam qui dixit: Stultus in tenebris ambulat, videtur omnino dixisse quod stultus non videat. Et rursum qui dixit: Oculi stultorum in finibus terrae, videtur dixisse, quod aliquid videant, vel ea quae sunt in finibus terrae. Quomodo ergo in tenebris ambulant, si vident? Quomodo autem non vident, si ea vident, quae sunt in finibus terrae? Sed sciendum est quod stulti non ideo in tenebris ambulare dicuntur, quod nihil videant: vident enim, 196Cquae sunt in finibus terrae, sed quod sive in his quae vident, sive in his quae non vident, veritatem non videant. Visibilia enim tamen per intentionem et desiderium vident, et invisibilia non vident. Et in his quae vident, putant bonum esse, quod non est; et in his quae non vident, nesciunt, bonum esse, quod est. Itaque nusquam veritatem vident, et ideo in tenebris ambulant etiam in his, quae vident. Excaecavit enim corda eorum delectatio carnis et illececebra voluptatum, ut veritatem non videant. Quia mens falsa dulcedine inebriata dum hoc solum, quod in praesenti dulce et jucundum videtur, cogitat, nec reminisci potest quanta dulcedo sit eorum bonorum a quibus aversione sua corruit, nec providere quanta sit amaritudo malorum supervenientium, ad quam 196Dsemper praecipitationis suae ruina festinat. Et nota quomodo se consequitur sententia veritatis. Superius namque iste considerata vanitate rerum mundanarum, contemptis omnibus ad contemplandam sapientiam se transtulit, dicens: Transivi ad contemplandam sapientiam, erroresque et stultitiam. Deinde considerans quod vera sapientia hominis alia non est, quam vera bona quaerere, et amare quae sursum sunt, ubi rex noster est: qui nos idcirco praecessit, illuc ascendens, ut quo sequeremur ostenderet. Attendens quoque quam difficile mentem terrenis delectationibus assuetam ad desideria aeternorum erigere, adjunxit et ait: Quid est homo, ut sequi possit regem factorem suum? Vides tamen 197Aquod corda, quae ad delectationes carnales se mergunt, a lumine veritatis tenebrescunt, quasi definitivam boni malique sententiam dedit, dicens: Vidi quod tantum praecederet sapientia stultitiam quantum differt lux a tenebris. Deinde studium utriusque commendans novissime adjunxit, et ait: Sapientis oculi in capite ejus stultus autem in tenebris ambulat. Quapropter ad summam recurrat sententia, et dicat: Difficile quidem est hominem mortalem ad contemplationem supernae sapientiae cor desideriis terrenis pressum erigere; sed tamen quia sapientia lux est, et omnes qui ab ejus contemplatione deficiunt, in tenebris sunt, necesse est, quantum possibilitas suppetit, etiam mortalem hominem quaerendae atque investigandae Sapientiae studium adhibere. 197BHaec est enim sapientia hominis in hac vita, Sapientiam quaerere et investigare. Nam invenire sapientiam et perfecte apprehendere verum, non huic vitae datum est, sed futurae repositum. Habet tamen ipsa inquisitio Sapientiae nunc lucem suam, qua discernit eos qui amant Sapientiam et quaerunt ab iis qui stultitiam amant, et ambulant in tenebris. Sed mens carnalis jucunditatem visibilis lucis amans, pro interna luce quaerenda labore vanum existimat; quia ejus claritatem post hanc lucem sublatam, in mentibus sanctis inexstinguibilem permanere aut dubitat aut prorsus ignorat. Nam quia pari sorte similique conditione sapientes patitur et stultos, ab hac luce visibili cernit post mortem carnis subtrahi: dubium ei fit etiam de luce 197CSapientiae, an ipsa possit in mentibus sanctis post mortem carnis inextinguibilis conservari. Propterea licet studium ipsius Sapientiae bonum ac laudabile esse consideret, utrum tamen tanto labore comparandum sit, dubitat, cujus fructus an perpetuus esse possit, nondum adhuc ei ratio ulla indubitata manifestat. Hanc ergo fluctuationem humani cordis iste in semetipso, et per contemplationem veritatis videns, et per affectum communis infirmitatis sentiens, per sententiam quoque assumit, ostendens qualiter quaesitam visamque sapientiam, ipsa eum mortalis vitae consideratio a studio sapientiae revocabat, et quod idcirco alios in sapientia procedere vanum omnino existimaverit, quia in reddendo mortis debito, 197Dparem caeteris se esse agnovit. Hoc est enim quod, post laudatam Sapientiam studiique ejus commendationem, subito nunc ad considerationem communis infirmitatis conversus infert, dicens:

Didici, quod unus utriusque esset interitus. Quia enim vidit utrumque, id est et sapientem et stultum uno mortis interitu ab hac vita subtrahi, etiam hoc dubitare coepit, utrum post hanc vitam diversa meritorum praemia secundum hanc ipsam diversam hujus vitae conversationem debeant inveniri. Et si hoc verum esse constat, quare una via ab hac vita exeunt, qui post hanc vitam ad unum praemium non pertingunt? Si vero quemadmodum unus cunctis transitus est, ita etiam universis fit una perventio: quare ante mortem dissimiliter laborando currerent, 198Aqui simili morte exeuntes ad dissimile post mortem praemium, non pervenirent? Hoc est enim quod sequitur: Et dixi in corde meo: Si unus, et stulti, et meus occasus erit, quid mihi prodest, quod majorem sapientiae dedi operam? His enim, qui hanc vitam solam esse credunt, studium Sapientiae vanum omnino existimatur: propterea quod ejus labor praesentis vitae est, praemium autem et fructus laboris futurae. Idcirco quia laborem vident, cito ipsum laborem fastidiunt, et facile ad ea convertuntur, quae etsi sapientia nequaquam appetenda esse doceat, quia tamen eorum fructus praesens est, commodiora existimant. Sed quia Sapientia etiam in hac vita laborem suum omnino infructuosum esse non sinit, eosque qui se sectantur, magna intus consolatione 198Brefovet, ac per illuminationem veritatis in hac mortalitatis miseria de aeternitatis praemio habere fiduciam suadet, iste statim postquam pro vitae carnalis defectu de fructu vitae perpetuae dubitare coeperat, pro eadem sua dubitatione ex intima se consideratione accusat, dicens:

Locutusque cum mente mea, animadverti quod hoc quoque esset vanitas. Et continuo causam adjungens quare supradictam dubitationem rem vanam esse testetur, et vanitatem ipsam cujus respectu veritatis ei in dubium venire potuisset infert, dicens:

Non enim erit memoria sapientis similiter, ut stulti in perpetuum. Sapientia enim, quae vitae praesenti mortalitatem non tollit futurae vitae tribuit 198Caeternitatem: et licet sapientis et stulti in exitu hujus vitae similis conditio sit, in futura tamen vita similis memoria non erit. Sicut enim hic eos dispar vivendi conversatio dividit, ita illic quoque cum in memoriam venerint ut ad judicium adducatur, dissimilis pro meritis suis retributio separabit. Neque enim futura tempora oblivione cuncta operient, sed venient in recordationem tempore suo cuncta quae facta sunt, ut in judicium advocetur omne opus, sive bonum sive malum sit. Propterea sapientis memoria non in perpetuum non erit similiter ut stulti, et futura tempora non operient cuncta oblivione, quia, cum tempus advenerit, et iste pro merito virtutis suae gloriam, et ille pro stultitiae suae excessu 198Dpoenam percipiet. Hoc est ergo pro quo vanum non est stultitiam devitare, et majorem sapientiae dare operam; quia, cum praemium retributionis percipitur, quantus sit justi laboris fructus manifestatur. Habet tamen justum quoddam taedium, haec ipsa nostrae mortalitatis consideratio; quia dignum est ut homo quod transitorium videt etiam prius quam finiatur despiciat? et pro eo adipiscendo, quod diu stare non potest, inani se labore non affligat. Propter hoc rursum de eadem pari mortalitatis conditione sententiam ingeminat, dicens:

Moritur doctus similiter ut indoctus: et idcirco taeduit me vitae meae. Merito siquidem talis vita in taedium venit, quae tota confusioni obnoxia, neque in bonis suis dum stare videtur, neque in malis suis 199Adum finitur, bonos a malis vel dignos ab indignis secernit. Bona siquidem ejus sine discretione ad indignos pariter ut ad dignos perveniunt, et mala illius bonos simul et malos parili sorte et eodem proventu affligunt. Unde, et bona quoque vitae hujus justis in despectum jure veniunt: quae et pro se laborantes variis doloribus affligunt, et saepe multo labore quaesita sine utilitate possidentium ad malos a bonis et a suis ad alienos transeunt. Quod iste considerans non solum, quae mala videntur hujus vita, sed ea quoque quae speciem boni praetendunt, re autem vera mala sunt, universa ad unam partem constituens, similique aestimatione adjudicans unam de cunctis sententiam dat, dicens:

Videns mala esse universa sub sole, et cuncta vanitatem, 199Bet afflictionem spiritus, rursus detestatus sum omnem industriam meam. Et ne forte putares eum illam hic industriam detestari qua majorem sapientiae dedit operam, et non illam potius qua eorum occupatione, quae sub sole vana sunt, distendebatur: mox quam industriam detestandam existimet, exponit dicens: Et quae [qua] sub sole studiosissime laboravi. Subauditur detestatus sum. Continuoque causam quare et haec, et eorum pariter industriam detestetur, aperit, cum subjungit:

Habiturus haeredem post me, quem ignoro, utrum sapiens an stultus futurus sit: et dominabitur in laboribus meis quibus desudavi, et sollicitus fui. Et novissime de hoc commendans judicium suum infert.

199CEt est quidquam tam vanum? Ac si diceret: Nihil ego tam vanum judico, quemadmodum cum alius avare congregans casso labore atteritur, alius et otiose, et luxuriose vivens in alienis laboribus dominatur. Multiplex enim vanitas est, ubi alius sine causa affligitur, alius illicite delectatur. Prima namque vanitas est non profutura appetere; secunda transeuntia congregare; tertia nostro labore parta aliis, et eis maxime quos quales futuri sint, nesciamus possidenda relinquere. Si enim vana essent haec omnia, etiam in nostros usus quaesita et retenta, quid erunt ad stultorum voluptatem transmissa? Unde ait:

Cessavi, renuntiavitque cor meum ultra laborare sub sole. Causam quoque quare a labore cessaverit 199Dingeminans subjungit, dicens:

Nam cum alius laboret in sapientia, et doctrina, et sollicitudine, homini otioso quaesita dimittit. Hoc ipsi contigit Salomoni, qui in sapientia, et doctrina, et sollicitudine laborans congregavit divitias, et opes cumulavit, et tandem omnia stulto haeredi possidenda reliquit. Reliquit enim stultitiam generis sui filium Roboam, qui in paternas opes succedens, omnia dissipavit, regnumque paternum, quod amplum satis et magnificum susceperat, minoratione sensus et cordis saturitate scissum turbatumque dereliquit. Sed et multi laborant sapientia, et doctrina, et sollicitudine cum magno labore, et studio secreta naturae, et arcana veritatis rimantes, et inventa memoriae 200Aposteritatis ad commendanda studia sua verbo pariter, et scripto transmittentes, ac saepe otiosis quaesita relinquunt, quia nonnunquam subsequentium negligentia hoc paratum in usum assumere respuit quod priorum sagax diligentia non sine grandi labore, et cura acquisivit.

Hoc ergo vanitas est, malum magnum. Vanum est idcirco in cognitione veritatis laborare, ut in notitiam illorum veniamus, qui veritatem nec propter se suscipere volunt, neque in aliis sciunt approbare. Hujusmodi ergo laborem fructus non sequitur, quia nec sibi profutura congregat, nec quibus congregata derelinquit, aliqua virtutis aemulatione ad studium boni provocantur. Si enim quaerenti labor est, et accipienti utilitas non est, quid prodest labor talis? 200BSed et malum magnum est, ut unde alius labore atteritur, alius otiose et illicite abutatur. Malum enim est magnum, quia et ille malo suo colligit et iste accipit in malum suum. Propterea vanitas est hoc et malum magnum.

Quid enim prodest homini de universo labore suo, et afflictione spiritus, quo sub sole cruciatus est? Si non ad aliud prodest, nihil prodest; imo vero si non ad aliud prodest, multum nocet, quia poenam magnam habet ejus inquisitio, sed fructum inventio non habet. Quae est enim poena nunquam esse sine poena?

Cuncti dies ejus doloribus, et aerumnis pleni sunt: nec per noctem mente requiescit. Multum miser est, qui nec illud tempus, quod naturaliter quieti datum 200Cest, quietum habere potest. Per diem labore atteritur, per noctem cura et sollicitudine laboris cruciatur. Quem enim vigilantem distensio laboris et inquietudo exagitat; dormientem quoque animo per imagines, et phantasias insomniorum ingesta fatigat. Nullum ergo tempus intermittitur requiei, totum dolori et labori occupatur, et nihil utilitati ac saluti acquiritur.

Et hoc nonne vanitas est? Vere vanitas est, et magna vanitas prorsus. Sed quid tunc? Si hoc vanitas est, quid ergo faciendum est?

Nonne melius est, inquit, comedere, et bibere, et ostendere animae suae bona de laboribus suis? Si vani sunt labores qui utilitatem non conferunt laborantibus, 200Dergo melius est laborare et fructum capere laborum suorum. Ratio manifesta videtur, sed multa habet exceptionem. Multo enim melius si dictum fuisset, et ubique verum constaret. Si vani sunt labores ex quibus laborantibus fructus non provenit, ergo ejusmodi labores omnino postponendi sunt, et laborandum potius in iis ubi et certus et verus laborantibus fructus proveniat. Nunc autem hac ratione vanitas mutata est, non dimissa, et alia alii vanitas successit, non omnis vanitas discessit. Vena sollicitudo reprehenditur, ut male secura mens per torporem, et otium, et incontinentiam ad turpitudinem relaxetur. Si enim ille, qui supervacuo labore se distendit, vere reprehensibilis cernitur, cur propterea, qui ad voluptatem et incontinentiam se resolvit 201Aplacere putatur? Sed carnalis animus difficile medium veritatis invenit; et propterea nonnunquam unum vitium deserere sponte acquiescit, quoniam per id sibi viam ad aliud, quod magis placet aperiri cernit. Et tanto audacius se in contrarium tota intentione effundit, quanto magis certum habet aliud malum esse, quod deserit. Jam enim se in suo malo non solum nulla reprehensione dignum existimat, verum etiam laudabilem suspicatur et cum malum manifeste committat, non se malum facere videri vult, sed potius malum devitare. Non enim considerat vitium declinando in vitium se corruisse, et idcirco nequaquam id quod agit malum sinistre notandum putat; quia in eo quasi non tam facere quam declinare malum laborat. Unde, et hic quoque 201Bcum vidisset eos, qui non profuturas sibi divitias cum labore et sollicitudine avare congregant, neque his quae possident utuntur, sed aliis post se possidenda et utenda relinquunt, miseros et reprehensione dignos, ut illorum devitet stultitiam, libere se in contrariam sententiam projicit, dicens: Nonne melius est comedere, et bibere, et ostendere animae suae bona de laboribus suis? Una omnium sententia est, qui proclives sunt in vitium. Semper adversa reprehendunt, ut sua commendent. Pereant avari, dicit vorax et prodigus, et devorat, et inebriatur, et distendit se ac replet usque ad suffocationem. Et proverbium illi est semper: Pereant avari. Et commendari se putat, quia talis non est, ne reprehensibiliter talis sit, qualis est. Imo etiam propterea talis 201Cesse, qualis est, videri vult, ne forte talis sit quales esse alios accusat, qualis esse non vult, quasi vero medium aliquod non sit, ubi fieri utrumque possit; et ne talis sit, quales esse alios accusat, et tamen talis non sit, qualem impudenti gloriatione se esse exsultat. Melius est comedere, et bibere, et ostendere animae suae bona de laboribus suis. Quam pulchra verba manducare, et bibere! Quis est qui obhorreat cum audit manducare et bibere, aut contra modestiam sive pudicitiam hic aliquid dictum putet? Sed latet impudens turpitudo velo pudicitiae tecta. Dicat ergo manifeste: Melius est devorare, et inebriari, et concupiscentiae suae desideriis effreni libertate servire. Si enim sic dixisset, qualis esset sententia? Et quidem 201Domnino sic dixit; quia hoc significare voluit in eo quod dixit: Melius est manducare, et bibere, et ostendere animae suae bona de laboribus suis.

Et hoc de manu Dei est. Dicunt hoc homines, et est hominum genus, qui hoc dicere solent: Devoremus, et inebriemur, et benefaciamus nobis ex iis quae Deus dedit nobis, quia hoc de manu Dei est; quia, et haec ideo nobis data sunt, ut bene nobis faciamus. Quare enim haec omnia facta sunt, nisi in usus hominum, ut eis utantur homines, et bene sit ipsis in iis quae dedit Deus ipsis? Et haec dicendo excaecantur, et rapiuntur sine mensura, et pudicitia in voluptates suas, ut applaudant sibi, quoniam haec omnia Deus ad utendum fecit; sed nesciunt neque considerant, quod etsi Deus bona omnia ad usum 202Afecit, ad pravos tamen et inordinatos usus nihil fecit.

Quis ita vorabit, et deliciis affluet ut ego? Mala gloriatio ista. Et sunt tamen qui in ejusmodi gloriantur: et istos quoque sapientia praeterire non debuit in numero vanitatum. Tales in alio loco propheta increpat, dicens: Vae qui potentes estis ad bibendum vinum, et viri fortes ad miscendam ebrietatem (Isa. V). Quis ita vorabit, et deliciis affluet ut ego? Qualis amator sapientiae? Quantum retrorsum conversus, imo quantum aversus et perversus ab illo, qui paulo ante lucem sapientiae vidit, eamque a stultitiae tenebris tam subtili consideratione divisit, dicens: Vidi quod tantum praecederet sapientia stultitiam, quantum differt lux a tenebris. Unde tam cito pessimatus 202B[pessundatus] est sensus iste putatis? An propter se non dixit, quod de se dixit, quod amator sapientiae fuit: et hoc non fuit quod dixit; sed quosdam tales significare voluit: propter quos hoc dixit, quod de se dixit? An, et hoc totum etiam ipse secundum aliquid vere fuit, et tamen amator sapientiae propter hoc esse non desiit; quia simul in uno homine, et sensus carnis secundum ingenitam corruptionem et peccatum, quod habitat in eo, suasit nequitiam et tamen spiritus secundum virtutis affectum, et judicium probitatis dilexit sapientiam? Videte tamen quid sit homo, sive in eo qui hoc dixit, et talis fuit, sive in iis propter quos dixit, quod de se dixit: quos tales esse significare voluit. Videte prorsus quid sit homo. Quis ita vorabit, et deliciis 202Caffluet ut ego? Quid gloriaris in malitia, qui potens es in iniquitate? (Psal. LI.) Si nemo potest quod tu potes, magnum est si bonum potest. Si vero amplius in malo potes, quid gloriaris? Malum enim posse potestas non est, sed infirmitas. Quis ita vorabit, et deliciis affluet ut ego? Quis enim est, ait, qui contradicat, cum Deus hoc jubeat? Deus enim laetitiam creavit, et voluit ut qui ei placent in ipsa jucundentur.

Peccatori autem dedit afflictionem, et curam surperfluam, ut laboret, ut distendatur, et congreget, et non possideat, sed tradat ei qui placet Deo. Ergo bona bonis, et mala malis. Considerate quanta est perversitas ista. Mentita est iniquitas sibi (Psal. 202DXXVI). Et de se mentita est iniquitas, et de Deo mentita est; et tamen nonnisi sibi mentita est. Dixit iniquitas: Bona bonis, et mala malis (Eccli. XXXIX). Et ubi est: Misericordia, et veritas obviaverunt sibi? (Psal. LXXXIV.) Ubi est: Universae viae Domini misericordia et veritas? (Psal. CXVIII.) Ubi est: Homines et jumenta salvabis, Domine: quemadmodum multiplicasti misericordiam tuam Deus? (Psal. XXXV.) Ubi est denique, quod Veritas ipsa et misericordia dicit: Estote misericordes, sicut et Pater vester misericors est: qui solem suum oriri facit super bonos et malos, et pluit super justos et injustos? (Matth. V.) Si bonis tantum bona data sunt, quid est quod dicit Scriptura de bonis: Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines justos caminus tribulationis? (Eccli. XXVII.) 203AEt: Omnes qui pie volunt vivere in Christo, necesse est ut persecutionem patiantur (II Tim. III). Circumierunt in melotis, in pellibus caprinis, egentes, nudi, angustiati, afflicti, quibus dignus non erat mundus (Hebr. XI). In fame et siti, in frigore et nuditate? (II Cor. XI.) Itaque mentita est iniquitas de Deo, cum dixit: Quod bonis tantum bona, et malis tantum mala dat Deus. Nam et bonis bona dat, et malis mala dat; et bonis mala, et malis bona. Bonis enim et bona dat ut foveantur, et mala dat ut exerceantur; et malis mala dat ut castigentur, et bona dat ut provocentur. Itaque mentita est iniquitas de Deo, cum dixit: bona bonis et mala malis dat Deus. Verum autem dixisset, si de veris bonis et de veris malis dixisset, quod vera bona et vera mala non nisi bonis bona, et 203Bmalis mala. Propterea ergo de Deo mentita est iniquitas. Sed et de se quoque mentita est iniquitas. Quando mentita est iniquitas de se? Quando se bonitatem dixit, tunc de se mentita est iniquitas, quia iniquitas bonitas non est. Et ubi iniquitas bonitatem se dixit? Quando dixit: Quis ita vorabit, et deliciis affluet ut ego? Tunc bonitatem se dixit: hoc enim iniquitas dixit, quia dictum iniquitatis et impuritatis est hoc contra bonitatem et honestatem. Ergo iniquitas hoc dixit, et in hoc bonitatem se dixit: quia hoc bonitatis tantum esse dixit, quod se facturam dixit, quia se bonitatem esse praesumpsit. Dixit enim:

Homini bono dedit Deus in conspectu suo sapientiam et scientiam, et laetitiam. Primum dedit sapientiam, et scientiam ut intelligat et sciat quaerere laetitiam 203Cin conspectu suo: quia eam fecit Deus ut exsultent in ea, qui placent ei. Quasi vero sapientia non sit et multo major sapientia, illam tristitiam quae secundum Deum est quaerere et amplecti, quam ineptam laetitiam, cum e contrario dicat Scriptura: Cor stulterum ubi laetitia, et cor sapientium ubi tristitia est (Eccle. VII), Verum quidem hoc est, quod Deus laetitiam electis suis in conspectu suo praeparavit, et sapientiam et scientiam in corde eorum posuit, ut sciant et intelligant quaerere eam ubi ipsa est. Sed haec non est illa laetitia qua laetantur qui male faciunt: qui exsultant in rebus pessimis (Prov. II). Non enim est in conspectu ejus illa laetitia, quia de iis qui eam amplectuntur dixit Scriptura: 203DPones eos deorsum, in reliquiis tuis praeparabis vultum eorum (Psal. XX). Ergo Deus homini bono laetitiam dedit, sed eam quae in conspectu suo est. De qua scriptum est: Justi epulentur, et exsultent in conspectu Dei: delectentur in laetitia (Psal. LXVII). Et iterum: Visita nos in salutari tuo, ad videndum in bonitate electorum tuorum: ad laetandum in laetitia gentis tuae, ut lauderis cum haereditate tua (Psal. CV). Et rursum dicit: Adimplebis me laetitia cum vultu tuo: delectationes in dextera tua usque in finem (Psal. XV). Hanc ergo laetitiam dedit Deus homini bono in conspectu suo.

Peccatori autem dedit afflictionem, et curam superfluam. Non malitiam inferendo, sed ad malitiam descendendo in occupationem pessimam.

204AUt addat et congreget, et tradat ei qui placuit Deo. Ideo tamen, quia ille per avaritiam divitias congregavit, et iste in usum misericordiae acceptas dispersit. Alioquin nec qui congregavit jure reprehenditur, nec qui possidet commendatur. Nunc autem omnia perverse dicuntur, cum dicitur quod qui devorat et deliciis affluit bonus est, et illi dedit Deus sapientiam, et scientiam, et laetitiam in conspectu suo, cum supradictum sit stultos esse qui oculos habent in finibus terrae; respicientes ad delectationes terrenas, et voluptati carnis servientes. Itaque mentita est iniquitas, quae dixit voluptatem praemium esse justitiae, fructumque sapientiae in ipsa consistere, et corporales delicias existimavit felicitatis summum continere. Sed non diu in gloria falsum judicium 204Bstare potest. Exit enim veritas, et prosternit mendacium. Ait quippe.

Sed et hoc vanitas est, et cassa sollicitudo mentis. Quid hoc? Non solum hoc ut peccator addat, et congreget, et non possideat, vanitas est, et cassa sollicitudo; sed hoc etiam vanitas, et cassa sollicitudo est, ut justus divitias peccatoris requirat, et concupiscat, aut, si acceperit, cor apponat. Totum ergo vanitas est, et cassa sollicitudo, quod nec utenti, nec quaerenti divitias, et voluptates, et gaudium, et laetitiam, quidquam sub sole permanere potest. Transeunt enim omnia et fluunt, et non subsistit quidquam sub sole, ut impleatur sententia: Vanitas vanitatum, vanitas vanitatum, et omnia vanitas (Eccle. I). Completur etenim in eo quoque vanitas 204Cquod, et ipsum cor hominis in eodem statu non permanet, sed semper a se alterum et sibi adversum atque extra se peregrinum, ab eo semper quod est elongat in id quod non est; et transit, et rapitur maxima vanitate, sive de vanis ad vera, sive de veris ad vana, ubique vanum et instabile, nunc summa appetens, nunc se in infima demergens. Illic approbans veritatem; hic anteponens vanitatem. Et videmus nunc fluctuationem istam maximam mentis humanae in uno homine universum genus hominum contemplantes, et mirabamur quomodo tam cito pessumdetur sensus mortalium, et post tam sublimem contemplationem veritatis, ire patiatur in aliena turpitudinis. Ex quo quidem non aliud datur intelligi, 204Dnisi ut cognoscamus miserabilem vanitatem nostram et in eo quod ad alta pertingimus, et potiora probamus, consideremus qualis homo ex natura factus sit: in eo vero quod tam misera et abjecta appetimus, intelligamus qualis homo ex culpa sua sit effectus, ut vel in hoc veritatis participes esse incipiamus, quod nostram veraciter vanitatem agnoscimus.

HOMILY XII. On that passage, according to another translation: The eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth; where our copy has: The fool walketh in darkness, and on the remainder of the second chapter.

190C

We have perhaps lingered longer over the discussion of these matters than the brevity of a treatise would require; but not fully so long as the difficulty of the subject would demand. Now therefore, since we have found an end, and an end, concerning which Scripture spoke when it said that Wisdom reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly; and since it was our purpose to seek these ends on account of the ends of the earth, where the eyes of fools are, who walk in darkness, lest perchance Wisdom, who reaches from end to end, should reach to the ends 190Dof the earth, and the light shine in the darkness in the ends of the earth, if Wisdom reaches to the ends of the earth, she who reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly. Since therefore we have found these ends. If nevertheless the things we have said about these ends are able worthily to fit their own truth to the interpretation of Scripture, and there be no other more excellent interpretation to which this one should by right give place, it now remains to inquire what these ends of the earth are that have been mentioned, and where they are; and also what that earth itself is, and where it is, in whose ends are the eyes of fools, who do not look back to their own head that they may see, and not walk in darkness. First, then, let us ask what this earth is, and where this earth is. Now we know that in this world there is earth and there is heaven, 191Aand between earth and heaven is whatever is in this world. For in the body of this world heaven is highest and earth lowest; and just as above heaven there is nothing of this kind which is not in heaven itself, so beneath the earth there is nothing, save perhaps what is in the earth. And if we say of this earth that the eyes of fools are in its ends, how this will not be able to stand. For we proclaim eyes keen-sighted rather than blind, which we assert are stretched out by their own vision even to the ends of the earth. Which of the just men has been able to do this, to survey the compass of the earth with his eyes, and to run through in a single seeing such far-off spaces as could scarcely be traversed by the labor of many years? It is ridiculous even to think this, that Scripture said it of bodily vision. Of this visible earth: The eyes of fools 191Bare in the ends of the earth, unless perhaps someone believe that in these words this is signified: that all fools and lovers of the carnal life, who with the whole intention of the mind always go about after earthly goods a terrena bona, run about in pursuit and search of them even to foreign nations, and often even to the uttermost bounds of the lands: and that they are therefore said to have their eyes there, because by thought and desire they always strain thither. But the wise man, who has raised his mind to the things that are above and directs his intention thither, he himself may have his eyes in his own head, in that he strains toward the attaining of that which is highest of all and chief. This could, so far as pertains to the truth of the interpretation, be brought in suitably enough, if Wisdom did not call us to a higher understanding, and to another earth, and to other ends, and to other eyes 191Cto be thought of. For if the head of the wise man is rightly understood spiritually, it is necessary that we interpret the earth also and its ends mystically and not bodily, on account of the eyes of fools. As, therefore, this visible world has its own earth and its own heaven, so man has his own earth and his own heaven. For man himself also is a world, and man has been called the lesser world. His earth is his flesh, and his heaven is his soul. But in this greater world the earth is within the heaven; in the lesser world, however, the heaven is within the earth. And yet the heaven of the lesser world is greater than the heaven of the greater world. But what is its earth compared to the earth of that other? How small it is? and yet its heaven is within its earth. What is heaven within 191Dearth? The soul within the body. The soul is heaven, the body is earth. The soul within the body; heaven within earth. And yet heaven is always above, earth below. For as this heaven is loftier than earth by its place, so that heaven is more sublime than its earth by its nature. Therefore in the greater world, the things that are in the earth are beneath the earth; the things that are outside the earth are above the earth. In the lesser world, the things that are within are above, the things that are without are beneath. What are the things within, and what the things without? Invisible things are within, visible things are without. Therefore invisible things are above, visible things beneath; and invisible things are above our heaven, invisible things beneath our earth. All earthly things are beneath our earth, because they were made for its service and ordained for its obedience. Therefore our earth is above the earth. And what shall I say? 192AIs not our earth also above heaven? Did he not carry it thither, and place it there, taken from us, he who took it for us? Therefore our earth is above heaven. Our earth had first been made by nature above the earth; afterward our earth went, through guilt, into the earth, and beneath the earth; but now, through grace, our earth has been raised above heaven. Therefore all earthly things are beneath our earth. And yet this same earth is joined to earthly things and coupled to them by a kind of friendship, as heaven is joined and allied to heavenly things; and earth reaches as far as earthly things, and heaven as far as heavenly things. Therefore earthly things are the ends of the earth, and heavenly things the ends of heaven; because earth reaches as far as earthly things and no farther, and heaven as far as heavenly things and no farther. Earth stretches itself through concupiscence as far as earthly things, and 192Bheaven stretches itself through wisdom as far as heavenly things. For the flesh, as the Apostle says, lusteth against the spirit; and the spirit against the flesh (Galat. V). For the spirit lusts upward and the flesh lusts downward: and therefore each of the two stretches itself in a direction contrary to the other. And when each has come whither it stretches, there it makes an end and stretches itself no farther. Therefore the ends of the earth are earthly things, whither the earth of the flesh is stretched by carnal desire. And our earth has indeed another end, that of judgment, but of desire it has no other end. Thus far it is stretched by desire, but by judgment it is led farther. Through desire, indeed, concupiscence is stretched toward earthly things; but through judgment, after earthly things it is led into the earth, after the earth to gehenna. Through concupiscence to pleasure, after 192Cpleasure to iniquity, after iniquity to death, after death to damnation. Every man, says Scripture, is tempted, being drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence. For concupiscence, when it hath conceived, bringeth forth sin; but sin, when it hath been completed, begetteth death (Jac. I). He hath conceived sorrow, and brought forth iniquity. His sorrow shall be turned upon his own head, and his iniquity shall come down upon his crown (Psal. VII).

And so the delights of carnal pleasures are the ends of the earth, and the death of the flesh follows upon the delights of the flesh. But the vengeance of damnation follows upon the death of the flesh. Therefore the ends of the earth have one end, death, by which they are received and consumed; but death 192Dhas damnation for its end, by which it is received and consummated. For carnal delights are consumed by death, so that they are no more; but the death of the flesh is consummated by damnation, so that it may be for ever. These ends fools are unwilling to consider, who have their eyes in the ends of the earth. For they gaze only at the first ends of the earth, round about the earth, where the earth itself is ended; not beyond, at the other end, where these ends are ended. They strain toward the ends of their own desire, not toward the ends of their own judgment. To the delight of their flesh, and to the enticements of their pleasures, they open their eyes, and they do not attend to what is to be thereafter beyond. Therefore they are fools who make an end in the middle of the way, where there is no end: and they do not look forward to the end where the end is. The heart of fools is where mirth is, and the heart of the wise where sadness is (Eccle. 193AVII) And another Scripture says: In all thy works all the days omnis diebus of thy life, remember thy last end, and for ever thou shalt not sin (Eccli. VII). For this reason fools do not fear to sin, because they look to the delight of sin alone, but do not look to what follows thereafter, the damnation of the delight. The eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth; the eyes of the wise man are in his head. What is the head of the wise man? Whatever is highest for anyone, this is his head. For the head is the highest part of a man. The head of the wise man, then, is that which is highest for the wise man. And what is highest for the wise man, save that which is highest of all. For he would not be wise who held for highest what was not the highest. And so that which is highest of all is the head of the wise man: and perhaps Wisdom herself is this head, whom 193Bhe who is wise sets before all things that seem to have anything to be desired, and in comparison with her he despises all things whatsoever. And rightly, because Wisdom is the highest of all; she herself is the head of the wise man, since this very thing, that he is wise, is from Wisdom herself, and what the wise man desires to be is wholly in her. Wherefore the head of the wise man is understood as nothing else more rightly than Wisdom herself; since from her is the origin of goodness, and in her consists the consummation of every good.

And so that which is highest of all is the head of the wise man, and this head is nothing other than Wisdom herself; since Wisdom is the highest of all. The highest good, then, is the head, and the highest evil the end. For there are two, the highest good and the highest evil, 193Cset on either side over against each other, and from the middle all goods and evils run back to these two ends. Every good to the highest good, and every evil to the highest evil. For there is no true good unless it leads to the highest good, nor a true evil unless it runs back to the highest evil. Therefore in like manner every evil is toward the highest evil, just as every good is toward the highest. But not in like manner is every evil from the highest evil, as every good is from the highest good. For every best giving, and every perfect gift, is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (Jac. I). And what of evils? The beginnings, he says, of sorrows are these (Matth. XXIV). Therefore every good is from the highest good, and every good is toward the highest good. In like manner 193Devery evil is toward the highest evil, but not every evil from the highest evil. Therefore the highest good is both the head and the end of all goods. The highest of all evils is not a head, but only an end. Therefore every good, apart from the highest good, is good just so far as it leads to the highest good; and every evil, apart from the highest evil, is evil just so far as it leads to the highest evil. For there have been many who had these middle goods, and they were not true goods to them, because through them they did not come to the highest good. And there have been many who bore grievous middle evils, and they were not evils to them, because through them they did not descend to the highest evil. And so the former, lifted up by false goods, fell headlong to the highest evil; the latter, exercised and humbled by false 194Aevils, advanced to the highest good. For this reason the wise man lifts his eyes as far as his own head, and nothing that is below suffices him, until he comes to that which is highest. For certain men have had their eyes upward and yet have not raised their eyes as far as the head, but have remained in the middle of the body. But what would the members do without the head? Could the members live, cut off from the head? So every good, without the highest good, is not a true good. You have seen a man abstaining from those things which are forbidden by the law, not committing murder, not committing adultery, not plundering, not bearing false witness, not coveting the goods of his neighbor, and you have called him a good man, of good life, of good conversation, worthy of praise, worthy of reward. 194BAnd how many have done these things and have not pleased God; because they did not do for God's sake what they did: and therefore they did not even do well, because they did not do it for the sake of the highest good. You have seen another climbing yet higher and doing greater goods, not only abstaining from evil, but even exercising himself in good, fasting, praying, bestowing many alms, showing compassion to the wretched, coming to the aid of those set in straits and tribulation, and you have proclaimed him great and worthy of imitation, as one near to God and chosen. And yet many have done all these things and have profited nothing; since they did not set God in the case. They did not have their eyes in their own head like the wise man, but bending downward into their own temptation, desiring to please either themselves or others, 194Cand glorying in their own good without God, they lost their own good, and did not come to the highest good. For deservedly could they not keep the members alive, who cut off the head from the body. Therefore the eyes of the wise man are in his head, that he may first go forward to the highest good by intention and desire of the mind, afterward follow after it by zeal and action, and then come to it by reward. Let him go forward by intention, so that all he does he may do for the attaining of it; let him follow after by zeal, so that he may persevere in it; let him come to it by reward, so that he may receive it as his prize. In this manner, therefore, the eyes of the wise man are in his head.

For this reason, indeed, when our head was below with us, lest perchance our intention also should remain below, 194Dthe head ascended above to the head, that it might draw us after it: and behold, above there are not two heads, but one head. For the head below was Christ the man in the world, and the head above was God the Father in heaven. Do you wish to know that Christ is the head? The head of the woman is the man, the head of the man is Christ (I Cor. XI). And Christ has been appointed by God head of the whole Church. And the Church herself, the bride of Christ and the body of Christ, what does she say of her bridegroom Christ? and of her head Christ? For she it is, the bride, who in Canticles, commending her beloved, after many such things and many others, adds this to his praise, saying: His head is the finest gold (Cant. V). Therefore Christ is the head, and Christ has a head. And what is the head of Christ? Hear the Apostle: The head of the woman is the man; the head 195Aof the man is Christ: The head of Christ is God (I Cor. XI). And so the head of Christ is God: and Christ himself, about to ascend into heaven, said: I ascend to my Father and your Father: my God and your God (Joan. XX). If therefore he ascends to God, he ascends to his own head; because the head of Christ is God. And this head is that finest gold which no rust consumes, no age wears away; because immortal divinity does not admit corruption. Behold, therefore, our head above is Christ, and our head above is God, and our one head is Christ and God; because Christ also is God, and the one God is Christ: and the head of Christ is God, and the one head is Christ, and the head of Christ is God; as Christ is the one beginning, and the head of Christ is God: I, he says, 195Bam the beginning, who also speak to you (Joan. VIII). For this beginning is itself our head: to which the wise man has raised his eyes, now straining toward him through faith, that afterward he may be able to have his eyes upon him, beholding him through sight. That we may lift our eyes to this beginning and to this head, Scripture admonishes us, saying: If you have risen again with Christ, savor the things that are above, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God; seek the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth. For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God (Coloss. III). For where we are dead, there we ought not to savor; but there we ought to savor, where we have life. If we are dead upon the earth, how do we savor upon the earth? For what dead man perceives? There, 195Ctherefore, we ought to perceive, where we have life; there to savor, where our life is hidden with Christ in God, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God. What is it to savor? To love him, that is to savor. For love itself is savor, and love itself is wisdom. And so to love the things that are above, this is to savor the things that are above; because love itself draws thither where that is which is loved: and meanwhile it has its own savor by which it is refreshed, until one comes to that which is loved. Since, therefore, what is loved through wisdom is above, for that reason Wisdom herself draws upward. And because what is loved through concupiscence, it is necessary that concupiscence itself also draw downward. But from that whereby Wisdom draws upward, and concupiscence downward, there is as it were a division of darkness from light: and the hearts which 195Ddescend downward fall away from the light; but those which ascend are in the light. For they who descend to vanity fall away from truth, and they who fall away from truth fall away from the light; because truth is light. And the light itself does not fail, but they themselves fall away from the light, when they become darkness; because darkness is not light, nor is it illumined by the light so as to shine. Nevertheless the light itself shines even in darkness, but the darkness does not comprehend it (Joan. I), so as to receive it into itself and become partakers of it, since darkness cannot have communion with light. These, then, are the darkness in which fools walk: they who savor earthly things and, not understanding their own honor, are compared to senseless beasts, and are become like to them (Psal. XLVIII). For 196Abecause after the manner of beasts they seek only earthly things, and seek after heavenly things with no affection of the mind, at length they are so blinded by the delight of the flesh, and so lulled asleep by the enticements of pleasures, that they are neither able valcant to think from what goods they have fallen, nor to look forward to what evils they are to come. What, then, do these do but walk in darkness, who are so blinded by a crooked delight that they can neither know true goods nor foresee true evils? What darkness do they suffer within, who do not see the light that is present, and cannot recognize that good whose presence they are able by no turning away to avoid? Why is this? unless because folly has blinded their eyes: which they have fixed in the ends of the earth, determining with themselves to turn their eyes down into the earth.

196BBut lest perchance anyone think it contrary, that here the fool is said to walk in darkness, and that there, as has been recalled, the eyes of fools are declared to be in the ends of the earth. For both seem to be affirmed, that they see and that they do not see, although both may nevertheless be true at once, that they see and that they do not see. For he who said: The fool walketh in darkness, seems to have said outright that the fool does not see. And again he who said: The eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth, seems to have said that they see something, namely those things which are in the ends of the earth. How then do they walk in darkness, if they see? And how do they not see, if they see those things which are in the ends of the earth? But it must be known that fools are said to walk in darkness not because they see nothing: for they see 196Cthe things which are in the ends of the earth, but because, whether in the things they see or in the things they do not see, they do not see the truth. For they do see visible things by intention and desire, and they do not see invisible things. And in the things they see, they think that to be good which is not; and in the things they do not see, they do not know that to be good which is. And so nowhere do they see the truth, and therefore they walk in darkness even in the things which they see. For the delight of the flesh and the illececebra of pleasures has blinded their hearts, so that they do not see the truth. Because the mind, made drunk with a false sweetness, while it thinks of this alone which seems sweet and pleasant in the present, can neither remember how great is the sweetness of those goods from which it fell by its own turning away, nor foresee how great is the bitterness of the evils that are coming upon it, toward which 196Dthe ruin of its own headlong fall always hastens. And note how the sentiment of truth follows upon itself. For above, this man, having considered the vanity of worldly things, despising all, betook himself to the contemplation of wisdom, saying: I passed over to the contemplation of wisdom, and errors and folly. Then considering that the true wisdom of man is nothing other than to seek true goods, and to love the things that are above, where our King is: who therefore went before us, ascending thither, that he might show whither we should follow. Noting also how difficult it is to raise up a mind accustomed to earthly delights toward the desires of eternal things, he added and said: What is man, that he can follow the King his maker? Yet you see 197Athat hearts which plunge themselves into carnal delights grow dark away from the light of truth — he gave, as it were, a definitive sentiment concerning good and evil, saying: I saw that wisdom went before folly as much as light differs from darkness. Then, commending the pursuit of both, he added at the last and said: The eyes of a wise man are in his head, but the fool walketh in darkness. Wherefore let the sentiment run back to its sum, and say: It is indeed difficult for mortal man to raise up to the contemplation of the wisdom above a heart pressed down with earthly desires; but nevertheless, because wisdom is light, and all who fail from the contemplation of it are in darkness, it is necessary that even mortal man, so far as his capacity supplies, apply his zeal to the seeking and searching out of Wisdom. 197BFor this is the wisdom of man in this life: to seek and to search out Wisdom. For to find wisdom and perfectly to lay hold of the truth is not granted to this life, but laid up for the life to come. Yet this very inquiry after Wisdom has now its own light, by which it distinguishes those who love and seek Wisdom from those who love folly and walk in darkness. But the carnal mind, loving the pleasantness of visible light, counts vain the labor for the inner light to be sought; because it either doubts or is wholly ignorant that its brightness, after this light has been taken away, remains inextinguishable in holy minds. For because it discerns that the wise and fools, by an equal lot and like condition, suffer to be withdrawn from this visible light after the death of the flesh, a doubt arises for it also concerning the light 197Cof Wisdom, whether it can be preserved inextinguishable in holy minds after the death of the flesh. Therefore, although it considers the pursuit of Wisdom itself to be good and praiseworthy, yet it doubts whether it is to be procured with so great a labor, since as to whether its fruit can be perpetual, no undoubted reason as yet makes anything manifest to it. This wavering of the human heart, then, this man, both seeing it in himself through the contemplation of truth and feeling it through the affection of the common infirmity, takes up also in a sentiment, showing how, wisdom having been sought and seen, that very consideration of mortal life was calling him back from the pursuit of wisdom, and that he therefore judged it wholly vain that others should advance in wisdom, because in paying the debt of death 197Dhe recognized himself to be equal with the rest. For this is what, after the praise of Wisdom and the commendation of the pursuit of it, he now suddenly brings in, turned to the consideration of the common infirmity, saying:

I learned that the destruction of both was one. For because he saw that both, that is, both the wise man and the fool, are withdrawn from this life by one destruction of death, he began to doubt this also: whether after this life diverse rewards of merits ought to be found according to this same diverse manner of life. And if it stands firm that this is true, why do they go out from this life by one way, who after this life do not attain to one reward? But if, just as the passage is one for all, so also there comes to be one arrival for all: why should they run before death by laboring unlike one another, 198Awho, going out by a like death, would not come after death to an unlike reward? For this is what follows: And I said in my heart: If the fall of the fool and my own shall be one, what does it profit me that I have given greater labor to wisdom? For by those who believe this life alone to be, the pursuit of Wisdom is judged wholly vain: for this reason, that its labor belongs to the present life, but the reward and fruit of the labor to the life to come. Therefore, because they see the labor, they quickly grow weary of the labor itself, and easily turn to those things which, even though wisdom teaches that they are by no means to be sought after, yet, because their fruit is present, they judge more convenient. But because Wisdom does not allow her labor to be wholly fruitless even in this life, and cherishes those who follow after her with a great inward consolation, 198Band through the illumination of truth persuades them to have confidence, in this misery of mortality, concerning the reward of eternity, this man, immediately after he had begun, because of the failing of the carnal life, to doubt concerning the fruit of the perpetual life, accuses himself out of his inmost consideration for this same doubt of his, saying:

And speaking with my own mind, I perceived that this also was vanity. And at once, adding the reason why he testifies that the aforesaid doubt is a vain thing, he brings in also the vanity itself in respect of which the truth could have come into doubt for him, saying:

For there shall not be remembrance of the wise man in like manner as of the fool for ever. For Wisdom, which does not take away mortality from the present life, grants 198Ceternity to the life to come: and although the condition of the wise man and of the fool is alike at the going out of this life, yet in the life to come the remembrance will not be alike. For as here an unlike manner of living divides them, so there too, when they shall have come into remembrance so that he may be brought to judgment, an unlike requital according to their own merits shall separate them. For future times shall not cover all things with oblivion, but all things that have been done shall come into recollection in their own time, so that every work, whether it be good or evil, may be called into judgment.
