Therefore the memory of the wise man shall not for ever not be in like manner as that of the fool, and future times shall not cover all things with oblivion, because, when the time shall have come, the one shall receive glory for the merit of his virtue, and the other shall receive punishment for the excess of his folly. 198DThis, then, is that for which it is not vain to shun folly, and to give greater labor to wisdom; because, when the reward of requital is received, it is made manifest how great is the fruit of just labor. Yet this very consideration of our mortality has a certain just weariness in it; because it is fitting that a man should despise what he sees to be transitory even before it comes to an end? and that he should not afflict himself with empty labor for the attaining of that which cannot long stand. On this account he again redoubles the sentiment concerning the same equal condition of mortality, saying:

The learned dieth in like manner as the unlearned: and therefore my life became wearisome to me. And deservedly indeed does such a life come into weariness, which, being wholly liable to confusion, neither in its goods while it seems to stand, nor in its evils while 199Ait comes to an end, separates the good from the evil or the worthy from the unworthy. For its goods come without discernment to the unworthy equally as to the worthy, and its evils afflict the good and the evil together by an equal lot and with the same outcome. Whence the goods also of this life rightly come into contempt with the just: goods which both afflict with various sorrows those who labor for them, and often, sought with much labor, pass over without profit to those who possess them, from the good to the wicked, and from their own to strangers. Considering which, this man, setting all things in one part — not only those which seem the evils of this life, but those also which put forward the appearance of good, while in real truth they are evils — and adjudging them by a like estimation, gives one sentiment concerning them all, saying:

Seeing that all things under the sun are evil, and all vanity, 199Band affliction of spirit, again I detested all my industry. And lest perchance you should think that he here detests that industry by which he gave greater labor to wisdom, and not rather that by which he was distended by the occupation of those things which are vain under the sun: presently he sets forth what industry he judges is to be detested, saying: And what [qua] under the sun I most studiously labored at. "I detested" is understood. And immediately he opens the reason why he detests both these things and equally the industry spent on them, when he subjoins:

Since I am to have an heir after me, whom I know not whether he will be wise or foolish: and he shall have dominion over my labors, in which I have toiled and been anxious. And lastly, commending his judgment concerning this, he brings in:

199CAnd is there anything so vain? As if he were to say: I judge nothing so vain as when one man, greedily gathering, is worn away with fruitless labor, and another, living both idly and luxuriously, has dominion over the labors of another. For manifold is the vanity where one man is afflicted without cause, and another is unlawfully delighted. For the first vanity is to seek after things that will not profit; the second, to gather things that pass away; the third, to leave the things gotten by our own labor to be possessed by others, and above all by those of whom we do not know what sort they will be. For if all these things were vain even when sought and kept for our own uses, what will they be when handed over to the pleasure of fools? Whence he says:

I ceased, and my heart renounced to labor any more under the sun. Redoubling also the reason why he ceased from labor, 199Dhe subjoins, saying:

For when one man labors in wisdom, and doctrine, and carefulness, he leaves what he has gotten to a man that is idle. This befell Solomon himself, who, laboring in wisdom and doctrine and carefulness, gathered riches and heaped up wealth, and at last left all to be possessed by a foolish heir. For he left the folly of his own stock, his son Rehoboam, who, succeeding to his father's wealth, scattered all, and left the kingdom of his father — which he had received ample enough and magnificent — torn and troubled by a diminishing of sense and a surfeit of heart. But many also labor in wisdom and doctrine and carefulness, searching out with great labor and zeal the secrets of nature and the hidden things of truth, and handing on what they have found to the memory 200Aof posterity, by word alike and by writing, for the commending of their own studies; and often they leave what they have gotten to idle men, because sometimes the negligence of those who come after refuses to take up for use this thing prepared, which the keen diligence of the earlier men acquired not without great labor and care.

This then is vanity, a great evil. It is therefore vain to labor in the knowledge of truth in order that we may come to the notice of those who neither wish to receive truth for its own sake, nor know how to approve it in others. Fruit, then, does not follow upon labor of this kind, because it neither gathers things that will profit itself, nor are those to whom it leaves what has been gathered stirred by any emulation of virtue to the pursuit of the good. For if there is labor for the one who seeks, and there is no profit for the one who receives, what does such labor profit? 200BBut it is also a great evil, that from what one man is worn away with labor, another should abuse idly and unlawfully. For it is a great evil, because both the one gathers to his own harm and the other receives to his own harm. Therefore this is vanity and a great evil.

For what does it profit a man of all his labor, and affliction of spirit, wherewith he has been tormented under the sun? If it does not profit toward anything else, it profits nothing; nay rather, if it does not profit toward anything else, it does much harm, because the searching after it has great punishment, but the finding has no fruit. For what a punishment it is never to be without punishment?

All his days are full of sorrows and hardships: nor does he rest in mind by night. Very wretched is he who cannot have quiet even in that time which is naturally given 200Cto quiet. By day he is worn away with labor, by night he is tormented with the care and anxiety of labor. For him whom, waking, the distension of labor and its restlessness harasses, it wearies also when he sleeps, being heaped upon his soul through the images and phantasies of dreams. No time, then, is allowed to pass for rest; the whole is taken up with sorrow and labor, and nothing is gained for profit and salvation.

And is not this vanity? Truly it is vanity, and utterly a great vanity. But what then? If this is vanity, what then is to be done?

Is it not better, he says, to eat and drink, and to shew his soul good things of his labors? If those labors are vain which confer no profit on those who labor, 200Dthen it is better to labor and to take the fruit of one's own labors. The reasoning seems plain, but it has many an exception. For it would have been much better if it had been said thus, and it would have stood true everywhere: If those labors are vain from which no fruit comes to those who labor, then labors of this sort are altogether to be set aside, and one must rather labor in those things wherein a fruit both certain and true may come to those who labor. But now by this reasoning vanity has been changed, not dismissed, and one vanity has succeeded another, not every vanity has departed. Vain Vena carefulness is rebuked, so that a mind harmfully free of care may be loosed through torpor and idleness and incontinence into baseness. For if that man who distends himself with superfluous labor is truly seen to be blameworthy, why on that account is he who dissolves himself into pleasure and incontinence 201Athought to please? But the carnal soul finds the middle of truth with difficulty; and therefore it sometimes willingly consents to forsake one vice, since through it it sees a way opened for itself to another which pleases it more. And it pours itself out into the contrary with its whole intention the more boldly, the more certain it holds it that what it forsakes is an evil. For now, in its own evil, it not only judges itself worthy of no rebuke, but even supposes itself praiseworthy; and although it manifestly commits evil, it does not wish to be seen to be doing evil, but rather to be shunning evil. For it does not consider that by turning aside from a vice it has fallen into a vice, and therefore it thinks that by no means is the evil which it does to be marked with ill repute; because in it, as it were, it labors not so much to do evil as to turn aside from it. Whence here too, 201Bwhen he had seen that those men are wretched and worthy of rebuke who greedily gather with labor and carefulness riches that will not profit them, and neither use the things they possess, but leave them to others to be possessed and used after them, in order to shun their folly he freely casts himself into the contrary sentiment, saying: Is it not better to eat and drink, and to shew his soul good things of his labors? There is one sentiment of all who are prone to vice. They always rebuke the opposite, that they may commend their own. Let the greedy perish, says the glutton and the spendthrift — and he devours, and gets drunk, and distends himself and fills himself to the point of choking. And his proverb is always: Let the greedy perish. And he thinks himself commended because he is not such a man, lest he be blameworthily such a man as he is. Nay, even for this reason he wishes to be seen to be such 201Cas he is, lest perchance he be such as he accuses others of being, which he does not wish to be — as though indeed there were no middle ground where both might come to pass; both that he be not such as he accuses others of being, and yet that he be not such as with shameless boasting he exults that he is. It is better to eat and drink, and to shew his soul good things of his labors. How fair are the words, to eat and to drink! Who is there that shudders when he hears "to eat and to drink," or thinks that anything has been said here against modesty or chastity? But a shameless baseness lies hidden, covered with the veil of chastity. Let him therefore say openly: It is better to devour, and to get drunk, and to serve the desires of one's concupiscence with unbridled liberty. For if he had spoken thus, what sort of sentiment would it be? And indeed 201Dhe did speak altogether thus; because he wished to signify this in that which he said: It is better to eat and drink, and to shew his soul good things of his labors.

And this is from the hand of God. Men say this, and there is a kind of men who are wont to say this: Let us devour, and let us get drunk, and let us do well by ourselves out of those things which God has given us, because this is from the hand of God; because these things too were given us for this, that we might do well by ourselves. For why were all these things made, save for the uses of men, that men might use them, and that it might be well with them in those things which God gave them? And by saying these things they are blinded, and are carried away without measure and without chastity into their own pleasures, so as to applaud themselves, since God made all these things for use; but they neither know nor consider that although God made all good things for use, 202Ayet he made nothing for crooked and disordered uses.

Who shall so devour, and abound with delights, as I? An evil boast is this. And yet there are those who glory in such things: and these too wisdom ought not to have passed over in the number of the vanities. Such men the prophet rebukes in another place, saying: Woe to you that are mighty to drink wine, and stout men at mingling drunkenness (Isa. V). Who shall so devour, and abound with delights, as I? What manner of lover of wisdom is this? How far turned backward, nay, how far turned away and perverted from him who a little before saw the light of wisdom, and divided it from the darkness of folly with so subtle a consideration, saying: I saw that wisdom went before folly as much as light differs from darkness. Whence, do you think, was this sense so quickly made worst 202B[pessundatus]? Did he not say for his own sake what he said of himself, that he was a lover of wisdom: and this was not what he said; but he wished to signify certain men of that sort, for whose sake he said this which he said of himself? Or was he himself also, in some respect, all this truly, and yet did not on that account cease to be a lover of wisdom; because at once in one man both the sense of the flesh, according to the inborn corruption and the sin that dwells in it, urged wickedness, and yet the spirit, according to the affection of virtue and the judgment of uprightness, loved wisdom? See, nevertheless, what man is, whether in him who said this and was such a man, or in those for whose sake he said what he said of himself: whom he wished to signify to be such. See indeed what man is. Who shall so devour, and abound with delights, 202Cas I? Why dost thou glory in malice, thou that art mighty in iniquity? (Psal. LI.) If no one can do what thou canst do, it is a great thing if he is able for good. But if thou art able for more in evil, why dost thou glory? For to be able for evil is not power, but weakness. Who shall so devour, and abound with delights, as I? For who is there, he says, to gainsay it, when God commands this? For God created gladness, and willed that those who please him should take joy in it.

But to the sinner he gave affliction, and superfluous surperfluam care, that he may labor, that he may be distended, and gather, and not possess, but hand it over to him who pleases God. Therefore good things to the good, and evil things to the evil. Consider how great is this perversity. Iniquity hath lied to itself (Psal. 202DXXVI). Iniquity has lied both about itself and about God; and yet it has lied to none but itself. Iniquity said: Good things to the good, and evil things to the evil (Eccli. XXXIX). And where is that word: Mercy and truth have met each other? (Psal. LXXXIV.) Where is that: All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth? (Psal. CXVIII.) Where is that: Men and beasts thou wilt save, O Lord: how hast thou multiplied thy mercy, O God? (Psal. XXXV.) Where, in short, is that which Truth herself and mercy says: Be ye merciful, as your Father also is merciful: who maketh his sun to rise upon the good and the bad, and raineth upon the just and the unjust? (Matth. V.) If good things have been given to the good alone, what is it that Scripture says of the good: The kiln trieth the potter's vessels, and the furnace of tribulation just men? (Eccli. XXVII.) 203AAnd: All who wish to live godly in Christ must needs suffer persecution (II Tim. III). They went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, being in want, naked, straitened, afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy (Hebr. XI). In hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness? (II Cor. XI.) And so iniquity lied about God, when it said: That God gives good things to the good alone, and evil things to the evil alone. For he both gives good things to the good, and gives evil things to the evil; and gives evil things to the good, and good things to the evil. For to the good he both gives good things that they may be cherished, and gives evil things that they may be exercised; and to the evil he gives evil things that they may be chastised, and gives good things that they may be called forth. And so iniquity lied about God, when it said: God gives good things to the good and evil things to the evil. But it would have spoken truth if it had spoken of true goods and of true evils, namely that true goods and true evils are goods to none but the good, and 203Bevils to none but the evil. For this reason, then, iniquity lied about God. But iniquity has also lied about itself. When did iniquity lie about itself? When it called itself goodness, then did iniquity lie about itself, because iniquity is not goodness. And where did iniquity call itself goodness? When it said: Who shall so devour, and abound with delights, as I? Then it called itself goodness: for iniquity said this, since this saying against goodness and honor belongs to iniquity and impurity. Therefore iniquity said this, and in this it called itself goodness: because it said that this alone belongs to goodness which it said it would do, since it presumed itself to be goodness. For it said:

To a good man God gave, in his own sight, wisdom and knowledge and gladness. First he gave wisdom and knowledge, that he might understand and know how to seek gladness 203Cin his sight: because God made it that those who please him might exult in it. As though indeed it were not wisdom, and much the greater wisdom, to seek and embrace that sadness which is according to God, rather than a foolish gladness, since on the contrary Scripture says: The heart of stulterum is where mirth is, and the heart of the wise where sadness is (Eccle. VII), This indeed is true, that God has prepared gladness for his elect in his sight, and has set wisdom and knowledge in their heart, that they may know and understand how to seek it where it is. But this is not that gladness with which they are glad who do evil: who rejoice in the worst things (Prov. II). For that gladness is not in his sight, because of those who embrace it Scripture said: 203DThou shalt set them downward [Vulg. dorsum, "the back"], in thy remnants thou shalt prepare their countenance (Psal. XX). Therefore God gave gladness to the good man, but that gladness which is in his sight. Of which it is written: Let the just feast, and exult in the sight of God: let them be delighted with gladness (Psal. LXVII). And again: Visit us with thy salvation, that we may see the good of thy elect: that we may be glad in the gladness of thy nation, that thou mayest be praised with thine inheritance (Psal. CV). And again he says: Thou shalt fill me with gladness with thy countenance: delights at thy right hand even unto the end (Psal. XV). This gladness, then, God gave to the good man in his sight.

But to the sinner he gave affliction, and superfluous care. Not by bringing in malice, but by descending to malice into the worst occupation.

204AThat he may add and gather, and hand it over to him who hath pleased God. Yet for this reason, because the one gathered riches through avarice, and the other, having received them, scattered them to the use of mercy. Otherwise neither is he who gathered rightly rebuked, nor is he who possesses commended. But now all things are said perversely, when it is said that he who devours and abounds with delights is good, and that to him God gave wisdom and knowledge and gladness in his sight — whereas it was said above that they are fools who have their eyes in the ends of the earth, looking to earthly delights and serving the pleasure of the flesh. And so iniquity lied, which said that pleasure is the reward of justice, and that the fruit of wisdom consists in it, and judged that bodily delights contain the sum of happiness. But a false judgment cannot long 204Bstand in glory. For truth comes forth, and lays falsehood low. He says, in fact.

But this also is vanity, and an empty carefulness of the mind. What is this? Not only is this vanity and empty carefulness, that the sinner should add and gather and not possess; but this too is vanity and empty carefulness, that the just man should seek after and covet the riches of the sinner, or, if he has received them, should set his heart upon them. The whole, then, is vanity and empty carefulness, because nothing under the sun can remain, either for him who uses or for him who seeks riches and pleasures and joy and gladness. For all things pass away and flow off, and nothing subsists under the sun, so that the sentiment may be fulfilled: Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all things vanity (Eccle. I). For vanity is filled full in this also, 204Cthat the very heart of man does not remain in the same state, but, always other than itself and adverse to itself and a stranger outside itself, always removes far from that which is into that which is not; and it passes over and is snatched away with the greatest vanity, whether from vain things to true or from true things to vain, everywhere vain and unstable, now seeking the highest things, now plunging itself into the lowest. There approving truth; here setting vanity before it. And we now see this greatest wavering of the human mind, contemplating in one man the whole race of men, and we were wondering how quickly the sense of mortals is brought to ruin, and, after so sublime a contemplation of truth, suffers itself to go into the alien things of baseness. From which indeed nothing else is given us to understand, 204Dexcept that we should know our own wretched vanity, and that in this, that we reach to high things and approve the better, we should consider what sort of being man was made by nature: but in this, that we seek after things so wretched and abject, we should understand what sort of being man has been made by his own guilt, so that at least in this we may begin to be partakers of truth, that we truly acknowledge our own vanity.

HOMILIA XIII. Quomodo omnia tempus suum habeant.

Multi sunt sermones hominis, quia cor hominis unum non est. Nisi enim prius mens a fonte veritatis introrsum se per multa desideria spargeret, nequaquam sermo foris per tam multas se assertiones derivaret. Nunc autem quia animus rector ab 205Aamore virtutis per varia desideria in concupiscentiam vanitatis scinditur: idcirco in approbatione ejusdem vanitatis vario ei inconstantique judicio lingua foris per verbum famulatur. Propterea ergo Salomon de vanitate disputans, toties in sermone sententiam mutat, ut videlicet sensum in cogitatione per amorem vanitatis mutatum ostendat. Cor namque humanum quod in desiderio aeternitatis fixum non est, nunquam stabile esse valet; quoniam aestu desideriorum carnalium toties a sua stabilitate concutitur, quoties ab iis quibus per amorem inhaeserat, ad alia concupiscenda movetur. Quia enim in rerum transeuntium usu fructum aeternitatis exquirit, et in iis, quae solum ad temporis consolationem facta sunt, felicitatis gaudium 205Binvenire se putat: ideo semper cum in rebus habitis, experientia docente, aut jucunditatem falsam aut veram miseriam invenerit, continuo ad alia se quasi potiora quibus, vel dolorem suum allevet, vel expleat jucunditatem, appetenda convertit. Hinc ergo semper futura appetit, praesentia fastidit: et fit miro quodam modo, ut qui semper in desiderio futurum fallitur, vix aliquando in experientia praesentium omnino decipiatur. Ipse enim sibi testis est homo; vera bona non esse haec ipsa quae diligit; quia dum semper animo futuris inhiat, et nunquam se in iis quibus fruitur vere felicem agnoscit: in hoc plane et ipse probat quod haec omnia licet possint a stultis, cum non habentur pro summa felicitate, appeti, nunquam tamen cum habentur, possunt 205Cad summam felicitatem possideri. Et tamen carnalis mens concupiscentiae suae tenebris caecata, plane videre non potest quod nec ipsa omnino ignorare potest, quod cum semper vanitatem videat in experientia praesentium, nunquam tamen se cohibet ab appetitu futurorum. Experta improbat, experienda laudat, et quo immoderatius in desiderio eorum quae nondum habet, per concupiscentiam effunditur, eo graviore in defectu eorum quae jam habet dolore vexatur. Hanc ergo fluctuationem mentis humanae hactenus nobis Ecclesiastes in semetipso expressit cum in rerum approbatione, vel pro fastidio praesentium, vel pro futurorum appetitu, mente mutata, toties judicium variavit. Putavit enim 205Din iis quae sub tempore volvuntur aliquid stabile invenire ubi animo requiesceret: et idcirco alia post alia quasi experiendo probans, et omnia experta improbans, agnovit tandem nihil esse in omnibus, quod fruentibus se, aut perpetuo consistere possit aut plenum jucunditatis fructum, dum praesens est, exhibere. Idcirco nunc arguens ignorantiam suam, pro eo quod in rebus mutabilibus permanentem credidit laetitiam possidere, ostendit, quod sicut omnia non solum prospera, sed adversa quoque suo tempore bene utenti bona sunt, ita iis qui perverso amore temporalia pro aeternis diligunt, et in eis felices se posse fieri sperant, nec ipsa prospera veram felicitatem conferre possunt. Male ergo fecit cum quaedam ex iis sibi quasi potiora prae omnibus 206Aad jucunditatem elegit; quia fortis animus, qui per temporalia ad aeternitatis statum festinat, non solum prospera hujus mundi interim ad consolationem expetit, sed adversa quoque cum tempus postulat, ad exercitationem virtutis suae libenter in usum assumit. Et ideo omnibus experimento probatis mutabilium tandem conditionem agnoscit, et quod nihil ex omnibus quae transeunt perpetuo stare possit, fatetur, dicens:

(ECCLE. V.) Omnia tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub coelo. Quare ergo tu hujus mundi, vel mala metuas, vel bona concupiscas, cum transeant universa sub coelo? Cum potius hoc veritati concordet, ut in omnibus iis nec aliquid, sive in bono, sive in malo pro summo habeas; quia transeunt 206Bomnia. Nec aliquid suo tempore abjiciendum existimes, quia juste ordinata sunt universa. Omnia enim tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub coelo. Omnia tempus habent, ut nihil perpetuum semperque permanens inveniatur: sed omne quod est aut aliud subsequatur ut non ab initio veniat, aut praecurrat aliud ut usque ad finem se non extendat. Tempus etiam habent omnia certum et determinatum, quando incipiant et quando finiantur; sive etiam quandiu subsistant, et quando subsistant singula ut nihil praeter rationem sit; et prudens animus sic se, et temporibus, et temporalibus aptare studeat ut et in iis quae transeunt quasi permanentibus fiduciam suam non constituat, et in iis quae bene ordinata sunt contra dispositionem 206CCreatoris murmurare non praesumat. In omni autem eventu veris, et permanentibus bonis se conformans, ita rerum mutabilium varietatem despiciat, ut licet unaquaque re pro tempore utatur dum praesens est, nunquam tamen in ejus transitu animum a statu suo declinare permittat. Ille enim prudentissimus est, qui sic scit transeuntia in usum vertere, ut tamen non norit in eorum defectu mentem a sua stabilitate inclinare. Omnia enim suo tempore bene utenti bona sunt, et tamen universa quae mutabilitati subjacent, licet in miseria qualemcunque consolationem praebeant, facilitatem tamen conferre non possunt. Nihil ergo suo tempore abjiciendum, et nihil non suo tempore eligendum, sed sic animus 206Dad usum temporis praeparetur ut tamen ad mutabilitatem temporis non mutetur. Omnia tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub coelo. Quare ergo eligatur ad omne tempus aliquid unum, cum omnia tempus habeant? Si enim unum aliquid ex omnibus omne tempus haberet, non omnia tempus haberent; quoniam ex duobus contrariis sibique repugnantibus si tempus esset, ut alterum semper esset, tempus esset ut alterum nunquam esset. Sicque hoc nullum tempus haberet, cum illud cum quo idem tempus habere non posset, omne tempus haberet. Nunc ergo, quia omnia tempus habent, nihil unum ex omnibus omne tempus habet; sed habet suum tempus unumquodque, quando ut sit bonum es et tempus quando bonum est, ut non sit. 207AQuando ergo tempus habet, bonum est ut sit, etiamsi bonum non est illud quod bonum est ut sit, et quando tempus non habet ut sit, bonum est ut non sit, etiamsi bonum est, quod bonum est ut non sit. Cognovit hoc Job, et suscepit bona laudans Deum in beneficiis suis, et putavit hostis, quod tempori subjaceret conscientia sancta. Tulit divitias et facultates; pignora interfecit; percussit carnem, opprobriis et injuriis lacessivit, ut frangeret adversis quem prosperis emollire non poterat. Ille autem sciens quod omnia tempus habent, sicut in bonis per continentiam semetipsum cohibuit, ita in malis quoque fortiter per patientiam adversa toleravit. Uxor autem ejus quia stulta fuit, et non intellexit quod omnia tempus habeant, putavit momentis 207Btemporum examinanda praemia meritorum: et ideo percussum videns et derelictum credens, frustra Deum coluisse increpuit, et quasi pro benedictione sua flagella meruisset, irrisit, dicens: Nunc benedic Deum, et morere (Job II). Cui ille respondit: Quasi una de stultis mulieribus locuta es. Si bona suscipimus de manu Domini, mala quare non suscipiemus? (Ibid.) Omnia enim tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub coelo. Si tempus est ut prosperis foveatur infirmus, tempus est ut adversis quoque perfectus exerceatur; si tempus est ut bona bonis et mala malis propter veritatem, et tempus est ut mala bonis et bona malis propter probationem. Omnia tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub coelo.

207CQuid causaris sub tempore omnes de legibus temporum? Temporis est subjacere mutabilitati, et pati vicissitudinem. Nam si haec omnia in tempore non fiunt, quando fieri habent? Extra tempora enim aeternitas erit, et mutabilitas non erit: et non erit ibi tunc, omnia tempus habent; sed omne quod erit, sic erit, ut pro tempore aliud et aliud esse non possit, sed quod erit semper erit. Ergo quandiu vivis sub tempore, patere leges temporis. Patere volens, ne forte etsi nolueris, tamen patiaris. Patere leges temporis, ut transeas per tempus ad statum aeternitatis. Non enim potest in tempore aeternitatem invenire, quia post tempora tunc demum venit aeternitas: et illi post tempora aeternitatem inveniunt, qui in fluxu temporum alternantium mente 207Din desiderio aeternitatis defixi, immutabiles consistunt. Omnia tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub coelo. Nam et ipsum coelum omnium temporum spatia metitur, et omnia quae sub coelo sunt tempore transeunt, et non transit ipsum coelum a quo est tempus. Quasi enim ex ipso coelo tempus est, et in ipso coelo tempus non est: et cum omnia quae sub coelo sunt tempus accipiant de coelo, in ipso tamen coelo aeternitas constat. Magnum spectaculum sapientiae visibilis imago est, ut ex visibilium contemplatione ad aemulationem invisibilium provocemur. Aspice coelum. Quasi moveri videtur, et mutari non videtur. Sed mutantur quae sub coelo sunt, et inde omnis motus origo est, ubi 208Amutabilitas nulla est. Ideo transeunt universa sub coelo, quia in coelo cuncta consistunt. Et ipsa quae transeunt esse suum metiuntur ex ipsis, quae subsistunt; quia non esset certa subsistentia transeuntium si subsistentium status non esset perpetuus. Illa enim, quae vere sunt, semper sunt; et semper sunt quod sunt; et sunt alia, quae vere non sunt, et ea quae vere sunt: quodammodo aemulantur, ut sint aliquid in eo quod sunt; et cum esse coeperint id quod sunt, transeunt in id quod non sunt; et non vere hoc sunt quod sunt, quia desinunt hoc esse, et jam non sunt, nec vere hoc sunt quod esse incipiunt, quia incipiunt tantum hoc esse, et nondum sunt. Ita sunt ista in vero esse errantia, et participare videntur in ipso transitu in quo currunt, esse 208Bquod non capiunt nec comprehendunt, licet attingere videantur, ne omnino nihil sint. Apparent enim ibi, et cum quaeruntur non sunt, quia abierunt in nihilum unde venerant, et non erant ex eo ubi erant. Ipsum enim in quo erant solum vere erat; et totum quod erat ipsum erat, nec aliunde acceperat quod erat; et in ipso admissa sunt haec omnia, ut ex eo quod ipsum vere erat, essent, et haec aliquid. Quantum ergo participant verum esse, tantum sunt omnia haec quae non habent in seipsis verum esse: quibus hoc totum est esse, quod sunt ipsum quod habet verum esse. Et cum in se unum sit, in ipsis tamen pro capacitate participantium aliud videtur esse, cum sint ipsa alia in eo, quod non est aliud. Habet ergo singula secundum participationem ejus, 208Cquod semper est, spatia subsistendi alia majora et alia minora; prout sunt in eo quod nec majus nec minus est, sed idem semper ipsum est. Ideo dividitur et mensuratur ex eo unicuique spatium suum et tempus suum alii breve, alii longum; et sunt dies et menses, et anni, et lustra, et saecula, et horae breves, et momenta, et instantia; et omnia haec tempus sunt in ipsis quae transeunt, et vere non sunt; et in ipso a quo sunt quod sunt, unum sunt et inveniuntur illic non tempus, sed aeternitas. Omnia tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub coelo. Ex omnibus enim quae sub coelo sunt nihil aeternum est, sed omnia tempori subjacent et mutabilitati. Omnia enim initium aliquando habuerunt, aliquando habitura finem: et inter initium, 208Det finem spatium est ipsum temporis, quod tempus est illi quod principium habet et finem; et ipsum aeternitas illi; quod nec principium habet nec finem. Ipsum enim quod coepit, antequam inciperet, non fuit; et cum desiit esse, jam non fuit; et tunc illi nihil fuit, quia illud nihil fuit; et tamen fuit etiam tunc quod semper fuit; et idem ipsum postea fuit cum hoc fuit; et hoc quod coepit, in illo coepit; et quod fuit, in illo fuit, quandiu fuit; et cum fuit hoc, quod non semper fuit, fuit, et illud quod semper fuit, quia hoc in illo fuit; et quod isti tempus fuit, quia non semper fuit; fuit illi aeternitas, quia semper fuit. Ita ex aeternitate omnia tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub 209Acoelo. Tempus habent quando incipiant, et quando finiantur tempus habent. Spatia habent quandiu subsistere habent: hoc enim spatium mora est subsistendi inter principium et finem; et ipsa spatia multorum similia, multorum dissimilia sunt; omnia tamen aequo judicio compensata. Et cum mora fit iis, qui in laetitia et gaudio vivunt, et in bonis ducunt dies suos, felicitas magna videtur; et cum iis qui in aerumnis sunt et adversis fatigantur, spatia longa procurrunt, magna miseria et infelicitas magna existimatur, et nescit tamen homo sortem suam neque judicium Dei super se scrutari potest: nam et ipsa tempora longa finem habent: et cum finem acceperint, ipsa jam non sunt, quae bona videbantur; similiter, et quae mala putabantur, jam 209Bnon sunt. Et succedunt saepe bonis transeuntibus mala mansura, et malis transeuntibus post finem, bona quae non habent finem: et tunc bona praeterita prodesse nil possunt in multitudine malorum, et mala praeterita in abundantia bonorum nihil obesse feliciter consummatis.

Non ergo glorietur homo pro tempore suo, ante tempus, neque temporum adversis frangatur, qui in tribulatione est; quia transeunt omnia, donec veniat tempus, quando remetietur in aeternitate quidquid in temporum spatiis tractum est, sive majus, sive minus. Tunc longa spatia temporum non placebunt impiis transacta felicitate temporum; et permanentibus culpis quae per tempora contraxerunt, cum aeterna viderint supplicia pro temporalibus 209Ccommissis. Justis autem tunc tempora sua longa etiam modica videbuntur, cum merita temporalia viderint praemiis aeternis compensari. Ante hoc tempus quidquid in tempore agitur, occultum est, sive longum sive breve sit, ut homo Dei judicium scrutari non audeat, sed paratus sit ad omne tempus, sive bonum sive malum sit, ut per bona et mala probatus transeat ad bona glorificandus. Et si interim longa sint spatia temporis, non praesumat in bonis, non corruat in malis; quia spatiis suis transeunt universa sub coelo, ut transeunte tempore sub coelo succedat aeternitas quae est in coelo.

Tempus nascendi, et tempus moriendi. Nunc 209Dexemplis succedentibus prosequitur quod generaliter praemiserat, dicens: Omnia tempus habent. Et enumerat hic et bona et mala: et post bona, mala, et item post mala, bona; nusquam sola mala, vel sola bona. hoc enim tempore vitae hujus, non est habere bona sine malis, nec mala sine bonis; quia mista sunt omnia, quandiu tempus est ut omnia habeant tempus.

Tempus nascendi et tempus moriendi; tempus plantandi et tempus evellendi; tempus occidendi et tempus sanandi; tempus destruendi et tempus aedificandi. Primum bona et mala: tempus nascendi et tempus moriendi. Postea mala et bona: tempus occidendi et tempus sanandi. Non sola bona, nec sola mala; sed et bona et mala. Nec solum post 210Abona mala, sed etiam post mala bona: prius tamen post bona mala, et deinde post mala bona subsequuntur. Duae quippe vitae sunt: una secundum carnem, altera secundum spiritum. Et scimus, testante Apostolo, quia non prius quod spirituale est, sed quod carnale est, prius est (I Cor. XV). Ergo duae vitae sunt, prima carnalis, secunda spiritualis. Et habet utraque vita bona sua et mala sua; quia universae viae Domini misericordia et veritas (Psal. XXIV); quoniam ipse salvat homines, et jumenta (Psal. XXXV); aperit manum suam, et implet omne animal benedictione (Psal. CXLIV). Proposuit enim omni homini et bona et mala. Bona quidem, quibus per misericordiam foveat; mala, quibus per justitiam culpas examinando addicat. Et habet omnis vita 210Bbona sua et mala sua, ut omnia tempus habeant, et suis spatiis transeant universa sub coelo; utrumque datur, et utrumque proponitur; alterum ex justitia, alterum ex misericordia. Universae viae Domini misericordia, veritas. Misericordia et veritas obviaverunt sibi: justitia et pax osculatae sunt (Psal. LXXXIV). Si sola mala, non esset misericordia. Si sola bona, non esset justitia. Igitur et bona et mala proponit Deus, et potestatem electionis homini relinquit, utra prius accipiat. Nam utraque gustaro oportet, sed utra prius, in ipso est. Carnalis autem quasi ad haereditatem festinans, et declinans judicium, ut careat benedictione in novissimo; prius bona eligit, et dat illi Deus bona temporalia quae finem habeant ut illis succedant mala mansura sine 210Cfine. Spiritualis vero prius probatur adversis ut ad prospera perducatur, et habeat ipse quoque mala sua et bona sua; sed mala in tempore, bona in aeternitate. Ita omnis vita alterna sorte ducitur in consummationem, altera de bonis ad mala, altera de malis ad bona. Et omnia tempus habent ut sint, et transeunt ut non sint, suis spatiis procurrentia ad finem, quandiu sint. Transeunt bona in malis, et mala in bonis; et dum transeunt aliquando moram faciunt, et habent spatia quaedam singula prout ordinantur, donec finem accipiant. Propterea enumerat quaedam alternantium in mundo, ut omnium mutabilium fluctuationem ostendat. Et primo ponit bona et mala, quasi vitae carnalis statum describens; 210Ddeinde mala et bona, spiritualis vitae exprimens conditionem. Post alternat, et mutat bona et mala; et mala et bona, ut alteram quamdam confusionem ostendat, quia nec malis usque in finem bona, nec bonis usque in finem mala. Sed et ante finem nunc bona et mala, nunc autem mala et bona subsequuntur. Omnis tamen variatio haec distributionis principium habet a bono in malum, cum dicitur: Tempus nascendi, et tempus moriendi; et finem a malo in bonum, cum dicitur tempus belli et tempus pacis. Quia prima vita primum bonum, et ultimum malum. Secunda vita primum malum, et ultimum bonum habet; in medio utriusque malis, et bonis incerta sorte fluctuantibus. In his autem omnibus quae enumerantur pro exemplo universorum 211Aquaedam sunt sumpta de ipsa vita humana, quaedam de iis quae pertinent ad vitam humanam, ut totum mutabile ostendatur, quod hominis est, qui fortassis totus in corruptionem non iret, si vel in se vel in suis saltem aliquatenus stare potuisset. Tempus nascendi et tempus moriendi, hoc est devita humana; tempus plantandi et tempus evelendi, quod plantatum est, hoc est de iis quae pertinent ad vitam humanam. Opus enim hominis simul cum homine interibit; quia sicut in homine quod nascitur, nascitur ut moriatur, ita quod plantatur ab homine, plantatur ut evellatur. Non enim in voluntate hominis tempus est omni rei sub coelo, sed in arbitrio Conditoris. Quoniam omni rei sub coelo tempus est cum vult Deus, etiam 211Bsi homo, cum tempus est, non vult quod vult Deus. Propterea, quae facit Deus, facit semper cum tempus est; quae vero facit homo, non semper cum tempus est facit, cum vel ignorantia, quod rectum est, nescit, vel voluntate prava appetit, quod est inordinatum. Ideo omnis rei tempus subest voluntati Creatoris, quando tempus est ut fiat, quod faciendum est in tempore, et omne quod fit in tempore; si ejus voluntati non concordat tempus erat cum fieret, sed non erat tempus cum fieri debuisset. Propterea sola opera hominum tempora sua non servant, etiam cum fiunt in tempore; quia in ea parte solus homo tempus statutum non sequitur, ubi arbitrii libertate abutens se sub Conditoris voluntate non moderatur.

211CAliud est ergo tempus quod unicuique rei per dispositionem Conditoris tribuitur; aliud quod praesumptione humana contra dispositionem Conditoris usurpatur. In illo tempore homo cum caeteris legem patitur; hic vero solus prae caeteris legem praevaricatur. Et idcirco illic recte cum eo agitur, etiam in eo quod ipse non vult; hic vero saepe contra rectum agit, non agendo nisi quod ipse vult. Tempus nascendi, et tempus moriendi. Nemo cum vult nascitur, etiam si quando vult aliquis moriatur. Et tamen multi cum moriuntur, voluntate non moriuntur, quando tempus est, et multi qui necessitate nascuntur, nascuntur quando tempus est. Etiam ii, qui ante tempus nascuntur, nascuntur quando tempus est; et 211Dqui post tempus nascuntur, nascuntur quando tempus est: quia tempus nascendi confert necessitas, tempus moriendi aliquando eligit prava voluntas. Ideo nemo cum nascitur offendit in tempore; et multi offendunt in tempore cum moriuntur. Nam etsi natura aliquando praeterit, voluntas tamen non offendit, quia pro culpa patienti non ponitur quod non ipsius circa se voluntas, sed dispositio desuper justa moderatur. Tunc ergo tempus est omni rei quando justum est ut fiat quod faciendum est, quidquid illud fuerit. Vel a Deo sine homine, vel ab homine, cum Deo. Nam sine Deo ab homine ut aliquid fiat, ita tempus nullum est, sicut justum nihil fieri sine Deo ab homine potest. Tempus nascendi et tempus moriendi. Tempus plantandi et tempus 212Aevellendi. Possumus hic summam quamdam atque universalem mutabilitatis omnium comprehensionem attendere, ut sicut in principio de tota operis serie distinximus, ita hic quoque primo illam cui omnia subjecta sunt mutabilitatem exprimat, ac deinde eam in qua humanae actiones fluctuant, latius prosequendo immaniorem cunctis plusque metuendam ostendat. Nam prima ista quatuor quae posita sunt ad illam specialiter mutabilitatem, quae inest rebus omnibus ortum et occasum habentibus, spectare videntur, caetera omnia ad eam proprie quae in actionibus humanis versatur pertinere. Quod enim omnia orta occidunt, et aucta senescunt, propter ea quae vivunt et sentiunt dictum est: Tempus nascendi et tempus moriendi; propter ea quae vivunt, et non 212Bsentiunt; tempus plantandi, et tempus evellendi; vel pro iis quae naturalem habent ortum, primum tempus nascendi, et tempus moriendi posuit; ac deinde pro iis quae studio et industria ad vivificationem aptantur: tempus plantandi, et tempus evellendi subjunxit. Haec est ergo illa magna vanitas, vanitas vanitatum, cui parum est, ut mutabilia sint omnia, nisi adhuc in contraria rapiantur, dum transeunt universa. Quantum est enim elongare et peregrinari a proprio esse, et ire ac pergere in contrarium esse, ubi non possis omnino esse quod esse incipias, nisi id quod es prorsus esse desieris? Illic ergo durus transitus est, ubi nulla ratione subsistere potest quod sequitur, nisi prius id quod praecedit totum perimatur. Et quid putas cum de bonis ad 212Cmala itur, cum bona in mala contraria commutantur, qualis est mutatio illa, maxime illic ubi recursus nullus est: neque reditus ullus sperari potest? Nam et mala aliquando in bona commutantur, et rursum bona in mala; et saepe fit hoc ut alternatim sibi succedant utraque. Nec grave omnino illud est, quod mutuo temperantur, ut nec magna sint mala, quibus bona succedunt, neque bona optima, quae malis subsequentibus terminantur et totum hoc sustineri potest, et comparationem habet quodcunque cum acciderit, ne nimium existimetur, unum est quod cum evenerit, quis poterit sustinere.

Tempus tacendi et tempus loquendi. Tempus congregandi et tempus perdendi. Tempus lugendi et tempus 212Dridendi. Omnia haec portabilia sunt: et cum evenerit homini unum aliquod horum, transit illud et venit aliud; et hoc quoque dum steterit tempore suo transit, et redit aliud quod transierat; et hoc usquequaque fit item et item quandiu vivitur; et nunquam permanet unum aliquid ut solum sit semper.

Tempus nascendi et tempus moriendi. Haec horum similia non sunt, neque recursum habent cum semel evenerit. Una est enim mors et una nativitas: et sicut post unam nativitatem una mors, ita ante unam mortem non nisi una nativitas. Et nemo moritur qui prius natus non fuerit; nec cum semel mortuus fuerit, deinde nasci potest aliquis. Principium vitae nativitas est, mors finis et de nativitate ad mortem itur, sed post mortem ad nativitatem 213Areditus non patet. A nativitate enim incipit tempus hominis, et morte finitur. Et propterea ista dissimiliter omnibus tempus habent; aliud, ut in eo tempus primum sit, et ipsum amplius non sit; aliud, ut in eo tempus amplius non sit, et illud semper sit. Hoc ergo gravius cunctis est, quod ita tempus habet, ut ipsum sit sine tempore, quia post ejus tempus non erit tempus quo possit denuo reparari quod abstulit et consumpsit ejus tempus. Propterea melius videtur tempus nascendi quam tempus moriendi, quia in tempore nascendi vita datur, in tempore autem moriendi tollitur vita. Et tamen qui nascuntur moriuntur, et qui moriuntur nascuntur, quoniam qui ad mortem nascuntur ex eo mori incipiunt, ex quo sub mortalitatis defectu vivere incipiunt; 213Bet qui ad vitam moriuntur, ex eo vivere veraciter incipiunt, ex quo post mortem jam mortales esse desierunt. Quocirca bona mors optanda magis est quam mala vita, quia bona morte ad bonam vitam pergitur, mala vita ad mortem malam pervenitur. Propterea omnia tempus habent, et nihil suo tempore abjiciendum: quoniam et tempus nascendi est, ut prima vita incipiat, quae per justitiam exercetur in tempore; et tempus moriendi, ut secunda vita succedat, quae praemio justitiae perfruitur in aeternitate. Postea adjungit quod sequitur:

Tempus plantandi, et tempus evellendi quod plantatum est. Hoc ergo secundum de opere est artificis, cum natura. Nam primum opus solius naturae erat, 213Cet ipsum transitorium erat. Nunc autem opus artificis cum natura simul subjungitur; et ipsum quoque transitorium esse demonstratur, ut nihil maneat sub sole, laetitia quae de nativitate vel plantatione suboritur mortis et eradicationis memoria temperetur. Deinde sequuntur opera solius artificis sine opere naturae, et ipsa plurima enumerantur, et omnia transitoria esse demonstrantur, ut in gradibus suis vanitas excrescat; et tamen universa haec sicut mutabilitate vana sunt, ita tempore congrua fiunt, ut in his omnibus homo, et si statum aeternitatis tenere non potest, servare tamen studeat ordinem rationis.

Tempus occidendi et tempus sanandi. Tempus destruendi et tempus aedificandi. Tempus flendi et tempus ridendi. Tempus lugendi et tempus saltandi. 213DEt multa alia quae enumerantur, et alia multa quae enumerari non possunt. Et in his omnibus vita humana vicissitudinem patitur, et subjacet mutabilitati. Transeunt enim ista omnia super eam, et incurrunt vicissim alia post alia; et subsequuntur quae praecesserant, et rursum quae secuta fuerant, praecedunt; et sine intermissione hoc agitur in undis magnarum fluctuationum. Venit post fletum risus, et post risum succedit fletus; et cum dolori gaudium successerit, iterum gaudia in dolorem commutantur. Et omnia haec tempus habent, cum voluntas hominis se per justitiam pro tempore divinae voluntati, vel ad haec agenda sponte conformat, vel ad patienda supponit. Tempus enim habent omnia, quando ea homo vel agit secundum Deum, vel patitur pro Deo, quia secundum 214ADeum ambulantem omnia in tempore suo si prospera eveniant, fovent; si contingant adversa, exercent. Ideo omnia tempus habent quae homo juste facere potest vel juste pati. Quod autem sine injustitia fieri non potest, non habet tempus unquam ut fiat, quia ad malum faciendum homo nullum tempus accepit, cui propter hoc solum tempus suum datum est, ut vel corrigat mala quae fecit, vel bona suppleat quae nondum fecit. Propterea peccata tempus non habent; et omnia tempus habent, quia in tempore suo omnia bene fieri habent; et bona sunt cum bene fiunt omnia, et ex omnibus non sunt peccata, quae bene fieri habent, nec sunt bona peccata, tametsi bonum est ut sint ipsa peccata. Ideo tempus non habent peccata, et permittuntur in tempore 214Bfieri peccata; et non juste fiunt quando fiunt, et juste fieri permittuntur quando fiunt; et cum facta fuerint, juste ordinantur; et fit tempus ut fieri permittantur, et non fit tempus ut fiant quia non bene fiunt, et bene permittuntur, ut juste ordinentur. Tempus plantandi, tempus lugendi, tempus saltandi, tempus acquirendi. Ubi est tempus luxuriandi et tempus inebriandi? Sed illa bene fieri possunt in tempore suo: ideo ipsa tempus habent. Ista tempus non habent, quia nunquam bene fieri habent. Sed forte contrarium videatur quod positum est tempus occidendi, tempus belli, tempus odii. Sed haec omnia bene fieri possunt; et ideo tempus habent, cum juste fieri habent. Nam est et gladius justitiae, 214Cquo reges et principes criminosos puniunt pro zelo aequitatis, et interficiunt homines damnatos pro sceleribus suis, secundum praecepta legis divinae accepta potestate in hoc ipso Deo servientes. Et hi pro defensione patriae, et pace Ecclesiarum, bella gerunt, et expugnant inimicos pacis, ne opprimant innocentes. Est et odium sanctum quo crimina odiuntur, non homines; et ipsum aliquando pro terrore salubri severitatem districtam exterius corrigendis vitiis irrogat, et intus dulcedinem dilectionis, qua salutem hominum sitit, inviolatam conservat. Propterea tempus est odii, et tempus belli: et omnia tempus habent, quando juste fieri habent. Profiteri licet mihi quod et in principio: quod ad alta et sublimia ista sensu minor sim ut narrem quod oporteat, quia 214Dquod non oportet et non convenit, hoc satis est declinasse si datur. Multa enim sunt in profundo sapientiae secreta abscondita, et non valet homo scrutari arcana ejus; et verba sapientiae ad sensum omnem excellentia spargunt de iis quae latent lumen aliquod, et ipsum modicum est ad totum. Propterea laborat homo cum videt illud, et existimat ingredi ut contempletur; et non valet nisi fuerit cum ipso sapientia, et ostendat illi intus secreta viarum suarum in parte qua gratiosus factus est ad eam. Et cum hauserit multum, hoc multum illi est, et exiguum est ipsum ad plenitudinem redundantem. Ideo multa diximus de fluctibus rerum et de agitatione contraria eorum quae sub coelo sunt; et parum est adhuc totum hoc ad totum; et erunt fortassis qui nos profusiores 215Aexistimaturi sunt in loquendo, quia non attendunt multitudinem dicendorum, et eorum quae dicta sunt profunditatem. Nos breviter hoc prolocuti sumus, ut novam iterum reportemus ad principium futurae narrationis dictionem, et animos habeamus alacriores.

HOMILY XIII. How all things have their own time.

Many are the words of man, because the heart of man is not one. For unless the mind first scattered itself inwardly, away from the fount of truth, through many desires, in no wise would speech derive itself outwardly through so many assertions. But now, because the ruling soul is torn away from 205Athe love of virtue, through various desires, into the concupiscence of vanity, therefore in the approving of that same vanity the tongue serves it outwardly by word with a various and inconstant judgment. For this reason, then, Solomon, disputing about vanity, so often changes his sentiment in his discourse, namely that he may show his understanding to have been changed in his thinking through the love of vanity. For the human heart, which is not fixed in the desire of eternity, is never able to be stable; since it is shaken from its own stability by the seething of carnal desires as often as it is moved, from those things to which it had clung by love, to the coveting of others. For because it seeks out the fruit of eternity in the use of things that pass away, and thinks that it can find the joy of happiness 205Bin those things which were made only for the consolation of a time: therefore always, when in the things it has, with experience teaching, it has found either a false pleasantness or a true misery, it straightway turns itself to the seeking of other things, as though better, by which it may either lighten its own sorrow or fill up its pleasantness. Hence, therefore, it always seeks things to come and loathes things present: and it comes about in a certain wondrous way that he who is always deceived in the desire of what is to come is scarcely ever wholly deceived in the experience of things present. For man is his own witness that these very things which he loves are not the true goods; because while he always gapes in mind after things to come, and never acknowledges himself truly happy in the things he enjoys, in this he plainly proves even himself that all these things, although they can be sought after by fools when they are not had, as though for the highest happiness, yet can never, when they are had, be 205Cpossessed unto the highest happiness. And yet the carnal mind, blinded by the darkness of its own concupiscence, cannot plainly see what it also cannot be wholly ignorant of: that although it always sees vanity in the experience of things present, yet it never restrains itself from the appetite of things to come. It disapproves what it has experienced, it praises what is yet to be experienced; and the more immoderately it pours itself out through concupiscence in the desire of the things it does not yet have, the more grievously is it vexed with sorrow in the failing of the things it already has. This wavering of the human mind, then, Ecclesiastes has thus far set forth to us in himself, when in the approving of things, whether from loathing of things present or from appetite for things to come, with a changed mind he so often varied his judgment. For he thought 205Dto find in those things which are rolled along under time something stable in which his soul might rest: and therefore, approving one thing after another as though by experiment, and disapproving all things once experienced, he acknowledged at last that there is nothing in them all which can either abide perpetually for those who enjoy it, or exhibit, while it is present, the full fruit of pleasantness. Therefore now, reproving his own ignorance, in that he believed himself to possess an abiding gladness in changeable things, he shows that just as all things, not only prosperous but adverse also, are good in their own time to him who uses them well, so to those who with a perverse love love temporal things instead of eternal, and hope that they can become happy in them, not even prosperous things can confer true happiness. He did ill, then, when he chose certain of them, as though better than all, 206Afor his own pleasantness; because a strong soul, which through temporal things hastens to the state of eternity, not only seeks prosperous things of this world meanwhile for consolation, but also willingly takes adverse things into use, when the time demands, for the exercising of its own virtue. And therefore, all things being proved by experiment, he at last acknowledges the condition of changeable things, and confesses that nothing out of all the things that pass away can stand perpetually, saying:

(ECCLE. V.) All things have their time, and all things pass in their own spaces under heaven. Why then should you either fear the evils of this world or covet its goods, since all things pass under heaven? Since rather this accords with truth: that in all these things you hold not anything, whether in good or in evil, for the highest; because all things 206Bpass away. Nor should you think anything is to be cast away in its own time, because all things have been justly ordered. For all things have their time, and all things pass in their own spaces under heaven. All things have their time, so that nothing is found perpetual and always abiding: but everything that is either follows something else, so that it does not come from the beginning, or runs before something else, so that it does not extend itself even to the end. All things have also a certain and determined time, when they begin and when they end; and likewise how long each subsists, and when each subsists, so that nothing is beside reason; and let the prudent soul study so to fit itself both to times and to temporal things that it neither set its confidence in the things that pass away as though they abided, nor presume to murmur, in the things that have been well ordered, against the disposition 206Cof the Creator. And in every event, conforming itself to true and abiding goods, let it so despise the variety of changeable things that, although it use each thing for a time while it is present, it never allow its soul, at the passing of that thing, to turn aside from its own state. For that man is most prudent who so knows how to turn passing things to use that nevertheless he does not know how to bend his mind from its own stability at their failing. For all things in their own time are good to him who uses them well, and yet all things whatsoever that lie subject to changeableness, although in misery they afford some sort of consolation, cannot nevertheless confer ease. Nothing therefore is to be cast away in its own time, and nothing is to be chosen not in its own time; but let the soul be so 206Dprepared for the use of a time that it nevertheless be not changed to the changeableness of the time. All things have their time, and all things pass in their own spaces under heaven. Why then should any one thing be chosen for every time, since all things have their time? For if some one thing out of them all had every time, all things would not have their time; since, of two things contrary and at odds with each other, if there were a time for the one always to be, there would be a time for the other never to be. And thus this one would have no time, since that one, with which it could not have the same time, would have every time. Now therefore, since all things have their time, no one thing out of them all has every time; but each thing has its own time, when that it should be is good es, and a time when it is good that it should not be. 207AWhen, therefore, it has its time, it is good that it should be, even if that is not good which it is good should be; and when it has not a time to be, it is good that it should not be, even if that is good which it is good should not be. Job knew this, and received good things, praising God in his benefits, and the enemy thought that a holy conscience lay subject to time. He took away riches and goods; he slew the pledges of his house; he smote the flesh, he assailed him with reproaches and injuries, that he might break by adverse things the man whom he could not soften by prosperous ones. But Job, knowing that all things have their time, just as in good things he restrained himself by continence, so in evil things also bravely bore adversities by patience. But his wife, because she was foolish, and did not understand that all things have their time, thought that the rewards of merits were to be weighed by the moments 207Bof times: and therefore, seeing him smitten and believing him forsaken, she rebuked him for having worshipped God in vain, and mocked him, as though he had deserved the scourges in return for his blessing, saying: Now bless God, and die (Job II). To whom he answered: Thou hast spoken like one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not receive evil? (Ibid.) For all things have their time, and all things pass in their own spaces under heaven. If there is a time for the weak to be cherished with prosperous things, there is a time also for the perfect to be exercised with adverse things; if there is a time for good things to the good and evil things to the evil for the sake of truth, there is a time also for evil things to the good and good things to the evil for the sake of testing. All things have their time, and all things pass in their own spaces under heaven.

207CWhy do you plead, all of you under time, about the laws of times? It belongs to time to lie subject to changeableness and to suffer vicissitude. For if all these things do not come to pass in time, when are they to come to pass? For beyond times there will be eternity, and there will be no changeableness: and there will not then be there, "all things have their time"; but everything that will be will so be that it cannot be now one thing and now another according to a time, but what will be will always be. Therefore, so long as you live under time, suffer the laws of time. Suffer them willingly, lest perchance, even if you were unwilling, you should nevertheless suffer them. Suffer the laws of time, that you may pass through time to the state of eternity. For one cannot find eternity in time, because eternity comes only after times: and those find eternity after times who, in the flowing of alternating times, fixed in mind 207Dupon the desire of eternity, stand unchangeable. All things have their time, and all things pass in their own spaces under heaven. For heaven itself also measures the spaces of all times, and all things that are under heaven pass away in time, and heaven itself does not pass away, from which time is. For time is, as it were, from heaven itself, and in heaven itself there is no time: and although all things that are under heaven receive their time from heaven, yet in heaven itself eternity stands firm. A great spectacle of wisdom is the visible image, that from the contemplation of visible things we may be roused to the emulation of invisible ones. Look upon heaven. It seems, as it were, to be moved, and it does not seem to be changed. But the things which are under heaven are changed, and thence is the origin of all motion, where 208Athere is no changeableness. Therefore all things pass away under heaven, because in heaven all things stand firm. And the very things which pass away measure their own being from those things which subsist; because there would be no certain subsistence of things passing away if the state of the things that subsist were not perpetual. For those things which truly are, always are; and always are what they are; and there are other things which truly are not, and those which truly are: in a certain way they emulate them, that they may be something in that which they are; and when they have begun to be what they are, they pass over into that which they are not; and they are not truly this which they are, because they cease to be this, and now are not; nor are they truly this which they begin to be, because they only begin to be this, and are not yet. So these things are wanderers in true being, and in the very passage in which they run they seem to partake of a being 208Bwhich they neither take in nor comprehend, although they seem to touch it, lest they be nothing at all. For they appear there, and when they are sought they are not, because they have gone away into the nothing whence they had come, and they were not out of that in which they were. For that alone in which they were truly was; and the whole of what it was, it itself was, nor had it received from elsewhere what it was; and in it all these things were admitted, so that out of that which itself truly was, these too might be something. As much, therefore, as they partake of true being, so much are all these things which do not have true being in themselves: to which this is the whole of being, that they are that very thing which has true being. And although in itself it is one, yet in them it seems to be another according to the capacity of those partaking, since they themselves are others in that which is not another. Each thing, then, has, according to its partaking of that 208Cwhich always is, its own spaces of subsisting, some greater and some lesser; according as they are in that which is neither greater nor lesser, but is always the same itself. Therefore from it there is divided and measured out to each its own space and its own time, to one short, to another long; and there are days and months, and years, and lustra, and ages, and short hours, and moments, and instants; and all these are time in the things themselves which pass away and truly are not; and in that from which they are what they are, they are one, and there is found there not time, but eternity. All things have their time, and all things pass in their own spaces under heaven. For out of all the things that are under heaven nothing is eternal, but all lie subject to time and to changeableness. For all things at some time had a beginning, and at some time will have an end: and between the beginning 208Dand the end is the space itself of time, which is time to that which has a beginning and an end; and that same space is eternity to that which has neither beginning nor end. For that very thing which began, before it began, was not; and when it ceased to be, it then was no longer; and then to it there was nothing, because that was nothing; and yet even then there was that which always was; and that same thing afterward was when this was; and this which began, began in that; and what was, was in that, so long as it was; and when this was, which was not always, that also was which always was, because this was in that; and what to the one was time, because it was not always, was to the other eternity, because it always was. So out of eternity all things have their time, and all things pass in their own spaces under 209Aheaven. They have a time when they begin, and they have a time when they end. They have spaces for as long as they are to subsist: for this space is the delay of subsisting between the beginning and the end; and these spaces are like for many, unlike for many; yet all are weighed out by an equal judgment. And when the delay comes to those who live in gladness and joy, and lead their days among good things, it seems a great happiness; and when for those who are in hardships and are wearied by adversities the long spaces run on, it is judged a great misery and a great unhappiness; and yet man does not know his own lot, nor can he search out the judgment of God upon himself: for the long times themselves also have an end; and when they have received their end, those things are now no more which seemed good; and in like manner the things also which were thought evil are now 209Bno more. And often upon passing goods there follow evils that will abide, and upon passing evils, after their end, goods which have no end: and then past goods can profit nothing in the multitude of evils, and past evils can hurt nothing, in the abundance of goods, to those happily brought to consummation.

Let not a man, therefore, glory on account of his own time, before the time, nor let him who is in tribulation be broken by the adversities of times; because all things pass away, until the time comes when there shall be measured back in eternity whatever was drawn out in the spaces of times, whether greater or lesser. Then the long spaces of times will not please the impious, the happiness of times being spent; and their faults abiding which they contracted through the times, when they shall have seen eternal punishments for temporal 209Cdeeds. But to the just their own long times will then seem even scant, when they shall have seen their temporal merits recompensed with eternal rewards. Before this time, whatever is done in time is hidden, whether it be long or short, so that man may not dare to search out the judgment of God, but may be prepared for every time, whether it be good or evil, so that, being proved through good things and evil, he may pass over to good things, to be glorified. And if meanwhile the spaces of time be long, let him not presume in good things, let him not fall in evil ones; because all things pass in their own spaces under heaven, so that, when the time under heaven passes away, there may succeed the eternity which is in heaven.

A time to be born, and a time to die. Now 209Dhe pursues, with examples following one upon another, what he had set forth generally, saying: All things have their time. And here he enumerates both goods and evils: and after goods, evils, and again after evils, goods; nowhere evils alone, or goods alone. For at this time of this life it is not possible to have goods without evils, nor evils without goods; because all things are mingled, so long as it is the time that all things have their time.

A time to be born and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to pluck up; a time to kill and a time to heal; a time to destroy and a time to build. First good things and evils: a time to be born and a time to die. Afterwards evils and good things: a time to kill and a time to heal. Not good things alone, nor evils alone; but both good things and evils. Nor only after 210Agood things evils, but also after evils good things: yet first after good things evils, and then after evils good things follow. For there are two lives: one according to the flesh, the other according to the spirit. And we know, on the Apostle's testimony, that not first that which is spiritual, but that which is carnal, is first (I Cor. XV). There are therefore two lives, the first carnal, the second spiritual. And each life has its own good things and its own evils; because all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Psal. XXIV); for he himself saves men and beasts (Psal. XXXV); he opens his hand, and fills every living thing with blessing (Psal. CXLIV). For he has set before every man both good things and evils. Good things indeed, by which he may cherish him through mercy; evils, by which through justice, examining his faults, he may condemn him. And every life has 210Bits own good things and its own evils, so that all things may have their time, and all things under heaven pass away in their own spans; both are given, and both are set forth; the one out of justice, the other out of mercy. All the ways of the Lord are mercy, truth. Mercy and truth have met one another: justice and peace have kissed (Psal. LXXXIV). If evils alone, there would be no mercy. If good things alone, there would be no justice. God therefore sets forth both good things and evils, and leaves to man the power of choosing which of the two he shall receive first. For it behooves him to taste gustaro both, but which of them first lies in himself. But the carnal man, hastening as it were to his inheritance and turning aside from judgment, so that he may lack the blessing at the last, chooses good things first; and God gives him temporal goods that have an end, so that evils that shall abide without 210Cend may follow upon them. But the spiritual man is first tried by adversities that he may be brought through to prosperity, and he too has his own evils and his own good things; but the evils in time, the good things in eternity. Thus every life is led to its consummation by an alternating lot, the one from good things to evils, the other from evils to good things. And all things have their time that they may be, and pass away that they may not be, running forward in their own spans to their end so long as they are. Good things pass away amid evils, and evils amid good things; and while they pass they sometimes make delay, and they have certain spans, each according as they are ordained, until they receive their end. Therefore he enumerates certain of the things that alternate in the world, that he may show the fluctuation of all mutable things. And first he sets down good things and evils, as though describing the state of the carnal life; 210Dthen evils and good things, expressing the condition of the spiritual life. Afterwards he alternates, and changes good things and evils, and evils and good things, that he may show a certain further confusion: because neither to the evil are there good things unto the end, nor to the good evils unto the end. But even before the end, now good things and evils, now evils and good things follow one upon another. Yet this whole variation of the distribution has its beginning from good into evil, when it is said: A time to be born, and a time to die; and its end from evil into good, when it is said, a time of war and a time of peace. Because the first life has good first, and evil last. The second life has evil first, and good last; in the middle of each, with evils and goods fluctuating by an uncertain lot. But among all these things which are enumerated for an example of all things, 211Acertain are taken from human life itself, certain from those things that belong to human life, so that the whole of what is man's may be shown mutable — man who perhaps would not go wholly into corruption, if he could have stood at least in some measure either in himself or in his own. A time to be born and a time to die, this is from human life itself devita humana; a time to plant and a time to pluck up what has been planted, this is from those things that belong to human life. For the work of man will perish together with man; because just as in man what is born is born that it may die, so what is planted by man is planted that it may be plucked up. For the time of every thing under heaven is not in the will of man, but in the judgment of the Maker. Since for every thing under heaven there is a time when God wills it, even 211Bif man, when the time is, does not will what God wills. Therefore the things that God does, he always does when the time is; but the things that man does, he does not always do when the time is, since either by ignorance he does not know what is right, or by a depraved will he desires what is disordered. Therefore the time of every thing lies under the will of the Creator, when it is time that what is to be done in time be done, and everything that is done in time; if it does not accord with his will, there was a time when it was being done, but it was not the time when it ought to have been done. Therefore the works of men alone do not keep their own times, even when they are done in time; because in that part man alone does not follow the appointed time, where, abusing the liberty of choice, he does not govern himself under the will of the Maker.

211CThere is therefore one time which is allotted to each thing by the disposition of the Maker; another which is usurped by human presumption against the disposition of the Maker. In that time man, with the rest, submits to the law; but here he alone, beyond the rest, transgresses the law. And therefore there it is rightly done with him, even in that which he himself does not will; but here he often acts against what is right, doing nothing but what he himself wills. A time to be born, and a time to die. No one is born when he wills, even if someone sometimes dies when he wills. And yet many, when they die, by will die not when the time is; and many who are born by necessity are born when the time is. Even those who are born before the time are born when the time is; and 211Dthose who are born after the time are born when the time is: because necessity confers the time of being born, while a depraved will sometimes chooses the time of dying. Therefore no one offends in the time when he is born; and many offend in the time when they die. For even if nature sometimes passes by, yet the will does not offend, because that is not laid to the fault of the sufferer which not his own will concerning himself, but a just disposition from above, governs. Then therefore is there a time for every thing, when it is just that what is to be done be done, whatever that shall have been. Either by God without man, or by man, with God. For that anything should be done by man without God — there is no time for it, just as nothing just can be done by man without God. A time to be born and a time to die. A time to plant and a time 212Ato pluck up. Here we may attend to a certain summary and universal comprehension of the mutability of all things, so that, as we distinguished at the beginning concerning the whole course of the work, so here too he may first express that mutability to which all things are subject, and then, pursuing more at large that one in which human actions fluctuate, may show it more monstrous than all and more to be feared. For these first four things which are set down seem to look especially to that mutability which is in all things that have a rising and a setting, and all the rest to belong properly to that which is engaged in human actions. For that all things that rise set, and that things increased grow old, was said on account of those things that live and feel: a time to be born and a time to die; on account of those things that live and do not 212Bfeel: a time to plant, and a time to pluck up; or else for those things that have a natural rising he set first a time to be born, and a time to die; and then for those that are fitted for quickening by care and industry he subjoined: a time to plant, and a time to pluck up. This therefore is that great vanity, vanity of vanities, for which it is too little that all things be mutable, unless they be further snatched into their contraries while all things pass away. For how great a thing it is to go far off and to sojourn away from one's own being, and to go and pass over into a contrary being, where you cannot at all be what you begin to be, unless you have utterly ceased to be what you are? There, then, the passage is hard, where by no reasoning can what follows subsist, unless first the whole of what precedes be destroyed. And what do you think, when there is a going from good things to 212Cevils, when good things are changed into their contrary evils — what a change that is, most of all there where there is no running back, nor can any return be hoped for? For evils too are sometimes changed into good things, and again good things into evils; and often it happens that the two succeed one another by turns. Nor is that altogether grievous which is mutually tempered, so that neither are the evils great upon which good things follow, nor the good things best which are ended by evils following after; and all this can be borne, and whatever it may be, when it has come to pass, has its comparison, that it be not reckoned too much: there is one thing which, when it has befallen, who will be able to bear?

A time to be silent and a time to speak. A time to gather and a time to lose. A time to mourn and a time 212Dto laugh. All these things are bearable: and when some one of them has befallen a man, that one passes and another comes; and this too, when it has stood its own time, passes, and that returns which had passed; and this happens everywhere again and again as long as one lives; and never does any one thing remain so as to be alone always.

A time to be born and a time to die. These are not like those, nor have they any running back once it has come to pass. For there is one death and one birth: and just as after one birth there is one death, so before one death there is not more than one birth. And no one dies who has not first been born; nor, when someone has once died, can he thereafter be born. Birth is the beginning of life, death the end, and there is a going from birth to death; but after death the way back to birth 213Adoes not lie open.
