For from birth the time of man begins, and by death it is ended. And therefore these have their time unlike all other things: the one, that in it the time is first, and it itself is no more; the other, that in it there is no more time, and it is always. This therefore is heavier than all, that it so has its time that it is itself without time, because after its time there will be no time in which what its time has taken away and consumed could be restored anew. Therefore the time to be born seems better than the time to die, because in the time of being born life is given, but in the time of dying life is taken away. And yet those who are born die, and those who die are born; since those who are born unto death begin to die from the moment they begin to live under the failing of mortality; 213Band those who die unto life begin truly to live from the moment when, after death, they have now ceased to be mortal. Wherefore a good death is more to be wished for than an evil life, because by a good death one proceeds to a good life, and by an evil life one arrives at an evil death. Therefore all things have their time, and nothing is to be cast away in its own time: since there is both a time to be born, that the first life may begin, which is exercised through justice in time; and a time to die, that the second life may follow, which enjoys the reward of justice in eternity. Afterwards he adds what follows:

A time to plant, and a time to pluck up what has been planted. This second thing therefore is of the work of the craftsman, together with nature. For the first work was of nature alone, 213Cand that too was transitory. But now the work of the craftsman together with nature is subjoined; and that too is shown to be transitory, so that nothing may remain under the sun, the gladness which springs up from birth or from planting be tempered by the memory of death and of uprooting. Then there follow the works of the craftsman alone without the work of nature, and these too are enumerated in great number, and all are shown to be transitory, so that vanity may increase by its degrees; and yet all these things, just as by their mutability they are vain, so in their time they become fitting, so that in all these things man, even if he cannot hold the state of eternity, may yet study to keep the order of reason.

A time to kill and a time to heal. A time to destroy and a time to build. A time to weep and a time to laugh. A time to mourn and a time to dance. 213DAnd many other things which are enumerated, and many others which cannot be enumerated. And in all these human life suffers vicissitude and lies subject to mutability. For all these things pass over it, and run in by turns, one after another; and those that had gone before follow after, and again those that had followed go before; and without intermission this is done in the waves of great fluctuations. After weeping comes laughter, and after laughter weeping succeeds; and when joy has succeeded grief, again joys are changed into grief. And all these things have their time, when the will of man conforms itself through justice, according to the time, to the divine will, either willingly for the doing of them, or submits itself for the suffering of them. For all things have their time when man either does them according to God or suffers them for God, because for the man who walks according to 214AGod all things in their own time, if prosperous things befall, cherish him; if adverse things happen, exercise him. Therefore all things have their time which man can justly do or justly suffer. But what cannot be done without injustice never has a time that it be done, because man has received no time for doing evil — man, to whom his time has been given for this alone, that he may either correct the evils he has done, or supply the good things he has not yet done. Therefore sins have no time; and all things have their time, because in their own time all things are to be well done; and things are good when all are well done, and out of all things sins are not among those that are to be well done, nor are sins good, although it is good that sins themselves should be. Therefore sins have no time, and sins are permitted to be done in time; 214Band they are not justly done when they are done, and they are justly permitted to be done when they are done; and when they have been done, they are justly ordered; and there comes a time that they be permitted to be done, and there comes no time that they be done, because they are not well done, and they are well permitted, that they may be justly ordered. A time to plant, a time to mourn, a time to dance, a time to acquire. Where is a time to be wanton and a time to get drunk? But those things can be well done in their own time: therefore they have their time. These have no time, because they are never to be well done. But perhaps it may seem to be the contrary that there has been set down a time to kill, a time of war, a time of hatred. But all these can be well done; and therefore they have their time, since they are to be justly done. For there is also a sword of justice, 214Cwith which kings and princes punish criminals out of zeal for equity, and put to death men condemned for their crimes, serving God in this very thing by a power received according to the precepts of the divine law. And these wage wars for the defense of the fatherland and the peace of the Churches, and fight down the enemies of peace, lest they oppress the innocent. There is also a holy hatred by which crimes are hated, not men; and this sometimes, for a wholesome terror, inflicts a strict severity outwardly for the correcting of vices, and inwardly preserves inviolate the sweetness of love, by which it thirsts for the salvation of men. Therefore there is a time of hatred, and a time of war: and all things have their time, when they are to be justly done. It is permitted me to confess what I confessed also at the beginning: that for these high and lofty matters I am too small in understanding to tell what is fitting, because 214Das for what is not fitting and does not agree, it is enough to have turned aside from this, if it be granted. For many are the secrets hidden in the deep of wisdom, and man is not able to search out her mysteries; and the words of wisdom, surpassing all understanding, scatter some light concerning the things that lie hidden, and that light is small in comparison with the whole. Therefore man labors when he sees it, and thinks to enter in that he may contemplate; and he is not able, unless wisdom be with him, and show him within the secrets of her ways in that part in which he has been made acceptable to her. And when he has drunk much, this much is much to him, and it is itself scant in comparison with her overflowing fullness. Therefore we have said many things about the waves of things and about the contrary agitation of those things that are under heaven; and all this is still little in comparison with the whole; and there will perhaps be those who will reckon us too lavish 215Ain speaking, because they do not attend to the multitude of things to be said, and to the profundity of the things that have been said. We have spoken this briefly, that we may bring back again a fresh utterance to the beginning of the narrative to come, and may have our minds more eager.

HOMILIA XIV. Reliquorum quae tempus suum habent declaratio et dictorum repetitio.

Omnia tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub coelo. Quaesierat supra Ecclesiastes unum aliquid in mundo in quo animo requiescere potuisset; et non invenit illud inter omnia, sive quia imperfecta erant singula, sive quia transitoria erant universa. Propterea coepit fastidire, 215Bet reprobare omnia; et tamen quaerere non desiit semper in his gaudium plenum et invenire non poterat. Tandem ergo aliquando mutabilium conditionem agnoscens, vidit se in utroque errasse, sive quod ea quae in genere suo bona erant, mala esse arguit, sive quod ea quae transitoria erant, perpetuo stare posse putavit. Nunc itaque corrigens semetipsum pro existimatione praeterita, profitetur omnia quae sub coelo sunt simul et tempore transeuntia et tempore suo bona. Quorum omnium mutabilitas et fluctuatio quanta sit, ut melius intelligi possit, universa haec non solum transire tempore, sed tempore quoque in contraria ire ostendit, dicens: Omnia tempus habent, et suis spatiis transeunt universa sub coelo. Et 215Cenumerat deinde universa in genere suo distinguens: Tempus nascendi et tempus moriendi. Primum secundum principium et finem describit cursum rerum mutabilium, ut postea eorum quae in medio versantur, mutabilitatem et vicissitudinem diligentius prosequatur. Sane quatuor sunt opera, quibus omnia temporalia et omnia tempore transeuntia explicantur. Primum est opus Dei, secundum est opus naturae; tertium est opus artificis cum natura; quartum est opus solius artificis sine natura. Opus Dei est essentiam rerum de nihilo creare materiam rerum in formam disponere, motum autem rerum sub certo ordine temperare. Propterea tria haec ad opus Dei pertinent, 215Did est essentia rerum, forma et ordo. Haec autem tria, sicut postea auctor ipse attestatur de operibus Dei, stabilia sunt, nec temporis capiunt mutabilitatem, quia et rerum essentiae hoc quod sunt nunquam esse desinunt, et rerum formae secundum primam Conditoris sui institutionem suis generibus perpetuam identitatem custodiunt, et motus rerum primi ordinis legem nunquam transcendunt. Neque enim vel essentiae rerum nihil esse, vel formae rerum aliter esse, vel ordo rerum dispositioque ab initio, aliter se habere potuerunt; sed servant omnia primae legis normam et antiquae institutionis pactum, nunquam secus currentia adhuc cuncta custodiunt. Propterea ergo permaneant opera Dei, quia stabile est in rebus 216Aomnibus quod Deus fecit, ut maneat semper. Opus itaque Dei est creare, formare, disponere universa. Opus naturae est semina rerum de occulto sinu per incrementum producere, eademque rursum marcescentia cum concidunt per defectum ad occultum sinum, unde prodierant revocare. Opus artificis cum natura est: ea quae oriuntur de terra, studio et industria adjuvare. Opus solius artificis est in subjecta rerum materia operari vel disjuncta componendo, vel conjuncta separando; ita ut nec creare cum Deo possit, ut sit quod non erat, nec cum natura fetibus rerum incrementum tribuere, ut majus sit quod minus crat

Tres itaque opifices sunt in hoc mundo, Deus, natura et artifex imitans naturam. Sed hi tres 216Bvalde dispari potentia id quod ad effectum producunt, efficiunt. Nam Deus in opere suo, nec naturae opera indiget, nec opificis imitantis naturam. Operatur enim Deus aliquando sine natura, aliquando in natura, aliquando supra naturam. Nam sine natura primum fecit ipsam naturam. Quando enim naturam fecit, cooperantem naturam non habuit. Non enim potuit quod nondum erat, semetipsum operari cum eo qui solus erat. Sic ergo primum naturam fecit sine natura, ut postea in natura, alia faceret cum natura, alia supra naturam. Cum natura quippe facit ea quae de natura secundum naturam producit; supra naturam facit, quando in natura, praeter naturae cursum solitum et posse primum, majori addita 216Cpotentia aliquid ad effectum producit. Quando ergo naturam operatur Deus, et quando supra naturam operatur natura, Deo non cooperatur; quia illic tantum natura accipit, quod non erat ut sit: hic vero accipit, quod non poterat ex eo, quod acceperat, ut possit. Ergo sine natura operari potest Deus; natura sine Deo non potest, quia quod natura facit, ex eo facit quod Deus facit, et cum eo quod Deus facit. Posse enim naturae primum Deus fecit; et ut ad effectum prodeat, rursum ipse facit cum ipsa natura quam facit. Omne ergo quod natura facit, Deus facit, sed non omne, quod Deus facit, natura etiam facit: qui sine natura naturam facit. Tertio loco sequuntur opera artificis 216Dimitantis naturam, et ipse quidem aliquando cum Deo operatur sine natura, aliquando cum natura sine Deo, aliquando cum Deo simul et cum natura, aliquando sine Deo pariter et sine natura. Cum Deo operatur quando opera justitiae operatur; quia rectae voluntati, et secundum justitiam ordinatae Deus cooperatur. Sine Deo operatur, quando opera iniquitatis operatur; quoniam peccata a Deo non sunt, nec per ejus cooperationem fieri habet, quod fit contra ejus voluntatem. Cum natura operatur artifex, quando seminibus rerum ac fetibus propagandis, quibus natura incrementum subjicit, foris industriam et studium apponit. Sine natura operatur, quando praeterea, quae ad propagationem seminum spectant, et nascentium 217Aatque eorum quae vegetationis sensusque vim habent, culturam in subjecta materia studium explicat, ut aliquid quodcunque ad effectum promoveat, in quo natura patitur tantum, non operatur, quia materiam operanti praebet, non effectum operandi exercet. Talia sunt omnia opera hominum, quae fiunt super terram, ex quibus multa mortalis vitae necessitas cogit, multa suadet cupiditas, multa vanitas operatur. Et in his omnibus, quia nihil stabile invenitur, et transeunt universa quae fiunt sub sole: quae vel natura producit, vel fingit artifex imitant naturam: cuncta subjicit vanitati sapientiae contemplator, sola opera Dei permanere probans; quoniam nec creata aliquando essentia consumitur, nec dispositionis 217Baut ordinis rerum ratio immutatur. Propterea ostendit primum naturae opera vanitati subjecta sive in iis quae natura sola operatur, quia orta occidunt, sive in iis quae cum natura artifex facit, quia aucta senescunt. Postea opera artificis imitantis naturam multa ac diversa enumerat: alia necessitatis, alia cupiditatis, alia vanitatis, et omnia vanitati subjicit quia mutabilitati obnoxia ostendit. Opus solius naturae narratur cum dicitur: Tempus nascendi et tempus moriendi.

Deinde opus artificis cooperantis naturae subinfertur, cum dicitur: Tempus plantandi et tempus evellendi. Postremo opus hominis sine naturae opera adjungitur, cum subinfertur: Tempus occidendi et tempus sanandi; tempus destruendi et 217Ctempus aedificandi. Et hoc deinde pluribus annumeratis multiplicius exponitur ut humani cordis vanitas quam multis implicata sit et late dispersa patenter demonstretur. Hoc enim ad rem maxime pertinuit ut vanitatem mentium humanarum, quae vitae mortalis incertum sequitur, quia illam arguendam suscepit et in narratione diligentius exponeret, et in comparatione anteferret. Ut caeterae omnes quasi ob hoc solum commemoratae videantur, ut illarum comparatione, haec quanta sit, agnoscatur. Tempus nascendi et tempus moriendi. Tempus nascendi est, quando ducendus est homo in hanc vitam. Tempus moriendi est, quando ab hac vita est evocandus. Interim autem post 217Dnativitatem ante mortem dum in hac vita mortali vivit, quae sustentamento indiget, et alimentis nutritur, ut subsistat. Tempus est plantandi et tempus evellendi, ut excolat homo terram de qua sumptus est, et seminet, et metat, et plantet, et carpat. Possunt autem et haec duo sequentia praecedentibus duobus per distinctionem conferri, hoc modo: Tempus nascendi et tempus plantandi; tempus moriendi et tempus evellendi. Nascente enim homine tempus est plantandi, ut fructibus terrenis alatur vita terrena. Moriente autem homine, tempus est evellendi; quia cum vita mortalis destruitur, etiam ea quae propter vitam mortalem condita fuerant, tolluntur. Quia autem infirmitati humanae post fructus terrae etiam carnis 218Ausus conceditur: idcirco post tempus plantandi et tempus evellendi, congrue etiam tempus occidendi subinfertur. In quo esu, quia mensura necessaria est, ne hoc caro ad incitamentum vitiorum sumat, quod ad sustentamentum infirmitatis accepit: statim post tempus occidendi adjungit tempus sanandi ut videlicet ipsorum animalium vitam, quae pro nostra infirmitate sustentanda in tempore opportuno, id est cum necessitas exigit, occidenda accepimus caeteris temporibus diligenti cura nutrire ac conservare studeamus. Hoc enim quasi infirmantia sanare est in quibus sibi non sufficiunt subveniendo, deficientia reparare. Unde fortasse, congrue cum dixisset: Tempus occidendi, non addidit, tempus sanandi 218Bquod occisum est. Sicut prius postquam dixerat tempus plantandi, statim adjunxit, et tempus evellendi, quod plantatum est. Quia scilicet plantata evelli possunt, sed occisa sanari non possunt. Sic fortasse si litterae sensum sequimur, nihil spirituali intelligentiae (quia postmodum vestiganda est) praejudicamus.

Tempus destruendi, et tempus aedificandi. Quando homo destruere debeat et quando aedificare, quispiam nequaquam quaerendum esse existimet; quoniam hic solum hoc demonstrari putet quod homo, si forte varia eventibus temporum subjicitur, ista dissimiliter etiam nolens patiatur. Nos autem ad faciliorem intelligentiam haec quae dicta 218Csunt applicantes, dicere possumus quod tempus occidendi sit, cum Deus peccata hominum punire volens, ad castigationem gladium interfectionis adducit; tempus vero sanandi, cum afflictos et tribulationum plagis saucios refovens, solita miseratione restituit. Et plane hoc magis veritati consonum esse videatur ut hic tempora rerum accipere debeamus, non quae humanae voluntati serviunt, sed quae divinae obtemperant dispositioni. Neque enim tempus est cujusque rei, cum homo vult, et Deus non vult. Quia et homo saepe vult cum tempus non est et cum vult Deus semper tempus est. Propterea omnia tempora ad divinam referuntur ordinationem: et dicitur tunc tempus esse omnis rei, cum a Deo juste disponitur, 218Dsive ad castigationem et correptionem criminis, sive ad consolationem infirmitatis. Tempus occidendi et tempus sanandi. Tempus destruendi et tempus aedificandi.

Tempus flendi et tempus ridendi. Tempus lugendi et tempus saltandi. Prius ubique mala enumerantur, postea adduntur bona; quia prius pro nostris peccatis juste affligimur, postea Dei miseratione benigne refovemur. Et manifestum est, qualiter horum omnium quotidie vicissitudinem vita humana patitur quoties occulta dispensatione Deus nos vel flagellis erudit, vel donis consolatur. Deinde sequitur:

Tempus spargendi lapides et tempus colligendi. Quid autem secundum litteram hoc sibi velit, merito 219Aquaeritur: cum tale aliquid ut inter humanas actiones tempus habere putetur, otiosum omnino atque incongruum videatur. Nisi forte ita intelligendum sit ut quia dicturus est in sequentibus: Tempus belli et tempus pacis, convenienter hic praemittat tempus spargendi lapides, et tempus colligendi, ut videlicet tempore belli instante colligantur lapides ad exstruendas munitiones et moenia murorum adversum obsidiones; tempore vero pacis, quia nulla pericula bellorum imminent, aggeres munitionum dispergantur, quatenus cunctis accessus sine contradictione patescant. Nec superfluum videri debet propterea quod supra dixerat: Tempus destruendi et tempus aedificandi quasi idem secundo repetitum sit; quia illud de aedificiis 219Bdomorum et habitaculis hominum convenientius dictum accipitur; hoc vero magis proprie ad munimenta murorum refertur. Potest tamen alius sensus fortassis magis idoneus sub his verbis intelligi. Nam quia supra praemiserat: Tempus occidendi et tempus sanandi, ne forte putaretur solos malos, et eos qui pro peccatis suis puniendi sunt ad interfectionem exponi: ostendit nunc justos etiam, aliquando Deo permittente, in exemplum malorum et castigationem cum impiis et peccatoribus et mortibus subdi, et exsiliis ac proscriptionibus dispergi, sicut per Petrum dicitur: Tempus est, ut incipiat judicium a domo Dei (I Petr. IV). Quod autem lapidum nomine justi significentur, per Jeremiam manifeste ostenditur, 219Ccum dicit: Dispersi sunt lapides sanctuarii in capite omnium platearum (Thren. IV). Et Isaias rursum: Ponam omnes muros tuos in lapides sculptos, omnes filios tuos doctos a Domino (Isa. LIV). Ergo tempus est spargendi lapides, ut justi in hac vita veram requiem non esse ex ipso sui dispersionis et concussionis labore intelligant. Et rursum tempus est lapides colligendi, ut post attritionem exsilii corporalis, ne deficiant animo iterum pace reddita temporali beneficio ad aeterna convalescant. Sic quod occultum est difficile in unam aliquam partem judicari potest: quoniam idcirco sermo divinus in quibusdam locis se a nobis dissimulat, ut se etiam illic ubi manifestus putabatur, scrutatione dignum 219Dostendat.

HOMILY XIV. A declaration of the remaining things that have their own time, and a repetition of what has been said.

All things have their time, and all things under heaven pass away in their own spans. Ecclesiastes had sought above some one thing in the world in which he might have rested in mind; and he did not find it among all things, whether because each one was imperfect, or because all were transitory. Therefore he began to loathe 215Band to reject all things; and yet he did not cease always to seek in them a full joy, and he could not find it. At length therefore, coming at last to know the condition of mutable things, he saw that he had erred in both: whether in that he charged those things which in their own kind were good with being evil, or in that he supposed that those things which were transitory could stand forever. Now therefore, correcting himself for his past estimate, he professes that all things under heaven are at once both passing away with time and good in their own time. And that the mutability and fluctuation of all these may be the better understood, how great it is, he shows that all these things not only pass away with time, but also with time go over into their contraries, saying: All things have their time, and all things under heaven pass away in their own spans. And 215Che then enumerates them all, distinguishing them in their own kind: A time to be born and a time to die. First he describes the course of mutable things according to its beginning and its end, that afterwards he may pursue more carefully the mutability and vicissitude of the things that turn in the middle. Now there are four works, by which all temporal things and all things passing away with time are unfolded. The first is the work of God; the second is the work of nature; the third is the work of the craftsman together with nature; the fourth is the work of the craftsman alone, without nature. The work of God is to create the essence of things out of nothing, to dispose the matter of things into form, and to temper the motion of things under a fixed order. Therefore these three belong to the work of God, 215Dthat is, the essence of things, their form, and their order. And these three, as the author himself afterwards testifies concerning the works of God, are stable, and do not admit the mutability of time; because the essences of things never cease to be what they are, and the forms of things, according to the first institution of their Maker, keep in their kinds a perpetual identity, and the motions of things never overstep the law of the first order. For neither could the essences of things be nothing, nor the forms of things be otherwise, nor the order and disposition of things from the beginning be otherwise than they are; but all things keep the norm of the first law and the covenant of the ancient institution; never running otherwise, they all still guard them. Therefore then let the works of God abide, because that which God made is stable in 216Aall things, so that it may remain always. The work of God, therefore, is to create, to form, to dispose all things. The work of nature is to bring forth the seeds of things out of the hidden bosom by increase, and again, when the same wither and fall through failure, to call them back to the hidden bosom whence they had come forth. The work of the craftsman together with nature is to help by care and industry the things that rise from the earth. The work of the craftsman alone is to work upon the underlying matter of things, either by composing what is disjoined or by separating what is joined; so that it can neither create with God, that there be what was not, nor with nature bestow increase upon the offspring of things, so that greater be that which was less crat

There are therefore three workers in this world: God, nature, and the craftsman who imitates nature. But these three 216Bbring about what they produce to effect with very unequal power. For God in his work needs neither the work of nature nor that of the craftsman who imitates nature. For God sometimes works without nature, sometimes in nature, sometimes above nature. For without nature he first made nature itself. For when he made nature, he had no nature working with him. For that which was not yet could not itself work together with him who alone was. Thus therefore he first made nature without nature, so that afterwards, in nature, he might make some things with nature, others above nature. For with nature he makes those things which he brings forth from nature according to nature; above nature he makes, when in nature, beyond nature's accustomed course and first power, by a greater power added, 216Che brings something forth to effect. When therefore God works nature, and when he works above nature, nature does not work together with God; because there nature only receives that it should be what it was not, but here it receives that it should be able to do what it could not do out of what it had received. God therefore can work without nature; nature cannot work without God, because what nature does, it does out of that which God does, and together with that which God does. For God made the first power of nature; and that it may come forth to effect, he again himself does it together with that very nature which he makes. Everything therefore that nature does, God does; but not everything that God does, nature also does: he who without nature makes nature. In the third place there follow the works of the craftsman 216Dwho imitates nature; and he indeed sometimes works with God without nature, sometimes with nature without God, sometimes with God and with nature together, sometimes without God and equally without nature. With God he works when he works the works of justice, because God works together with a right will, one ordered according to justice. Without God he works when he works the works of iniquity, since sins are not from God, nor does that which is done against his will come to be through his cooperation. With nature the craftsman works when he applies outwardly his industry and care to the propagating of the seeds and offspring of things, to which nature supplies the increase. Without nature he works when, besides the things that look to the propagation of seeds, and to the tending of things being born 217Aand of those things that have the power of growth and of sense, he unfolds his effort upon the underlying matter, so as to advance something, whatever it be, to effect; in which nature only suffers, and does not work, because it furnishes the matter to the worker, and does not exercise the effecting of the work. Such are all the works of men that are done upon the earth, of which many the necessity of mortal life compels, many desire urges, many vanity works. And in all these, because nothing stable is found, and all things pass away that are done under the sun — those which either nature brings forth, or the craftsman imitating imitant nature fashions — the contemplator of wisdom subjects all things to vanity, proving that the works of God alone abide; since neither is a created essence ever consumed, nor is the reason of the disposition 217Bor order of things changed. Therefore he shows first the works of nature made subject to vanity, whether in those things which nature alone works, because things that rise set; or in those things which the craftsman does together with nature, because things increased grow old. Afterwards he enumerates many and diverse works of the craftsman who imitates nature: some of necessity, some of desire, some of vanity; and he subjects all to vanity, because he shows them liable to mutability. The work of nature alone is told when it is said: A time to be born and a time to die.

Then the work of the craftsman working together with nature is brought in, when it is said: A time to plant and a time to pluck up. Last of all the work of man without the work of nature is added, when it is brought in: A time to kill and a time to heal; a time to destroy and 217Ca time to build. And this is then set forth more manifoldly, with more things numbered up, that it may be plainly shown in how many things the vanity of the human heart is entangled and how widely it is scattered. For this pertained most of all to the matter: that the vanity of human minds, which follows the uncertainty of mortal life — because he had undertaken to reprove it — he should both set forth more diligently in the narrative, and set before the rest in the comparison; so that all the others might seem to have been recalled for this alone, that by comparison with them it might be recognized how great this one is. A time to be born and a time to die. It is a time to be born, when man is to be led into this life. It is a time to die, when he is to be called forth from this life. But meanwhile, after 217Dbirth and before death, while he lives in this mortal life, which needs sustenance and is nourished with food, that it may subsist. It is a time to plant and a time to pluck up, that man may till the earth from which he was taken, and sow, and reap, and plant, and gather. Now these two following things can also be compared with the two preceding by a distinction, in this way: A time to be born and a time to plant; a time to die and a time to pluck up. For when a man is born it is a time to plant, that earthly life may be fed with earthly fruits. But when a man dies, it is a time to pluck up; because when mortal life is destroyed, those things also which had been established for the sake of mortal life are taken away. And because to human infirmity, after the fruits of the earth, the use of flesh 218Ais also granted, therefore after the time to plant and the time to pluck up there is fittingly brought in also a time to kill. And because in this eating a measure is necessary, lest the flesh take for an incitement to vices what it has received for the sustaining of its infirmity, immediately after the time to kill he adds a time to heal: namely, that in all other times we may study with careful concern to nourish and preserve the life of those very animals which we have received to be killed at the opportune time — that is, when necessity demands — for the sustaining of our infirmity. For this is, as it were, to heal the ailing, by coming to their aid in those things wherein they are not sufficient for themselves, and to repair what is failing. Whence perhaps, fittingly, when he had said, A time to kill, he did not add, a time to heal 218Bwhat has been killed. As before, after he had said a time to plant, he immediately added, and a time to pluck up what has been planted. Namely because things planted can be plucked up, but things killed cannot be healed. Thus perhaps, if we follow the sense of the letter, we prejudge nothing of the spiritual understanding (which is to be traced out afterwards).

A time to destroy, and a time to build. When man ought to destroy and when to build, someone may reckon is by no means to be asked; since he may think that here this alone is shown: that man, if by chance he is subjected to various things by the events of the times, suffers these things unequally, even unwilling. But we, applying to an easier understanding these things which have been 218Csaid, can say that it is a time to kill when God, willing to punish the sins of men, brings the sword of slaughter for chastisement; but a time to heal when, cherishing again the afflicted and those wounded by the strokes of tribulations, he restores them with his wonted compassion. And plainly this may seem more consonant with truth, that here we ought to take the times of things not as those which serve the human will, but as those which obey the divine disposition. For neither is it the time of anything when man wills and God does not will. Because man often wills when it is not the time, and when God wills it is always the time. Therefore all times are referred to the divine ordinance; and it is said to be then the time of every thing, when it is justly disposed by God, 218Dwhether for the chastisement and correction of a crime, or for the consolation of infirmity. A time to kill and a time to heal. A time to destroy and a time to build.

A time to weep and a time to laugh. A time to mourn and a time to dance. Everywhere evils are enumerated first, afterwards good things are added; because first we are justly afflicted for our sins, afterwards we are kindly cherished again by God's compassion. And it is manifest in what way human life daily suffers the vicissitude of all these things, as often as by a hidden dispensation God either instructs us with scourges or consoles us with gifts. Then there follows:

A time to scatter stones and a time to gather. But what this means according to the letter is rightly 219Aasked, since such a thing, if it be thought to have a time among human actions, seems altogether idle and unfitting. Unless perhaps it is to be understood thus: that, because he is going to say in what follows, A time of war and a time of peace, he fittingly sets before it here a time to scatter stones and a time to gather; namely, that when a time of war is at hand the stones may be gathered for building fortifications and the ramparts of walls against sieges; but in a time of peace, because no perils of wars are threatening, the mounds of the fortifications may be scattered, so that access may lie open to all without hindrance. Nor ought it to seem superfluous, on the ground that he had said above, A time to destroy and a time to build, as though the same thing were repeated a second time; because that is taken as more fittingly said of the buildings 219Bof houses and the dwellings of men, whereas this refers more properly to the defenses of walls. Yet perhaps another sense, more suitable, may be understood under these words. For because he had set before, A time to kill and a time to heal, lest perhaps it should be thought that only the evil, and those who are to be punished for their sins, are exposed to slaughter, he now shows that the just also are sometimes, by God's permitting, for an example and chastisement of the evil, subjected together with the impious and with sinners to deaths as well, and scattered by exiles and proscriptions, as is said through Peter: It is time that judgment begin at the house of God (I Petr. IV). And that by the name of stones the just are signified is manifestly shown through Jeremiah, 219Cwhen he says: The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of all the streets (Thren. IV). And Isaiah again: I will make all thy walls of graven stones, all thy sons taught of the Lord (Isa. LIV) [Vulg. omnes terminos tuos in lapides desiderabiles, "all thy borders of desirable stones"]. Therefore it is a time to scatter stones, that the just may understand from the very labor of their scattering and shaking that there is no true rest in this life. And again it is a time to gather stones, that after the wearing down of bodily exile, lest they fail in mind, when peace has been restored they may again grow strong by a temporal benefit unto things eternal. Thus what is hidden can with difficulty be judged toward any one side: since the divine word for this reason dissembles itself from us in certain places, that even there where it was thought to be manifest it may show itself worthy 219Dof searching out.

HOMILIA XV. De tempore et tempori subjectis per aliam interpretationem.

Non nos igitur pigeat iterato parabolarum istarum duritiam attentare: donec forsitan usu sermonis attrito cortice verbi ejus interiora patescant. In temporibus enim sumus, et volvitur nobiscum sermo noster, donec stabiliamur in eo quod tempore non mutatur: hoc autem est, ut humanas maxime actiones contemplemur: quia in illis est, quod ingemiscimus, totum vanitatis.

Tempus occidendi et tempus sanandi. Quae fuerunt tempora occidendi, et tempora sanandi? Miserabile principium humanarum actionum, ab occisione et 220Ainterfectione. Sic incipere debuit opus vitae morti addictae, ut sententiam sequeretur auctoris: Maledicta saeviens in necem suam. Percurramus animo tempora praeterita, et videamus bella et interfectiones ab initio facta, usque adhuc, gentium et gentium, et innumerabilium populorum. Et sustinuit Deus humanum genus saevire in viscera sua: et in his omnibus operatus est judicia sua, furores hominum intorquens ad vindictam justitiae suae, ut alii juste paterentur, quod alii injuste voluerunt. Et surrexerunt alii et multi interficiebantur et damnabantur; et multi interficiebantur et salvabantur; et alii a morte interfectionis liberabantur, et ad damnationem servabantur, et alii liberabantur, ne damnarentur si interficerentur. In omnibus his justum judicium 220Bcomplevit super eos: ut castigaret et parceret secundum moderamen aequitatis qua disponit universa Deus. Propterea tempus est occidendi et tempus sanandi: et alii faciunt quod voluit, alii patiuntur quod nolunt, et sedet desuper Arbiter justus, faciens quod vult, et disponens omnia ut timeatur. Tempus occidendi et tempus sanandi: Tempus destruendi et tempus aedificandi. Quanta a principio aedificaverunt amatores hujus saeculi, et nomen suum in terra sua vocaverunt, ut famam haberent apud posteros gloriosam. Laboraverunt enim labore gravi in operibus suis, ut starent post ipsos monumenta jactantiae illorum: et invaluerunt usque ad aliquid magna industriae suae signa posteris relinquentes; et apparent adhuc vestigia quaedam ruinarum in ipsis, praeteritorum 220Csaeculorum: et miramur ipsos quos non videmus, quod talia potuerunt, et magis ingemiscimus super eos: quia cum essent ipsi homines ad aeternitatem conditi, vana dilexerunt: et evanuerunt, quia vani facti sunt in ipsis. Perierunt enim ipsi: et post ipsos opera eorum ceciderunt, et successerunt alii: et fecerunt ipsi quoque opera magna, et abierunt post haec in nihilum: et destructa sunt omnia, quae fecerant, pariter cum ipsis. Et iterum alii surrexerunt, et aedificaverunt, et non intellexerunt ubi esset prior generatio, et opera ejus: ut viderent vanitatem quae est sub sole. Et permisit eos Deus frustra laborare, ut aedificarent peritura: ut intelligat homo vanitatem suam, ut destruatur quod 220Daedificatum est, et iterum quod destructum est aedificetur: et non sit stabile opus hominis super terram. Ideo omnia tempus habent: ut erudiatur homo de vanitate sua, et de incerto vitae mortalis per quam ambulat.

Tempus flendi et tempus ridendi: tempus lugendi et tempus saltandi. Fletus et risus ad animum pertinent. Luctus vero, vel, ut magis proprie dicatur, planctus, et saltatio ad corpus. Fletu itaque et risu dolor et laetitia mentis exprimuntur: planctus autem et saltatio eadem ipsa significant, sed quando per corporis motum demonstrantur. Tempus flendi, et tempus ridendi: templus plangendi, et tempus saltandi. Habent omnia haec tempus suum in hominibus, dum currit vita ista mortalis: et permittit Deus varia sorte, et eventu dispari, 221Asecundum altitudinem judiciorum suorum, et profundum consilii sui, quo disponit nos, ut haec currant et varientur super nos, prospera adversis alternando, et adversa prosperis commutans in tempore. Et veniunt tempora laeta, et rident homines, et saltant, et putant bene sibi esse: et obliviscuntur saepe Creatoris sui, et se morituros esse non animadvertunt. Sola enim praesentia respiciunt, et laetantur in eis quasi permansura sint semper; nec conditionem suam et vitae mortalis dubium attendunt, neque cogitant pericula superventura. Et ideo secure peccant, et effundunt se in voluptates noxias, et ambulant post desideria cordis sui in intuitu oculorum suorum, ut faciant quae non oportet, et multiplicent iram et indignationem. Et videt hoc Deus, et super seminat 221Bdolores, et amaritudines lasciviis male dulcium voluptatum: et revocat ac cohibet effluentes ut non eant in omnem abalienationem. Tunc venit tempus flendi, et tempus plangendi: et dolent homines, et causantur saepe Deum quando bene cum eis agitur. Ipse autem dissimulat pravitatem illorum, et post tempus miscet iterum prospera adversis, ne deficiant: et rursum cum tempus est, adversa prosperis, ne praesumant: et hoc saepe agit nutriens et exercens, castigans et refovens hominem, ut discat esse timoratus: et sciat quoniam apud Dominum est potestas vitae, et mortis. Propterea est tempus flendi, et tempus ridendi: tempus plangendi, et tempus saltandi. Et succedit his tempus spargendi lapides, et tempus colligendi. Hoc tempus post illa enumeratum est, sed 221Cordinatum in illis: quia in tempore saepe simul sunt causae, quae unam temporis rationem conducunt. Tempus spargendi lapides, et tempus colligendi. Omnis mundus exsilium est iis quibus coelum patria esse debuisset: sed tamen animi mortalium usu coalescunt, et incipiunt homines diligere loca sua, et terras suas in quibus nati fuerant, vel nutriti; et succedit grandis oblivio aeternorum pro temporalium affectu: et nisi Deus tergeret istas passionum inolitas suavitates, non erat quo intraret ad nos desiderium ejus. Propterea dat judicia sua, et veniunt commotiones, et concussiones gentium, et transmigrationes populorum: et surgunt alii, ut rapiant non sua, et alii diripiuntur, et disperguntur, et iterum fortiores quibus posse datum est, et ipsi cum venerint, 221Dejiciunt eos, qui aliena violenter rapuerant, et possident non sua, et fluctuat mundus in semetipso: ut videat homo non esse hic stabilem mansionem, et assuescat paulatim abstrahere animum, et solvere a vinculis terrenarum delectationum. Propterea venit tempus spargendi lapides, ut non sit stabilis mansio super terram: et cogatur homo suspirare in exsilio suo ad patriam, ubi manent gaudia inconcussa, et pacis securitas nulla superveniente infestatione turbatur. Hoc ergo facit dispersio lapidum in tempore suo. Sed quia humana infirmitas corruit cito, et non potest diu in adversis salva consistere, venit post tempus dispersionis tempus collectionis: ut quiete temporis convalescat in hoc ipso admonita 222Asapere, et experiri quanta sint gaudia venturae quietis; ut ad illam festinet ubi timor dispersionis non est, neque exsilii aerumna metuitur, quibus aeternitas vitae in patria data est. Tempus spargendi lapides, et tempus colligendi. Deinde iterum aliud tempus sequitur post tempus istud: et nominantur alia quae et ipsa tempus habent saepe cum iis, quae dicta sunt temporibus, unum: saepe extra tempora ista tempore suo seorsum aliud.

Tempus amplexandi, et tempus longe fieri ab amplexibus. Castis amplexibus tempus datum est, ut seminetur caro in propagationem, et humani generis seges, quae quotidie per totum mundum morte metitur, studio generationis reparetur. Pactum enim institutionis primae, qua ex carne caro sumenda erat 222Bsine carnis contagio, post peccatum primae praevaricationis in carne peccati, per indulgentiam confirmatur, non solum pro explendo officio, sed etiam pro conferendo remedio: ne scilicet motus carnis immoderatius jam effervens turpius in omnem praevaricationem proflueret, si licite nusquam laxari potuisset. Praescribitur itaque meta usquequo se sine pudicitiae damno extendere possit carnis affectus: ut quod in matrimonii castimonia per concessionem agitur, etsi ad infirmitatem pertineat, ad turpitudinem tamen non imputetur. Sed ne rursum blandimenta voluptatis avertant animum in oblivionem Conditoris, salubri dispensatione aliquando homo et a concessis suspenditur: ne forte si his, quae in praesenti dulcia videntur, immoderatius inhiet, ad ea quae aeterna 222Csunt non festinet. Propterea datum est tempus amplexandi, et tempus longe fieri ab amplexibus. Tempus enim amplexandi datum est, ut reparetur mortalitas et excipiatur mortalium infirmitas: tempus longe fieri ab amplexibus datum est, ut, dum caro a carnis delectatione subtrahitur, ad spiritualem animus delectationem nutriatur. Tempus amplexandi et tempus longe fieri ab amplexibus. Quando enim colliguntur lapides, tempus est amplexandi; quando vero disperguntur, tempus longe fieri ab amplexibus: quoniam idcirco tempora augustiae data sunt, ut caro afflicta a suis se delectationibus temperet: ut post in tempore gaudii et consolationis se cum timore et reverentia ab excessu castiget. Sunt et amplexus charorum et contubernia 222Dsocietatis amicae, in qua praeter carnis experientiam, convictus dulcis gratissimo foederatur consensu qui et ipsi solvuntur tempore suo, ne cor hominis in homine requiescat, donec veniat quod non solvitur pactum charitatis aeternae. Propter haec omnia tempus est amplexandi, et tempus longe fieri ab amplexibus: ut in tempore non quaerat homo quod aeternum est, et qui hominis viventis societatem diligit, cogitet semper morituri separationem.

Tempus acquirendi, et tempus perdendi. Quae sunt bona quae primum acquiruntur, et postea perduntur? Perdita enim fuerant quaedam bona et acquisita sunt postea, ut deinceps perdi non possint. Et erant rursum alia bona non similia prioribus, 223Aquae tamen bona visa sunt: et erat vere aliquid in eis ad bonum, sed non ut prima bona quae vera erant. Et ista bona non bona erant hominis ad verum bonum: et venit homo postquam vera amiserat, et acquisivit falsa bona, felicem se existimans in illis. Voluit enim consolari et habere in tempore quod aeternitas confert: et collegit peritura, quae tenere non posset; et concessit hoc Deus, ut boni distantiam agnosceret, et erudiretur vanitate sua, ad convertendum se in ea quae vera sunt. Propterea ergo dimisit Deus cor ejus, ut congreget ea quae stare non possunt et ea ipsa in tempore suo nunc tribuit acquirenda, nunc acquisita subtrahit: probans hominem in cunctis operibus suis, et ostendens vana omnia esse sub coelo. Propter hoc datur tempus 223Bacquirendi; et tempus perdendi: ut dum adeptus fuerit homo quae concupierat, discat experiendo quod possint haec gaudia conferre iis qui magni aestimant peritura: cum vero habita perdit agnoscat quod omnia quae invito tolli poterant, fuerant etiam cum possidebantur extranea.

Tempus custodiendi, et tempus abjiciendi. Bona temporalia tempore suo custodienda sunt, quantum vitae temporalis necessitas postulat; sed quia in morte carnis omne quod ad vitae carnalis jucunditatem pertinet, necessitate amittitur, dignum est ut etiam ante mortem ab amore cordis voluntate abjiciatur.

Tempus scindendi, et tempus consuendi. Qui scindit, unita dividit: qui autem consuit, divisa et 223Cseparata conjungit. Omnia haec in vita hominum, quousque mutabilitati subjacet, sine cessatione agi iste prospexerat: in qua societas humanae conversationis, nunc quia utilitatis aliquid conferre videtur, appetenda est; nunc vero quia saepe eadem detrimentum adducit, fugienda. Habet ergo consutionem suam tempore suo consensus socialis; habet et scissionem suam in tempore suo zelus justae contradictionis; ut et bene volentibus et bona agentibus assensu et opere uniamur; ab his autem qui prava diligunt et iniqua operantur, animo pariter et operatione dividamur. Sed ne forte haec sententia eadem videatur cum illa qua supradictum est: tempus amplexandi et tempus longe fieri ab amplexibus: quoniam in illa similiter de conjunctione et separatione 223Dsocialis dilectionis tractari asseruimus, possunt non inconvenienter quae illic dicta sunt tantum de amore ac dilectione significanda accipi: quae vero hic memorantur, ad quamcunque societatem sive pactionem quamlibet in qua idem consensus est et concordiae placitum, figurandam referri. Sic se similitudines rerum praestant ad sapientiam intelligendam: et utitur ipsa sapientia operibus suis ut se manifestet in nobis. Multa sunt quae in parabolis dicuntur et profunda scrutatione digna; sed non cuncta exire volunt, ut semper intus requirantur.

Tempus tacendi, et tempus loquendi. Prius tempus tacendi, postea tempus loquendi. Sapientia enim de 224Acorde exit, nec aliunde lingua habet quod recte proferre possit, nisi prius verbum intelligentia formet. Propterea prius est tempus tacendi, post tempus loquendi: ut prius in silentio sagax cogitatio in se sapientiam colligat, quam lingua postmodum ad audientiam aliorum per verbum emittat. Propter hoc etiam tempus est tacendi et tempus loquendi, quoniam auditores verbi aliquando illud cum desiderio et amore suscipiunt, aliquando vero sine reverentia abjiciendo contemnunt. Quapropter tempus tacendi est, cum auditores admonitionis omnimodo impatientes aspicimus; tempus autem loquendi, cum eos verbum vel desiderare vel saltem sustinere velle videmus. Propter hoc quoque tempus tacendi est, quia in iis quae discutere non possumus, praesumere non 224Bdebemus. Et item tempus loquendi: quia alia quae possumus comprehendere, propter eruditionem proximorum necesse est non reticere. Unde non solum opera hominum, sed et verba fugientis vitae incertum sequuntur, ut totum vanitas occupet: et nihil stabile vel constans relinquatur: cum nec semper dicere possimus quae scimus, nec semper quae novimus, retinere: et nunc tacuisse noceat, quae dicenda fuerant: nunc vero dixisse culpa sit, quae fuerant reticenda. Item saepe non possumus, cum volumus: et sapere non volumus, cum possumus: saepius autem utrumque non debemus, cum facimus. In hoc magnum est incertum, et caligo ignorationis profundae: ut jactetur homo de tempore ad tempus, et non intelligat tempus suum in omni opere 224Csuo.

Tempus dilectionis, et tempus odii. Multa sunt quae diliguntur in hoc mundo, et similiter odiuntur plurima. Et in omnibus, quae diliguntur, pauci veritatem diligunt: et in iis, quae odiuntur, pauci odiunt iniquitatem. Propter hoc diligunt homines, et putant saepe bene se diligere, et male diligunt: quia in iis, quae diligunt, veritatem non diligunt: nec ea diligunt, propter veritatem. Similiter odia exercent plurimi, et jactant zelum suum pro justitia et aequitate: et latet intus rixa in corde, et furor saevus odio se pascens iniquo. Et propterea non possunt discernere tempus suum primitus amor, et odium: quia non sequuntur judicium justitiae et veritatis, sed suo nutu feruntur in appetitus pravos, ut faciant quae volunt. 224DDiligunt, et odiunt, amant, et zelant, saepe, quae non debent, saepe quando non debent: et confusio fit magna amoris et odii, et dispergitur cor in universam vanitatem fugiens, quae recta sunt et quae prava sunt concupiscens. Propterea positum est homini tempus amoris et odii: ut intelligat et discernat quando ex iis, quae pro tempore bona et mala esse possunt, aliquid vel appetere debeat vel declinare. Nam extra tempora quaedam sunt quae tempore non mutantur, ut aliud esse possint: et sunt in his bona et mala. Et quae bona sunt, aeterna sunt, ut semper bona sint, et quae mala sunt, similiter aeterna sunt, ut semper sint mala. Non de illis tibi dicitur: Tempus dilectionis, et tempus odii. Nam illi aeterna dilectio est, et odium 225Aaeternum: quoniam quae diligenda sunt, ibi semper diligenda sunt: et quae odienda sunt, semper sunt odienda. Interim autem nunc in tempore dum cuncta incerta sunt, ea quae transeuntibus nobis occurrunt, pro tempore se commutant, ut alteri in malum cedat quod alteri faustum exstiterat: et quod iste adversum doluit, ille sibi feliciter provenisse cognoscat. Propterea in iis omnibus, quae tempore transeunt, tempus est dilectionis et tempus odii: ut non firmet cor suum homo ad ea vel dilectione, vel odio: quae possunt et odio habita iterum juste diligi, et dilecta rursum juste odio haberi.

Tempus belli, et tempus pacis. Propter tempus occidendi, tempus belli ordinatur: propter tempus sanandi, 225Btempus pacis subsequitur. Et erat illud primum, hoc autem novissime commemoratum est: ut principium, et finis, cum mediis omnibus laboribus et periculis concludatur: ut vita hominis nunquam tuta sit, quae pertransit ut desinat. Exivit enim homo ut recederet, et non staret cum Deo: et fecit pactum dilectionis ad voluptatem hujus mundi, ut requiesceret in ea. Et noluit Deus foedus istud sustinere ut permaneret in abalienatione: et suscitavit contra eum quae perverse dilexerat, ut adversarentur, et affligerent illum: et factum est homini bellum cum omnibus quae in mundo sunt, ut dolorem et afflictionem inveniat in eis donec revertatur ad pacem cum Deo. Tunc ad pacem ejus se component omnia: ut subjecta sint humili quae fuerant adversa 225Celato. Primum enim cuncta pacata fuerant, sicut in novissimo pacabuntur universa: ut in medio quae transeant incerta sorte percurrant; donec veniant ut vel sub judicio cadenti in perpetuum adversa sint omnia, vel feliciter consummatio, subjecta sint universa. Ubi enim odium aeternum erit, illic erit et bellum perpetuum: et ubi erit aeterna dilectio, ibi pax sempiterna constabit. Neque ibi dicetur tempus pacis, et tempus belli, sicut non dicetur tempus dilectionis, et tempus odii: sed erit bellum, et pax: bellum sine fine, et sine fine pax. Non ergo existimet homo valde metuendum bellum, cui potest pax succedere: neque pacem illam veram, quam bellum subsequens potest perturbare: quia cuncta, quae transeunt, vana in hoc ipso reputanda sunt quod in 225Dbono, similiter et in malo, semper permanere non possunt.

Quid habet amplius homo de labore suo? Ergo in incerto currit labor hominis: quia amplius habere non potest de labore suo, ne contentus sit homo iis quae labore suo constant: quia vana sunt omnia, et tempore transeunt, tempore finienda.

HOMILY XV. On time and on the things subject to time, according to another interpretation.

Let it not therefore irk us to attempt once again the hardness of these parables, until perhaps, the bark being worn away by the use of speech, the inward parts of its word may lie open. For we are in times, and our discourse rolls along with us, until we be made stable in that which is not changed by time; and this is, that we should contemplate above all human actions, because in them is the whole of vanity, over which we groan.

A time to kill and a time to heal. What were the times of killing and the times of healing? A pitiable beginning of human actions, from slaying and 220Aslaughter. So must the work of a life given over to death have begun, so as to follow the sentiment of its author: Accursed, raging unto its own slaughter. Let us run over in mind the times past, and see the wars and slaughters made from the beginning until now, of nation upon nation and of innumerable peoples. And God bore with the human race raging against its own bowels; and in all these things he wrought his judgments, twisting the furies of men to the vindication of his justice, so that some justly suffered what others unjustly willed. And others rose up, and many were slain and were damned; and many were slain and were saved; and some were freed from the death of slaughter and were kept for damnation; and others were freed lest they be damned if they were slain. In all these he fulfilled his just judgment 220Bupon them, so as to chastise and to spare according to the governance of that equity by which God disposes all things. Therefore there is a time to kill and a time to heal; and some do what he willed, others suffer what they do not will, and the just Arbiter sits above, doing what he wills and disposing all things that he may be feared. A time to kill and a time to heal: A time to destroy and a time to build. How great things from the beginning have the lovers of this world built, and have called their own name upon their own land, that they might have a glorious fame among those who come after. For they labored with heavy labor in their works, that the monuments of their boasting might stand after them; and they prevailed to a certain point, leaving to posterity great signs of their industry; and there still appear certain traces of ruins among them, of ages 220Cgone by; and we marvel at those very men whom we do not see, that they could do such things, and we groan the more over them, because, though they themselves were men created for eternity, they loved vain things and vanished away, because they were made vain in themselves. For they themselves perished, and after them their works fell, and others came in their place; and these too did great works, and after these went into nothing; and all that they had made was destroyed together with them. And again others rose up and built, and did not understand where the former generation was, and its works, so as to see the vanity which is under the sun. And God permitted them to labor in vain, and to build things that would perish, that man might understand his own vanity; that what has been 220Dbuilt be destroyed, and again that what has been destroyed be built; and that the work of man upon the earth be not stable. Therefore all things have their time, that man may be instructed concerning his own vanity, and concerning the uncertainty of the mortal life through which he walks.

A time to weep and a time to laugh: a time to mourn and a time to dance. Weeping and laughter pertain to the mind. But mourning — or, to speak more properly, wailing — and dancing pertain to the body. By weeping, then, and by laughter, the grief and gladness of the mind are expressed; but wailing and dancing signify these same things, only when they are shown forth by the motion of the body. A time to weep, and a time to laugh: templus to wail, and a time to dance. All these things have their time among men, while this mortal life runs on; and God permits, by a varying lot and by unequal outcome, 221Aaccording to the height of his judgments and the depth of his counsel by which he disposes us, that these things should run and be varied over us, alternating prosperity with adversity, and changing adversity into prosperity in due time. And glad times come, and men laugh and dance and think it is well with them; and they often forget their Creator, and do not consider that they are to die. For they look upon present things alone, and rejoice in them as though they were to abide always; nor do they attend to their own condition and to the doubtfulness of mortal life, nor do they think of the perils that are to come upon them. And therefore they sin securely, and pour themselves out into harmful pleasures, and walk after the desires of their heart in the gaze of their eyes, so as to do what is not fitting, and to multiply wrath and indignation. And God sees this, and sows over them 221Bgriefs and bitternesses upon the wantonness of ill-sweet pleasures; and he calls back and restrains them as they flow forth, that they may not go into utter estrangement. Then comes a time to weep, and a time to wail; and men grieve, and often lay the blame upon God when it is dealt well with them. But he dissembles their depravity, and after a time mingles prosperity again with adversity, lest they fail; and again, when it is time, adversity with prosperity, lest they presume; and this he often does, nourishing and exercising, chastising and cherishing man, that he may learn to be fearful, and may know that with the Lord is the power of life and of death. Therefore there is a time to weep, and a time to laugh: a time to wail, and a time to dance. And upon these there follows a time to scatter stones, and a time to gather. This time is enumerated after those, but 221Cis ordered among them: because in time there are often together causes that lead to one reckoning of time. A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather. The whole world is an exile to those for whom heaven ought to have been the fatherland: yet the minds of mortals grow together with it by use, and men begin to love their own places, and their own lands in which they were born or reared; and a great forgetfulness of things eternal succeeds, for the sake of affection for things temporal; and unless God wiped away these ingrown sweetnesses of the passions, there was no way by which desire for him might enter in to us. Therefore he gives his judgments, and there come commotions and shakings of nations and migrations of peoples; and some rise up to snatch what is not their own, and others are plundered and scattered; and again the stronger, to whom the power has been given, when they too have come, 221Dcast out those who had violently snatched what belonged to others, and possess what is not their own; and the world fluctuates within itself, so that man may see that there is here no stable dwelling, and may accustom himself little by little to draw back his mind and loose it from the bonds of earthly delights. Therefore there comes a time to scatter stones, that there be no stable dwelling upon the earth, and that man may be forced to sigh in his exile for the fatherland, where joys remain unshaken, and the security of peace is troubled by no infestation coming upon it. This, then, is what the scattering of stones does in its own time. But because human infirmity quickly collapses, and cannot long stand unharmed amid adversities, after the time of scattering there comes a time of gathering: that by the quiet of the season it may grow strong, being admonished in this very thing 222Ato be wise, and to learn by experience how great are the joys of the rest to come; that it may hasten to that place where there is no fear of scattering, nor is the hardship of exile dreaded, to whom eternity of life in the fatherland has been given. A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather. Then again another time follows after that time; and others are named which themselves also have their time — often one time together with those times that have been spoken of, often, apart from those times, another separately in its own time.

A time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces. A time has been given to chaste embraces, that flesh may be sown for propagation, and that the harvest of the human race, which daily throughout the whole world is reaped by death, may be repaired by the care of generation. For the covenant of the first institution, by which flesh was to be taken from flesh 222Bwithout the contagion of the flesh, is after the sin of the first transgression confirmed in the flesh of sin by indulgence, not only for the fulfilling of a duty, but also for the conferring of a remedy: namely, lest the motion of the flesh, now boiling up too immoderately, should flow out more shamefully into every transgression, if it could nowhere be lawfully relaxed. A boundary is therefore prescribed, up to which the affection of the flesh may extend itself without loss of chastity: so that what is done in the chastity of matrimony by concession, even if it belong to infirmity, may yet not be imputed to shamefulness. But lest again the blandishments of pleasure turn the mind aside into forgetfulness of the Maker, by a wholesome dispensation man is sometimes suspended even from what is conceded: lest perhaps, if he gape too immoderately after these things that seem sweet in the present, he should not hasten to those things that are eternal 222C. Therefore a time to embrace has been given, and a time to be far from embraces. For a time to embrace has been given, that mortality may be repaired and the infirmity of mortals sustained; a time to be far from embraces has been given, that while the flesh is withdrawn from the delight of the flesh, the mind may be nourished unto spiritual delight. A time to embrace and a time to be far from embraces. For when the stones are gathered, it is a time to embrace; but when they are scattered, a time to be far from embraces: since for this reason the times of augustiae have been given, that the afflicted flesh may temper itself from its own delights, and that afterwards, in the time of joy and consolation, it may chastise itself with fear and reverence from excess. There are also the embraces of dear ones and the fellowships 222Dof friendly society, in which, apart from the experience of the flesh, a sweet companionship is bound together by a most welcome consent — and these too are loosed in their own time, lest the heart of man rest in man, until there come that covenant of eternal charity which is not loosed. On account of all these things there is a time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces: so that in time man may not seek what is eternal, and that he who loves the society of a living man may always think of the separation of one who is to die.

A time to acquire, and a time to lose. What are the good things that are first acquired and afterwards lost? For certain good things had been lost and were afterwards acquired, so that thenceforth they could not be lost. And there were again other good things unlike the former, 223Awhich nevertheless seemed good: and there was truly something in them toward good, but not as the first good things which were true. And these good things were not the good things of man toward the true good: and man came, after he had lost the true, and acquired false good things, reckoning himself happy in them. For he willed to console himself and to have in time what eternity confers; and he gathered things that would perish, which he could not hold; and God granted this, that he might recognize the distance of the good, and be instructed by his own vanity, so as to turn himself to those things that are true. Therefore, then, God let go his heart, that he might gather together those things that cannot stand; and these very things, in their own time, he now grants to be acquired, now takes away when acquired: testing man in all his works, and showing that all things under heaven are vanity. For this a time is given 223Bto acquire, and a time to lose: that while man has obtained what he had coveted, he may learn by experience what these joys can confer upon those who greatly esteem things that perish; but when he loses what he had, he may recognize that all things which could be taken from him against his will had been foreign to him even while they were possessed.

A time to keep, and a time to cast away. Temporal goods are to be kept in their own time, as much as the necessity of temporal life demands; but because in the death of the flesh everything that belongs to the pleasantness of carnal life is of necessity lost, it is worthy that even before death it be cast away by the will from the love of the heart.

A time to rend, and a time to sew. He who rends divides what is united; but he who sews joins together what is divided and 223Cseparated. All these things this man had foreseen to be done without ceasing in the life of men, so long as it lies subject to mutability: in which life the fellowship of human converse is now to be sought after, because it seems to confer something of usefulness; and now to be fled, because often the same brings loss. Social consent, therefore, has its own sewing in its own time; the zeal of a just contradiction has also its own rending in its own time: so that both with those who wish well and with those who do good we may be united in assent and in work; but from those who love depraved things and work iniquities we may be divided in mind and equally in working. But lest perhaps this sentiment seem the same as that in which it was said above, a time to embrace and a time to be far from embraces — since in that place likewise we asserted that the conjunction and separation 223Dof social love was treated of — the things that were said there can not unfittingly be taken as signifying only love and affection, while the things that are recalled here are referred to the figuring of any fellowship whatever, or of any compact in which there is the same consent and the same pleasure of concord. Thus do the likenesses of things offer themselves for the understanding of wisdom: and wisdom herself uses her own works that she may manifest herself in us. There are many things that are said in parables and worthy of deep searching; but they do not all wish to come out, that they may always be sought within.

A time to be silent, and a time to speak. First a time to be silent, afterwards a time to speak. For wisdom goes out from 224Athe heart, nor has the tongue from anywhere else what it may rightly bring forth, unless understanding first form the word. Therefore first there is a time to be silent, after that a time to speak: so that first, in silence, shrewd thought may gather wisdom into itself, before the tongue afterwards sends it forth by word to the hearing of others. For this reason too there is a time to be silent and a time to speak, since the hearers of the word sometimes receive it with desire and love, but sometimes without reverence despise it by casting it away. Wherefore it is a time to be silent, when we see hearers in every way impatient of admonition; but a time to speak, when we see that they either desire the word or at least are willing to bear it. For this reason also there is a time to be silent, because in those things which we cannot discuss we ought not 224Bto presume. And likewise a time to speak: because as for other things that we can comprehend, it is necessary, for the instruction of our neighbors, not to keep silent. Whence not only the works of men, but their words also, follow the uncertainty of fleeting life, so that vanity occupies the whole and nothing stable or constant is left: since we can neither always say what we know, nor always retain what we have learned; and now it may be harmful to have kept silent the things that ought to have been said, but now it may be a fault to have said the things that ought to have been kept silent. Likewise we often cannot when we will, and we do not will to be wise when we can; but more often we ought not to do either, when we do it. In this there is great uncertainty, and the gloom of a deep ignorance: so that man is tossed from time to time, and does not understand his own time in all his work 224C.

A time of love, and a time of hatred. Many are the things that are loved in this world, and likewise very many that are hated. And in all the things that are loved, few love truth; and in those that are hated, few hate iniquity. For this reason men love, and often think that they love well, and love ill: because in the things they love they do not love truth, nor do they love them on account of truth. Likewise very many practice hatreds, and boast of their zeal for justice and equity; and within there lurks strife in the heart, and a savage fury feeding itself on unjust hatred. And therefore love and hatred cannot at the first discern their own time: because they do not follow the judgment of justice and truth, but are borne by their own inclination into depraved appetites, so that they do what they will. 224DThey love and they hate, they cherish and they are zealous, often for things they ought not, often when they ought not; and there comes a great confusion of love and hatred, and the heart is scattered into universal vanity, fleeing the things that are right and coveting the things that are depraved. Therefore a time of love and of hatred has been set before man: that he may understand and discern when, out of those things which according to the time can be good and evil, he ought either to seek after something or to turn aside from it. For outside the times there are certain things which are not changed by time so as to be able to be otherwise: and among these there are good things and evil. And the things that are good are eternal, so that they are always good; and the things that are evil are likewise eternal, so that they are always evil. It is not of those that it is said to thee: A time of love, and a time of hatred. For to those belongs eternal love, and eternal 225Ahatred: since the things that are to be loved are there always to be loved, and the things that are to be hated are always to be hated. But meanwhile, now in time, while all things are uncertain, the things that meet us as we pass by change themselves according to the time, so that what had stood as fortunate for one gives way into evil for another; and what this man has grieved over as adverse, that man recognizes as having turned out happily for himself. Therefore in all these things that pass away with time there is a time of love and a time of hatred: so that man may not fix his heart upon them either by love or by hatred; things which, when held in hatred, can again be justly loved, and, when loved, can again be justly held in hatred.

A time of war, and a time of peace. On account of the time to kill, a time of war is ordained; on account of the time to heal, 225Ba time of peace follows. And that was the first, but this was recalled last of all: so that the beginning and the end may be enclosed with all the labors and perils that lie between; so that the life of man, which passes through only to cease, may never be safe. For man went out that he might withdraw and not stand with God; and he made a covenant of love with the pleasure of this world, that he might rest in it. And God would not endure that covenant, that man should abide in estrangement; and he raised up against him the things he had perversely loved, that they might oppose and afflict him; and there came about for man a war with all things that are in the world, that he might find grief and affliction in them until he return to peace with God. Then all things will compose themselves to peace with him, so that the things that had been adverse to the exalted may be subject 225Cto the humble. For at the first all things had been at peace, just as at the last all things will be pacified: so that in the middle the things that pass may run their course by an uncertain lot; until they come to this, that either, for one falling under judgment, all things be adverse forever, or, happily, consummation, all things be made subject. For where hatred will be eternal, there will also be perpetual war; and where there will be eternal love, there everlasting peace will stand fast. Nor will it be said there, a time of peace and a time of war, just as it will not be said, a time of love and a time of hatred: but there will be war, and peace; war without end, and without end peace. Let not man therefore reckon that war greatly to be feared to which peace can succeed; nor that peace true which a war following after can disturb: because all things that pass away are to be reckoned vain in this very thing, that in 225Dgood, and likewise in evil, they cannot always remain.

What more has man from his labor? Therefore the labor of man runs in uncertainty: because he cannot have more from his labor, lest man be content with those things that consist in his own labor; because all things are vanity, and pass away with time, to be ended with time.

HOMILIA XVI. De spirituali intelligentia eorum quae de tempore dicta sunt.

Sed jam tempus est ut post excursum temporum, secundum ea quae foris volvuntur in tempore, spiritualis etiam intelligentiae recordemur. Paulatim 226Anamque promovet se sermo sapientiae ad spiritualia contingenda, ut exercitatum animum ad interiora subducat. Duas ergo vitas supra distinximus: unam secundum carnem, alteram secundum spiritum. Vita autem carnalis tempore prior est, eo quod omnis homo prius in carne nascitur quam in spiritu renascatur: et omnis qui vivit in carne, vel secundum carnem ambulat, et vitam spiritualem nondum attigit: vel secundum spiritum ambulat, et vitam carnalem abdicavit. Quapropter omnis spiritualis ex carnali spiritualis factus est: sed non omnis carnalis ex spirituali carnalis est effectus. Vita enim carnalis semper vel sola est, vel prima, ut illam omnis homo vel solam teneat, ut spiritualem vitam nunquam inchoet: vel prius habitam spiritualis vitae 226Bstudio subsequente commutet. Utraque haec vita sectatores suos habet: carnalis quidem eos qui vitae praesentis gaudia diligunt; spiritualis vero eos qui futurae vitae jucunditatem inquirunt. Quorum illi quidem blandimentis terrenarum delectationum carnem fovent, hi vero studio virtutum in spe ac desiderio futurorum spiritum exercent. Cum duobus istis populis mundus per temporum mutabilitatem ad finem decurrit, donec veniat ut statuto pacto justitiae amborum judicium fiat. Placuit enim Deo ut ostenderet divitias gloriae superventurae in vasa misericordiae, etiam vasa irae in sustentatione per temporalem misericordiam traducere: et ipsa similiter vasa misericordiae, ut justitia et veritas adimpleatur, nunc interim molestiis tentationum exercere: ut habeat 226Comnis vita et quod de misericordia gratuitum accipiat, ne bonitas relinquatur incognita; et quod de justitia districtum sentiat, ut veritas fiat manifesta. Propterea itaque proposuit Deus omni homini et bona et mala, ut utrumque demonstraret, misericordiam scilicet et veritatem: alterum, quo sine merito gratis beneficium tribuit; alterum, quo malo merito poenam dignam rependit. Propterea disposuit ut utrumque accipiat homo; et reliquit potestatem homini quid prius velit ut accipiat. Apposuit autem conditionem electionis in utroque, ne forte excusabilis sit concupiscentia prava: ut si homo bona temporalia in hac vita ad jucunditatem eligeret, aeterna adipisci non valeret; et si se hic flagello castigationis in judicio veritatis sponte supponeret, in 226Dfutura vita tormenta damnationis non sentiret. Reprobi autem qui vitam temporalem diligunt, et ejus jucunditatem vitae perpetuae gaudiis anteponunt, bona praesentia toto desiderio amplectuntur, atque in eis omnem felicitatem suam constituunt: electi vero temporales dolores patienter sustinent, ut ad ea, quae promissa sunt, gaudia aeternitatis possint pervenire: et in eorum respectu quidquid transitorium est, si amarum videtur, non metuunt; si dulce, non concupiscunt. Unde accidit ut carnalis vitae amatores prius habeant bona, deinde mala accipiant: spirituales vero prius adversis exerceantur, deinde ad bona pertingant. Illis prima bona, ultima mala: istis prima mala, ultima bona. Sed quia 227Arursum omnia, quae in tempore transeunt, confusa sunt et permista, ut ordinem non servent, sive de bono in malum, sive de malo in bonum, idcirco nunc interim inter principium et finem multiplex vicissitudo incurrit: ut scilicet nunc post bona mala, nunc post mala bona, et malis pariter et bonis incerta sorte contingant. Omnia ista dum de temporum volubilitate, et vicissitudine eorum, quae in tempore variantur, distinctionem quamdam proponeret Ecclesiastes, pro exemplo universorum diligenter expressit, ut et bonorum et malorum simul sortem provectumque in contraria currentem ostenderet. Cum enim dixisset omnia quae sub coelo sunt temporis rotatu variari et in contraria ferri, subjunxit exempla, et enumeravit multa de omnibus ut 227Bomnium natura patesceret. Et in iis quae enumeravit, quaedam sunt in quibus commemorantur bona et mala - quaenam in quibus mala et bona, ut et carnalium et spiritualium pariter status et conditio agnoscatur. Septem enim sunt in quibus bona prius commemorantur, postea mala; et iterum septem in quibus mala prius dicuntur postea bona, ut universitas in utraque parte usque in finem decurrat. Septenario quippe tota haec vita praesens exprimitur: quae septem dierum curriculo provolvitur usque ad finem suum. Habent ergo mali septenarium suum, et boni similiter septenarium suum habent; quia tota haec vita malorum est de bono in malum, et tota bonorum de malo in bonum cuntium. Cujus 227Cvitae principium malorum est in bono, et finis in malo; bonorum autem principium in malo, et finis in bono, mediis alternatim fluctuantibus. Media enim incerta sunt: et ob hoc etiam quod medium positum est, dubie est pronuntiatum, sive de bono in malum, sive de malo in bonum. Medium enim fuit tempus spargendi lapides et tempus colligendi: et ipsum ambiguam expositionem suscepit, sive de bello sive de pace significans, ut media incerta relinquantur.
