Neque enim potest homo rixando et murmurando contra Deum ejus dispositionem immutare: et ideo melius est ejus judicia cum timore suscipere, quam in ejus injuria pro nostra laesione murmurare. Nam et ideo Deus judicia sua abscondit a nobis, ut, dum ea nec nostro intellectu penetrare, nec pro nostro arbitrio immutare possumus, amplius timeamus. Idcirco prosequitur et dicit:

Didici quod omnia opera quae fecit Deus, perseverent in aeternum. Non possumus eis quidquam addere nec auferre quae fecit Deus, ut timeatur. Non solum de operibus Dei quibus essentias rerum 242Ccreavit: creatisque per singula genera, et species rerum formam modumque imposuit, hoc verum est, quod opera Dei perseverent in aeternum: pro eo quod ejus dispositio in eis non mutatur, et servant singula, ut sint quod ea esse instituit: et si transeunt, non ex ipso hoc est, quod id quod sunt ex ipso sunt; quod autem esse desinunt, ex semetipsis habent: sicut et hoc quod antequam essent, nihil fuerunt, ex semetipsis habuerunt. Non solum itaque verum est hoc de operibus Dei quibus creaturam mundi disponit, quod sine immutatione et confusione ordinis maneant in aeternum; sed etiam de dispositione et praedestinatione judiciorum ejus quibus facta hominum examinat, hoc verum est, quod 242Dmaneant in aeternum, et legem providentiae suae, et statutum cogitationis ipse non mutat. Et sicut operibus ejus rerum generibus neque addere possumus creando, ut sit quod non erat, neque auferre perimendo, et destruendo, ut omnino nihil sit quod aliquid erat: sic neque judicia ejus immutare possumus, vel addendo ut fiat quod ipse non disposuit, vel auferendo ut non fiat quod ipse fieri ordinavit. Ut enim solus ipse timeatur, et ad eum omni tempore in misericordia respectus sit conscientiae humanae, idcirco soli sibi potestatem servavit operum, et judiciorum suorum, ut nemo immutare possit quod ipse legibus aeternis fixum constituit, ut adimpleret. Propter hoc non disputet homo in universis quae illi adveniunt, sed suscipiat judicia Dei cum 243Areverentia et timore: et cum quidem prospera tribuit Deus, et placita condonat, casta exsultatione laetetur in beneficiis ejus; cum vero adversa egrediuntur, et molesta occurrunt, mala sua merita confitens, justitiam illius commendet et veritatem. Quod si quando molestiis ingruentibus, patientiam suam labefactari conspexit, contra murmurationis et impatientiae vitium dona munificentiae Creatoris sui opponat: ut animus qui pondere tentationis premitur, ne aliquatenus in blasphemiam erumpat, recordatione beneficiorum Dei mitigetur. Tunc enim incipiet benefacere, et laetari in vita sua, et videre bona de labore suo: non solum quando bonis hujus mundi industria sua acquisitis cum gratiarum actione perfruitur; sed tunc etiam quando in adversis 243Bconstitutus, pro patientiae suae labore spe futurae consolationis laetatur. Comedet enim et laetabitur in donis Dei, quando in prosperis exsultabit de munere, et in adversis hilarescet de retributione. Sic se omni tempore componet ad pacem cum Deo, ut videat et intelligat quod cuncta bona facit in tempore suo, ut non juste accusetur ab homine in omnibus quae acciderint. Rata enim sunt judicia ejus: et de legibus illius, in aeternum stantibus, non potest immutari magnum vel parvum aliquid. Nam sicut in cunctis rerum generibus quae videntur imminui vel deperire, in iis quae transeunt, in supervenientibus et succedentibus restaurantur, ut dispositio universitatis ordinem suum ratum immobilemque conservet; et permaneat semper primae dispositionis statutum 243Cinviolabile, ut neque ultra transgrediatur vel infra remaneat operum Dei certa moderatio: sic et judicia ejus secundum certam providentiam currunt, ut his neque addi neque minui aliquid possit. Et si quando ipse aliter facere videtur, et aliter judicare, dispensatio occulta est qua non mutatur consilium, sed opus variatur et judicium exercetur. Nam et hoc ipsum judicium est: quod judicium differtur aliquando ut tempore suo restauretur, ut non pereat aliquid ex omnibus quae facta sunt, ut maneant semper. Semper enim hoc est, ut culpa poenam habeat, et justitia praemium consequatur. Sed est poena occulta, et poena manifesta. Similiter praemium occultum est, et praemium manifestum. Et saepe Deus malos tolerat, et differt poenam illorum 243Dmanifestam: et habet tamen omnis malitia poenam occultam. Et judicat Deus, et videtur differre judicium vel facta hominum omnino non attendere ab iis qui non vident nisi ea quae foris sunt. Similiter aliquando probat Deus justos, adversitatibus et tribulationibus exercet, et videtur justitia non habere praemium apud ipsum: et tamen nunquam caret retributione sua occulta: et manifesta aliquando differtur, ut interrogarentur de perseverantia sua conscientiae hominum. Et quia ea quae in manifesto sunt dissimiliter currunt, fluctuant eorda hominum, et mirantur ubi sit judicium veritatis; cum in hoc mundo innocentia premitur, et malitia prosperatur; propter hoc subjunxit, et ait:

HOMILY XVII. On the confusion of minds arising from the passing of times.

236D

Just now we have come out from the times, but would that we had come through to eternity! For many things still remain, and very many are rolled about us: and again the times repeat their circuit on every side, so that there is no end until all things shall have been consummated. For upon the mutability of things there follows a grievous confusion of minds: since hearts go along upon the rollings and passings of times, so that they do not stand in truth, but flow away with the things which go that they may pass. Therefore he ceases from all these things which totter without, and fluctuate, as though all these were small and not working greatly unto peril: and he turns himself inward, and there redoubles his complaint concerning the vanity 237Awhich is hidden: and he examines that one with grievous expostulation over the one which appears without as alien. For the mutability of things would not have harmed, if the mutability of minds had not been: since this very thing was good, that transitory things should change their appearance for a time, but it was not good that the judgments of human minds should desert truth. And so we do not lay the blame that times are various, since it is good: but we lay the blame that human judgments are various: since this is not good. For truth cannot of itself be other: because what is good in truth is not evil: and what is not good in truth, is evil. Why therefore is it judged that this is good, and this is evil; and is it judged that this is evil, and this is good: when in truth either 237Bit is not good, if it is evil, or it is not evil, if it is good. One says, It is good, and another says, It is evil: and he who says, This is good, says That is evil: and he who says This is evil, says That is good: and all speak ill, because the whole is good. But this alone is not good, that they speak ill of that which is good. Wherefore all things are good: and those alone are evil who beyond all the rest ought to have been good. For all the rest are what they ought to have been, and they alone are not what they ought to have been: because they are not truthful, and are not in truth; and therefore all things are good in that which they are, but they themselves are not good in that which they are, because they are not what they ought to have been. This therefore, among the other vanities, is itself also reckoned for a great vanity, 237Cand alone is set before all vanities by comparison. And he says:

I saw the affliction which God gave to the sons of men, that they should be distended in it. For what is that affliction?

He hath made all things good in their time: and he hath delivered the world to their disputation; that man may not find the work which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end. Therefore the mutability of things does not afflict man, but his own disputation afflicts him. And rightly: because disputation always signifies restlessness and struggle. And therefore the mutability of things is not man's labor; but that he himself has been made restless, this is his labor. And that restlessness itself is the great disputation 237Dwhich man has in his own instability, so that he does not feel the same thing: since he is divided, and made another, so that he is not one whole. Consider now the great disputation which man carries on upon the earth. For it is much, and long, and exceedingly involved: so that it cannot easily have an end, until man himself receives his end. And now, that you may believe, see how many sentiments concerning the works of God those curious of wisdom have formed from the beginning: and there has been no one until now who could impose an end upon this so great business. And they wrangle still daily, and fight with struggles as they dispute: and one says This is so, and another says It is not, but it is otherwise; and many things are said, and lies of opinions are feigned as though wrought by craft concerning the judgment of things. And very many assert 238Athat there is nothing except that very thing which is seen, and others come, and testify that nothing truly is except that very thing which is not seen. And in all these things they heap up and multiply their arguments, and weave reasons, and as it were reasons: and each man's reason is his own estimation. For God has set forth his work before the eyes of men, that he may question their hearts concerning it: and he himself lies hidden behind, until they may make trial of our exercise in it. And they draw with sense, and judge with heart, and bring forth very many things out of the treasury of their judgments, and out of the deep abyss of their fantasies, and of their false opinions and empty thoughts. And some say that nature alone is, and there is nothing else; and God is nothing, but empty fear has devised all things; and so it always was, 238Bwhat is from the beginning, and before the beginning without beginning. And the ages revolve, and nature works itself, and renews itself, and cannot be other than it always was. Others on the contrary cry out and wrangle for the wrong done to the Creator, and think that they defend him whom they themselves assail with their lies. They say that there is a craftsman who from matter co-eternal with himself has fashioned all things, that he might give a better form; and these men do not know the power of the Creator, but deny that anything has been made from nothing: and they deny that any of these things which are can slip back into nothing: but that the Founder's work consists only in the alterations of things. After these others follow, wrangling and disputing, and they promise to take away error and to make truth manifest; and these themselves confess that all things were made from nothing, and that he was not made 238Cthrough whom all things were made; and that there was once a time when nothing was created, and that then he was who always was. And these men have in their teachings as it were a good beginning, but an evil end follows. For those who think as it were truly concerning the creation of things, lie exceedingly concerning the subsistence of things, and there is no end of the disputations and inventions of men. They feign essences, and forms, and atoms, and ideas of the principal constitutions, and very many elements, and infinite births, and invisible motions and procreative efficiencies. And in all these things the likenesses of reasons are multiplied, and very many disputations are made, and truth is not in them all. For likewise he who speaks, speaks falsely, and he who contradicts, 238Dspeaks falsely, because by disputing and by lying they have all by one vanity gone far away from truth. For neither shall man be able to find the work which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end. Out of all the things which have been made from the beginning and which are to be made unto the end, man will not be able to find any one thing so as to comprehend it, and know the whole of what it is. For even if certain men seem to have found very many things, all things had been set forth, and the things which were hidden could in no way be found. For God delivered the world to their disputation, and set before them his works, that they might see them and judge. And in these he manifested many things which he willed to be known, and the things which he willed to be hidden could not be found. Therefore God manifested in them all the things which are known; and man did not find them 239Aby his own sense, until they were revealed in him so far as God willed. For certain things were set forth without, and certain things were revealed within, and man found nothing, so as to go by his own sense to those things which were hidden, until they were made manifest in him. And if he should wish to contend that he himself found some things, could he nevertheless find all the things which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end? And in the very things which he found, could he find the whole of what was, and did there not remain over something hidden and secret to which his sense was not admitted, so that he might find the whole? For if man had found the whole, there would be no disputation at all, nor would opinions run in opposite directions concerning all those things which are in the world. For we all alike see this world: and it is placed before our eyes, 239Bthat it might be delivered to our disputation; and we see this whole before us, and we do not know whence it came hither. For he who made it lies hid, and stretches his work out before himself, that he may be hidden, and be made manifest in it. For the image that has been made, receiving human contemplation from near at hand, brings it about that one can neither see his Creator manifestly, nor likewise be wholly ignorant of him. Therefore the understanding of man, exercised by the appearance of things, rises up, and from that which offers itself to manifestation strives, according to its emulation of truth, to search out inward things; and it has in the works of God the beginning of first contemplation, but it does not come through unto the end of the works of God, so as to grasp the whole of what is hidden. For if it had been able to come through to the end, it would assuredly have found God, since from him from whom 239Call things are, there do all things have their end and consummation. It does not therefore come to the end, since it could not find God, until he himself should manifest himself in us; and they that search searchings have been confounded, since they have failed (Psal. LXIII), and have not availed to comprehend and to make an end of their disputations. Therefore God hath made foolish the wisdom of the world (I Cor. V), because he placed the world in their disputation, himself remaining hidden until the disputers and those seeking empty things should fail. And man shall not find every work which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end. After these things God revealed himself and came forth that he might be found, when man could no longer glory as though he himself by his own sense and wisdom had known God, who had failed in 239Dsearching out the work of God. To this end therefore it profited that the world was for a time delivered to their disputation, that man might not find invenirit every work which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end. These are the disputations of men seeking with vain curiosity the hidden things of the works of God, which they multiply for themselves by fabricating lies concerning the things they do not know, and they fortify their errors with concortationibus. And there are yet certain other disputations in the desires of men, exceedingly manifold and various, and out of them arise the pursuits of many vanities. For every man prefers what he himself loves, and the hearts of all are drawn into infinite rendings, so that they never agree in one. Some follow wantonness and luxury and pleasure: to be drunken and to play and to laugh and to dance, and 240Athey reckon this to be the happiness of man and the sweetest delight. Others court honors, and dignities, and great fame among the peoples, and commend their own pursuits, and dispute with grievous struggle, that this portion is better in the life of man. Others heap up moneys and pile up wealth, and think to procure security, and great confidence against oncoming want in the time of straitness. And these men praise foresight and say that solicitude is better, though they wish nevertheless to be secure themselves. And thus indeed all are carried away into their own appetites, each one apart with contrary approval; and they dispute by quarreling, and by dissenting with importunate desires. And the world is delivered to their disputation, that in its affluence each one may make trial of his own pleasures and prove them, and 240Bsee, and consume them into arguments one against the other about themselves out of its plenty, each man of that thing which he himself shall have chosen in the approval of his own desires. And each one snatches with great obstinacy what he has chosen for himself; and each praises his own part, and there comes to be a great disputation and altercation of wills in the various estimations which many desires bring forth. And in all these things man does not find the work which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end. For the beginning of the works of God is the use of temporal things; but the end and consummation, the fruit of eternal things. Therefore he who establishes his disputation in the things of the world, and seeks out the approval of his own desires, cannot find in the works which God hath wrought anything from the beginning unto the end; since, 240Calthough he is allowed to make trial how great delight there can be in the goods of this world, yet that ineffable pleasantness which confers consummated happiness he does not lay hold of in the contemplation of God. For this reason the world has been delivered to the lovers of the world, to whom it is not given to deserve to find the works of God from the beginning unto the end; because to those from whom the sweetness of eternal goods is taken away, carnal delights have been given, and the joys of the world set forth unto the dissipation of their evil desires. We find yet other disputations in the judgments of men, grievous and manifold, and horrendous stirring up quarrels rigas coacitantes, so that they grow even into blasphemy of the Creator, and men say the things they ought not. For men violently seize the place 240Dof God, and set themselves up as judges of the world, and dispute concerning the world and concerning the works of God, and his providence, and the judgments by which he disposes the whole world. And some say, God has done this well; and others murmur, and say, That was not well done. For these are the complaints of men, and the presumptions by which they provoke the wrath of God; because they will not be subjected to his laws, but dispute concerning his works, and reprehend his judgments. Someone has perished by a cruel death or by grievous loss, and has been crushed by a miserable chance; and his enemy comes and says: God has done well; he has judged an impious and sinful man according to his malice; and his friend murmurs, and raises a complaint against God, why he permitted an innocent man to perish, and did not guard the just man. And that man is condemned 241Afor his malice; and this one is judged for his rashness. And yet men do not cease to dispute concerning the works of God, and to weigh his judgments by their own estimation; and God is reprehended by the thoughts of malignant men. For men say that God ought not to have created harmful things, nor to have placed among his works the things which are hostile and do harm; and they curse the good creatures of God, and blaspheme their Creator. Frogs, and flies, and serpents, and all venomous things, and all adverse and pestilential things — why did God make them? For he would have done better, if he had made all things good. For evil things are very many, and all evil things are not good. And he indeed made all things good in their time; but man alone is evil, not understanding goodness nor retaining the judgment 241Bof truth, and with an evil will disagrees with goodness: and when that comes to pass which he himself evilly does not will, he says that it is ill done; whereas it is well done, and he himself evilly wills. Therefore evil wills and wicked concupiscences blind the hearts of men, so that they do not understand what is right, because they do not love nor will what is good. And they reprehend God because he made harmful things; and yet no one reprehends when his own enemy is hurt, though they themselves all are enemies of God, and adversaries of truth. For this reason man does not understand the work which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end. For the carnal man perceiveth not the things that are of God (I Cor. II). For he follows his own concupiscence, and praises the delight of his own desires, and when what he loves is given him, he thinks that it goes well with him. when rather this comes to pass 241Cunto his harm; and when his desires are withstood, he murmurs and raises a complaint; and he lays blame, as though it were ill done when it is justly ordained; and he does not understand the works which God works from the beginning unto the end. From the time when he is brought forth out of the earth, until he is called back into the earth: he does not understand the works which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end. For God works many things about man from his beginning and unto the end of him, and man does not find to what end all these things are done, until he himself receives his end. But then he shall understand, and then he shall find the things which God hath wrought in him from his own beginning unto his own end, whether in mercy or in judgment, that he might lead him to such an end as he approved by his works from the beginning unto the end, that 241Dhe should come into consummation. But meanwhile, until the end comes, from the beginning unto the end all things lie hidden, so that man does not find the work which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end. Therefore he can dispute concerning the works of God, which God works from the beginning unto the end; but he cannot find the work which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end. But if man cannot find the work which God works from his own beginning unto his own end, so as to understand at least this which he himself has seen, how then shall he find the works which God hath wrought from the beginning of the world unto the end of the age, which he himself could not see? Let man therefore cease to dispute concerning the judgments of God, by which he governs and disposes the whole world from the beginning unto the end; because man was placed by God neither as ruler 242Anor as judge of the world, but as possessor; nor that by his own strength or power he should rule the elements of the world or dispense the outcomes of times at his own choice, but that he should receive the fruits of the world, and the changes of times, according to the Creator's dispensation, for the use of nourishing his own weakness. Therefore he added and said:

I have known that there was nothing better than to be glad and to do well in one's life. For every man that eateth and drinketh, and seeth good of his labor, this is the gift of God. For every man who contends and disputes concerning the works of God, and lays blame on the judgments of God, and accuses his dispositions in the world: this is not the gift of God, nor is it from God, but against God; and he does better who lawfully uses in this world the gifts of God acquired by just labor, 242Bthan he who quarrels against God over those things which in this world come to pass contrary to his own will or estimation. For man cannot by quarreling and murmuring against God change his disposition: and therefore it is better to receive his judgments with fear, than to murmur, in wrong done to him, over our own hurt. For to this end also God hides his judgments from us, that, while we can neither penetrate them by our own understanding nor change them at our own choice, we may fear the more. Therefore he goes on and says:

I have learned that all the works which God hath made continue for ever. We cannot add anything to them nor take away the things which God hath made, that he may be feared. Not only of the works of God by which he created the essences of things, 242Cand imposed upon the things created, through their several genera and species, form and measure, is this true, that the works of God continue for ever: in that his disposition in them is not changed, and each thing keeps to being what he appointed it to be: and if they pass away, this is not from him, since what they are they are from him; but that they cease to be, they have from themselves: just as this also, that before they were, they were nothing, they had from themselves. And so not only is this true of the works of God by which he disposes the creation of the world, that they remain for ever without change and confusion of order; but also of the disposition and predestination of his judgments, by which he examines the deeds of men, this is true, that they 242Dremain for ever, and he himself does not change the law of his own providence, and the decree of his own thought. And just as to his works, to the genera of things, we can neither add by creating, so that there should be what was not, nor take away by destroying and demolishing, so that what was something should be nothing at all: so neither can we change his judgments, either by adding, so that what he himself has not disposed should come to pass, or by taking away, so that what he himself has ordained to be done should not come to pass. For that he alone might be feared, and that at all times the regard of the human conscience might be toward him in mercy, therefore he has reserved to himself alone the power of his works and of his judgments, that no one may change what he himself has fixed by eternal laws, to be fulfilled. For this reason let not man dispute in all the things which come upon him, but let him receive the judgments of God with 243Areverence and fear: and when indeed God bestows prosperity and grants pleasant things, let him be glad with chaste exultation in his benefits; but when adverse things come forth, and troublesome things meet him, confessing his own evil deserts, let him commend God's justice and truth. But if at any time, when troubles press upon him, he has seen his own patience giving way, let him set against the vice of murmuring and impatience the gifts of his Creator's munificence: so that the mind which is pressed by the weight of temptation may, lest it break out in any degree into blasphemy, be softened by the remembrance of God's benefits. For then he will begin to do well, and to be glad in his life, and to see good things of his labor: not only when with thanksgiving he enjoys the goods of this world acquired by his own industry; but then also when, set 243Bin adversities, he is glad, for the labor of his patience, in the hope of consolation to come. For he shall eat and shall be glad in the gifts of God, when in prosperity he shall exult over the gift, and in adversity shall be gladdened over the recompense. Thus at all times he will compose himself unto peace with God, so that he may see and understand that he makes all things good in their time, so that he may not justly be accused by man in all the things that shall have befallen. For his judgments are established: and of his laws, standing for ever, nothing great or small can be changed. For just as in all the genera of things which seem to be diminished or to perish, in those things which pass away, they are restored in the things that come upon them and succeed, so that the disposition of the universe may keep its own order established and immovable; and the ordinance of the first disposition may remain always 243Cinviolable, so that the sure moderation of the works of God neither passes beyond nor remains short: so also his judgments run according to a sure providence, so that nothing can be added to them or diminished from them. And if at any time he himself seems to do otherwise, and to judge otherwise, there is a hidden dispensation by which the counsel is not changed, but the work is varied and the judgment exercised. For this very thing also is a judgment: that judgment is sometimes deferred, that in its own time it may be restored, so that nothing may perish of all the things which have been made, but that they may remain always. For this is always so, that fault has its punishment, and justice obtains its reward. But there is a hidden punishment, and a manifest punishment. Likewise there is a hidden reward, and a manifest reward. And often God tolerates the evil, and defers their manifest punishment: 243Dand yet all malice has its hidden punishment. And God judges, and seems to defer judgment, or not to attend at all to the deeds of men, in the eyes of those who see nothing but the things which are without. Likewise God sometimes proves the just, exercises them with adversities and tribulations, and justice seems not to have its reward with him: and yet it never lacks its own hidden recompense: and the manifest one is sometimes deferred, that the consciences of men might be questioned concerning their perseverance. And because the things which are in the open run dissimilarly, the eorda of men fluctuate, and they wonder where the judgment of truth is; when in this world innocence is oppressed, and malice prospers; for this reason he subjoined and said:

HOMILIA XVIII. De perversis hominum moribus: et quid ex eis censuerit Ecclesiastes.

244A

Vidi sub sole in loco judicii impietatem, et in loco justitiae iniquitatem. Et dixi in corde meo: Justum et impium judicabit Dominus, et tempus omnis rei tunc erit. Quia vero mentibus humanis de judiciis Dei et de rerum omnium proventu contrario gravis aborta est disputatio, et subjiciendae nunc sunt rationes, quare corda hominum adversus ipsum moveantur, et in murmurationem consurgant, breviter superiora repetemus ut eorum quae dicenda sunt, ex ipsis sententiam quasi a principio dicamus. Superius demonstraverat Ecclesiastes nihil in hoc mundo perpetuo in eodem posse consistere; sed temporum 244Bvices contrariis euntibus sine cessatione raptari: quae videlicet rerum mutabilitas licet a Creatore rerum omnium recte ordinetur, tamen cor humanum per impatientiam in murmurationem et blasphemiam adversus ipsum concutitur. Et ideo subjunxit post enumerata rerum tempora, et ait: Vidi afflictionem quam dedit Deus filiis hominum, ut distendantur in ea. Cuncta fecit bona in tempore suo, et mundum tradidit disputationi eorum. Haec est ergo afflictio hominum, disputatio eorum adversus Deum; quia in eo quod judiciis Dei humiliter subdi nolunt, et ejus dispositionem, quae bona est in rebus omnibus, cum quid contra voluntatem eorum pravam agitur, contumaciter reprehendunt, non solum eos exterius poena adversitatis, et tribulationis molestia 244Catterit, sed multo magis intus furor, et impatientia murmurationis affligit. Quam afflictionem Deus illis dedisse dicitur, non mentem illorum pravitate corrumpendo, sed judicia sua juste, ut probentur ipsi, quod mali sunt, ab eorum cognitione subtrahendo; ut, cum videre non valent qua justitia fiat quod circa eos agitur, amplius per impatientiae suae vitium a cognitione veritatis excaecentur. Idcirco dedit illis afflictionem, quando disputationem dedit celando judicia sua, ut non inveniat homo omne opus, quod operatur Deus ab initio usque ad finem. Nam praecedunt aliquando quaedam causae manifestae in hoc mundo judicia Dei, cum Deus facta hominum in praesenti vita subsequente retributione vel bona remunerat, vel punit mala. Et in his tantum valent 244Daliquatenus discerni judicia Dei, ut aliquid judicium habeat homo occultae veritatis, quatenus illa etiam quae penetrare non potest, veneretur.

Cum vero causae praecedentes occultae sunt, vel quae subsequuntur latent, oriuntur disputationes plurimae et contradictiones, et affligunt se mentes hominum pravae rixando, et murmurando contra Deum, cum penetrare non possint judicia ipsius, neque invenire opus quod operatus est Deus ab initio usque ad finem. Non enim penetrare possunt in tanta caligine, quo fine fiat aliquid, etsi quaedam in principio causae exstare videntur, sed occulta sunt omnia propter finem. Idcirco non invenit homo omne opus Dei ab initio usque ad finem; quoniam 245Aet si quaedam videre videtur non penetrat totum, et fit dubium totum, quia non manifestatur totum; propterea ne rixetur homo in dubiis contra Deum, et murmuret in adversis constitutus, dono Dei conceduntur prospera multa, et placita plurima, ut licite utatur homo bonis justo labore acquisitis, et gaudeat, et laetetur, et mitiget conscientiam suam adversus Deum. Et bene sentiat de illo, et non disputet neque contendat adversus illum, quasi adversetur Deus qui bona largitus est. Hoc enim sibi vult quod subjungitur, dicens: Et cognovi, quod non esset melius nisi laetari, et facere bona in vita sua. Qui enim sibi benefacit in vita sua de his quae dono Dei concessa sunt hominibus ad fruendum ut laetetur et gaudeat in Deo suo, melius facit quam qui 245Bdisputat et contendit adversus Deum. Omnis enim homo qui comedit, et bibit, et videt bonum de labore suo, hoc donum Dei est. Idcirco hoc quia donum Dei est, et licite concessum a Deo, melius est quam disputare, et contendere, et murmurare: quod donum Dei non est, nec concessum hominibus a Deo; quia malum est et afflictio magna. Multum quippe affligitur qui neque amare vel approhare potest, quod sustinet; nec quod odit, immutare. Idcirco multum affligitur qui disputat, et rixatur contra Deum, blasphemans judicia ejus et opera ejus detestans, cum ea quae operatur Deus homo mullatenus possit immutare.

Propterea quod sequitur et dicit: Didici, quod omnia opera quae fecit Deus perseverarent in aeternum. 245CSicut enim opera conditionis in generibus suis ordinem divinae institutionis non transeunt, ita quoque opera judiciorum ejus, quibus facta hominum et totum mundum disponit, sententiam praedestinationis et providentiae ejus in aeternum fixam non confundunt. Neque enim addere illis quidquam possumus, ut amplius sit quam provisum est; neque auferre, ut sint minus quae facta sunt, ut timeatur Deus. Propter hoc namque dispositio rerum visibilium in cursu transeuntium rerum et succedentium vicissitudine ordinem non confundit, ut sciat homo et intelligat providentiam esse aeternam, quae ab initio rata constantique praecepti sui examinatione quemadmodum proventus suos temporibus suis 245Dconsequerentur, cuncta disposuit. Ut illam quoque in factis suis discat metuere, cujus omnipotentiam cernit in cunctis suis operibus, et judiciis constantiam atque immutabilem permanere. Rata quippe dispositio operis et certa moderatio, qua cuncta temporibus suis ad effectum producit Deus, manifeste demonstrat, quod sicut sua sapientia in discernendo non fallitur, ita quoque consilium suum in judicando non mutatur. Quod factum est ipsum permanet. Sicut in hoc toto rerum conditarum corpore quod factum est permanet, quia dispositionis ordo non confunditur, etiamsi natura mutabilis varietur, ita etiam in judiciis ejus quod factum est permanet, quia in eo etiam quod secundum ineffabilem dispensationem, variationem temporum dissimiliter 246Aordinat, providentiae suae sententiam non immutat. Idcirco quod factum est, permanet, et in rerum universitate, quantum pertinet ad ordinem dispositionis, et in judicii ejus exhibitione, quantum ad sententiam praedestinationis spectat. Quae futura sunt jam fuerunt. In utroque etenim quae futura sunt, jam fuerunt; quia et in generibus rerum omnium quod fuerunt ea quae jam non sunt, hoc idem secundum naturae similitudinem et identitatem procursus in genere suo singula futura sunt, quae nondum sunt. Et in judiciis divinis quam veritatem in praeteritis servatam audivimus, eamdem in supervenientibus exhibendam exspectamus. Instaurat enim Deus ubique quod abiit; quia sicut rerum transeuntium defectum per succedentium in suis generibus 246Bmultiplicationem reparat, ita quotidie facta hominum judicando, antiquam judiciorum suorum, quae ab initio exercuit veritatem, licet intermissa ad templum videretur, integram se tenuisse demonstrat. Semper enim apud ipsum malitia poenam habet, et praemium virtus. Sed quia poenarum quaedam occulta est, quaedam manifesta: dum impios et peccatores Deus per patientiam tolerat, et eis statim poenam manifestam non irrogat, humana stultitia eum aut nescire aut non curare facta hominum, sive etiam, quod pejus est, pravitatem malignantium approbare putat. Inde ergo cor hominis adversus Deum concutitur, unde Deus ab hominibus amplius diligendus et laudandus demonstratur. Conqueritur homo, quod malus homo a Deo toleratur, 246Ccum manifestum sit quod nullus homo fuisset bonus, si nullus aliquando fuisset toleratus malus. Et tamen scandalizantur infirmantium corda, dum vident in hoc mundo impios prosperari et premi innocentes; quia ad sola ea quae foris sunt in manifesto respiciunt, et illa quae vel intrinsecus latent occulta, vel in futuro manifesta exhibenda servantur, non attendunt. Quorum querela ex qua causa surgat, aperitur cum subditur:

Vidi sub sole in loco judicii impietatem et in loco justitiae iniquitatem. Vidit quippe, quod in hoc mundo Deus impios judices esse permittit, et potestatem obtinere ut dominentur et opprimant innocentes, et facta hominum iniqua, quae justa esse debuerunt, 246Det in his omnibus confusionem magnam esse sub sole. Quia enim Deus potestatem in hoc mundo perversis tribuit, propterea impietas est in loco judicii, et in loco justitiae iniquitas: ut ibi sit impietas ubi esse deberet judicium, et ibi iniquitas ubi justitia. Nam, quia praelati sunt impii, idcirco sunt iniqui subjecti, quia nisi illi per impietatem innocentiam opprimerent, isti per iniquitatem justitiam non impugnarent. Propterea namque inferiores ad iniquitatem perpetrandam audaces sunt, quia superiores ad tutandam innocentiam pii non sunt; quia si illi injuriam patientibus judicium facerent, isti ad inferendam injuriam tam prompti non fuissent. Sed in hoc quoque sub sole impietas est in loco judicii, et in loco justitiae iniquitas: quod omnis 247Ahomo mala proximi sui sine misericordia persequitur, sua vero mala unusquisque contra justitiam etiam quantum potest, defensare conatur. In causa quippe proximi sui impius est omnis judex, et in sua causa adversus proximum iniquus, quia cum mala proximi judicanda sunt, misericordiae non meminit; cum vero acta sua adversus proximum examinanda sunt, justitiam non custodit. Et in hunc modum perversa sunt judicia omnia sub sole, et nutant mentes hominum, et mirantur ubi sit judicium Dei qui haec sustinet.

Adhuc possumus, et alio intellectu fortassis commodiore sub sole in loco judicii impietatem, et in loco justitiae iniquitatem considerare. Est quippe sub sole in loco judicii impietas, et iniquitas in loco justitiae, 247Bquando in hoc mundo, et justus sustinet poenam iniqui, et iniquus capit praemium justi. Boni namque in hac vita tantum judicantur, ut pro suis excessibus hic flagella Dei suscipiant, et ad futurum praemium transeant purgatiores. Mali vero, quia ad futurum servantur judicium, saepe in hoc mundo non solum nulla adversa sustinent, sed desideria quoque sua implere permittuntur, ut cuncta illis ad jucunditatem et felicitatem vitae praesentis pro voto succedant. Et videntur dissimiliter currere retributiones ut boni mala, et mali bona accipiant, et impium esse judicium justorum, ut opprimantur innocentes, et poenam sustineant iniquorum, et ut praemium justorum tollant iniqui: et confusa omnia, et permista, quia Deus non statim exercet judicium ut 247Cinnocentes eripiat, et justos de oppressione impiorum, et eos puniat qui operantur iniqua. Inde gravis concussio nascitur animorum, et succenduntur zelo pusillanimes qui non vident, nisi quae foris sunt solum, et putant quasi Deus humana non curet, et fortunae commiserit universa, et nihil judicio fiat. Et, quod crudelius est, saepe in tantam itur perversitatem ut blasphemetur Deus, et dicatur quasi approbet iniquitatem, et impietas apud ipsum sit, nec cognoscat judicium verum. Et hoc totum ex eo oritur, quod sub sole impietas est in loco judicii, et in loco justitiae iniquitas, et quasi in vanitate quae sub sole est, confusa sint omnia, et dissimiliter cuncta proveniant. Et tamen, cum considerat homo opera 247DDei, et videt qualiter rata constantique moderatione universa disponit, intelligit quod omnium inspector est Deus et moderator: et quod cassari non possunt judicia ejus, et quod facta hominum quae in hac vita non judicat, in posterum examinanda conservat. Si enim, quemadmodum ex operum ejus dispositione probatum est, justus judex est Deus, superest ut quod in praesenti in factis hominum judicandis non agitur, in futuro perficiendum sine dubitatione credatur. Propterea, ut proponeret querelam infirmorum in eo quod Deus in hujus vitae volubilitate, et transitu omnia quasi indiscussa relinquit, et facta hominum dissimili meritis retributione disponit, dixit: Vidi sub sole impietatem in loco judicii et in loco justitiae iniquitatem. Statim 248Avero, considerans quod justa judicia Dei cassari omnino non possent, intellexit differri tantum judicium, non auferri, et ait:

Dixi in corde meo: Justum et impium judicabit Dominus, et tempus omnis rei sub coelo tunc erit.

Tunc quando justum et impium judicabit Dominus, tempus erit omnis ei rei sub coelo: quia omne quod in vita agitur, sive bonum sive malum sit, tunc ad judicium perducetur. Et nunc quidem in hac vita justum et impium judicat Dominus, sed occultae sunt retributiones istae, et quae manifestae erunt differuntur in futurum. Et idcirco parvicordes murmurant, et queruntur, et putant non esse judicium justum; quia retributiones non vident. Tamen, et nunc judicium justum agitur: et unusquisque 248Bsecundum merita sua judicatur. Sed hoc totum intus est, quo carnis oculus non attingit. Et quae manifesta sunt, differuntur donec judicium illorum adveniat; et tunc omnia occulta, et manifesta erunt manifestata, et judicabuntur omnia secundum judicium justum. Et tunc justum et impium judicabit Dominus; et tempus omnis rei sub coelo tunc erit. Interim autem obscura sunt omnia, et permista currunt ad finem suum. Et una sorte involvuntur justi cum impiis, donec pariter currunt in via, ut, cum simul exierint, discernantur et ordinentur dispariter. Usque illuc enim nulla discretio est in omnibus quae foris apparent sub sole. Sed sicut simul oriuntur omnia, sic vivunt simul, et simul pertranseunt universa. Et hoc totum fit, ut probentur 248Ccorda hominum: an vivat in eis aliquid de cognitione veritatis, et affectu boni quod absconditum est, si forte ex illo argumentum fidei sumere incipiant se esse amplius, quam id quod videtur solum. Nam extra nihil est unde hoc possit agnosci, et tolluntur foris argumenta omnia ut operari incipiat, quod intus est, et probetur quantum sit. Nam, si cognoverit se ex eo homo magnum est, et pro merito constat quod Deum requirit per fidem, quem non videt per speciem. Recessit enim primum, et avertit se quando praesentem contemplabatur: et erat reatus magnus et culpa gravis lucem praesentem odisse; et constitutum est homini ad remedium placationis, si requisierit absentem et absconditum desideraverit; 248Det sciat esse quod non videtur, ut manifestum fiat tempore suo. Ideo nunc subtrahuntur omnia, et absconduntur quae invisibilia sunt, et relinquitur homo foris solus cum alienis, ut nihil videat de suo, ut probetur si forte recordatio in illo superest aliqua ad convertendum ad requisitionem illius. Propterea nunc iste altius considerans profunditatem judiciorum Dei, videt non esse mirum, si in hujus vitae nubilo inter justum et impium non discernitur, cum tanta sit involuta caligine nostra mortalitas, ut in ea homo etiam bestiis similis videatur. Propterea infert, et dicit:

Dixi in corde meo, de filiis hominum ut probaret eos Deus, et ostenderet similes esse bestiis. Idcirco unus est interitus hominis, et jumentorum, et aeque 249Autriusque conditio. Idcirco enim mortalis factus est homo, et ideo moriuntur filii hominum similiter ut jumenta ut probentur, et ostendantur similes esse bestiis. Duo quippe in homine facta erant, unum ad similitudinem Dei, alterum ad similitudinem jumenti. Et illud quidem quod creatum est ad similitudinem Dei, natura factum est immortale, sicut immortalis fuit Deus, ad cujus similitudinem factum est. Illud vero, quod ad similitudinem jumenti factum fuerat, corruptibile erat natura, sicut illa ad quorum similitudinem factum erat. De terra enim utraque sumpta sunt, et erat terra utriusque materia; et ipsa terra natura erat corruptibilis, sicut illa, quae facta sunt de terra. Ita ergo duo in homine facta sunt, unum terrenum, alterum coeleste; unum natura 249Bcorruptibile, alterum immortale; unum similitudo jumenti, alterum Dei. Et erat quidem corpus terrenum natura corruptibile, factum ad similitudinem jumenti; anima vero coelestis erat, natura immortalis, condita ad imaginem Dei. Et conjuncta sunt in homine corpus et anima, duo in unum: et datum est corpori beneficium societatis, ut participaret de immortalitate animae ad incorruptionem: et hoc totum ad gloriam animae factum est, quia placita erat Deo in justitia et veritate consistens, ut non attereretur vestimentum ejus si perseveraret obedientia illius. Et coopertum est gloria incorruptionis, quod erat similitudo jumenti in homine ut quasi dissimularetur; nec videret illud in confusionem dilectionis, sed in toto conspiceret illius formam, quod amabat, 249Cet non elongaret alicubi. Postea avertit se anima in abalienationem amoris, et oblita est quod melius erat suum, et intuita est foris pulchritudinem alienam. Et intendit in fucum pallii sui, ut se oblectaret ibi; et coepit fornicari ad illecebras corporales, et subtracta est ab oculis ejus dilectio spiritualis. Et iratus est Deus, et non placuit ipsi aversio ista, et voluit hominem revocare intus ad id quod verum erat, ut semper non haereret super imagines fucatas intuitus fallacis. Et abstraxit gloriam indumenti ejus ut iret in corruptionem, et jussit animam reverti ne vegetaret illud, et portaret ad aeternitatem; et concidit vestimentum ejus ut ostenderet homini quod non esset in eo gloria ejus ubi se bestiis similem esse videret. Et cecidit homo, et dilapsum est 249Dquod erat terrenum corruptibile, et fluere coepit ut rediret unde venerat. Factumque est ut probaretur homo, an meminisset boni sui, et si nosset requirere illud dum cogitur speciem vanam relinquere, et exire ab eo qui perverse inhaeserat.

Propterea ut probaret Deus filios hominum, et ostenderet eos similes esse bestiis. Idcirco unus est interitus hominis et jumentorum, et aequa utriusque conditio; sicut moritur homo, sic et illa moriuntur. In morte ergo una est hominis et jumenti conditio; quia sicut homo moritur, ita etiam et illa moriuntur. Sed tamen conditio mortalitatis homini ex judicio est, jumento ex natura. Et quod similiter habent ex simili causa non habent; quia homo ut moriatur ex 250Aculpa habuit, jumentum vero ex natura ut moriatur, accepit. Tamen probatur homo, et ostenditur similis esse bestiis; quia unus est interitus hominis et jumentorum, et similis utriusque conditio: et sic homo moritur sicut illa moriuntur.

Et similiter spirant omnia. Id est, et ille, et ipse similem habent vitam, et spiraculum simile vivificationis. Et in his omnibus:

Nihil habet homo jumento amplius. Quia communis utriusque est, et ortus, quoniam pariter de terra facta sunt; et procursus, quia simul:

Omnia vanitati, et mutabilitati subjecta sunt. Et transeunt universa, et consummatio finis eadem moriuntur similis, et revertuntur ad terram de qua primum sumpta fuerunt. Sic, et prius homini cum 250Bjumentis una origo erat in corpore, quod sumptum est de terra, et una vivendi conditio cum jumentis, ut similiter corpus terrenum aleretur de terra; sed unus finis cum jumentis homini non erat, quia factus erat homo ut non moreretur, neque in terram reverteretur de qua factus est. Ita tunc per incorruptionem corporis humilis origo tegebatur, et dissimulatum erat per immortalitatem ne veniret in exprobrationem quod homo similis esset bestiis; neque ostendere voluit homini Deus unde esset ignobilitas ejus, ut eum in ipsius conditione totum exponeret. Sed vestivit eum pulchritudine immortalitatis, et posuit seorsum extra genus suum in sortem alteram. Cum vero peccasset homo Deo, privavit eum gloria sua, et remisit ad originem suam, ut per id, quo ibat, 250Cagnosceret unde venerat. Propterea unus est interitus hominis et jumentorum, et aequa utriusque conditio; quia sicut homo moritur, sic et illa moriuntur: et similiter spirant omnia, et in his omnibus nihil habet homo jumento amplius, sed cuncta pariter subjacent vanitati.

Et pergunt omnia ad unum locum. Id est ad terram matrem suam, et originis principium, quia:

De terra facta sunt, et in terram pariter revertuntur. Et si quis dicere voluerit: quod habet homo amplius jumento in eo, quod spiritus filiorum Adam vadit sursum, ut occidente in mortem corpore, superstes in vita remaneat: et spiritus jumentorum descendat deorsum, id est, pariter cum morte corporis 250Ddefluat in corruptionem: quis novit hoc? Non tamen quia verum non est, sed quia occultum est: ideo:

Quis novit hoc? Non enim dixit falsum est hoc, sed quis novit hoc? Nemo hoc novit. Non enim sciri potest hoc ab homine, et tamen credi potest. Et verum est, quia creditur: et quod creditur, verum est, et ipsa credulitas non dubia scientia firma est; et tamen nemo hominum hoc scit qualiter sciuntur ea quae videntur, et audiuntur, et tanguntur, et caeteris sensibus percipiuntur; et qualiter sciuntur ea, de quibus naturaliter dubitari non potest, et quae incredulis etiam dubitantibus, indubitabili ratione demonstrantur. Sola enim fide hoc percipitur, et ideo dubitatio magna est fidem non habentibus super 251Ahoc, quia illud nesciunt, nec demonstrari eis potest ab iis qui fide hoc capiunt, quia ipsi fidem non capiunt. Propterea putant ipsi hominem nihil prorsus jumento habere amplius, quia nesciunt quod spiritus filiorum Adam vadit sursum, et spiritus jumentorum deorsum. Et cum dicitur eis: quod homo jumento amplius habet, quia spiritus hominis sursum vadit ad vitam, et spiritus jumentorum ad mortem deorsum, dicunt: Quis novit hoc? Non enim putant sciri aliquid posse, nisi oculo carnis videatur, et contingatur sensu, et ideo scientiam fidei non recipiunt, qua sola homo ad id revocatur in quo jumento habet amplius. Et quia videre non possunt illud, nec contingere in manifesto ut comprehendant quid hoc est, quod habet homo jumento amplius: 251Bdesperant omnino de vita perpetua, et increduli fiunt iis quae dicuntur, et se in delectationes vitae praesentis tota intentione projiciunt, quasi haec sit portio illorum sola, et nihil amplius sint accepturi postea. Nesciunt enim, quod ideo absconditum est, ut credatur quod habet homo jumento amplius, et probetur homo ipse ignorantia sua in fide a Deo. Si enim videretur non crederetur, sed sciretur; nec esset meritum, nec probaretur homo, nec convincerentur iniqui, nec boni exercerentur. Propterea absconditum est ut non videatur, quod habet homo jumento amplius, ut fides meritum habeat, et infidelitas locum. Et sunt multi infideles, et dicunt: Quis novit hoc? Et probant certa pro incertis non esse relinquenda; et incipiunt praesentia amplecti, 251Cet ea quae videntur rapere, ut teneant quae certa sunt; et ludificantur in incerto quia transeunt, et elabuntur dum teneri putantur; et succedunt quae certa sunt, quae putabantur incerta. Haec omnia demonstrat iste, et format narrationem suam huc et illuc, ut sequatur mentes hominum, quoniam in hunc modum ipsae nutant, et fluctuant in incerto vitae caliginosae. Dixit enim dubitationem hominum de vita sua, quia ignorant an habeat homo jumento amplius, et non inveniunt quis noverit, si post mortem corporis spiritus hominis superstes in vita remaneat; nunc ipsorum vocem in approbationem praesentium delectationum pro hac ipsa sua dubitatione, ac desperatione vitae futurae assumit, dicens:

Deprehendi: nihil esse melius quam laetari hominem 251Din opere suo: et hanc esse partem illius. Qui enim futuram vitam esse non credunt, ii partem hominis hanc solam esse putant, ut laetetur in opere suo et in hac vita labore suo perfruatur; quoniam qui mercedem post opus consummatum subsecuturam non existimant, ii operis emolumentum non post opus, sed in opere capiendum arbitrantur, atque illum felicem solum esse qui sui laboris fructum in praesenti ad usum praeparat, non eum qui sui operis mercedem in posterum capiendam reservat.

Quis enim cum adducet, ut post se futura cognoscat? Ex quo ab hac vita semel egressus fuerit homo, non adducitur amplius, nec revocatur ultra in hanc vitam ut experiatur, et sentiat rursum quae 252Aaguntur in hoc saeculo ut possit denuo delectationibus ejus perfrui, et percipere jucunditatem illius quae futura est post eum. Ideo quandiu vivit, capiat quantum potest, et utatur hoc mundo antequam abeat, et educatur ex illo; quia non revertetur amplius, nec reducetur ut post se futura cognoscat. Et fieri potest ut iis, quibus ipse uti noluit, alius post ipsum abutatur, et gaudeat, et exsultet in bonis ejus alienus, et non possint amplius ad usum ipsius reduci, cum semel ablatus fuerit. Propter hoc et hujuscemodi putant homines hanc esse partem suam, ut fruantur voluptate mundi dum vivunt; et ob hoc solum factos se existimant, nec futuros post haec aliquid, cum finem acceperit vita ista. Et multiplicant rationes, et argumenta, et quae sibi sunt rationes coacervant 252Balias post alias, ut seipsos decipiant et confirmentur corda eorum in malum, et credant quod falsum est. Et aedificant mendaciis murum inter se et veritatem, ut non videant eam; et proponunt cuncta, et exquirunt diligenter omnia, quibus possint verisimiliter demonstrare quod vita alia non est, et haec sola bona est: et propter hanc vitam tantum factus est homo, et alia post ipsam non erit. Et haec tota concussio de caligine judiciorum Dei consurgit; quia in dubio hominem posuit ut probaret eum, nec videret quod habet homo jumento amplius. Et tamen ipse errorem istum rursum aliis judiciis prosequitur, et ostendit bonam non esse vitam istam in qua mala plurima regnant; nec potest vera delectatio vel requies tranquilla inveniri. Et ideo superseminat 252Cadversa, et convertitur retrorsum ad se, et elongat, ut oppressos non liberet, ut valde affligantur, et dolore, ac tristitia, mala dulcedo, et delectatio iniqua tergatur. Et idcirco qui volunt in vita ista jucundari, et pactum faciunt amoris cum saeculo, et inique proponunt non requirere veritatem, coguntur veris judiciis videre mala, quae sub sole sunt, ut non placeant sibi nimis in aversione sua. Propterea iste cum dixisset bonum esse hominis laetari in opere suo, et hanc esse partem illius, et definitionem dedisset ad requiescendum in istis, movetur alia consideratione, quod non, sic vita ista est, ut requies in ea esse possit. Propterea adjungit, et dicit:

252DVerti me ad alia (Eccles. IV). Ad alia quippe recte conversus dicitur, quia iis quae nunc visurus est, aliud ab eo quod prius existimaverat, credere admonetur. Haec enim omnia, quae videbuntur tunc, alibi doceat esse verum bonum hominis, quam in hac vita, quae tantis miseriis et doloribus subjecta est, in qua innocentia premitur, et dolor consolationem non meretur: hoc itaque aliud, et longe aliud ab eo, quod prius videbatur et putabatur, iste considerabat, et ait:

HOMILY XVIII. On the perverse morals of men: and what Ecclesiastes judged concerning them.

244A

I saw under the sun in the place of judgment impiety, and in the place of justice iniquity. And I said in my heart: The just and the impious shall the Lord judge, and then shall be the time of every thing. But because in human minds a grievous disputation has arisen concerning the judgments of God and concerning the contrary outcome of all things, and because the reasons must now be set forth why the hearts of men are moved against him, and rise up into murmuring, we shall briefly repeat what went before, so that of the things which are to be said we may speak the sentiment out of those very things as though from the beginning. Above, Ecclesiastes had shown that nothing in this world can stand perpetually in the same state; but that the changes 244Bof times are hurried along without ceasing by contraries going their way: which mutability of things, although it be rightly ordered by the Creator of all things, nevertheless the human heart is through impatience shaken into murmuring and blasphemy against him. And therefore, after the times of things had been enumerated, he subjoined and said: I saw the affliction which God gave to the sons of men, that they should be distended in it. He hath made all things good in their time, and hath delivered the world to their disputation. This therefore is the affliction of men, their disputation against God; because, in that they will not be humbly subjected to the judgments of God, and contumaciously reprehend his disposition, which is good in all things, when anything is done contrary to their depraved will, not only does the punishment of adversity and the trouble of tribulation 244Cwear them down outwardly, but much more does fury within, and the impatience of murmuring, afflict them. Which affliction God is said to have given them, not by corrupting their mind with depravity, but by withdrawing his judgments justly from their knowledge, that they themselves may be proved to be evil; so that, when they cannot see by what justice that is done which is done concerning them, they may the more, through the vice of their own impatience, be blinded away from the knowledge of truth. Therefore he gave them affliction when he gave disputation by concealing his judgments, that man might not find every work which God works from the beginning unto the end. For sometimes certain manifest causes go before the judgments of God in this world, when God, by a recompense that follows in the present life, either rewards the good deeds of men or punishes the evil. And in these alone 244Dthe judgments of God avail to be discerned in some degree, so that man may have some judgment of the hidden truth, in so far as he may venerate even those things which he cannot penetrate.

But when the preceding causes are hidden, or those which follow lie concealed, very many disputations and contradictions arise, and the depraved minds of men afflict themselves by quarreling and murmuring against God, since they cannot penetrate his judgments, nor find the work which God hath wrought from the beginning unto the end. For they cannot penetrate, in so great a darkness, to what end anything is done, even if certain causes seem to stand forth at the beginning, but all things are hidden because of the end. Therefore man does not find every work of God from the beginning unto the end; since, 245Aeven if he seems to see certain things, he does not penetrate the whole, and the whole becomes doubtful, because the whole is not made manifest; therefore, lest man quarrel against God in doubtful things, and murmur when set in adversities, by the gift of God many prosperous things are granted, and very many pleasant ones, that man may lawfully use goods acquired by just labor, and rejoice, and be glad, and soften his own conscience toward God. And let him think well of him, and not dispute nor contend against him, as though God were adverse who has bestowed good things. For this is what is meant by that which is subjoined, saying: And I have known that there was nothing better than to be glad, and to do good things in one's life. For he who does good to himself in his life out of those things which by the gift of God have been granted to men to enjoy, that he may be glad and rejoice in his God, does better than he who 245Bdisputes and contends against God. For every man that eateth, and drinketh, and seeth good of his labor, this is the gift of God. Therefore, because this is the gift of God, and lawfully granted by God, it is better than to dispute, and contend, and murmur: which is not the gift of God, nor granted to men by God; because it is evil and a great affliction. For he is much afflicted who can neither love nor approve approhare what he endures; nor change what he hates. Therefore he is much afflicted who disputes and quarrels against God, blaspheming his judgments and detesting his works, since man can by no means mullatenus change the things which God works.

Therefore that which follows, and he says: I have learned that all the works which God hath made continue for ever. 245CFor just as the works of creation in their own genera do not pass beyond the order of the divine institution, so also the works of his judgments, by which he disposes the deeds of men and the whole world, do not confound the sentence of his predestination and providence fixed for ever. For neither can we add anything to them, that there should be more than has been provided; nor take away, that the things which have been made should be less, that God may be feared. For for this reason the disposition of visible things does not confound its order in the course of things passing away and in the vicissitude of things succeeding, so that man may know and understand that providence is eternal, which from the beginning disposed all things, by the established and constant examination of its own precept, in what manner their outcomes should follow 245Din their own times. And that he may also learn to fear in his own deeds him whose omnipotence he discerns in all his works, and in his judgments a constancy that remains unchangeable. For the established disposition of the work, and the sure moderation by which God brings all things to effect in their own times, manifestly demonstrates that, just as his wisdom is not deceived in discerning, so also his counsel is not changed in judging. What is done, the same remaineth. Just as in this whole body of created things what is done remains, because the order of the disposition is not confounded, even if mutable nature be varied, so also in his judgments what is done remains, because even in that which, according to his ineffable dispensation, he ordains dissimilarly for the variation of times, 246Ahe does not change the sentence of his own providence. Therefore what is done remains, both in the universe of things, so far as pertains to the order of the disposition, and in the exhibition of his judgment, so far as regards the sentence of predestination. The things which are to come have already been. For in both, the things which are to come have already been; because both in the genera of all things, what those things were which now are not, this same thing, according to the likeness of nature and the identity of the course, are the several things in their own kind to be, which are not yet. And in the divine judgments, the truth which we have heard was kept in things past, the same we expect to be exhibited in things that come after. For God everywhere restores what has gone away; because just as he repairs the failing of things that pass away by the multiplication of those that succeed in their own genera, 246Bso, by judging daily the deeds of men, he demonstrates that he has held entire the ancient truth of his judgments, which he exercised from the beginning, although it seemed to have been interrupted unto the temple. For with him malice always has its punishment, and virtue its reward. But because of punishments one is hidden, another manifest: while God through patience tolerates the impious and sinners, and does not straightway inflict upon them a manifest punishment, human folly thinks that he either does not know or does not care about the deeds of men, or even, what is worse, that he approves the depravity of the malignant. Thence therefore the heart of man is shaken against God, whence God is shown to be the more to be loved and praised by men. Man complains that an evil man is tolerated by God, 246Cwhen it is manifest that no man would have been good, if no evil man had ever been tolerated. And yet the hearts of the weak are scandalized, while they see in this world the impious prospering and the innocent oppressed; because they look only to those things which are without in the open, and do not attend to those which either lie hidden within, or are kept to be exhibited manifest in the future. From what cause their complaint arises is opened when it is added:

I saw under the sun in the place of judgment impiety and in the place of justice iniquity. He saw indeed that in this world God permits the impious to be judges, and to obtain power so that they lord it over and oppress the innocent, and that the deeds of men are iniquitous which ought to have been just, 246Dand that in all these things there is great confusion under the sun. For because God grants power in this world to the perverse, therefore there is impiety in the place of judgment, and in the place of justice iniquity: so that there is impiety where judgment ought to be, and there iniquity where justice ought to be. For, because those set over are impious, therefore the subjects are iniquitous, because unless those oppressed innocence through impiety, these would not assail justice through iniquity. For inferiors are bold to perpetrate iniquity for this reason, that superiors are not dutiful to protect innocence; because if those did judgment for them that suffer wrong, these would not have been so ready to inflict wrong. But in this too under the sun there is impiety in the place of judgment, and in the place of justice iniquity: that every 247Aman pursues without mercy the evils of his neighbor, but each one strives, even against justice, as far as he can, to defend his own evils. For in his neighbor's cause every judge is impious, and in his own cause against his neighbor iniquitous, because when his neighbor's evils are to be judged, he does not remember mercy; but when his own acts against his neighbor are to be examined, he does not keep justice. And in this manner all judgments under the sun are perverse, and the minds of men totter, and they wonder where is the judgment of God who endures these things.

We can still, with another and perhaps more convenient understanding, consider impiety under the sun in the place of judgment, and iniquity in the place of justice. For there is under the sun impiety in the place of judgment, and iniquity in the place of justice, 247Bwhen in this world both the just man endures the punishment of the iniquitous, and the iniquitous receives the reward of the just. For the good are judged in this life only, that here they may receive the scourges of God for their own excesses, and may pass more purified to the reward to come. But the evil, because they are kept for the judgment to come, often in this world not only endure no adverse things, but are also permitted to fulfill their own desires, so that all things fall out for them according to their wish, unto the pleasantness and happiness of the present life. And recompenses seem to run dissimilarly, so that the good receive evils and the evil goods, and the judgment of the just seems to be impious, so that the innocent are oppressed and endure the punishment of the iniquitous, and so that the iniquitous take away the reward of the just: and all things confused and mingled, because God does not straightway exercise judgment so as 247Cto rescue the innocent, and the just from the oppression of the impious, and to punish those who work iniquitous things. Thence arises a grievous shaking of minds, and the pusillanimous who see nothing but what is without alone are kindled with zeal, and think as though God did not care for human things, and had committed all things to fortune, and that nothing came to pass by judgment. And, what is more cruel, often men go into such perversity that God is blasphemed, and it is said as though he approved iniquity, and as though impiety were with him, and he did not know true judgment. And all this arises from this, that under the sun impiety is in the place of judgment, and in the place of justice iniquity, and that, as it were in the vanity which is under the sun, all things are confused, and all come forth dissimilarly. And yet, when man considers the works 247Dof God, and sees in what manner he disposes all things with established and constant moderation, he understands that God is the inspector and moderator of all: and that his judgments cannot be made void, and that the deeds of men which he does not judge in this life he keeps to be examined hereafter. For if, as has been proved from the disposition of his works, God is a just judge, it remains that what is not done in the present in judging the deeds of men be without doubt believed to be brought to completion in the future. Therefore, in order to set forth the complaint of the weak in that God, in the fickleness and passing of this life, leaves all things as it were undiscussed, and disposes the deeds of men with a recompense unlike their merits, he said: I saw under the sun impiety in the place of judgment and in the place of justice iniquity. But straightway, 248Aconsidering that the just judgments of God could not at all be made void, he understood that judgment was only deferred, not taken away, and he said:

I said in my heart: The just and the impious shall the Lord judge, and then shall be the time of every thing under heaven.

Then, when the Lord shall judge the just and the impious, there shall be the time of every thing under heaven: because everything which is done in life, whether it be good or evil, shall then be brought to judgment. And even now indeed in this life the Lord judges the just and the impious, but those recompenses are hidden, and those which shall be manifest are deferred unto the future. And therefore the small-hearted murmur, and complain, and think that the judgment is not just; because they do not see the recompenses. Yet even now just judgment is done: and each one 248Bis judged according to his own merits. But all this is within, whither the eye of the flesh does not reach. And the things which are manifest are deferred until their judgment comes; and then all hidden things also shall be made manifest, and all things shall be judged according to just judgment. And then the Lord shall judge the just and the impious; and then shall be the time of every thing under heaven. But meanwhile all things are obscure, and run mingled toward their end. And the just are wrapped up in one lot with the impious, so long as they run together on the way, so that, when they shall have gone forth together, they may be distinguished and set in order unlike. For up to that point there is no distinction in all the things which appear without under the sun. But just as all things arise together, so they live together, and all things pass away together. And all this comes to pass, that the hearts of men may be proved: 248Cwhether there live in them anything of the knowledge of truth, and of the affection for the good which is hidden, if perchance out of that they may begin to take an argument of faith that they are something more than that alone which is seen. For outside there is nothing whence this can be known, and all arguments are taken away without, that what is within may begin to work, and be proved how great it is. For, if a man shall have known himself out of that, it is a great thing, and it stands to his merit that he seeks God through faith, whom he does not see through sight. For he first withdrew, and turned himself away when he was contemplating him present: and it was a great guilt and a grievous fault to have hated the light that was present; and it has been appointed for man as a remedy of propitiation, if he shall seek him who is absent and shall desire him who is hidden; 248Dand that he may know that to be which is not seen, that it may be made manifest in its own time. Therefore now all things are withdrawn, and the things which are invisible are hidden, and man is left outside alone with things not his own, so that he may see nothing of his own, that it may be proved whether perchance any remembrance remains in him for turning to the seeking of him. Therefore now this man, considering more deeply the profundity of the judgments of God, sees that it is no wonder if in the cloud of this life no distinction is made between the just and the impious, since our mortality is wrapped in so great a darkness that in it man may even seem like to the beasts. Therefore he infers and says:

I said in my heart concerning the sons of men, that God might prove them, and show them to be like the beasts. Therefore there is one destruction of man and of the beasts, and equally 249Athe condition of both. For man was made mortal for this reason, and therefore the sons of men die in like manner as beasts, that they may be proved and shown to be like the beasts. For two things had been made in man, one to the likeness of God, the other to the likeness of a beast. And that indeed which was created to the likeness of God was made immortal by nature, as God was immortal, to whose likeness it was made. But that which had been made to the likeness of a beast was corruptible by nature, as were those things to whose likeness it had been made. For both were taken from earth, and earth was the matter of both; and that earth was corruptible by nature, as were the things which were made of earth. So then two things were made in man, one earthly, the other heavenly; one by nature 249Bcorruptible, the other immortal; one the likeness of a beast, the other of God. And the body indeed was earthly, by nature corruptible, made to the likeness of a beast; but the soul was heavenly, by nature immortal, founded to the image of God. And body and soul were joined in man, two into one: and to the body was given the benefit of the fellowship, that it might share of the immortality of the soul unto incorruption: and all this was done for the glory of the soul, because it was pleasing to God, standing in justice and truth, so that its garment might not be worn away if its obedience persevered. And that which was the likeness of a beast in man was covered with the glory of incorruption, so that it might as it were be dissembled; nor might it see it unto the confusion of love, but might behold wholly the form of that which it loved, 249Cand might not go far off anywhere. Afterward the soul turned itself away into the estrangement of love, and forgot that which was better, its own, and gazed without upon an alien beauty. And it bent itself upon the dye of its own cloak, that it might delight itself there; and it began to commit fornication with bodily enticements, and spiritual love was withdrawn from its eyes. And God was angry, and this turning away did not please him, and he willed to call man back within to that which was true, so that the gaze of the deceiver might not always cleave upon painted images. And he drew away the glory of its garment, that it might go into corruption, and commanded the soul to turn back, lest it should quicken it and bear it to eternity; and he cut down its garment, that he might show man that his glory was not in that wherein he should see himself like to the beasts. And man fell, and that slipped away 249Dwhich was earthly and corruptible, and it began to flow so as to return whence it had come. And it came to pass that man was proved, whether he remembered his own good, and whether he knew how to seek it while he is compelled to leave the vain appearance, and to go out from that to which he had perversely clung.

Therefore, that God might prove the sons of men, and show them to be like the beasts. Therefore there is one destruction of man and of the beasts, and the condition of both equal; as man dieth, so also they die. In death therefore the condition of man and of the beast is one; because as man dies, so also they die. But nevertheless the condition of mortality is for man from judgment, for the beast from nature. And what they have alike they do not have from a like cause; because man had it from 250Afault that he should die, but the beast received it from nature that it should die. Nevertheless man is proved, and is shown to be like the beasts; because there is one destruction of man and of the beasts, and the condition of both alike: and so man dies as they die.

And all things breathe alike. That is, both the one and the other have a like life, and a like breath of quickening. And in all these things:

Man hath nothing more than the beast. Because common to both is both their rising, since they were alike made of earth; and their course, since together:

All things are subject to vanity and to mutability. And all things pass away, and the consummation of the end the same, they die similar, and they return to the earth of which they were first taken. So also formerly man had with the beasts one origin in the body, which was taken from earth, and one 250Bcondition of living with the beasts, so that the earthly body should likewise be nourished from the earth; but man did not have one end with the beasts, because man had been made that he should not die, nor return into the earth of which he was made. So then through the incorruption of the body his lowly origin was covered, and it was dissembled through immortality, lest it should come into reproach that man was like the beasts; nor did God will to show man whence his ignobility was, so as to expose him wholly in his own condition. But he clothed him with the beauty of immortality, and set him apart outside his own kind into another lot. But when man had sinned against God, he deprived him of his glory, and sent him back to his origin, so that by that whither he was going 250Che might know whence he had come. Therefore there is one destruction of man and of the beasts, and the condition of both equal; because as man dies, so also they die: and all things breathe alike, and in all these things man has nothing more than the beast, but all alike lie subject to vanity.

And all things go to one place. That is, to the earth their mother, and the beginning of their origin, because:

They were made of earth, and into earth they alike return. And if anyone should wish to say: that man has this more than the beast, that the spirit of the sons of Adam goes upward, so that, the body falling into death, it remains surviving in life; and that the spirit of the beasts descends downward, that is, together with the death of the body 250Dflows away into corruption: who knows this? Yet not because it is not true, but because it is hidden: therefore:

Who knoweth this? For he did not say, This is false, but, Who knows this? No one knows this. For this cannot be known by man, and yet it can be believed. And it is true, because it is believed: and what is believed is true, and that belief itself is not doubtful but firm knowledge; and yet no man knows this in the manner in which those things are known which are seen, and heard, and touched, and perceived by the other senses; and in the manner in which those things are known concerning which one naturally cannot doubt, and which are demonstrated by indubitable reason even to unbelievers who doubt.
